paras.html: "Members of the Supreme Court" include the Chief Justice: The "members of the Supreme Court" used in the 1987 Constitution who are within the President's appointing power refer not only to the fourteen Associate Justices but also to the Chief Justice. Hence, the JBC may accept applications and nominations for Chief Justice, and the President may appoint one (applying Dulay v. JBC).
paras.text: "Members of the Supreme Court" include the Chief Justice: The "members of the Supreme Court" used in the 1987 Constitution who are within the President's appointing power refer not only to the fourteen Associate Justices but also to the Chief Justice. Hence, the JBC may accept applications and nominations for Chief Justice, and the President may appoint one (applying Dulay v. JBC).

paras.html: The 90-day duty to fill a vacancy is imperative: Sec. 4(1), Art. VIII imposes on the President the "imperative duty" to appoint a Member of the Supreme Court within 90 days from the occurrence of the vacancy; failure to do so is "a clear disobedience to the Constitution."
paras.text: The 90-day duty to fill a vacancy is imperative: Sec. 4(1), Art. VIII imposes on the President the "imperative duty" to appoint a Member of the Supreme Court within 90 days from the occurrence of the vacancy; failure to do so is "a clear disobedience to the Constitution."

paras.html: The 90-day limit cannot be defeated by pending cases: The 90-day limitation is a special provision establishing a definite mandate for the President as the appointing power (De Castro v. JBC), and it cannot be defeated by the pendency of petitions questioning the Senate's jurisdiction in the impeachment case.
paras.text: The 90-day limit cannot be defeated by pending cases: The 90-day limitation is a special provision establishing a definite mandate for the President as the appointing power (De Castro v. JBC), and it cannot be defeated by the pendency of petitions questioning the Senate's jurisdiction in the impeachment case.

paras.html: Prohibition against legislative inquiries: under the Court's expanded jurisdiction (Art. VIII, Sec. 1), "the power of the Court to enjoin a legislative act is beyond cavil"; certiorari and prohibition lie against any branch or instrumentality for grave abuse of discretion (Villanueva v. JBC). But the petitioner must show that the inquiry violates the Constitution or is attended by grave abuse; a mere apprehension of arrest is not enough.

paras.html: Habeas corpus and concurrent jurisdiction: the release of the detainees moots a habeas corpus petition. The SC, CA, and RTC have concurrent jurisdiction; once the CA acquires it, it holds it "to the exclusion of all others, including this Court." The SC's administrative supervision (Art. VIII, Sec. 6) and its power to transfer cases concern venue, not jurisdiction.

paras.html: Amparo; Congress vs. the Judiciary: the writ of amparo is confined to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, or threats thereof. Congress's contempt power cannot reach CA Justices, who are non-impeachable and under the SC's sole authority; judicial privilege exempts the Judiciary from compulsory processes only as to internal deliberations and actions in adjudication.

paras.html: The SC (Constitution), the CA (BP 129; RA 7902), and the RTC (BP 129) have concurrent jurisdiction over habeas corpus (also Family Courts for minors' custody, and first-level judges in the absence of RTC judges); Rule 102, Sec. 2. Having been filed with the CA, the CA "acquired jurisdiction over said petition to the exclusion of all others, including this Court"; jurisdiction once acquired continues until the case ends, to avoid conflicting decisions.

paras.html: Rule 102, Sec. 6: even a lower court to which the writ is made returnable acquires authority to decide the merits (Medina v. Yan; Saulo v. Cruz). Concurrency gives no absolute freedom to choose the court; the hierarchy of courts guides the forum for extraordinary writs.

paras.html: Art. VIII, Sec. 6 (administrative supervision) refers to the supervision the DOJ used to exercise over courts (ConCom: Guingona, Regalado). Under the Administrative Code (Book IV, Ch. 7, Sec. 38(2)), administrative supervision means overseeing operations "without interference with day-to-day activities". The OCA (PD 828, as amended) has no function of assuming jurisdiction over pending cases.

Majaducon did not finally settle that prohibition does not lie against legislative functions; it recognized Congress's power of inquiry, so that if the constitutional requirements are met, courts cannot prohibit committees from requiring attendance. Holy Spirit Homeowners Association involved invalidating quasi-legislative implementing rules, for which an ordinary action for nullification (not prohibition) was proper.

paras.html: Villanueva v. JBC: the SC's certiorari and prohibition reach "any act of grave abuse of discretion ... by any branch or instrumentality of the Government, even if the latter does not exercise judicial, quasi-judicial or ministerial functions", per Art. VIII, Sec. 1's expanded jurisdiction (distinct from traditional jurisdiction). "The power of the Court to enjoin a legislative act is beyond cavil," as in Garcillano (enjoining the "Hello Garci" inquiry for unpublished rules).

paras.html: The power and its limits: inquiry is express in Sec. 21, Art. VI; an "essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function" (Arnault); broad enough to cover executive officials (Senate v. Ermita). Limits: it must further a legitimate legislative task, so "investigations conducted solely to gather incriminatory evidence and punish those investigated" must be struck down; it must follow duly published rules; and Bill of Rights guarantees (due process; against self-incrimination) must be respected.

paras.html: Scope: under Sec. 1 of the Amparo Rule and Secretary of National Defense v. Manalo, amparo is confined to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, or threats thereof. Elements of enforced disappearance (Navia v. Pardico; Sec. 3(g), RA 9851): deprivation of liberty; by or with the acquiescence of the State or a political organization; refusal to acknowledge or disclose the person's fate; intent to remove the person from the law's protection for a prolonged time (also Lozada v. Macapagal-Arroyo). Petitioners admit the petition covers neither → dismissible on this ground alone.

paras.html: The Court addressed the House–CA standoff for guidance. Congress's contempt, arrest, and detention powers are "indeed awesome" but cannot deprive the Court of its duty to supervise lower-court judges. "The fact remains that the CA Justices are non-impeachable officers. As such, authority over them primarily belongs to this Court and to no other" (Maceda v. Vasquez: only the SC oversees judges' compliance with laws; no other branch may intrude).

Congress's contempt, arrest, and detention powers are "indeed awesome" but cannot deprive the Court of its duty to supervise lower-court judges. "The fact remains that the CA Justices are non-impeachable officers. As such, authority over them primarily belongs to this Court and to no other" (Maceda v. Vasquez: only the SC oversees judges' compliance with laws; no other branch may intrude).

paras.html: Judicial privilege: separation of powers exempts the Judiciary's Justices, officials, employees, and confidential information from compulsory processes, including the power of inquiry (citing Senate v. Ermita). But it is limited to "internal deliberations and actions of the Court in the exercise of the Members' adjudicatory functions." Reiterating the Feb. 14, 2012 Per Curiam Resolution (Corona impeachment), privileged matters include: raffle results and agenda actions; deliberations; predecisional and deliberative records (notes, drafts, memoranda); confidential information, even after the term of office; and records of pending cases.

paras.html: Not privileged (citing J. Carpio's separate opinion in that Resolution): information on crimes, misconduct, Code of Judicial Conduct violations, and financial, budgetary, personnel, and administrative matters. Judicial privilege also cannot defeat impeachment, a sui generis constitutional process whose importance outweighs it (citing the concurring and dissenting opinion of CJ Sereno [spelled "Sereneo"] in that Resolution); e.g., a Justice may testify on bribery but not on internal debates.

paras.html: Legislative inquiry and the Judiciary: Congress' powers to cite in contempt, arrest and detain cannot be used to deprive the Court of its constitutional duty to supervise judges of lower courts; CA Justices are non-impeachable, so authority over them primarily belongs to the SC. Judicial privilege exempts the Judiciary from compulsory processes, including inquiries in aid of legislation, but only as to matters forming part of its internal deliberative adjudicatory functions, and it cannot defeat a positive constitutional duty such as impeachment.
paras.text: Legislative inquiry and the Judiciary: Congress' powers to cite in contempt, arrest and detain cannot be used to deprive the Court of its constitutional duty to supervise judges of lower courts; CA Justices are non-impeachable, so authority over them primarily belongs to the SC. Judicial privilege exempts the Judiciary from compulsory processes, including inquiries in aid of legislation, but only as to matters forming part of its internal deliberative adjudicatory functions, and it cannot defeat a positive constitutional duty such as impeachment.

paras.html: Prohibition against legislative inquiries: Under the Court's expanded jurisdiction (Sec. 1(2), Art. VIII), prohibition lies against any branch, including Congress, for grave abuse of discretion. But an inquiry in aid of legislation under Sec. 21, Art. VI will not be enjoined absent a showing that it violates the Constitution or is attended by grave abuse; a mere apprehension of arrest is not enough.

paras.html: Habeas corpus and Amparo: Release of the detainees renders a habeas corpus petition moot; illegal restraint is jurisdictional. Where the SC, CA and RTC have concurrent jurisdiction, the court that first acquires it keeps it to the exclusion of all others, including the SC; the SC's administrative supervision (Sec. 6, Art. VIII) does not include the power to assume a case pending in a lower court. The writ of Amparo is confined to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances, or threats thereof.

paras.html: Limited: it covers only matters that are part of the internal deliberations and actions of the Court in the exercise of the Members' adjudicatory functions.

paras.html: The Court reiterates the Feb. 14, 2012 Per Curiam Resolution (Corona impeachment) listing privileged matters: (1) court actions such as raffle results and actions on agenda items (except a party's request for raffle results, Rule 7, Sec. 3, IRSC); (2) court deliberations; (3) predecisional and deliberative records (notes, drafts, research, internal memoranda); (4) confidential information obtained by court personnel in their functions, privileged even after their term; (5) records of cases pending decision, except pleadings, orders and resolutions made public.

paras.html: JBC nomination is only a qualification for appointment: Under Sec. 9, Art. VIII, nomination by the JBC is a qualification for appointment, but this "only means that the President cannot appoint an individual who is not nominated by the JBC." The JBC's power to recommend cannot restrict the President's power to appoint: "As long as in the end, the President appoints someone nominated by the JBC, the appointment is valid."
paras.text: JBC nomination is only a qualification for appointment: Under Sec. 9, Art. VIII, nomination by the JBC is a qualification for appointment, but this "only means that the President cannot appoint an individual who is not nominated by the JBC." The JBC's power to recommend cannot restrict the President's power to appoint: "As long as in the end, the President appoints someone nominated by the JBC, the appointment is valid."

paras.html: Clustering is unconstitutional: For simultaneous vacancies in a collegiate court, the JBC cannot cluster nominees into separate numbered shortlists. The President may appoint from all the nominees "as if embodied in one JBC list," provided there are at least three nominees per vacancy. The rule also applies to closely successive vacancies to which the President makes appointments on the same occasion, regardless of whether the JBC ran combined or separate application processes.

The rule also applies to closely successive vacancies to which the President makes appointments on the same occasion, regardless of whether the JBC ran combined or separate application processes.

paras.html: Seniority is part of the appointing power: Seniority among Sandiganbayan Associate Justices is fixed by law according to the dates (or order of issuance) of their commissions (Sec. 1, PD 1606). By numbering the vacancies, the JBC unduly arrogates a vital part of the President's power of appointment.

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the Court DISMISSES the instant Petition for Quo Warranto and Certiorari and Prohibition for lack of merit. The Court DECLARES the clustering of nominees by the JBC UNCONSTITUTIONAL, and the appointments of respondents Associate Justices Musngi and Econg, together with the four other newly appointed Associate Justices of the Sandiganbayan, as VALID. The Court further DENIES the Motion for Intervention of the JBC, but ORDERS the Clerk of Court En Banc to docket as a separate administrative matter Item No. 2 (the deletion of Rule 8, Sec. 1 of JBC-009 from JBC No. 2016-1) and Item No. 3 (the removal of incumbent Senior Associate Justices as JBC consultants). The Court DIRECTS the JBC to file its comment on Items 2 and 3 within thirty (30) days from notice.

paras.html: Practice of law is a privilege, not a right: "The right to practice law is not a natural or constitutional right but is a privilege." It is limited to persons of good moral character with special qualifications. "The practice of law is a privilege that can be withheld even from one who has passed the bar examinations, if the person seeking admission had practiced law without a license."
paras.text: Practice of law is a privilege, not a right: "The right to practice law is not a natural or constitutional right but is a privilege." It is limited to persons of good moral character with special qualifications. "The practice of law is a privilege that can be withheld even from one who has passed the bar examinations, if the person seeking admission had practiced law without a license."

paras.html: What counts as practice of law: any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training, and experience (Cayetano v. Monsod). Appearing as counsel before a Municipal Board of Election Canvassers and filing pleadings there is practice of law.

paras.html: When one becomes a lawyer: passing the bar is not the only qualification. "It is the signing in the Roll of Attorneys that finally makes one a full-fledged lawyer"; the lawyer's oath administered by the Court and the signature in the Roll are the two remaining essential requisites.

paras.html: Philippine Lawyers Association v. Agrava: practice of law is not limited to the conduct of cases in court. It embraces the preparation of pleadings and other papers incident to actions and special proceedings, the management of such proceedings on behalf of clients, and, in general, "all advice to clients, and all action taken for them in matters connected with the law."

paras.html: Cayetano v. Monsod: "practice of law" means any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience; to practice law is to perform acts usually performed by members of the legal profession, or to render any kind of service requiring legal knowledge or skill.

paras.html: Diplomatic negotiations privilege: "Diplomatic negotiations ... are recognized as privileged in this jurisdiction" (PMPF v. Manglapus; Chavez v. PCGG). The final text of a treaty may not be kept perpetually confidential, but "the offers exchanged by the parties during the negotiations continue to be privileged even after the [treaty] is published." The privilege is presumptive, not absolute, and it may be invoked against citizens and in legislative investigations alike.
paras.text: Diplomatic negotiations privilege: "Diplomatic negotiations ... are recognized as privileged in this jurisdiction" (PMPF v. Manglapus; Chavez v. PCGG). The final text of a treaty may not be kept perpetually confidential, but "the offers exchanged by the parties during the negotiations continue to be privileged even after the [treaty] is published." The privilege is presumptive, not absolute, and it may be invoked against citizens and in legislative investigations alike.

paras.html: Burden and showing of need: the Executive must first give precise and certain reasons; once it shows the information is covered by a recognized privilege, the burden shifts to the requesting party, "whether that party is Congress or a private citizen," to make a "strong showing of need", i.e., that the information is vital to effective and reasonable participation in decision-making, "not simply for the satisfaction of its curiosity."

paras.html: Treaty negotiation and waiver: the power to negotiate treaties belongs to the President alone; Senate concurrence goes only to validity. Because the privilege is an exemption to Congress's power of inquiry, the Executive does not waive it by failing to assert it against mere requests that are not compulsory process.

paras.html: Against PMPF v. Manglapus: that case involved national security (military bases), not an economic treaty; its petitioners were all media, while here members of Congress sue; and the socio-political context has changed (the "incompatibility hypothesis" is outdated). The privilege applies only at certain stages of negotiation (Chavez v. PCGG; Chavez v. PEA). The House members also invoke Congress's power over foreign commerce (Art. VI, Sec. 28(2); PD 1464, Secs. 401–402). The privilege was raised too late (only in the Comment).

paras.html: There is no rigid test of public concern; courts decide case by case (Legaspi v. CSC). From the JPEPA's nature as an international trade agreement, the offers are matters of public concern; respondents do not dispute this. But neither the right to information nor full public disclosure is absolute; privileged matters are exceptions (Almonte, Chavez v. PCGG, Chavez v. PEA, Senate v. Ermita). Validity depends on the ground invoked and the context; here the ground is diplomatic negotiations then in progress.

paras.html: Chavez v. PCGG: "information on inter-government exchanges prior to the conclusion of treaties and executive agreements may be subject to reasonable safeguards for the sake of national interest."

paras.html: PMPF v. Manglapus (RP-US Military Bases negotiations): "secrecy of negotiations with foreign countries is not violative" of free speech, press, or access to information. Diplomacy requires centralized authority and confidentiality (Secretary Stimson: "who would ever trust American Delegations"); an "ill-timed speech" or a frank declaration of concessions leads to "widespread propaganda to block the negotiations"; and once a treaty is drafted and published, there is "ample opportunity for discussion before it is approved." It adopted U.S. v. Curtiss-Wright: the President is "the sole organ of the nation in its external relations"; into negotiation "the Senate cannot intrude; and Congress itself is powerless to invade it."

paras.html: Application: the final text may not be kept perpetually confidential, but the offers "continue to be privileged even after the JPEPA is published." The Japanese submitted offers expecting "historic confidentiality"; disclosure could impair dealings with Japan and other governments, and would discourage Filipino negotiators from frank expression. Negotiations involve quid pro quo: conceding in areas of lesser importance to win greater national interests; publicity breeds "grandstanding" and freezes positions (Duval).

paras.html: The privilege resembles the presidential communications and deliberative process privileges (NLRB v. Sears): all protect a frank exchange of exploratory ideas; diplomatic negotiations protect the President's independence as sole organ in external relations and, like deliberative process, are privileged because they are part of a process of deliberation, not because of content.

paras.html: Fulbright & Jaworski v. Dept. of Treasury (U.S.-French tax treaty notes): "Negotiations between two countries to draft a treaty represent a true example of a deliberative process"; drafts of treaties deserve the same protection as draft regulations. CIEL v. USTR (U.S.-Chile FTA) ordered disclosure only because documents exchanged with Chile were not "inter-agency" under FOIA Exemption 5, and it did not reach deliberative process; Fulbright was not overturned. The Philippines has no FOIA counterpart, so courts may focus directly on whether public policy supports the privilege, even for documents not purely internal. → "No reason to modify, much less abandon, the doctrine in PMPF v. Manglapus."

paras.html: Art. VI, Sec. 28(2) concerns fixing tariff rates and quotas, not negotiating treaties. The power to negotiate rests on Art. VII, Sec. 21, and treaty-making is exclusive to the President (BAYAN v. Executive Secretary; Pimentel v. Executive Secretary), subject only to two-thirds Senate concurrence for validity. The President's authority under PD 1464 acknowledges a power already inherent in the office and cannot make the President accountable to Congress for negotiations. → Congress "may not interfere in the field of treaty negotiations"; only the Senate, not Congress as a whole, concurs.

paras.html: Indirect intrusion (Agan v. PIATCO): what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly; opening the negotiations to the House "would have made a mockery" of vesting direct negotiation solely in the President (Hamilton on excluding the House). The Philippine Senate, unlike the U.S. Senate, does not even advise on treaties; much less the House.

paras.html: No real legislative need shown: the House Committee never pursued its subpoena and did not sue as a body (unlike the Senate in Ermita); the members did not show how the lack of offers would hinder legislation (Senate Select: need depends on the function and the degree to which the material is necessary). Since publication, the final text is available for any legislative purpose.

paras.html: One test for Congress and citizens: different criteria (e.g., "clear and present danger" for citizens) would make it harder for Congress than for private citizens to obtain executive information, an absurdity. The "need" shown is part of the context of every claim. The Court has balanced interests before (Secretary of Justice v. Lantion); the dispute with the dissent is only on the result.

paras.html: Public concern vs. need: whether information is covered by the right to information depends only on public concern, not need. But once privilege is established, the requester must show the information is vital "for its ability to effectively and reasonably participate in social, political, and economic decision-making." → "The balance in this case tilts in favor of executive privilege."

NAFTA's text was released before signing, and FTAA drafts were public.

paras.html: Test: the diplomatic secrets privilege is qualified (ConCom: "subject to reasonable safeguards on the national interest"; U.K. FOIA 2000 treats foreign-relations exemptions as qualified). But the proper test is balancing of interests, not "showing of need": the Court has never required people to show a need to exercise constitutional rights; Nixon, Senate Select, and In re Sealed Case involved institutions with functions, not citizens. Contested provisions (e.g., fisheries and Art. XII, Sec. 2; agricultural export subsidies) show the need for informed debate.

paras.html: Jurisdiction over "application or operation": Under Sec. 4(2), Art. VIII, the Court en banc hears cases involving the constitutionality, application or operation of "other regulations" such as PNP CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112. It may therefore require the production of police reports on how they were implemented, but only to determine the reports' existence, whether they were prepared as mandated, and whether they facially show compliance — not the veracity of their contents, since the Court is not a trier of facts.

paras.html: Relevance is for the Court to determine: Whether evidence is relevant rests largely in the Court's discretion, exercised according to logic and everyday experience (Sec. 4, Rule 128); a party cannot arrogate that determination to itself.

paras.html: No blanket national-security or regularity shield: Records of routine police operations against illegal drugs are not state secrets; the presumption of regularity does not attach because deaths are not supposed to occur in police operations; and willful suppression of the records will lead the Court to presume they are adverse (Sec. 3(e), Rule 131).

paras.html: 17 November 2017 – Advisory. The Court framed the issues: (1) the constitutionality of CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112, including their legal basis and whether they direct any unlawful act; (2) whether the acts authorized or conducted under them violate Art. II, Sec. 11 and Art. III, Secs. 1, 2, 12, 14, and 17 of the Constitution, RA 7438, the buy-bust and stop-and-frisk case law, Art. 125 RPC, PNP operational procedures, and DOJ Circular No. 61; (3) whether they violate international obligations (ICCPR, Minnesota Protocol); and (4) whether the writ of amparo ought to issue, plus procedural sub-issues (class suit, standing, jurisdiction, joinder, verification).

paras.html: J. Carpio: The SG said 3,806 were killed in "legitimate" drug operations since 1 July 2016 and about 4,000 fall under "deaths under investigation" (DUI). He said 419 Chinese nationals were arrested (a mix of users, pushers, and drug lords) and that drug users rose from 1.8 million (2015, per the CMC) to about 4 million, conceding the earlier figure was "understated." Carpio asked why the campaign targets street-level pushers rather than the bulk smugglers the CMC itself identifies.

paras.html: 5 December 2017 – Resolution. The Court directed the SG to submit, for police drug operations and for DUIs from 1 July 2016 to 30 November 2017: the place, date, and time; the PNP team; pre-operation plans; whether warrants were issued; the media, NGO, and barangay representatives present; the names, addresses, genders, and ages of those killed; post-operation reports; the DUI investigators, investigation reports, and charges filed; and, for the Daño petition, the list of San Andres Bukid buy-busts since Tokhang began and the pre- and post-operation reports of the 25 fatal buy-busts. Memoranda and documents were due in 30 days, extended to 60 days on the SG's motion because of their volume.

paras.html: Jurisdiction over "application or operation": Under Sec. 4(2), Art. VIII, the Court en banc hears cases involving the constitutionality, application or operation of "other regulations" such as PNP CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112. It may therefore require the production of police reports on how they were implemented, but only to determine the reports' existence, whether they were prepared as mandated, and whether they facially show compliance — not the veracity of their contents, since the Court is not a trier of facts.
paras.text: Jurisdiction over "application or operation": Under Sec. 4(2), Art. VIII, the Court en banc hears cases involving the constitutionality, application or operation of "other regulations" such as PNP CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112. It may therefore require the production of police reports on how they were implemented, but only to determine the reports' existence, whether they were prepared as mandated, and whether they facially show compliance — not the veracity of their contents, since the Court is not a trier of facts.

paras.html: Relevance is for the Court to determine: Whether evidence is relevant rests largely in the Court's discretion, exercised according to logic and everyday experience (Sec. 4, Rule 128); a party cannot arrogate that determination to itself.
paras.text: Relevance is for the Court to determine: Whether evidence is relevant rests largely in the Court's discretion, exercised according to logic and everyday experience (Sec. 4, Rule 128); a party cannot arrogate that determination to itself.

paras.html: No blanket national-security or regularity shield: Records of routine police operations against illegal drugs are not state secrets; the presumption of regularity does not attach because deaths are not supposed to occur in police operations; and willful suppression of the records will lead the Court to presume they are adverse (Sec. 3(e), Rule 131).

paras.html: 17 November 2017 – Advisory. The Court framed the issues: (1) the constitutionality of CMC 16-2016 and DILG MC 2017-112, including their legal basis and whether they direct any unlawful act; (2) whether the acts authorized or conducted under them violate Art. II, Sec. 11 and Art. III, Secs. 1, 2, 12, 14, and 17 of the Constitution, RA 7438, the buy-bust and stop-and-frisk case law, Art. 125 RPC, PNP operational procedures, and DOJ Circular No. 61; (3) whether they violate international obligations (ICCPR, Minnesota Protocol); and (4) whether the writ of amparo ought to issue, plus procedural sub-issues (class suit, standing, jurisdiction, joinder, verification).

paras.html: 5 December 2017 – Resolution. The Court directed the SG to submit, for police drug operations and for DUIs from 1 July 2016 to 30 November 2017: the place, date, and time; the PNP team; pre-operation plans; whether warrants were issued; the media, NGO, and barangay representatives present; the names, addresses, genders, and ages of those killed; post-operation reports; the DUI investigators, investigation reports, and charges filed; and, for the Daño petition, the list of San Andres Bukid buy-busts since Tokhang began and the pre- and post-operation reports of the 25 fatal buy-busts. Memoranda and documents were due in 30 days, extended to 60 days on the SG's motion because of their volume.

paras.html: The President had no factual basis for declaring a state of emergency, especially in the Province of Sultan Kudarat and the City of Cotabato, where no critical violent incidents occurred.
paras.text: The President had no factual basis for declaring a state of emergency, especially in the Province of Sultan Kudarat and the City of Cotabato, where no critical violent incidents occurred.

paras.html: Since not all areas under the ARMM were placed under a state of emergency, the take-over of the entire ARMM by the DILG Secretary had no basis either.

paras.html: The President acted under her calling-out power as Commander-in-Chief (first sentence of Sec. 18, Art. VII). The determination of the need to exercise it rests solely on her wisdom.
paras.text: The President acted under her calling-out power as Commander-in-Chief (first sentence of Sec. 18, Art. VII). The determination of the need to exercise it rests solely on her wisdom.

paras.html: She must use her judgment, based on intelligence reports and the best information available to her, to call out the armed forces to suppress and prevent lawless violence wherever and whenever it arises.

paras.html: The principal victims were members of the Mangudadatu family and the main perpetrators were members and followers of the Ampatuan family → the military and police had to prepare for and prevent reported retaliatory actions from the Mangudadatus and additional offensive measures from the Ampatuans.

paras.html: Senate contempt detention is not indefinite: "the period of imprisonment under the inherent power of contempt by the Senate during inquiries in aid of legislation should only last until the termination of the legislative inquiry under which the said power is invoked."
paras.text: Senate contempt detention is not indefinite: "the period of imprisonment under the inherent power of contempt by the Senate during inquiries in aid of legislation should only last until the termination of the legislative inquiry under which the said power is invoked."

paras.html: When the inquiry terminates: (1) upon the approval or disapproval of the Committee Report; or (2) upon the expiration of one (1) Congress. Detention may continue during recess, but only until the Committee Report is approved or disapproved.

paras.html: Inherent vs. statutory contempt: to detain beyond the inquiry, Congress must resort to statutory contempt (e.g., Art. 150, RPC, or a new or amended law), which is tried before the courts with a definite penalty and all the rights of the accused.

paras.html: 11:29 a.m.: Sen. Poe asked petitioner whether he was the president of AJ Fraternity. He invoked his right against self-incrimination and refused twice. Lacson warned that he could be cited in contempt. Poe noted the alleged "Code of Silence" texts and that his signature appeared on the fraternity's application for recognition and organizational sheet as president. He again invoked the right.

paras.html: Poe moved to cite him in contempt, seconded by Sens. Villanueva and Zubiri. Lacson ruled the motion properly seconded and ordered the Sergeant-at-Arms to detain him after the hearing. paras.html: 1:19 p.m.: On Villanueva's question about who decided to bring Atio to Chinese General Hospital instead of UST Hospital, petitioner apologized and moved to lift the contempt. He admitted membership but said he did not know who the president was because he was then enrolled in another school. On Villanueva's repeated question, he again invoked self-incrimination. Villanueva said the contempt would remain; Lacson noted his many chances. He was placed in the Sergeant-at-Arms' custody.

paras.html: The Court may decide a moot case when there is: (1) a grave constitutional violation; (2) the exceptional character of the case; (3) paramount public interest; (4) an opportunity to guide the bench, the bar, and the public; or (5) a case capable of repetition yet evading review.

paras.html: The legislative contempt power is sourced from the American system (citing Arnault).

paras.html: Anderson v. Dunn (1821): though the offense may be undefinable, the punishment need not be indefinite; since the legislative body ceases to exist upon adjournment, imprisonment under the contempt power must terminate with adjournment.

paras.html: Hence the US Congress enacted Sec. 102 of the Revised Statutes (1857): fine of US$100–1,000 and imprisonment of 1 to 12 months, prosecuted and heard in the courts (later codified as 2 U.S.C. § 192 on June 22, 1938).

paras.html: Lopez v. De los Reyes (1930): the House cited Lopez in contempt for assaulting a member after the Congress where it happened had adjourned → invalid. Imprisonment for a term not exceeding the session is the limit of the power to deal directly by contempt. The power rests on self-preservation; "where punishment as such is to be imposed, a criminal prosecution must be brought," with all Bill of Rights protections.

paras.html: Arnault v. Nazareno (1950): the Senate is a continuing body, so "there is no limit as to time" to its contempt power; the HOR's contempt runs until the final adjournment of the last session of that Congress. The Court assumed the Senate would not abuse it, and refused to limit it because committees may conduct inquiries during recess.

paras.html: Neri v. Senate (2008), reiterated in Garcillano v. HOR and Romero II v. Estrada: the Senate as an institution is continuing, but in its day-to-day business, the Senate of each Congress acts separately. Under Sec. 123, Rule XLIV of the Senate Rules, all pending matters and proceedings, including legislative investigations, terminate upon the expiration of one Congress; the next Congress may take them up only as if presented for the first time.

paras.html: Sec. 21, Art. VI: Congress must respect the rights of persons appearing in or affected by inquiries. Under Arnault, a witness could be detained "for a day, a month, a year, or even for a lifetime depending on the desire of the perpetual Senate" → the right to liberty cannot be respected under indefinite detention without due process.

paras.html: Nature of the power: per Lopez, it rests solely on self-preservation and is "a means to an end and not the end itself." Even if not entirely punitive (it secures information or removes an obstruction), it still restricts liberty.

paras.html: Intent to punish (citing Alejano v. Cabuay): courts infer intent to punish when restrictions are arbitrary and purposeless, or excessive in relation to the purpose → an indefinite and unspecified detention is an excessive restriction.

paras.html: Importance of the power acknowledged: a legislature cannot legislate wisely without information; requests are often unavailing → compulsion is essential. But despite the presumption that the Senate will not abuse the power, the possibility of indefinite imprisonment remains while no period is fixed.

paras.html: First – approval or disapproval of the Committee Report. Under Secs. 22–23 of the Senate Rules, the committee begins considering its Report within 15 days after the inquiry concludes; the Report is approved by a majority vote of all members, otherwise it is disapproved; it is then filed and included in the next Order of Business and referred to the Committee on Rules. → The Committee Report is "the culmination of the legislative inquiry"; its approval or disapproval ends the inquiry, and the witness should be released.

paras.html: Second – expiration of one Congress (at the final adjournment of its last session). Per Neri, legislative investigations terminate then.

paras.html: Arnault's fears (losing an essential means; having to repeat contempt proceedings every session) are insufficient to permit indefinite imprisonment.

paras.html: Statutory contempt: if Congress wants imprisonment beyond the inquiry or beyond final adjournment, it may enact or amend a law. The charge is tried before the courts, the witness is heard, and the law fixes the exact penalty and period. This is distinct from the inherent power (recognized in Chapman, Jurney, and Lopez).

Whether to augment the power is in Congress's sole discretion.

paras.html: Inherent: self-preservation, coercive, imposed by the Senate itself, ends with the inquiry. Statutory: punitive, tried in courts with full rights of the accused, fixed term (e.g., Art. 150, RPC). Note the tension: the Court calls Art. 150 a recourse for the Senate's "statutory power of contempt," though prosecution is by the executive and trial by the courts.

paras.html: The Court may decide a moot case when there is: (1) a grave constitutional violation; (2) the exceptional character of the case; (3) paramount public interest; (4) an opportunity to guide the bench, the bar, and the public; or (5) a case capable of repetition yet evading review.

paras.html: Re: Foreign roots – the contempt power must have a limit
paras.text: Re: Foreign roots – the contempt power must have a limit

paras.html: The legislative contempt power is sourced from the American system (citing Arnault).
paras.text: The legislative contempt power is sourced from the American system (citing Arnault).

paras.html: Anderson v. Dunn (1821): though the offense may be undefinable, the punishment need not be indefinite; since the legislative body ceases to exist upon adjournment, imprisonment under the contempt power must terminate with adjournment.
paras.text: Anderson v. Dunn (1821): though the offense may be undefinable, the punishment need not be indefinite; since the legislative body ceases to exist upon adjournment, imprisonment under the contempt power must terminate with adjournment.

paras.html: Hence the US Congress enacted Sec. 102 of the Revised Statutes (1857): fine of US$100–1,000 and imprisonment of 1 to 12 months, prosecuted and heard in the courts (later codified as 2 U.S.C. § 192 on June 22, 1938).

paras.html: In re Chapman (1897): the statute is valid; it aids each House in discharging its functions.
paras.text: In re Chapman (1897): the statute is valid; it aids each House in discharging its functions.

paras.html: Jurney v. MacCracken (1935): the statute did not impair the inherent power; it was enacted because imprisonment limited to the session was not sufficiently drastic, so it merely supplements the inherent power.

paras.html: Re: Philippine jurisprudence before Balag
paras.text: Re: Philippine jurisprudence before Balag

paras.html: Lopez v. De los Reyes (1930): the House cited Lopez in contempt for assaulting a member after the Congress where it happened had adjourned → invalid. Imprisonment for a term not exceeding the session is the limit of the power to deal directly by contempt. The power rests on self-preservation; "where punishment as such is to be imposed, a criminal prosecution must be brought," with all Bill of Rights protections.

Imprisonment for a term not exceeding the session is the limit of the power to deal directly by contempt. The power rests on self-preservation; "where punishment as such is to be imposed, a criminal prosecution must be brought," with all Bill of Rights protections.

paras.html: Arnault v. Nazareno (1950): the Senate is a continuing body, so "there is no limit as to time" to its contempt power; the HOR's contempt runs until the final adjournment of the last session of that Congress. The Court assumed the Senate would not abuse it, and refused to limit it because committees may conduct inquiries during recess.

paras.html: Neri v. Senate (2008), reiterated in Garcillano v. HOR and Romero II v. Estrada: the Senate as an institution is continuing, but in its day-to-day business, the Senate of each Congress acts separately. Under Sec. 123, Rule XLIV of the Senate Rules, all pending matters and proceedings, including legislative investigations, terminate upon the expiration of one Congress; the next Congress may take them up only as if presented for the first time.

paras.html: Re: Why detention cannot be indefinite
paras.text: Re: Why detention cannot be indefinite

paras.html: Sec. 21, Art. VI: Congress must respect the rights of persons appearing in or affected by inquiries. Under Arnault, a witness could be detained "for a day, a month, a year, or even for a lifetime depending on the desire of the perpetual Senate" → the right to liberty cannot be respected under indefinite detention without due process.

paras.html: Nature of the power: per Lopez, it rests solely on self-preservation and is "a means to an end and not the end itself." Even if not entirely punitive (it secures information or removes an obstruction), it still restricts liberty.

paras.html: Intent to punish (citing Alejano v. Cabuay): courts infer intent to punish when restrictions are arbitrary and purposeless, or excessive in relation to the purpose → an indefinite and unspecified detention is an excessive restriction.
paras.text: Intent to punish (citing Alejano v. Cabuay): courts infer intent to punish when restrictions are arbitrary and purposeless, or excessive in relation to the purpose → an indefinite and unspecified detention is an excessive restriction.

paras.html: Importance of the power acknowledged: a legislature cannot legislate wisely without information; requests are often unavailing → compulsion is essential. But despite the presumption that the Senate will not abuse the power, the possibility of indefinite imprisonment remains while no period is fixed.

paras.html: Link to legitimacy of the inquiry: per Arnault, obedience may be enforced if the subject is within legitimate legislative inquiry → once the inquiry concludes, the power ceases and there is no more genuine necessity to penalize the detained witness.

paras.html: Re: 3.1 – The two instances when the inquiry terminates
paras.text: Re: 3.1 – The two instances when the inquiry terminates

paras.html: First – approval or disapproval of the Committee Report. Under Secs. 22–23 of the Senate Rules, the committee begins considering its Report within 15 days after the inquiry concludes; the Report is approved by a majority vote of all members, otherwise it is disapproved; it is then filed and included in the next Order of Business and referred to the Committee on Rules. → The Committee Report is "the culmination of the legislative inquiry"; its approval or disapproval ends the inquiry, and the witness should be released.

Under Secs. 22–23 of the Senate Rules, the committee begins considering its Report within 15 days after the inquiry concludes; the Report is approved by a majority vote of all members, otherwise it is disapproved; it is then filed and included in the next Order of Business and referred to the Committee on Rules. → The Committee Report is "the culmination of the legislative inquiry"; its approval or disapproval ends the inquiry, and the witness should be released.

paras.html: Second – expiration of one Congress (at the final adjournment of its last session). Per Neri, legislative investigations terminate then.

paras.html: Arnault's fears (losing an essential means; having to repeat contempt proceedings every session) are insufficient to permit indefinite imprisonment.
paras.text: Arnault's fears (losing an essential means; having to repeat contempt proceedings every session) are insufficient to permit indefinite imprisonment.

paras.html: Statutory contempt: if Congress wants imprisonment beyond the inquiry or beyond final adjournment, it may enact or amend a law. The charge is tried before the courts, the witness is heard, and the law fixes the exact penalty and period. This is distinct from the inherent power (recognized in Chapman, Jurney, and Lopez).

The charge is tried before the courts, the witness is heard, and the law fixes the exact penalty and period. This is distinct from the inherent power (recognized in Chapman, Jurney, and Lopez).

paras.html: Art. 150, RPC (disobedience to summons of Congress, including refusal "to answer any legal inquiry") already provides a definite penalty (arresto mayor or a fine of ₱200–1,000, or both) not limited by the period of the inquiry → "another recourse" for the Senate. Whether to augment the power is in Congress's sole discretion.

Whether to augment the power is in Congress's sole discretion.

paras.html: Recess: the Senate may still exercise contempt during hearings in recess, but imprisonment lasts only until the Committee Report is approved or disapproved → the power stays "potent and compelling" while detention is not indefinite.

paras.html: Summary: the Senate may exercise contempt immediately upon a contemptuous act, subject to its rules and the witness's constitutional rights; beyond the inquiry, it may file a criminal case under the existing statute or enact a new law.

paras.html: Sec. 21, Art. VI, 1987 Constitution: inquiries in aid of legislation must follow duly published rules, and the rights of persons appearing in or affected by them shall be respected → the textual anchor for limiting detention.

paras.html: Inherent: self-preservation, coercive, imposed by the Senate itself, ends with the inquiry. Statutory: punitive, tried in courts with full rights of the accused, fixed term (e.g., Art. 150, RPC). Note the tension: the Court calls Art. 150 a recourse for the Senate's "statutory power of contempt," though prosecution is by the executive and trial by the courts.

paras.html: Power to reorganize: The President has the power to reorganize the offices and agencies in the Executive Department in line with the constitutionally granted power of control over executive offices and by virtue of a previous delegation of the legislative power to reorganize under existing statutes (Sec. 31, Book III, Administrative Code; GAA provisions). Concomitant to the express powers under Sec. 31 to abolish, consolidate, merge, and transfer, the President implicitly has the power to effect "less radical or less substantive changes" to the functional and internal structure of the OP, including the modification of functions of executive agencies.
paras.text: Power to reorganize: The President has the power to reorganize the offices and agencies in the Executive Department in line with the constitutionally granted power of control over executive offices and by virtue of a previous delegation of the legislative power to reorganize under existing statutes (Sec. 31, Book III, Administrative Code; GAA provisions). Concomitant to the express powers under Sec. 31 to abolish, consolidate, merge, and transfer, the President implicitly has the power to effect "less radical or less substantive changes" to the functional and internal structure of the OP, including the modification of functions of executive agencies.

paras.html: Limits: This delegated legislative power to reorganize pertains only to the OP and the departments, offices, and agencies of the Executive Branch; it does not include the Judiciary, the Legislature, or constitutionally created or mandated bodies. The reorganization must also be carried out in good faith (Dario v. Mison); whoever alleges bad faith bears the burden of proving it.

paras.html: Background – EO 285 and the NPO:
paras.text: Background – EO 285 and the NPO:

paras.html: July 25, 1987: President Corazon Aquino, while still exercising legislative powers under the Freedom Constitution, issued EO 285 (abolishing the General Services Administration and transferring its functions). Sec. 6 created the National Printing Office (NPO) out of the merger of the Government Printing Office and the relevant printing units of the Philippine Information Agency (PIA). The NPO was attached to the PIA.
paras.text: July 25, 1987: President Corazon Aquino, while still exercising legislative powers under the Freedom Constitution, issued EO 285 (abolishing the General Services Administration and transferring its functions). Sec. 6 created the National Printing Office (NPO) out of the merger of the Government Printing Office and the relevant printing units of the Philippine Information Agency (PIA). The NPO was attached to the PIA.

paras.html: Under Sec. 6, the NPO had exclusive printing jurisdiction over: (a) printing, binding, and distribution of all standard and accountable forms of national, provincial, city, and municipal governments, including government corporations; (b) official ballots; and (c) public documents such as the Official Gazette, the GAA, the Philippine Reports, and PIA development information materials. It could accept other government printing jobs, but not on an exclusive basis.

It could accept other government printing jobs, but not on an exclusive basis.

paras.html: The assailed EO 378:
paras.text: The assailed EO 378:

paras.html: October 25, 2004: President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (PGMA) issued EO 378, amending Sec. 6 of EO 285 by, inter alia, removing the NPO's exclusive jurisdiction over the printing requirements of government agencies and instrumentalities:
paras.text: October 25, 2004: President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (PGMA) issued EO 378, amending Sec. 6 of EO 285 by, inter alia, removing the NPO's exclusive jurisdiction over the printing requirements of government agencies and instrumentalities:

paras.html: SECTION 1. The NPO shall continue to provide printing services to government agencies and instrumentalities as mandated by law. However, it shall no longer enjoy exclusive jurisdiction over the printing services requirements of the government over standard and accountable forms. It shall have to compete with the private sector, except in the printing of election paraphernalia which could be shared with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, upon the discretion of the Commission on Elections . . . .
paras.text: SECTION 1. The NPO shall continue to provide printing services to government agencies and instrumentalities as mandated by law. However, it shall no longer enjoy exclusive jurisdiction over the printing services requirements of the government over standard and accountable forms. It shall have to compete with the private sector, except in the printing of election paraphernalia which could be shared with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, upon the discretion of the Commission on Elections . . . .

paras.html: SECTION 2. Government agencies/instrumentalities may source printing services outside NPO provided that: 2.1 The printing services to be provided by the private sector is superior in quality and at a lower cost than what is offered by the NPO; and 2.2 The private printing provider is flexible in terms of meeting the target completion time of the government agency.
paras.text: SECTION 2. Government agencies/instrumentalities may source printing services outside NPO provided that: 2.1 The printing services to be provided by the private sector is superior in quality and at a lower cost than what is offered by the NPO; and 2.2 The private printing provider is flexible in terms of meeting the target completion time of the government agency.

paras.html: SECTION 3. In the exercise of its functions, the amount to be appropriated for the programs, projects and activities of the NPO in the General Appropriations Act (GAA) shall be limited to its income without additional financial support from the government.
paras.text: SECTION 3. In the exercise of its functions, the amount to be appropriated for the programs, projects and activities of the NPO in the General Appropriations Act (GAA) shall be limited to its income without additional financial support from the government.

paras.html: Facts bearing on the class suit: The petition did not state how many NPO employees would be affected. The OSG pointed out that the NPO had about 549 employees. There were 67 petitioners; 32 later executed an Affidavit of Desistance and one signed a letter denying that he ever signed the petition (ostensibly leaving 34). Of the 67 who signed the Verification/Certification, only 20 were named in the jurat as having subscribed before the notary. Petitioners' counsel challenged the desistance and insinuated it was due to pressure from people "close to the seat of power." The President of the National Printing Office Workers Association (NAPOWA) filed a Manifestation of Desistance expressing NAPOWA's opposition to the filing of the petition in any court.

Zamora: the Administrative Code gives the President continuing authority to reorganize and redefine the functions of the OP (Sec. 31, Chapter 10, Title III, Book III). Quoting Canonizado v. Aguirre, reorganization "involves the reduction of personnel, consolidation of offices, or abolition thereof by reason of economy or redundancy of functions," and occurs when there is an alteration of the existing structure of government offices, including the lines of control, authority, and responsibility between them.

paras.html: Dario v. Mison: reorganizations are valid if pursued in good faith, i.e., for the purpose of economy or to make the bureaucracy more efficient. In that event no dismissal actually occurs because the position itself ceases to exist, and "security of tenure would not be a Chinese wall." But if the "abolition" is done for political reasons or purposely to defeat security of tenure, no valid abolition takes place and it is void ab initio – e.g., a mere change of nomenclature of positions, or claims of economy belied by ample funds.

The NPO is an agency attached to the OP, not part of the OP Proper.

paras.html: PD 1416 is an undue delegation: creating and abolishing offices is legislative; neither the Executive nor the Judiciary inherently possesses the power to reorganize. "National government" covers all three branches; PD 1416 surrenders the core legislative power to re-mold the bureaucracy, and its authority to "transfer appropriations" and "standardize salaries" conflicts with Sec. 25(5), Art. VI and Sec. 5, Art. IX-B. Like Sec. 68 of the old Revised Administrative Code struck down in Pelaez, it offends potestas delegata non delegari potest.

paras.html: PD 1416 was meant for the transition to a parliamentary system (last "Whereas" clause); at the very least, legislative powers under it ceased upon the convening of the First Congress (Sec. 6, Art. XVIII). The majority's sweeping caveats (limits to the Executive; compliance with the Constitution) will not erase PD 1416 from the statute books.

paras.html: Amnesty distinguished from pardon: Pardon is granted by the Chief Executive alone, is a private act that must be pleaded and proved, is granted after conviction, and looks forward (it forgives the punishment). Amnesty is proclaimed by the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress, is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, is granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses (generally before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction), and looks backward: it abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself.
paras.text: Amnesty distinguished from pardon: Pardon is granted by the Chief Executive alone, is a private act that must be pleaded and proved, is granted after conviction, and looks forward (it forgives the punishment). Amnesty is proclaimed by the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress, is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, is granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses (generally before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction), and looks backward: it abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself.

paras.html: No admission required: To be entitled to the benefits of the Amnesty Proclamation, it is not necessary that the accused, as a condition precedent or sine qua non, admit having committed the offense and allege amnesty as a defense; it is sufficient that the evidence, either of the complainant or the accused, shows that the offense comes within the terms of the Proclamation.

paras.html: Non-waivable: Once established by the evidence, the right to the benefits of amnesty cannot be waived, because it is of public interest that one whom the law regards as innocent, and as a patriot or hero, is not punished as a criminal.

paras.html: "all persons who committed any act penalized under the Revised Penal Code in furtherance of the resistance to the enemy or against persons aiding in the war effort of the enemy, and committed during the period from December 8, 1941 to the date when each particular area of the Philippines was actually liberated from the enemy control and occupation. This amnesty shall not apply to crimes against chastity or to acts committed from purely personal motives."

paras.html: Once established by the evidence (of the prosecution or of the defense), the right can not be waived, because it is of public interest that one whom the Proclamation, which has the force of a law, regards not only as innocent but as a patriot or hero cannot be punished as a criminal.

paras.html: A fortiori argument: courts cannot convict a person who, per the evidence, committed an act not punishable by law even if he confesses guilt; so also, they cannot convict one whom the law considers a patriot and hero.

paras.html: But although motive is a subjective state of mind, it need not be testified to by the defendant himself. It is generally established by witnesses' testimony on the acts or statements of the accused before or immediately after the offense, from which motive may be inferred.

paras.html: Amnesty distinguished from pardon: Pardon is granted by the Chief Executive alone, is a private act that must be pleaded and proved, is granted after conviction, and looks forward (it forgives the punishment). Amnesty is proclaimed by the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress, is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, is granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses (generally before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction), and looks backward: it abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself.
paras.text: Amnesty distinguished from pardon: Pardon is granted by the Chief Executive alone, is a private act that must be pleaded and proved, is granted after conviction, and looks forward (it forgives the punishment). Amnesty is proclaimed by the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress, is a public act of which courts take judicial notice, is granted to classes of persons or communities who may be guilty of political offenses (generally before or after prosecution, sometimes after conviction), and looks backward: it abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself.

paras.html: No admission required: To be entitled to the benefits of the Amnesty Proclamation, it is not necessary that the accused, as a condition precedent or sine qua non, admit having committed the offense and allege amnesty as a defense; it is sufficient that the evidence, either of the complainant or the accused, shows that the offense comes within the terms of the Proclamation.

paras.html: Non-waivable: Once established by the evidence, the right to the benefits of amnesty cannot be waived, because it is of public interest that one whom the law regards as innocent, and as a patriot or hero, is not punished as a criminal.

paras.html: Before the period for perfecting an appeal expired, Jimenez learned of Proclamation No. 8 (September 7, 1946), issued by President Manuel Roxas with the concurrence of Congress under Art. VII, Sec. 10, par. 6 of the Constitution [1935 Constitution].

paras.html: Its operative part declares an amnesty in favor of:
paras.text: Its operative part declares an amnesty in favor of:

paras.html: "all persons who committed any act penalized under the Revised Penal Code in furtherance of the resistance to the enemy or against persons aiding in the war effort of the enemy, and committed during the period from December 8, 1941 to the date when each particular area of the Philippines was actually liberated from the enemy control and occupation. This amnesty shall not apply to crimes against chastity or to acts committed from purely personal motives."
paras.text: "all persons who committed any act penalized under the Revised Penal Code in furtherance of the resistance to the enemy or against persons aiding in the war effort of the enemy, and committed during the period from December 8, 1941 to the date when each particular area of the Philippines was actually liberated from the enemy control and occupation. This amnesty shall not apply to crimes against chastity or to acts committed from purely personal motives."

paras.html: Its whereas clauses state that the fact that such acts were committed in furtherance of the resistance is not a valid defense under Philippine law, and that the persons so accused "should not be regarded as criminals but rather as patriots and heroes".
paras.text: Its whereas clauses state that the fact that such acts were committed in furtherance of the resistance is not a valid defense under Philippine law, and that the persons so accused "should not be regarded as criminals but rather as patriots and heroes".

paras.html: It created Guerrilla Amnesty Commissions to examine the facts and circumstances surrounding each case and, if necessary, conduct summary hearings of witnesses for both the complainant and the accused. Upon finding that a case falls within the Proclamation, the Commission so declares, and the accused is forthwith released or discharged.
paras.text: It created Guerrilla Amnesty Commissions to examine the facts and circumstances surrounding each case and, if necessary, conduct summary hearings of witnesses for both the complainant and the accused. Upon finding that a case falls within the Proclamation, the Commission so declares, and the accused is forthwith released or discharged.

paras.html: Administrative Order No. 11 (October 2, 1946) created the Commissions: cases pending in the CFI of the province, and cases decided by the CFI but not yet elevated on appeal, go to the respective Amnesty Commission; cases pending appeal go to the Seventh Amnesty Commission.

paras.html: By Proclamation of the Chief Executive with the concurrence of Congress; a public act of which courts should take judicial notice.

paras.html: Looks backward: abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself, so that the person released "stands before the law precisely as though he had committed no offense".

paras.html: Once established by the evidence (of the prosecution or of the defense), the right can not be waived, because it is of public interest that one whom the Proclamation, which has the force of a law, regards not only as innocent but as a patriot or hero cannot be punished as a criminal.

paras.html: A fortiori argument: courts cannot convict a person who, per the evidence, committed an act not punishable by law even if he confesses guilt; so also, they cannot convict one whom the law considers a patriot and hero.

paras.html: But although motive is a subjective state of mind, it need not be testified to by the defendant himself. It is generally established by witnesses' testimony on the acts or statements of the accused before or immediately after the offense, from which motive may be inferred.

paras.html: The accused's own statement at arraignment or hearing about his motive generally cannot be relied on, especially against contrary evidence, since it may be an afterthought or colored by his interest.

paras.html: Totality of evidence in amparo: The privilege of the writ of amparo may be granted on the totality of evidence standard, which may extend to relevant circumstantial evidence; hearsay testimony that is consistent with the admissible evidence adduced may also be admitted and appreciated. The flexibility derives from the State's often virtual monopoly of access to pertinent evidence and its deliberate use of power to destroy evidence. It is not automatic admissibility in all amparo proceedings; it is determined case to case.

The flexibility derives from the State's often virtual monopoly of access to pertinent evidence and its deliberate use of power to destroy evidence. It is not automatic admissibility in all amparo proceedings; it is determined case to case.

paras.html: Substantial evidence and threats: Amparo is a summary proceeding requiring only substantial evidence. Acts that merely threaten the rights to life, liberty, and security, or that are preliminary steps to a probable extrajudicial killing or enforced disappearance, can justify the writ; courts need not wait for the irreversible to happen.

paras.html: Extraordinary diligence of public officials: A public official named as amparo respondent must prove extraordinary diligence and cannot invoke the presumption of regularity (Sec. 17). Merely issuing orders to subordinates and relying on their reports, without independent investigation, does not discharge the two-fold burden. Failure to prove the involvement of government forces does not bar an order for further investigation.

paras.html: Razon, Jr. v. Tagitis adopted the totality of evidence standard for amparo, given the unique evidentiary difficulties of enforced disappearances, which call for standards responsive to the circumstances "without transgressing the due process requirements that underlie every proceeding."

paras.html: The rule: consider all the evidence in its totality, and consider any evidence otherwise inadmissible under the usual rules to be admissible if it is consistent with the admissible evidence adduced. The rules are reduced to the most basic test of reason: relevance to the issue and consistency with the other evidence. → Even hearsay may be admitted if it meets this minimum test.

paras.html: The Rome Statute established the International Criminal Court (ICC), with jurisdiction over "the most serious crimes of international concern" (genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression), "complementary to the national criminal jurisdictions." paras.html: May 9, 2003: US Ambassador Francis Ricciardone sent Embassy Note No. 0470 proposing a non-surrender bilateral agreement. May 13, 2003: via Exchange of Notes No. BFO-028-03, the RP, through DFA Secretary Ople, accepted the US proposals and put the Agreement into effect. It aims to protect "persons" of both countries from "frivolous and harassment suits" in international tribunals; the US had similar agreements with 33 other countries.

May 13, 2003: via Exchange of Notes No. BFO-028-03, the RP, through DFA Secretary Ople, accepted the US proposals and put the Agreement into effect. It aims to protect "persons" of both countries from "frivolous and harassment suits" in international tribunals; the US had similar agreements with 33 other countries.

paras.html: Terms: (1) "persons" are current or former Government officials, employees (including contractors), military personnel, or nationals of a Party; (2) persons of one Party in the other's territory shall not, absent the express consent of the first Party, be surrendered or transferred to any international tribunal (unless established by the UN Security Council), nor to a third country for that purpose; (3)–(4) neither Party, when extraditing a person of the other to a third country, will agree to that country's surrender of the person to such a tribunal without consent; (5) it remains in force until one year after notice of termination.

paras.html: The Agreement is void ab initio as immoral or contrary to universally recognized principles of international law (it "leaves criminals immune"). It is invalid without two-thirds Senate concurrence: it involves political issues and permanent arrangements, which belong in treaties (Commissioner of Customs v. Eastern Sea Trading); its subject is outside the listed categories for executive agreements; and an exchange of notes cannot amend a treaty (Adolfo v. CFI of Zambales). The exchange of notes is not a valid medium.

paras.html: Under the doctrine of incorporation (Art. II, Sec. 2), the Philippines adopts generally accepted principles of international law. An exchange of notes falls "into the category of inter-governmental agreements". UN Treaty Reference Guide: a record of a routine agreement in which each party holds the document signed by the other; used for speed or "to avoid the process of legislative approval." "Exchange of notes" and "executive agreements" are used interchangeably; executive agreements take the form of exchanges of notes or more formal agreements or protocols (Sayre). → E/N BFO-028-03 "is a recognized mode of concluding a legally binding international written contract among nations."

Foreign affairs have grown more complex (human rights, environment, the sea); US executive agreements (1980–2000) covered defense, arms limitation, nuclear safety, and more. Treaty-authorized and treaty-implementing executive agreements also exist.

Ne bis in idem (Art. 20(3)) underscores State primacy. The ICC comes into play only when States are unwilling or unable to prosecute.

paras.html: RA 9851 defines the crimes, provides penalties, and establishes special courts for the State's primary jurisdiction; nothing in it goes against the Agreement. Sec. 17's second paragraph (authorities "may" dispense with prosecution and "may" surrender to an international court or another State under applicable extradition laws and treaties) "is simply permissive": "may" denotes discretion.

Genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity are customary law, even jus cogens, supporting universal jurisdiction.

paras.html: Custom requires state practice (generality, uniformity and consistency, duration) and opinio juris (Bernas). As of Oct. 12, 2010, only 114 of 194 States (about 58.76%) had ratified the Rome Statute after it entered into force on July 1, 2002; no overwhelming consensus that these crimes be handled by a particular international court. "The Philippines ... does not even feel bound by the Rome Statute. Res ipsa loquitur": eight years after signing, it has not been transmitted to the Senate. Without practice, opinio juris is absent. The Statute rejects universal jurisdiction (requiring State consent) and requires ratification → "the ICC ... is not declaratory of customary international law."

paras.html: RA 9851, Secs. 2(e) and 17: the State policy that serious international crimes "must not go unpunished" and the State's jurisdiction over persons in the Philippines regardless of citizenship impose a duty to prosecute. If it declines, the Philippines has only two options: surrender to an appropriate international court, or to another State "pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties," and only if that court or State is already investigating or prosecuting.

paras.html: No applicable extradition treaty: the RP-US Extradition Treaty requires dual criminality; the US lacks equivalent laws (no implementing legislation for the Geneva Conventions; Medellin v. Texas; the Holt and Dallas report on gaps such as apartheid, persecution, enslavement, extermination). The Agreement itself is not one either. Requiring US consent before surrender to the ICC, and dispensing with the "already investigating" condition, derogates from Sec. 17, which needs an amendatory law or treaty.

paras.html: Executive agreements cannot amend laws: echoing his Suplico dissent, an executive agreement has the force of law but cannot amend or repeal prior laws and is deemed repealed by an inconsistent subsequent law (Civil Code, Art. 7); only a Senate-concurred treaty acquires the status of municipal law (also the US State Department view).

paras.html: Incorporation: generally accepted principles, including custom, form part of Philippine law even without treaty obligations (Kuroda v. Jalandoni). The duty to prosecute or surrender, reflected in Art. 89(1) of the Rome Statute, has that status; derogating from it requires Senate ratification [he cites "Section 17 of RA 8951" at one point; the statute is RA 9851].

The exception for UN Security Council tribunals suits the US because of its veto.

paras.html: Executive agreements need no Senate concurrence: international agreements may be treaties (requiring legislative concurrence after executive ratification) or executive agreements (no concurrence; usually less formal and narrower). An exchange of notes is a recognized form of executive agreement. The Eastern Sea Trading list of subjects for executive agreements "is not cast in stone"; "the primary consideration in the choice of the form of agreement is the parties' intent", and the Constitution does not classify which subjects require a treaty (save Art. XVIII, Sec. 25).

paras.html: The Rome Statute established the International Criminal Court (ICC), with jurisdiction over "the most serious crimes of international concern" (genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression), "complementary to the national criminal jurisdictions." Dec. 28, 2000: the Philippines signed it through Chargé d'Affaires Enrique Manalo; it is subject to ratification, and as of the petition only 92 of 139 signatories had ratified. The Philippines had not.

paras.html: May 9, 2003: US Ambassador Francis Ricciardone sent Embassy Note No. 0470 proposing a non-surrender bilateral agreement. May 13, 2003: via Exchange of Notes No. BFO-028-03, the RP, through DFA Secretary Ople, accepted the US proposals and put the Agreement into effect. It aims to protect "persons" of both countries from "frivolous and harassment suits" in international tribunals; the US had similar agreements with 33 other countries.

May 13, 2003: via Exchange of Notes No. BFO-028-03, the RP, through DFA Secretary Ople, accepted the US proposals and put the Agreement into effect. It aims to protect "persons" of both countries from "frivolous and harassment suits" in international tribunals; the US had similar agreements with 33 other countries.

paras.html: Terms: (1) "persons" are current or former Government officials, employees (including contractors), military personnel, or nationals of a Party; (2) persons of one Party in the other's territory shall not, absent the express consent of the first Party, be surrendered or transferred to any international tribunal (unless established by the UN Security Council), nor to a third country for that purpose; (3)–(4) neither Party, when extraditing a person of the other to a third country, will agree to that country's surrender of the person to such a tribunal without consent; (5) it remains in force until one year after notice of termination.

paras.html: Respondents gravely abused their discretion by concluding the Agreement after signing the Rome Statute: they abandoned the only recourse to try "persons" for grave international crimes, abdicating sovereignty; good faith (Vienna Convention, Art. 18) bars acts impairing the signed Statute; the Agreement defeats the Statute's object and purpose and breaches Arts. 27, 86, 89, and 90; it falls outside Art. 98.

paras.html: The Agreement is void ab initio as immoral or contrary to universally recognized principles of international law (it "leaves criminals immune"). It is invalid without two-thirds Senate concurrence: it involves political issues and permanent arrangements, which belong in treaties (Commissioner of Customs v. Eastern Sea Trading); its subject is outside the listed categories for executive agreements; and an exchange of notes cannot amend a treaty (Adolfo v. CFI of Zambales). The exchange of notes is not a valid medium.

When a citizen asserts a public right, "the mere fact that he is a citizen satisfies the requirement of personal interest" (Francisco v. Nagmamalasakit).

paras.html: Under the doctrine of incorporation (Art. II, Sec. 2), the Philippines adopts generally accepted principles of international law. An exchange of notes falls "into the category of inter-governmental agreements". UN Treaty Reference Guide: a record of a routine agreement in which each party holds the document signed by the other; used for speed or "to avoid the process of legislative approval." "Exchange of notes" and "executive agreements" are used interchangeably; executive agreements take the form of exchanges of notes or more formal agreements or protocols (Sayre). → E/N BFO-028-03 "is a recognized mode of concluding a legally binding international written contract among nations."

paras.html: Vienna Convention, Art. 2: a treaty is "an international agreement concluded between states in written form and governed by international law ... whatever its particular designation." International agreements may be (1) treaties needing legislative concurrence after executive ratification or (2) executive agreements, similar but needing no concurrence, usually less formal and narrower.

paras.html: Under international law, treaties and executive agreements have no difference in binding effect if negotiators stayed within their powers; domestically, neither is valid if it violates the Constitution. A treaty has greater "dignity" (backed by the President, Senate, and people) and, unlike an executive agreement, takes precedence over prior statutes.
