paras.html: Eastern Sea Trading: its observation that political issues and permanent arrangements usually take the form of treaties, and its list of subjects for executive agreements, are "not cast in stone." "The primary consideration in the choice of the form of agreement is the parties' intent and desire"; form "takes a back seat" since both bind under pacta sunt servanda. Foreign affairs have grown more complex (human rights, environment, the sea); US executive agreements (1980–2000) covered defense, arms limitation, nuclear safety, and more. Treaty-authorized and treaty-implementing executive agreements also exist.

paras.html: Complementarity: the ICC "shall be complementary to national criminal jurisdictions" (Art. 1). The sixth preambular paragraph declares "the duty of every State to exercise its criminal jurisdiction" → primary jurisdiction rests with the State; the ICC acts secondarily (Art. 17(1)). Ne bis in idem (Art. 20(3)) underscores State primacy. The ICC comes into play only when States are unwilling or unable to prosecute.

paras.html: Signatory vs. State-Party: a signatory is only obliged to refrain from acts defeating the object and purpose (Vienna Convention, Art. 18); a State-Party must follow all provisions. The Philippines is only a signatory "for lack of ratification by the Senate" [the decision's phrase; Pimentel, which it cites later, vests ratification in the President, with Senate concurrence]. → Arts. 27, 86, 89, and 90 bind only State-Parties; arguing otherwise is premature.

paras.html: Custom requires state practice (generality, uniformity and consistency, duration) and opinio juris (Bernas). As of Oct. 12, 2010, only 114 of 194 States (about 58.76%) had ratified the Rome Statute after it entered into force on July 1, 2002; no overwhelming consensus that these crimes be handled by a particular international court. "The Philippines ... does not even feel bound by the Rome Statute. Res ipsa loquitur": eight years after signing, it has not been transmitted to the Senate. Without practice, opinio juris is absent. The Statute rejects universal jurisdiction (requiring State consent) and requires ratification → "the ICC ... is not declaratory of customary international law."

paras.html: RA 9851, Secs. 2(e) and 17: the State policy that serious international crimes "must not go unpunished" and the State's jurisdiction over persons in the Philippines regardless of citizenship impose a duty to prosecute. If it declines, the Philippines has only two options: surrender to an appropriate international court, or to another State "pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties," and only if that court or State is already investigating or prosecuting.

paras.html: No applicable extradition treaty: the RP-US Extradition Treaty requires dual criminality; the US lacks equivalent laws (no implementing legislation for the Geneva Conventions; Medellin v. Texas; the Holt and Dallas report on gaps such as apartheid, persecution, enslavement, extermination). The Agreement itself is not one either. Requiring US consent before surrender to the ICC, and dispensing with the "already investigating" condition, derogates from Sec. 17, which needs an amendatory law or treaty.

paras.html: Executive agreements cannot amend laws: echoing his Suplico dissent, an executive agreement has the force of law but cannot amend or repeal prior laws and is deemed repealed by an inconsistent subsequent law (Civil Code, Art. 7); only a Senate-concurred treaty acquires the status of municipal law (also the US State Department view).

paras.html: Executive agreements need no Senate concurrence: international agreements may be treaties (requiring legislative concurrence after executive ratification) or executive agreements (no concurrence; usually less formal and narrower). An exchange of notes is a recognized form of executive agreement. The Eastern Sea Trading list of subjects for executive agreements "is not cast in stone"; "the primary consideration in the choice of the form of agreement is the parties' intent", and the Constitution does not classify which subjects require a treaty (save Art. XVIII, Sec. 25).

paras.html: May 9, 2003: US Ambassador Francis Ricciardone sent Embassy Note No. 0470 proposing a non-surrender bilateral agreement. May 13, 2003: via Exchange of Notes No. BFO-028-03, the RP, through DFA Secretary Ople, accepted the US proposals and put the Agreement into effect. It aims to protect "persons" of both countries from "frivolous and harassment suits" in international tribunals; the US had similar agreements with 33 other countries.

paras.html: Terms: (1) "persons" are current or former Government officials, employees (including contractors), military personnel, or nationals of a Party; (2) persons of one Party in the other's territory shall not, absent the express consent of the first Party, be surrendered or transferred to any international tribunal (unless established by the UN Security Council), nor to a third country for that purpose; (3)–(4) neither Party, when extraditing a person of the other to a third country, will agree to that country's surrender of the person to such a tribunal without consent; (5) it remains in force until one year after notice of termination.

paras.html: The Agreement is void ab initio as immoral or contrary to universally recognized principles of international law (it "leaves criminals immune"). It is invalid without two-thirds Senate concurrence: it involves political issues and permanent arrangements, which belong in treaties (Commissioner of Customs v. The exchange of notes is not a valid medium.

paras.html: Under the doctrine of incorporation (Art. II, Sec. 2), the Philippines adopts generally accepted principles of international law. An exchange of notes falls "into the category of inter-governmental agreements". UN Treaty Reference Guide: a record of a routine agreement in which each party holds the document signed by the other; used for speed or "to avoid the process of legislative approval." "Exchange of notes" and "executive agreements" are used interchangeably; executive agreements take the form of exchanges of notes or more formal agreements or protocols (Sayre). → E/N BFO-028-03 "is a recognized mode of concluding a legally binding international written contract among nations."

paras.html: RA 9851 defines the crimes, provides penalties, and establishes special courts for the State's primary jurisdiction; nothing in it goes against the Agreement. Sec. 17's second paragraph (authorities "may" dispense with prosecution and "may" surrender to an international court or another State under applicable extradition laws and treaties) "is simply permissive": "may" denotes discretion.

Genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity are customary law, even jus cogens, supporting universal jurisdiction.

paras.html: Custom requires state practice (generality, uniformity and consistency, duration) and opinio juris (Bernas). As of Oct. 12, 2010, only 114 of 194 States (about 58.76%) had ratified the Rome Statute after it entered into force on July 1, 2002; no overwhelming consensus that these crimes be handled by a particular international court. "The Philippines ... does not even feel bound by the Rome Statute. Res ipsa loquitur": eight years after signing, it has not been transmitted to the Senate. Without practice, opinio juris is absent. The Statute rejects universal jurisdiction (requiring State consent) and requires ratification → "the ICC ... is not declaratory of customary international law."

paras.html: RA 9851, Secs. 2(e) and 17: the State policy that serious international crimes "must not go unpunished" and the State's jurisdiction over persons in the Philippines regardless of citizenship impose a duty to prosecute. If it declines, the Philippines has only two options: surrender to an appropriate international court, or to another State "pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties," and only if that court or State is already investigating or prosecuting.

paras.html: No applicable extradition treaty: the RP-US Extradition Treaty requires dual criminality; the US lacks equivalent laws (no implementing legislation for the Geneva Conventions; Medellin v. Texas; the Holt and Dallas report on gaps such as apartheid, persecution, enslavement, extermination). The Agreement itself is not one either. Requiring US consent before surrender to the ICC, and dispensing with the "already investigating" condition, derogates from Sec. 17, which needs an amendatory law or treaty.

paras.html: Executive agreements cannot amend laws: echoing his Suplico dissent, an executive agreement has the force of law but cannot amend or repeal prior laws and is deemed repealed by an inconsistent subsequent law (Civil Code, Art. 7); only a Senate-concurred treaty acquires the status of municipal law (also the US State Department view).

paras.html: Incorporation: generally accepted principles, including custom, form part of Philippine law even without treaty obligations (Kuroda v. Jalandoni). The duty to prosecute or surrender, reflected in Art. 89(1) of the Rome Statute, has that status; derogating from it requires Senate ratification [he cites "Section 17 of RA 8951" at one point; the statute is RA 9851].

The exception for UN Security Council tribunals suits the US because of its veto.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy: It contemplates "a guarantee of full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require"; it "means freedom from outside control." A veto that withholds the Chief Justice's authority to augment items from savings is "tantamount to dictating to the Judiciary how its funds should be utilized" and violates Sec. 3, Art. VIII, under which Judiciary appropriations, once approved, "shall be automatically and regularly released."

paras.html: Item veto: The President may veto only a particular item — "an indivisible sum of money dedicated to a stated purpose" — in an appropriation, revenue, or tariff bill. paras.html: The veto is a constitutionally vested power, but "the veto power is not absolute." Sec. 27(2), Art. VI allows the President to veto "any particular item or items in an appropriation, revenue or tariff bill," but "the veto shall not affect the item or items to which he does not object."

paras.html: The OSG is correct that, generally, the veto is all or nothing: the President "cannot act like an editor crossing out specific lines, provisions, or paragraphs in a bill."

paras.html: Exception – appropriation, revenue, or tariff bills: the Administration needs the money to run the government and cannot veto the entire bill → it would be compelled to approve undesirable parts → hence the item veto, "to avoid inexpedient riders being attached to an indispensable appropriation or revenue measure."

paras.html: The Court's position papers before Congress: the DBM sets the parameters for budget proposals, submits its own version to Congress "without informing the agency of major alterations and mutilations," and expects the agency to defend proposals not of its making. After enactment, it controls releases through guidelines, Work and Financial Plans, allotments, notices of cash allocation, and accountability reports. Since it prunes budgets "to below subsistence levels," the CJ, the ConCom chairs, and the Ombudsman must make "pilgrimages to DBM" for additional funds.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy: It contemplates "a guarantee of full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require"; it "means freedom from outside control." A veto that withholds the Chief Justice's authority to augment items from savings is "tantamount to dictating to the Judiciary how its funds should be utilized" and violates Sec. 3, Art. VIII, under which Judiciary appropriations, once approved, "shall be automatically and regularly released."
paras.text: Fiscal autonomy: It contemplates "a guarantee of full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require"; it "means freedom from outside control." A veto that withholds the Chief Justice's authority to augment items from savings is "tantamount to dictating to the Judiciary how its funds should be utilized" and violates Sec. 3, Art. VIII, under which Judiciary appropriations, once approved, "shall be automatically and regularly released."

paras.html: Item veto: The President may veto only a particular item — "an indivisible sum of money dedicated to a stated purpose" — in an appropriation, revenue, or tariff bill. She cannot veto part of an item and approve the rest, and provisions (e.g., authority to augment from savings, or the manner of drawing from a fund) are not items.

paras.html: Separation of powers: The veto power cannot be used to repeal an existing law (RA 1797) or to set aside a final resolution of the Supreme Court; the President's power is merely to execute the laws.

paras.html: Background – the pension laws:
paras.text: Background – the pension laws:

paras.html: June 20, 1953: RA 910 provided retirement pensions for Justices of the SC and the CA who have rendered at least 20 years of service in the Judiciary or any other branch of government, and who either reach age 70 or resign by reason of incapacity. The retired Justice receives, for the rest of his life, the salary he was receiving at retirement.
paras.text: June 20, 1953: RA 910 provided retirement pensions for Justices of the SC and the CA who have rendered at least 20 years of service in the Judiciary or any other branch of government, and who either reach age 70 or resign by reason of incapacity. The retired Justice receives, for the rest of his life, the salary he was receiving at retirement.

paras.html: June 21, 1957: RA 1797 amended RA 910 by adding Sec. 3-A, the automatic readjustment clause:
paras.text: June 21, 1957: RA 1797 amended RA 910 by adding Sec. 3-A, the automatic readjustment clause:

paras.html: "In case the salary of Justices of the Supreme Court or of the Court of Appeals is increased or deceased [sic], such increased or decreased salary shall, for purposes of this Act, be deemed to be the salary or the retirement pension which a Justice ... who retired was receiving at the time of his cessation in office. Provided, that any benefits that have already accrued prior to such increase or decrease shall not be affected thereby."

paras.html: The veto is a constitutionally vested power, but "the veto power is not absolute." Sec. 27(2), Art. VI allows the President to veto "any particular item or items in an appropriation, revenue or tariff bill," but "the veto shall not affect the item or items to which he does not object."
paras.text: The veto is a constitutionally vested power, but "the veto power is not absolute." Sec. 27(2), Art. VI allows the President to veto "any particular item or items in an appropriation, revenue or tariff bill," but "the veto shall not affect the item or items to which he does not object."

paras.html: The OSG is correct that, generally, the veto is all or nothing: the President "cannot act like an editor crossing out specific lines, provisions, or paragraphs in a bill."
paras.text: The OSG is correct that, generally, the veto is all or nothing: the President "cannot act like an editor crossing out specific lines, provisions, or paragraphs in a bill."

paras.html: Exception – appropriation, revenue, or tariff bills: the Administration needs the money to run the government and cannot veto the entire bill → it would be compelled to approve undesirable parts → hence the item veto, "to avoid inexpedient riders being attached to an indispensable appropriation or revenue measure."
paras.text: Exception – appropriation, revenue, or tariff bills: the Administration needs the money to run the government and cannot veto the entire bill → it would be compelled to approve undesirable parts → hence the item veto, "to avoid inexpedient riders being attached to an indispensable appropriation or revenue measure."

paras.html: Only a particular item may be vetoed. The power to disapprove items "does not grant the authority to veto a part of an item and to approve the remaining portion of the same item" (*Gonzales v. Macaraig, Jr.*).

paras.html: The Court's position papers before Congress: the DBM sets the parameters for budget proposals, submits its own version to Congress "without informing the agency of major alterations and mutilations," and expects the agency to defend proposals not of its making. After enactment, it controls releases through guidelines, Work and Financial Plans, allotments, notices of cash allocation, and accountability reports. Since it prunes budgets "to below subsistence levels," the CJ, the ConCom chairs, and the Ombudsman must make "pilgrimages to DBM" for additional funds.

paras.html: Retired AFP officers and men number in the tens of thousands and retire much younger (some generals at 50 or earlier), while retired Justices are few and retire at 70. paras.html: The inquiry must be in aid of legislation: the power of inquiry under Sec. 21, Art. VI is not absolute or unlimited. The inquiry must be "material or necessary to the exercise of a power ... vested by the Constitution" (Arnault), and its character is judged by the speech or resolution under which it is made. An inquiry whose aim is to find out whether private persons violated a law (here, Sec. 5, RA 3019) is not in aid of legislation; it is a matter "more within the province of the courts." There is "no general authority to expose the private affairs of individuals" (Watkins).

paras.html: The inquiry must be in aid of legislation: the power of inquiry under Sec. 21, Art. VI is not absolute or unlimited. The inquiry must be "material or necessary to the exercise of a power ... vested by the Constitution" (Arnault), and its character is judged by the speech or resolution under which it is made. An inquiry whose aim is to find out whether private persons violated a law (here, Sec. 5, RA 3019) is not in aid of legislation; it is a matter "more within the province of the courts." There is "no general authority to expose the private affairs of individuals" (Watkins).

paras.html: Kilbourn v. Thompson (1880) is dated. McGrain v. Daugherty: courts presume a legitimate legislative object where the subject is one on which legislation could be had; an express avowal is better but not indispensable. US cases (Josephson, Barsky, Shelton, Deutsch): the measure is the potentiality of legislation; hearings need not result in legislation. Bernas: in the Philippines, Congress holds the totality of legislative power, so "in aid of legislation" is easily satisfied.

paras.html: Source of the power to create the PTC: The creation of the PTC does not fall within the power to reorganize under Sec. 31 of the Administrative Code, which contemplates the alteration of an existing structure ("[t]he creation of an office is nowhere mentioned, much less envisioned"); nor is it justified by the power of control, which is "entirely different from the power to create public offices"; nor by PD 1416, which is functus officio. It finds justification in the faithful-execution clause (Sec. 17, Art. VII): the President's power to conduct investigations, and to create ad hoc bodies to do so, is inherent in his powers as Chief Executive. Funding from existing OP appropriations is an allotment, not an appropriation.

It finds justification in the faithful-execution clause (Sec. 17, Art. VII): the President's power to conduct investigations, and to create ad hoc bodies to do so, is inherent in his powers as Chief Executive. Funding from existing OP appropriations is an allotment, not an appropriation.

paras.html: Fact-finding vs. adjudication: Fact-finding is not adjudication; the PTC has no quasi-judicial power, and since the Ombudsman's and DOJ's investigative powers are not exclusive, it complements rather than supplants them.

paras.html: Equal protection (the decisive ruling): The equal protection clause covers all official state action, including the Executive's. Singling out the "previous administration" – "but just a member of a class, that is, a class of past administrations" – is arbitrary where the distinctions are not substantial and the exclusion is deliberate. "The PTC must, at least, have the authority to investigate all past administrations. While reasonable prioritization is permitted, it should not be arbitrary."

paras.html: Before the May 2010 elections, then Senator Benigno Simeon Aquino III condemned graft and corruption with the slogan "Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap." He was elected President.
paras.text: Before the May 2010 elections, then Senator Benigno Simeon Aquino III condemned graft and corruption with the slogan "Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap." He was elected President.

paras.html: To transform this into reality, President Aquino found a need for a special body to investigate reported graft and corruption allegedly committed during the previous administration.
paras.text: To transform this into reality, President Aquino found a need for a special body to investigate reported graft and corruption allegedly committed during the previous administration.

paras.html: July 30, 2010: President Aquino signed EO 1, "Creating the Philippine Truth Commission of 2010" (PTC). Its Whereas clauses invoke Art. XI, Sec. 1 (public office is a public trust), state a need for "a separate body dedicated solely to investigating and finding out the truth concerning the reported cases of graft and corruption during the previous administration," and cite Sec. 31, Chapter 10, Book III of EO 292 (continuing authority to reorganize the OP).
paras.text: July 30, 2010: President Aquino signed EO 1, "Creating the Philippine Truth Commission of 2010" (PTC). Its Whereas clauses invoke Art. XI, Sec. 1 (public office is a public trust), state a need for "a separate body dedicated solely to investigating and finding out the truth concerning the reported cases of graft and corruption during the previous administration," and cite Sec. 31, Chapter 10, Book III of EO 292 (continuing authority to reorganize the OP).

paras.html: Sec. 1: the PTC "shall primarily seek and find the truth on . . . reports of graft and corruption of such scale and magnitude that shock and offend the moral and ethical sensibilities of the people, committed by public officers and employees, their co-principals, accomplices and accessories from the private sector, if any, during the previous administration; and thereafter recommend the appropriate action." It has a Chairman and four members acting as an "independent collegial body."
paras.text: Sec. 1: the PTC "shall primarily seek and find the truth on . . . reports of graft and corruption of such scale and magnitude that shock and offend the moral and ethical sensibilities of the people, committed by public officers and employees, their co-principals, accomplices and accessories from the private sector, if any, during the previous administration; and thereafter recommend the appropriate action." It has a Chairman and four members acting as an "independent collegial body."

paras.html: Sec. 2: it has all the powers of an investigative body under Sec. 37, Chapter 9, Book I of the Administrative Code; it conducts a fact-finding investigation of cases involving third-level public officers and higher during the previous administration and submits findings and recommendations to the President, Congress, and the Ombudsman. Among others, it may require executive agencies to produce documents; obtain records from Congress and the courts upon proper request; invite or subpoena witnesses and administer oaths; recommend state witnesses; and (g) turn over evidence to prosecutorial authorities "when in the course of its investigation" it finds reasonable ground to believe officials are liable.

paras.html: Sec. 9: government personnel who refuse to obey a subpoena, take an oath, or testify face administrative discipline; private persons "may be dealt with in accordance with law." Sec. 11: the OP shall provide the necessary funds. Sec. 14: term until December 31, 2012. Sec. 17: "If and when in the judgment of the President there is a need to expand the mandate . . . to include the investigation of cases and instances of graft and corruption during the prior administrations, such mandate may be so extended accordingly by way of a supplemental Executive Order." Sec. 18: separability clause.

paras.html: Nature of the PTC (as described by the Court):
paras.text: Nature of the PTC (as described by the Court):

paras.html: A mere ad hoc body formed under the OP; though described as "independent," it is essentially an entity within the Office of the President Proper and subject to his control; it is a public office, as an ad hoc body is one.
paras.text: A mere ad hoc body formed under the OP; though described as "independent," it is essentially an entity within the Office of the President Proper and subject to his control; it is a public office, as an ad hoc body is one.

paras.html: It is not a quasi-judicial body: it cannot adjudicate, arbitrate, or render awards; it has subpoena powers but no power to cite for contempt or order arrest; it cannot determine probable cause or impose criminal, civil, or administrative sanctions.
paras.text: It is not a quasi-judicial body: it cannot adjudicate, arbitrate, or render awards; it has subpoena powers but no power to cite for contempt or order arrest; it cannot determine probable cause or impose criminal, civil, or administrative sanctions.

paras.html: It differs from truth commissions abroad, which investigate serious human rights violations as mechanisms of transitional justice (e.g., South Africa's reconciliatory commission); the PTC's "marching order" is the identification and punishment of perpetrators.

paras.html: G.R. No. 193036: special civil action for certiorari and prohibition by Reps. Lagman, Albano, Datumanong, and Fua as incumbent HOR members. Their grounds: (a) EO 1 usurps Congress's power to create a public office and appropriate funds; (b) Sec. 31 cannot legitimize it because reorganizing the OP does not include creating a new office; (c) EO 1 vests quasi-judicial powers duplicating or superseding the Ombudsman and DOJ; (d) it violates equal protection by targeting only the previous administration; (e) it violates the international practice of limiting truth commissions to human rights violations; (f) it is "an adventure in partisan hostility" and populist propaganda; and (g) the lack of past challenges to similar bodies is immaterial.

paras.html: OSG (Consolidated Comment): petitioners lack standing; EO 1 does not usurp Congress because the President's executive power and control include the inherent power to investigate, supported by the Constitution, EO 292, PD 1416 (as amended by PD 1772), RA 9970, and jurisprudence; there is no appropriation, only an allocation of funds already appropriated; the PTC is fact-finding, not quasi-judicial; and the EO pursues laudable purposes. It cited past bodies such as the PCAC (Magsaysay), PCAPE (Garcia), and PARGO (Marcos).

paras.html: Biraogo: The PTC is a public office, not a mere adjunct of the OP; to create one, the President must be empowered by the Constitution or a statute, and no law authorizes a truth commission. Sec. 31 uses only the verbs "reorganize," "transfer," "consolidate," "merge," and "abolish"; if it vested the power to create offices, it would be inconsistent with the separation of powers and must be deemed repealed.

paras.html: Lagman et al.: Creating a public office is for Congress. The delegated power under Sec. 31: (1) does not permit creating a public office; (2) is limited to the OP's administrative structure; (3) is limited to restructuring the internal organs of the OP Proper and transferring functions and agencies; and (4) is only to achieve simplicity, economy, and efficiency.

paras.html: The allocation of power to the three branches is a grant of all powers inherent in them. paras.html: Equal protection is embraced in due process but is a separate, more specific guaranty: arbitrariness in general may be challenged under due process, but where an act partakes of unwarranted partiality or prejudice, "the sharper weapon to cut it down is the equal protection clause."

paras.html: It requires that all persons or things similarly situated be treated alike, both as to rights conferred and responsibilities imposed; the state may not draw distinctions on differences irrelevant to a legitimate objective.

paras.html: It is aimed at all official state actions, not just those of the legislature; its inhibitions cover all departments, including the political and executive, through whatever agency or guise.

paras.html: It permits classification if reasonable: (1) rests on substantial distinctions; (2) germane to the purpose of the law; (3) not limited to existing conditions only; and (4) applies equally to all members of the same class. Elizalde Rope Workers' Union).

paras.html: The powers of the President
paras.text: The powers of the President

paras.html: Sec. 31 expressly grants continuing authority to reorganize the OP, which "necessarily includes the power to create offices within the Office of the President Proper" (contrary to the majority); all Presidents under the 1987 Constitution have created, abolished, or merged units there.

paras.html: The power to find facts is inherent in executive (as in legislative and judicial) power; Lagman admitted this in oral arguments (Evangelista v. Jarencio).
paras.text: The power to find facts is inherent in executive (as in legislative and judicial) power; Lagman admitted this in oral arguments (Evangelista v. Jarencio).

paras.html: Two routes: the President can create the PTC as a public office under Sec. 31(1), or as an ad hoc fact-finding body whose members are appointed Special Assistants/Advisers — no public office is created then. PD 1416 is no basis (a dictatorial-era delegation, now functus officio). Control does not involve the power to create a public office.

paras.html: No usurpation of appropriation: Sec. 11 does not release unappropriated Treasury funds; the OP's budget always contains a Contingent Fund that can fund ad hoc bodies.

paras.html: Not quasi-judicial: Lagman admitted no EO 1 provision grants such power; findings bind no one.
paras.text: Not quasi-judicial: Lagman admitted no EO 1 provision grants such power; findings bind no one.

paras.html: No usurpation of the Ombudsman: three kinds of executive fact-finding (purely fact-finding, administrative investigation, preliminary investigation); the Ombudsman's primary jurisdiction covers criminal/quasi-criminal Sandiganbayan cases and is not exclusive (Honasan II v. DOJ Panel); the PNP and NBI also investigate crimes under the President's control.

paras.html: The PTC has subpoena powers (Sec. 37, Book I) but no contempt powers; the name "Truth Commission" cannot invalidate EO 1, and the public will not be deceived that its findings are final (e.g., the Agrava Board).

paras.html: No violation of equal protection
paras.text: No violation of equal protection

paras.html: Sec. 17 of EO 1 mirrors Sec. 2(b) of the PCGG Charter, which the Court has consistently upheld (Virata); Sec. 17 merely prioritizes the Arroyo administration.

paras.html: Reasonable grounds: prescriptive periods (20, 15, and 12 years); the Marcos, Ramos, and Estrada administrations were already investigated (PCGG, Saguisag Commission, Estrada's plunder conviction); most past Presidents are dead; recent evidence is fresher; and the PTC has only 29 months.

paras.html: Fact-finding by nature has a specific focus (Feliciano, Melo, Zeñarosa Commissions; Roberts, Warren, 9/11 Commissions). "Earlier past administrations" spanning 111 years are not similarly situated and cannot be one class.

paras.html: The right claim would be that similarly situated administrations were not investigated (US v. Armstrong) — which is false. Deciding what to investigate is the Executive's "special province." Only those adversely affected may raise selective prosecution (Nuñez v. Sandiganbayan); granting relief to non-parties is itself discriminatory. People v. dela Piedra and Art. 7, Civil Code: others' impunity is no defense.

paras.html: The ruling imperils the PCGG Charter, gives every administration "a cloak of immunity," and disregards that public officers are accountable "at all times."

paras.html: Standing: legislators' standing is confined to injuries to Congress's powers; the equal protection claim of the previous administration has nothing to do with impairment of Congress's powers (Pimentel v. Executive Secretary). They cannot take up the cudgels for the previous administration. Biraogo's memorandum never raised equal protection; transcendental importance cannot make the Court resolve an issue never raised.

paras.html: Substantial distinction: proximity and magnitude of recent events (as with the Feliciano Commission for Oakwood and the Zenarosa Commission for Maguindanao); other administrations already have complete and definitive reports (PCGG, Saguisag, and earlier bodies; Estrada's plunder judicially ascertained).

paras.html: Not discriminatory: the classification rests on period, not personalities; it even reaches current officials who acted during the previous administration. She would void EO 1 if it exempted turncoats. "Partisan hostility" is undefined, turning "a political creature" into "a legal animal."

paras.html: Germane: the purpose of EO 1 is to gather information for the President, not to "stamp out" corruption; deliberate classification is not intentional discrimination; good faith is presumed; one step at a time is allowed (Quinto v. COMELEC).

paras.html: Not limited to existing conditions / applies equally: the requirement goes to operational details, and nothing in EO 1 excludes unreported cases in the class; no one complains of prejudice (dela Piedra principle).

Carpio Morales).

paras.html: Control over bonuses: The President's issuance of AO 268 and AO 29 – capping productivity incentive benefits, enjoining heads of agencies from granting them without prior presidential approval, and directing refund of the excess – is a valid exercise of the power of control over executive departments (Sec. 17, Art. VII). Control is "the power of an officer to alter or modify or set aside what a subordinate officer had done in the performance of his duties and to substitute the judgment of the former for that of the latter," and the President may exercise it motu proprio.

paras.html: No encroachment on the CSC: The AOs did not revoke the privilege; they merely regulated its grant and amount. Sound management and effective utilization of financial resources of government are basically executive functions, not the CSC's; under Sec. 35, Chapter 5, Book V of EO 292, it is the President or the head of the department or agency who is authorized to incur the expense. Bodies with fiscal autonomy (Judiciary, CSC, COA, COMELEC, Ombudsman) are not covered by the amount fixed by the President.

paras.html: February 21, 1992: President Corazon Aquino issued AO 268, granting each official and employee productivity incentive benefits of up to 30% of one month's basic salary, but not less than P2,000, for those with at least one year of service as of December 31, 1991. paras.html: March 6, 1995: On appeal, the COA denied the appeal, reasoning that: (1) under Sec. 1(a) of the Supplemental Rules Implementing RA 6971, the law covers business enterprises, including GOCCs performing proprietary functions that are established solely for business or profit, excluding those created in pursuance of a State policy or whose officers and employees are covered by the Civil Service; the PTA was created to implement DOT policies (Sec. 9, PD 189) and its personnel are subject to Civil Service law (Sec. 21); and RA 6971's provisions (referring to the NWPC, BIR, and NCMB) show that it pertains to private enterprises covered by the Labor Code; (2) AO 29 prohibits payment of similar benefits in future years unless authorized by the President; (3) the matter was settled by COA Memorandum No. 92-758; and (4) the title of RA 6971 (encouraging productivity and industrial peace through incentives "to both labor and capital") shows it pertains to the private sector.

CIR).

paras.html: Applying this to the PTA's charter (PD 189, as amended by PD 564): of its general purposes, the 1st, 3rd, 4th, and 6th are governmental, while the 2nd (develop tourist zones) and 5th (assure land availability for private investors) are proprietary. Of its specific powers, the 1st (planning) and 4th (zone administration) are governmental, the 5th (project and investment promotions) is proprietary, and the 2nd, 3rd, 6th, and 7th are partly governmental and partly proprietary; 7(e) and 7(i) may be either, depending on the circumstances.

paras.html: Chairman Veloso's statement referred to GOCCs incorporated under the general corporation law, because only workers in private corporations and such GOCCs have the right to bargain collectively. paras.html: Qualifications not limited to the Constitution: The qualifications for President are not limited to those enumerated in Sec. 2, Art. VII; a COC may also be cancelled under statutory grounds such as the OEC. "Eligible" in Sec. 74, OEC means having all the qualifications and none of the ineligibilities; perpetual disqualification is an ineligibility and is therefore material under Sec. 78.

paras.html: Court vs. PET: The SC sitting as the PET takes cognizance of an election contest only if (a) a petition is filed before it, and (b) it is filed against a candidate who has been validly proclaimed, taken the oath, and assumed office. Before then, Rule 64/65 petitions from the COMELEC stay with the Court; the PET is the same Court, not a separate body. Qualification is not waived by election, so the petitions were not moot.

paras.html: No disqualification: Failure to file an income tax return is not a crime involving moral turpitude (it may result from mere neglect and is not fraudulent per se). The penalty of perpetual disqualification under Sec. 286(c), 1977 NIRC (as amended by PD 1994) is not automatically imposed; unless explicitly provided in the fallo, it is not deemed imposed. A final judgment imposing only fines cannot be modified.

paras.html: COMELEC Second Division (Jan. 17, 2022): denied the Buenafe petition. Though it could be summarily dismissed for invoking disqualification grounds, the Division ruled on the merits: no perpetual disqualification in the CA Decision; BBM was a private individual when he failed to file his 1985 ITR (left the Philippines Feb. 25, 1986); non-filing is not moral turpitude (Republic v. Marcos II); no intent to deceive. Comm. Kho (now Justice) separately opined that perpetual disqualification under the NIRC is a principal penalty that must be expressly imposed.

paras.html: Moral turpitude: acts "contrary to justice, modesty, or good morals; an act of baseness, vileness or depravity"; it excludes acts not immoral in themselves whose illegality lies only in being positively prohibited (Teves v. COMELEC; Zari v. Flores). The Court traced the concept from US immigration law (J. Brion in Teves; Jordan v. De George: fraud is the touchstone), Call v. State Bar, In re Grimes (willful failure to file a tax return is not per se moral turpitude), and Philippine cases (In re Basa; Tak Ng; Ao Lin; In re Lanuevo: a question of fact depending on all circumstances), listing 40 crimes held to involve it.

paras.html: Zari: tax evasion involves moral turpitude, but failure to file ≠ tax evasion. Evasion requires actual, intentional fraud with (a) underpayment, (b) an evil or willful state of mind, and (c) an unlawful act or omission. Failure to file "may be committed by neglect, without any fraudulent intent and/or willfulness": the NIRC distinguishes failure to file (25% surcharge) from willful neglect to file (50% fraud penalty) (Sec. 248, 1997 NIRC; Sec. 72, 1939 NIRC) → "omission to file a tax return is not fraudulent per se."

paras.html: Background: disqualification is a long-established penalty (Acts of the Philippine Commission; Election Law of 1907; Old Penal Code Arts. 31–36 required accessory penalties to be expressly imposed, People v. Perez); under the RPC (Arts. 30, 32; Lacuna v. Abes), Art. 73 presumes accessory penalties imposed with the principal. Special laws (RA 9165, 10845, 10863, 11479) and administrative rules also provide disqualification.

paras.html: Good-faith reorganization does not violate security of tenure: "Valid abolition of offices is neither removal nor separation of the incumbents." A reorganization is in good faith if it is for the purpose of economy or to make the bureaucracy more efficient; if the "abolition" is done for political reasons or purposely to defeat security of tenure, it is void ab initio (citing Dario v. Mison).

paras.html: President's power to reorganize: As a general rule, the power to abolish a public office is lodged with the legislature (the power to create includes the power to destroy), except where the office was created by the Constitution itself. Exception: as to bureaus, agencies, or offices in the executive department, the President's power of control may justify him to inactivate the functions of a particular office, or certain laws may grant him broad authority to carry out reorganization measures (Larin v. Executive Secretary; Sec. 77, RA 8745; Sec. 78, RA 8760; Sec. 31, Book III, EO 292).

paras.text: Background on the EIIB:

paras.html: June 30, 1987: President Corazon Aquino issued EO 127 establishing the Economic Intelligence and Investigation Bureau (EIIB) as part of the structural organization of the Ministry of Finance. [The decision's footnote 3 says EO 127 was "Approved on January 30, 1987"; the body says June 30, 1987.]
paras.text: June 30, 1987: President Corazon Aquino issued EO 127 establishing the Economic Intelligence and Investigation Bureau (EIIB) as part of the structural organization of the Ministry of Finance. [The decision's footnote 3 says EO 127 was "Approved on January 30, 1987"; the body says June 30, 1987.]

paras.html: EIIB functions (Sec. 26, EO 127): (a) receive, gather, and evaluate intelligence on illegal activities affecting the national economy, such as economic sabotage, smuggling, tax evasion, and dollar-salting, investigate them, and aid in prosecution; (b) coordinate with external agencies in monitoring financial and economic activities that may adversely affect national financial interest; (c) provide the Ministry's intelligence units with the general framework and guidelines for intelligence and investigation work; (d) supervise, monitor, and coordinate all intelligence and investigation operations of the Ministry's operating bureaus and offices; (e) investigate, hear, and file, upon clearance by the Minister, anti-graft cases against Ministry personnel; and (f) perform other functions assigned by the Minister.

paras.html: Precursors (fn. 4): the Anti-Smuggling Action Center (ASAC), created by President Marcos through EO 11 (1966), later transferred to the DND (EO 220, 1970) and placed under the Secretary of Finance (EO 303, 1971); PD 1458 (1978) created the Finance Department Intelligence and Investigation Bureau.

paras.html: At first glance, the case seems to hinge on whether the "deactivation" of the EIIB constitutes "abolition" of an office. But the ultimate queries are: (a) Does the President have the authority to reorganize the executive department? and (b) How should the reorganization be carried out?

paras.html: Re: Deactivation vs. abolition
paras.text: Re: Deactivation vs. abolition

paras.html: To "deactivate" means to render inactive or ineffective, or to break up by discharging or reassigning personnel; to "abolish" means to do away with, annul, abrogate, or destroy completely. Abolition denotes an intention to do away with the office wholly and permanently.
paras.text: To "deactivate" means to render inactive or ineffective, or to break up by discharging or reassigning personnel; to "abolish" means to do away with, annul, abrogate, or destroy completely. Abolition denotes an intention to do away with the office wholly and permanently.

paras.html: In abolition, the office ceases to exist; in deactivation, the office continues to exist, albeit dormant or inoperative. "Be that as it may, deactivation and abolition are both reorganization measures."
paras.text: In abolition, the office ceases to exist; in deactivation, the office continues to exist, albeit dormant or inoperative. "Be that as it may, deactivation and abolition are both reorganization measures."

paras.html: The OSG invoked the distinction only "on the mistaken assumption that the President has no power to abolish an office."
paras.text: The OSG invoked the distinction only "on the mistaken assumption that the President has no power to abolish an office."

paras.html: Re: General rule and exception
paras.text: Re: General rule and exception

paras.html: General rule: the power to abolish a public office is lodged with the legislature. This proceeds from the precept that the power to create includes the power to destroy. A public office is created by the Constitution, by statute, or by authority of law; thus, except where the office was created by the Constitution itself, it may be abolished by the same legislature that brought it into existence (fn. 16, Eugenio v. CSC).

A public office is created by the Constitution, by statute, or by authority of law; thus, except where the office was created by the Constitution itself, it may be abolished by the same legislature that brought it into existence (fn. 16, Eugenio v. paras.html: While Task Force Aduana was created to take the place of the EIIB, "its creation does not entail expense to the government":

paras.html: First, no new personnel. Under EO 196, the staffs are composed of people already in the public service, being employees of other existing agencies. [The decision says "the technical, administrative and special staffs of EIIB"; in context it refers to the Task Force's staffs.] Their tenure with the Task Force is only temporary, by way of detail or assignment; they retain their employment with their agencies and are sent back when the need ceases.
paras.text: First, no new personnel. Under EO 196, the staffs are composed of people already in the public service, being employees of other existing agencies. [The decision says "the technical, administrative and special staffs of EIIB"; in context it refers to the Task Force's staffs.] Their tenure with the Task Force is only temporary, by way of detail or assignment; they retain their employment with their agencies and are sent back when the need ceases.

paras.html: Second, a smaller base. EO 196's thrust is "to have a small group of military men under the direct control and supervision of the President" as the base of the anti-smuggling campaign, with the power to enlist the assistance and use the personnel, facilities, and resources of any department, bureau, or office, and to recruit from the PSG and ISAFP. The idea is to use existing resources "instead of maintaining an independent office with a whole set of personnel and facilities." The EIIB had proven burdensome because it maintained separate offices in every region.

paras.html: "Nothing is better settled in our law than that the abolition of an office within the competence of a legitimate body if done in good faith suffers from no infirmity. Valid abolition of offices is neither removal nor separation of the incumbents."

paras.html: Dario v. Mison (through J. Abraham F. Sarmiento): if the reorganization is in good faith, "no dismissal (in case of dismissal) or separation actually occurs because the position itself ceases to exist. And in that case, security of tenure would not be a Chinese wall."

paras.html: But if the "abolition," which is nothing else but a separation or removal, is done for political reasons or purposely to defeat security of tenure, otherwise not in good faith, no valid abolition takes place and whatever abolition is done is void ab initio. There is an invalid abolition "where there is merely a change of nomenclature of positions, or where claims of economy are belied by the existence of ample funds."

paras.html: SC's exclusive administrative supervision over court personnel: By virtue of Sec. 6, Art. VIII, "it is only the Supreme Court that can oversee the judges' and court personnel's administrative compliance with all laws, rules and regulations." No other branch may intrude into this power without running afoul of the separation of powers. → The CSC has no disciplinary jurisdiction to try and decide an administrative case against a court employee, even one arising from a civil service examination anomaly.
paras.text: SC's exclusive administrative supervision over court personnel: By virtue of Sec. 6, Art. VIII, "it is only the Supreme Court that can oversee the judges' and court personnel's administrative compliance with all laws, rules and regulations." No other branch may intrude into this power without running afoul of the separation of powers. → The CSC has no disciplinary jurisdiction to try and decide an administrative case against a court employee, even one arising from a civil service examination anomaly.

paras.html: Standard procedure: When a court employee violates the Civil Service Law, the CSC brings its complaint before the Office of the Court Administrator (OCA) (Ampong v. CSC).
paras.text: Standard procedure: When a court employee violates the Civil Service Law, the CSC brings its complaint before the Office of the Court Administrator (OCA) (Ampong v. CSC).

paras.html: No estoppel: A court employee who denied the charge, did not appear at the formal investigation, and raised lack of jurisdiction on appeal to the CSC is not estopped from assailing the CSC's jurisdiction (distinguishing Ampong, where the employee admitted guilt and actively participated without questioning the CSC's authority).

paras.html: Congress cannot expand the CA's confirmation power: Confirmation is required only for the officers in the first sentence of Sec. 16, Art. VII. A law requiring CA confirmation of other presidential appointees is unconstitutional because it amends by legislation the first sentence (adding appointments needing confirmation) and the second sentence (imposing confirmation on appointments entrusted to the President alone).

paras.html: Doctrines deduced: (1) confirmation only for first-sentence appointees, including officers whose appointments are expressly vested by the Constitution (sectoral representatives; members of the COA, CSC, COMELEC); (2) no confirmation for officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by law or whom the President is authorized by law to appoint (e.g., CHR); and, per Mison, when Congress creates inferior offices but omits to provide for appointment, or provides for it unconstitutionally, those officers are among those "not otherwise provided for by law."

paras.html: March 1989: RA 6715 (Herrera-Veloso Law), amending the Labor Code (PD 442), was approved. Sec. 13 (amending Art. 215) provides: "The Chairman, the Division Presiding Commissioners and other Commissioners shall all be appointed by the President, subject to confirmation by the Commission on Appointments. Appointments to any vacancy shall come from the nominees of the sector which nominated the predecessor. The Executive Labor Arbiters and Labor Arbiters shall also be appointed by the President, upon recommendation of the Secretary of Labor and Employment, and shall be subject to the Civil Service Law, rules and regulations."

paras.html: Endencia and Jugo v. David: the legislature cannot pass a declaratory act giving binding weight to its own reading of the law; nor can it validate an unconstitutional law by declaring it shall be construed not to violate the Constitution. The legislature makes laws but does not interpret them, especially the Constitution; otherwise a final court ruling could be undermined by a later legislative interpretation, violating the separation of powers.

Butler).

paras.html: The writ of amparo covers only extralegal killings and enforced disappearances: Its coverage, "in its present form, is confined to these two instances or to threats thereof" (Manalo; Lozada). It is not the proper remedy for obtaining parental authority and custody of a minor child.
paras.text: The writ of amparo covers only extralegal killings and enforced disappearances: Its coverage, "in its present form, is confined to these two instances or to threats thereof" (Manalo; Lozada). It is not the proper remedy for obtaining parental authority and custody of a minor child.

paras.html: No enforced disappearance where the State discloses the person's whereabouts: Under the elements in Navia v. Pardico (Sec. 3(g), RA 9851), there must be a refusal to acknowledge or give information on the person's fate or whereabouts, with intent to remove him from the protection of the law for a prolonged period. Where the DSWD disclosed the child's whereabouts and produced him in court, the third and fourth elements are missing.

paras.html: Custody disputes require the proper remedies: The RTC (affirmed by the SC without prejudice to the petitioner's proper legal remedies) held that the mother should have filed a custody case under the Family Code and the Rule on Custody of Minors, or a petition for habeas corpus if there is extreme urgency.

paras.html: Petitioner Ma. Christina Yusay Caram (Christina) had a relationship with Marcelino Gicano Constantino III and became pregnant without the benefit of marriage. She misled Marcelino into believing she had an abortion but carried the child to term, intending to have him adopted through Sun and Moon Home for Children (Parañaque) to spare her family the embarrassment of a second illegitimate son.
paras.text: Petitioner Ma. Christina Yusay Caram (Christina) had a relationship with Marcelino Gicano Constantino III and became pregnant without the benefit of marriage. She misled Marcelino into believing she had an abortion but carried the child to term, intending to have him adopted through Sun and Moon Home for Children (Parañaque) to spare her family the embarrassment of a second illegitimate son.

paras.html: July 26, 2009: Christina gave birth to Baby Julian at Amang Rodriguez Memorial Medical Center, Marikina. Sun and Moon paid all hospital and medical expenses.
paras.text: July 26, 2009: Christina gave birth to Baby Julian at Amang Rodriguez Memorial Medical Center, Marikina. Sun and Moon paid all hospital and medical expenses.

paras.html: August 13, 2009: Christina voluntarily surrendered Baby Julian to the DSWD through a Deed of Voluntary Commitment.
paras.text: August 13, 2009: Christina voluntarily surrendered Baby Julian to the DSWD through a Deed of Voluntary Commitment.

paras.html: November 26, 2009: Marcelino died of a heart attack without knowing of his son. At the wake, Christina told his family that they had a son whom she gave up for adoption due to financial distress and embarrassment. The family sympathized and vowed to help her recover and raise the baby.

paras.html: August 5, 2010: The OSG entered its appearance for the State and was allowed to participate. Judge Sale narrowed the issues for position papers: (1) jurisdiction; (2) whether the petition is the proper remedy; and (3) whether custody should be given to the biological mother. In the same order, she noted that the child was brought before the court and Christina was allowed to see and photograph him.

Judge Sale narrowed the issues for position papers: (1) jurisdiction; (2) whether the petition is the proper remedy; and (3) whether custody should be given to the biological mother. paras.html: August 17, 2010: The RTC dismissed the petition without prejudice to the appropriate action. Christina availed of the wrong remedy; she should have filed a civil case for custody under the Family Code and the Rule on Custody of Minors and Writ of Habeas Corpus in Relation to Custody of Minors. paras.html: Sec. 1, Rule on the Writ of Amparo: the writ is a remedy available to any person whose right to life, liberty, and security is violated or threatened by an unlawful act or omission of a public official or employee, or of a private individual or entity. "The writ shall cover extralegal killings and enforced disappearances or threats thereof."
paras.text: Sec. 1, Rule on the Writ of Amparo: the writ is a remedy available to any person whose right to life, liberty, and security is violated or threatened by an unlawful act or omission of a public official or employee, or of a private individual or entity. "The writ shall cover extralegal killings and enforced disappearances or threats thereof."

paras.html: Secretary of National Defense v. Manalo: the Amparo Rule was intended to address the "intractable problem" of extralegal killings and enforced disappearances; its coverage, "in its present form, is confined to these two instances or to threats thereof."

paras.html: Extralegal killings: "killings committed without due process of law, i.e., without legal safeguards or judicial proceedings."
paras.text: Extralegal killings: "killings committed without due process of law, i.e., without legal safeguards or judicial proceedings."

paras.html: Enforced disappearances: an arrest, detention, or abduction by a government official or organized groups or private individuals acting with the government's direct or indirect acquiescence, plus the State's refusal to disclose the person's fate or whereabouts or to acknowledge the deprivation of liberty, placing the person outside the protection of law.

paras.html: One representative of Congress, one full vote: By using the singular "a representative of the Congress" in Sec. 8(1), Art. VIII, the Framers intended Congress to have only one seat in the JBC, and that lone representative carries one full vote. The JBC has seven members, not eight; splitting one vote between two representatives is a constitutional circumvention.

The JBC has seven members, not eight; splitting one vote between two representatives is a constitutional circumvention.

paras.text: Background on judicial appointments:

paras.html: Under the Malolos and 1935 Constitutions, the President appointed members of the Judiciary subject to confirmation by the Commission on Appointments → the "deplorable practice" of aspirants trying to ingratiate themselves with legislators.
paras.text: Under the Malolos and 1935 Constitutions, the President appointed members of the Judiciary subject to confirmation by the Commission on Appointments → the "deplorable practice" of aspirants trying to ingratiate themselves with legislators.

paras.html: Under the 1973 Constitution (executive and legislative powers fused), the appointment power became exclusive and absolute to the Executive, subject only to qualifications.
paras.text: Under the 1973 Constitution (executive and legislative powers fused), the appointment power became exclusive and absolute to the Executive, subject only to qualifications.

paras.html: To rid judicial appointments of political pressure and partisan activity, the 1986 ConCom created the JBC, a separate body representative of all stakeholders, to recommend nominees to the President. Sec. 8(1), Art. VIII provides:

paras.html: ① Allowing only one representative of Congress leads to absurdity given its bicameral nature; ② the Framers' failure to adjust the provision when they shifted from unicameralism to bicameralism was a plain oversight; ③ two representatives would not subvert the intent to insulate the JBC from politics; ④ the Court's rationale that a seven-member body solves stalemates is not exactly correct.

paras.html: Starting only from "a" gives an unworkable result that undermines the bicameral Congress implied in the 114 other places the Constitution uses "Congress." Reading "representative of Congress" and "ex officio" too still follows verba legis but reveals ambiguity → resort to ratio legis et anima and ut magis valeat quam pereat (Macalintal v. PET; Civil Liberties Union v. Exec. Sec.). "Text is authoritative, but it is not exhaustive of the entire universe of meaning."

paras.html: Congress has no checking role in the JBC: "perplexing." Congress is represented because (1) it crafts statutes; (2) judicial review lets courts nullify its acts, so it has an interest in nominees' judicial philosophy; (3) it is a political organ whose members periodically face the electorate. Its JBC representatives may be instructed by their chambers → they do not sit to represent themselves.

paras.html: One representative of Congress, one full vote: By using the singular "a representative of the Congress" in Sec. 8(1), Art. VIII, the Framers intended Congress to have only one seat in the JBC, and that lone representative carries one full vote. The JBC has seven members, not eight; splitting one vote between two representatives is a constitutional circumvention.

The JBC has seven members, not eight; splitting one vote between two representatives is a constitutional circumvention.

paras.html: Under the Malolos and 1935 Constitutions, the President appointed members of the Judiciary subject to confirmation by the Commission on Appointments → the "deplorable practice" of aspirants trying to ingratiate themselves with legislators.

paras.html: Under the 1973 Constitution (executive and legislative powers fused), the appointment power became exclusive and absolute to the Executive, subject only to qualifications.

paras.html: The Framers were not keen on adjusting the provision because the JBC is not in the exercise of Congress's primary function — to legislate. The JBC was created to support the executive power to appoint, and Congress, as one whole body, was merely assigned a contributory non-legislative function.

paras.html: In its legislative functions (Sec. 27, Art. VI) and non-legislative functions (appropriation, Sec. 24, Art. VI; declaring war, Sec. 23(1), Art. VI; canvassing presidential returns, Sec. 4, Art. VII; impeachment, Sec. 3, Art. XI), the dichotomy of the Houses must be recognized because of their interplay: each House's powers consider (1) its relationship with the other chamber and (2) checks and balances with the other branches.

paras.html: The provision also says the representation is "ex officio" (by virtue of one's office). Under Senate rules and House rules, the chairperson of each chamber's Justice Committee is automatically its JBC representative → two persons hold separate offices with the attached function. A literal reading means no representative of Congress would qualify as ex officio, denying Congress the representation the Framers intended.

paras.html: Starting only from "a" gives an unworkable result that undermines the bicameral Congress implied in the 114 other places the Constitution uses "Congress." Reading "representative of Congress" and "ex officio" too still follows verba legis but reveals ambiguity → resort to ratio legis et anima and ut magis valeat quam pereat (Macalintal v. PET; Civil Liberties Union v. Exec. Sec.). "Text is authoritative, but it is not exhaustive of the entire universe of meaning."

paras.html: Congress has no checking role in the JBC: "perplexing." Congress is represented because (1) it crafts statutes; (2) judicial review lets courts nullify its acts, so it has an interest in nominees' judicial philosophy; (3) it is a political organ whose members periodically face the electorate. Its JBC representatives may be instructed by their chambers → they do not sit to represent themselves.

paras.html: Stricter prohibition: Sec. 13, Art. VII imposes a stricter prohibition on the President, VP, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants than Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B imposes on appointive officials generally. "Unless otherwise provided in this Constitution" refers only to exceptions in the Constitution itself (VP as Cabinet member; VP acting as President; Secretary of Justice in the JBC), not to the "allowed by law or by the primary functions" exceptions of Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B. The prohibition covers public and private office.

paras.html: Ex officio positions: The prohibition does not cover posts held in an ex officio capacity, as provided by law and as required (not merely allowed) by the primary functions of the official's office, without additional compensation. These are additional duties, not "any other office." Any per diem, honorarium, or allowance for them is prohibited "by whatever name it is designated."

paras.html: Under Marcos's martial law legislative powers, there was a proliferation of agencies and GOCCs with Cabinet members on their boards, drawing salaries, per diems, and perquisites, leading to self-enrichment. The 1983 COA report showed Ongpin on 29 boards, Imelda Marcos on 23, Virata on 22, and others on 10 to 15. This was "one of the serious causes of discontent" with the regime, and ending it was "one of the strongest selling points" of the 1987 Constitution during ratification (as observed by J. Cruz).

paras.html: Comparison of wording: the disqualifications for Members of Congress, active AFP members (Sec. 5(4), Art. XVI), and appointive officials (Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B) all refer to office "in the Government." Sec. 13, Art. VII is not so qualified → "the disqualification is absolute… all-embracing and covers both public and private office or employment." Its second sentence also bars practicing a profession, participating in business, or financial interest in government contracts, "proof of the intent… to treat the President and his official family as a class by itself."

Reading "unless otherwise provided" as referring to Art. IX-B would "render nugatory" the stricter prohibition and erase the distinction between Assistant Secretary and up versus civil servants below.

paras.html: It would also make parts of the Constitution inoperative: the VP, an elective official, is absolutely ineligible for any other appointment under Sec. 7(1), Art. IX-B, yet the Constitution lets the VP be a Cabinet member (Sec. 3, Art. VII) and act as President (Sec. 7, Art. VII). Only reading Art. IX-B as the general rule and Sec. 13 as the exception avoids this absurdity.

Embroidery and Apparel Control Board: designated officials "merely perform duties in the Board in addition to those already performed under their original appointments"). E.g., the DOTC Secretary as ex officio chair of the PPA and LRTA.

paras.html: Primary functions: the chief or principal functions (may be plural). The additional duties must be not only closely related to, but "required" by (fn. 22: obligatory, as opposed to "allowed," which is permissive) the primary functions. E.g., Finance and Budget Secretaries on the Monetary Board; DOTC Secretary chairing MARINA and the CAB.

paras.html: Not covered: functions "merely incidental, remotely related, inconsistent, incompatible, or otherwise alien" to the primary function (e.g., the Press Undersecretary on the PAGCOR Board); likewise positions conferring management functions and/or monetary compensation, such as GOCC chairmanships or directorships.

paras.html: Prior concurrence of the Monetary Board (Sec. 20, Art. VII): The requirement is not read literally as full MB approval before the loan is signed. It is “enabled through a more detailed and elaborate procedure”: an Approval-in-Principle before negotiations, signing subject to its conditions, and a Final Approval after signing but before the borrower may draw on the loan. Only the Approval-in-Principle is, strictly speaking, prior action, but the MB's participation does not end there.
paras.text: Prior concurrence of the Monetary Board (Sec. 20, Art. VII): The requirement is not read literally as full MB approval before the loan is signed. It is “enabled through a more detailed and elaborate procedure”: an Approval-in-Principle before negotiations, signing subject to its conditions, and a Final Approval after signing but before the borrower may draw on the loan. Only the Approval-in-Principle is, strictly speaking, prior action, but the MB's participation does not end there.

paras.html: Public information on foreign loans (Sec. 21, Art. XII): “Shall be made available to the public” is proactive and unqualified. A confidentiality clause that keeps all terms secret, requires the lender's prior consent, and allows disclosure only to government bodies cannot, for future purposes, withstand constitutional scrutiny (pronounced as guidance; the disclosure issue was moot).

paras.html: Filipino First Policy and foreign-funded procurement: Foreign loan arrangements that are executive agreements may adopt their own (hybrid) procurement rules despite deviating from RA 9184, but pacta sunt servanda cannot override the Constitution: bidding rules for such projects “must give preference, or at least equal opportunity, to qualified Filipinos.” The Filipino First Policy is not a Filipino monopoly.

paras.html: October 20, 2016: The GRP, through the DOF, and the Chinese government-owned Export-Import Bank of China (EXIM Bank) signed a Memorandum of Understanding on Financing Cooperation (MOU). Under Arts. 1.1, 2.3, 4.1, and 4.2, the MOU was a precursor to more binding and detailed loan agreements for GRP-nominated priority infrastructure projects; it was not legally binding except Arts. 3 to 7, and each loan agreement's terms were left to further negotiation.
paras.text: October 20, 2016: The GRP, through the DOF, and the Chinese government-owned Export-Import Bank of China (EXIM Bank) signed a Memorandum of Understanding on Financing Cooperation (MOU). Under Arts. 1.1, 2.3, 4.1, and 4.2, the MOU was a precursor to more binding and detailed loan agreements for GRP-nominated priority infrastructure projects; it was not legally binding except Arts. 3 to 7, and each loan agreement's terms were left to further negotiation.

paras.text: January 20, 2017: The DFA sent the PRC Embassy Note Verbale No. 17-0330, proposing how the financing arrangement “under the MOA” [sic: MOU] would be activated. paras.html: (1) the DOF requests concessional loan financing for priority projects through the PRC Embassy; (2) the Chinese Government gives its considerations and a list of at least three qualified, legitimate, and reputable Chinese contractors; (3) the implementing agency (IA) conducts Limited Competitive Bidding (LCB) among them and signs the commercial contract; (4) the DOF submits documents to EXIM Bank for due diligence; and (5) the DOF and EXIM Bank sign the loan agreement (and guarantee agreement, if any).

paras.html: The President cannot be sued during tenure, regardless of the nature of the suit. Immunity is not written in the 1987 Constitution but is “understood in present jurisprudence” (Fr. Bernas to Comm. Suarez in the ConCom); Rubrico v. Macapagal-Arroyo confirmed it survives.

paras.html: Unlike the U.S. version, Philippine immunity does not distinguish official from personal acts or turn on the nature of the suit. Rationale: free the President from hindrance or distraction (Soliven v. Makasiar); protect the dignity of the office (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo). The President need not personally invoke it first.

paras.html: Scope of the foreign borrowing power: The power to contract or guarantee foreign loans under Sec. 20, Art. VII is construed broadly. The Constitution "makes no prohibition on the issuance of certain kinds of loans or distinctions as to which kinds of debt instruments are more onerous than others." Bond conversion (a bond is a loan) and debt buyback (a necessary implied power of the borrowing power) are within it. The only restrictions are the prior concurrence of the Monetary Board and such limitations as may be provided under law (e.g., RA 245, as amended by PD 142).
paras.text: Scope of the foreign borrowing power: The power to contract or guarantee foreign loans under Sec. 20, Art. VII is construed broadly. The Constitution "makes no prohibition on the issuance of certain kinds of loans or distinctions as to which kinds of debt instruments are more onerous than others." Bond conversion (a bond is a loan) and debt buyback (a necessary implied power of the borrowing power) are within it. The only restrictions are the prior concurrence of the Monetary Board and such limitations as may be provided under law (e.g., RA 245, as amended by PD 142).

paras.html: Exercise by alter ego: Under the doctrine of qualified political agency, the Secretary of Finance may exercise the foreign borrowing power as the President's alter ego. It does not belong to the exceptional class of powers that the President must exercise in person (declaring martial law, suspending the privilege of the writ, pardoning). However, the alter ego must secure the President's prior consent or subsequent ratification, and the President's repudiation of the alter ego's acts is binding.

paras.html: Limits of judicial review: The Art. II state policies are "not a panacea that can annul every governmental act." That petitioners prefer another debt-relief approach goes into the wisdom of the executive act, which courts do not review; the assailed acts enjoy a strong presumption of validity.

paras.html: The Financing Program was the culmination of efforts begun under President Corazon Aquino to manage the external debt through a negotiation-oriented debt strategy (cooperation and negotiation with foreign creditors), as opposed to a default approach.

paras.html: The 1992 Financing Program
paras.text: The 1992 Financing Program

paras.html: On 28 February 1992, the Philippine Debt Negotiating Team, chaired by respondent Pelaez, negotiated with the country's Bank Advisory Committee (representing all foreign commercial bank creditors) the Philippine Comprehensive Financing Program for 1992, which respondents called "a multi-option financing package." It was scheduled for execution on 24 July 1992.
paras.text: On 28 February 1992, the Philippine Debt Negotiating Team, chaired by respondent Pelaez, negotiated with the country's Bank Advisory Committee (representing all foreign commercial bank creditors) the Philippine Comprehensive Financing Program for 1992, which respondents called "a multi-option financing package." It was scheduled for execution on 24 July 1992.

paras.html: Petitioners alleged that respondents had already implemented the "buyback component" before execution: on 15 May 1992, the Philippines bought back P1.26 billion of external debts under the Program.

paras.html: Petitioners' description: a package of two debt-relief options:
paras.text: Petitioners' description: a package of two debt-relief options:

paras.html: Option 1: a cash buyback of portions of the Philippine foreign debt at a discount.
paras.text: Option 1: a cash buyback of portions of the Philippine foreign debt at a discount.

paras.html: Option 2: conversion of existing debt instruments into bonds/securities: (a) new money bonds with a five-year grace period and 17-year final maturity, the purchase of which would let creditors convert eligible debt papers into bearer bonds with the same terms; (b) interest-reduction bonds, 25-year maturity; and (c) principal-collateralized interest-reduction bonds, 25-year maturity.
paras.text: Option 2: conversion of existing debt instruments into bonds/securities: (a) new money bonds with a five-year grace period and 17-year final maturity, the purchase of which would let creditors convert eligible debt papers into bearer bonds with the same terms; (b) interest-reduction bonds, 25-year maturity; and (c) principal-collateralized interest-reduction bonds, 25-year maturity.

paras.html: Respondents' description: the Program would cover about US$5.3 billion of foreign commercial debts, deal comprehensively with the commercial bank debt problem, and pave the way for access to capital markets. Creditors could choose among three options: (a) lend new money; (b) exchange existing restructured debts for an interest-reduction bond; or (c) exchange them for a principal-collateralized interest-reduction bond. The deal consisted of three agreements (the PCIRB, Philippine Bond, and IRB Issuance and Exchange Agreements).

paras.html: Unilateral repudiation by the executive, possibly without prior court determination, would bring adverse repercussions (e.g., cross-default clauses). The Court quoted Dr. Felipe Medalla (former NEDA Director General): repudiation, even selective, could provoke concerted sanctions from banks, multilateral institutions, and creditor governments, affecting credit, export markets, and development aid; repudiation is unattractive if net payments can be cut by agreement.

paras.html: On bonds: a loan creates a definite creditor-debtor relationship, while bonds do not. A loan can be restructured or novated, but by converting debts to bearer bonds "the Philippines surrenders the novatable character of a loan contract for the irrevocable and unpostponable demandability of a bearer bond." The Constitution prohibits the President from issuing bonds that are "far more onerous" than loans.

paras.html: Only restrictions: prior Monetary Board concurrence, and limitations provided by law. RA 245, as amended by PD 142 (1973), allows the Secretary of Finance, with the President's approval and after consultation with the MB, to borrow and issue evidences of indebtedness, including treasury bonds, notes, and securities (one to 25 years). Sovereign bonds may thus be issued not only for expenditures but also for the purchase, redemption, or refunding of any government obligation.

paras.html: Villena v. Secretary of the Interior (adopted from American jurisprudence): the Constitution establishes a single, not plural, Executive. Department heads hold office in an advisory capacity, and their "personality is in reality but the projection of that of the President." Per Chief Justice Taft (Myers v. United States), "each head of a department is, and must be, the President's alter ego in the matters of that department where the President is required by law to exercise authority."

paras.html: Mootness: "An issue or a case becomes moot and academic when it ceases to present a justiciable controversy so that a determination thereof would be without practical use and value." There is then no actual substantial relief to which the petitioner would be entitled and which would be negated by dismissal. Corona's petition was "mooted by supervening events and his own acts": his conviction, his acceptance of the verdict, and his vacating the office.

paras.html: December 12, 2011: At a caucus of the House majority bloc, the leadership of the Committee on Justice submitted a verified impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Renato C. Corona. After a brief presentation, it was voted on in session the same day, and 188 Members signed and endorsed it, "way above the one-third vote required by the Constitution" (the direct mode under Art. XI, Sec. 3(4) [the Resolution writes "Art. XI, par. 4, Sec. 3" (sic)]).
