paras.html: Charges: culpable violation of the Constitution, betrayal of public trust, and graft and corruption, in eight Articles: (I) partiality and subservience to the Arroyo administration, up to his "midnight" appointment as Chief Justice; (II) failure to disclose his SALN under Sec. 17, Art. XI; (III) failure to meet the standards of Sec. 7(3), Art. VIII (acting on letters causing "flip-flopping" decisions, entanglement with Mrs. Arroyo through his wife's appointment, discussing pending cases with litigants); (IV) the status quo ante order against the House in the Gutierrez impeachment; (V) disregarding res judicata in the 16 cities and Dinagat cases; (VI) creating a committee to investigate a Justice; (VII) the TRO in favor of former President Arroyo and her husband; and (VIII) failure to account for the JDF and SAJ collections.

paras.html: December 26, 2011: Corona's Answer assailed the "blitzkrieg" signing and transmittal, attributing the impeachment to President Aquino's party mates, supporters, and "hidden forces," citing the President's open rejection of his appointment and attacks on the Court. He denied the charges (admitting only that he once served the Offices of the President and Vice-President under PGMA, and that he granted only VACC's Dante Jimenez a courtesy call, Lauro Vizconde appearing uninvited). He prayed for outright dismissal for failure to meet constitutional requirements, or acquittal.

paras.html: The prosecution panel held a press conference on supposed evidence; front pages reported high-priced condominium units and properties in Fort Bonifacio and Quezon City possibly omitted from his non-public SALN. Senators scolded the prosecutors, since the Senate Rules of Procedure on Impeachment Trials (Rule XVIII) bar public comment on the merits. Five petitions had by then been filed with the Court to enjoin the trial (improper verification; lack of due process).

paras.html: Filed "without submitting themselves to the jurisdiction" of the Court and without conceding the House's exclusive power to initiate and the Senate's exclusive power to try.

paras.html: The petition raises matters purely political in character, for the Senate and House alone. Citing Nixon v. United States, letting an impeached official raise any and all substantive issues before the Court would make the process so long it may outlast the Senator-Judges' terms.

paras.html: Limits on the pardoning power are constitutional only: the power under Sec. 11(6), Art. VII (1935 Constitution) has two limitations, namely that it be exercised after conviction and that it does not extend to cases of impeachment. "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

VII (1935 Constitution) has two limitations, namely that it be exercised after conviction and that it does not extend to cases of impeachment. "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

paras.html: Effect of an absolute pardon: "An absolute pardon not only blots out the crime committed, but removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction," including accessory and resultant disabilities. When granted after the term of imprisonment has expired, it removes all that is left of the consequences of conviction, such as a statutory disqualification from voting that rests on that conviction.

paras.html: Sec. 11(6), Art. VII of the 1935 Constitution: the President may grant reprieves, commutations, and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, after conviction, for all offenses, except in cases of impeachment, upon such conditions and with such restrictions and limitations as he may deem proper [the CD Asia text reads "deem pro to impose" (sic)]; he may grant amnesty with the concurrence of the National Assembly.
paras.text: Sec. 11(6), Art. VII of the 1935 Constitution: the President may grant reprieves, commutations, and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, after conviction, for all offenses, except in cases of impeachment, upon such conditions and with such restrictions and limitations as he may deem proper [the CD Asia text reads "deem pro to impose" (sic)]; he may grant amnesty with the concurrence of the National Assembly.

paras.html: Only two limitations: (a) the power must be exercised after conviction; and (b) it does not extend to cases of impeachment.
paras.text: Only two limitations: (a) the power must be exercised after conviction; and (b) it does not extend to cases of impeachment.

paras.html: "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action." It "must remain where the sovereign authority has placed it and must be exercised by the highest authority to whom it is entrusted."

paras.html: TLDR: The pardon did not lift the Sec. 94(b) disqualification, so Santos remained disqualified from voting. [The dissent states no disposition of its own in the file; its reasoning would require granting the exclusion.] It rests on three conclusions: (1) the pardon had no object; (2) a pardon remits the penalty but does not erase the commission of the crime or the conviction; and (3) Sec. 94(b) is, properly speaking, neither a penalty nor a disability resulting from the conviction.

paras.html: The majority misread "disability resulting from conviction." The disabilities flowing from a conviction are those the law attaches to it: here, arresto mayor with the accessory suspension of suffrage for its duration, which ended with the sentence. When Santos finished serving it, no other law deprived him of suffrage, since the Election Code had not yet been enacted.

paras.html: There is no conflict. Under Title V, Art. 1 (Suffrage) of the 1935 Constitution, suffrage may be exercised by qualified citizens "not otherwise disqualified by law" → fixing disqualifications belongs exclusively to the Legislature. Any injustice or error can be cured only by the Legislature (amendment or repeal) or by the Judiciary (declaring the law void).

paras.html: Limits on the pardoning power are constitutional only: the power under Sec. 11(6), Art. VII (1935 Constitution) has two limitations, namely that it be exercised after conviction and that it does not extend to cases of impeachment. "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

VII (1935 Constitution) has two limitations, namely that it be exercised after conviction and that it does not extend to cases of impeachment. paras.html: Effect of an absolute pardon: "An absolute pardon not only blots out the crime committed, but removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction," including accessory and resultant disabilities. When granted after the term of imprisonment has expired, it removes all that is left of the consequences of conviction, such as a statutory disqualification from voting that rests on that conviction.

paras.html: Re: Nature and limits of the pardoning power
paras.text: Re: Nature and limits of the pardoning power

paras.html: Sec. 11(6), Art. VII of the 1935 Constitution: the President may grant reprieves, commutations, and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, after conviction, for all offenses, except in cases of impeachment, upon such conditions and with such restrictions and limitations as he may deem proper [the CD Asia text reads "deem pro to impose" (sic)]; he may grant amnesty with the concurrence of the National Assembly.
paras.text: Sec. 11(6), Art. VII of the 1935 Constitution: the President may grant reprieves, commutations, and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, after conviction, for all offenses, except in cases of impeachment, upon such conditions and with such restrictions and limitations as he may deem proper [the CD Asia text reads "deem pro to impose" (sic)]; he may grant amnesty with the concurrence of the National Assembly.

paras.html: Only two limitations: (a) the power must be exercised after conviction; and (b) it does not extend to cases of impeachment.
paras.text: Only two limitations: (a) the power must be exercised after conviction; and (b) it does not extend to cases of impeachment.

paras.html: TLDR: The pardon did not lift the Sec. 94(b) disqualification, so Santos remained disqualified from voting. paras.html: The majority misread "disability resulting from conviction." The disabilities flowing from a conviction are those the law attaches to it: here, arresto mayor with the accessory suspension of suffrage for its duration, which ended with the sentence. When Santos finished serving it, no other law deprived him of suffrage, since the Election Code had not yet been enacted.

paras.html: There is no conflict. Under Title V, Art. 1 (Suffrage) of the 1935 Constitution, suffrage may be exercised by qualified citizens "not otherwise disqualified by law" → fixing disqualifications belongs exclusively to the Legislature. Any injustice or error can be cured only by the Legislature (amendment or repeal) or by the Judiciary (declaring the law void).

paras.html: Ancestral lands (Sec. 3[b]): lands occupied by individuals, families, and clans of ICCs, "including residential lots, rice terraces or paddies, private forests, swidden farms and tree lots," "occupied, possessed and utilized" by them or their ancestors "since time immemorial, continuously to the present."

paras.html: "The time-tested standards for the exercise of judicial review are: (1) the existence of an appropriate case; (2) an interest personal and substantial by the party raising the constitutional question; (3) the plea that the function be exercised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) the necessity that the constitutional question be passed upon in order to decide the case." (Dumlao v. COMELEC, citing People v. Vera)
paras.text: "The time-tested standards for the exercise of judicial review are: (1) the existence of an appropriate case; (2) an interest personal and substantial by the party raising the constitutional question; (3) the plea that the function be exercised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) the necessity that the constitutional question be passed upon in order to decide the case." (Dumlao v. COMELEC, citing People v. Vera)

paras.html: "An 'actual case or controversy' means an existing case or controversy which is both ripe for resolution and susceptible of judicial determination, and that which is not conjectural or anticipatory, or that which seeks to resolve hypothetical or feigned constitutional problems. A petition raising a constitutional question does not present an 'actual controversy,' unless it alleges a legal right or power. Moreover, it must show that a conflict of rights exists, for inherent in the term 'controversy' is the presence of opposing views or contentions."

paras.html: "In the case at bar, there exists a live controversy involving a clash of legal rights. A law has been enacted, and the Implementing Rules and Regulations approved. Money has been appropriated and the government agencies concerned have been directed to implement the statute. It cannot be successfully maintained that we should await the adverse consequences of the law in order to consider the controversy actual and ripe for judicial resolution."

paras.html: "It is precisely the contention of the petitioners that the law, on its face, constitutes an unconstitutional abdication of State ownership over lands of the public domain and other natural resources. Moreover, when the State machinery is set into motion to implement an alleged unconstitutional statute, this Court possesses sufficient authority to resolve and prevent imminent injury and violation of the constitutional process."

Since the government, as the guardian of the national patrimony, holds it for the benefit of all Filipinos without distinction as to ethnicity, it follows that a citizen has sufficient interest to maintain a suit to ensure that any grant of concessions covering the national economy and patrimony strictly complies with constitutional requirements. paras.html: "First, according to petitioners, the King of Spain under international law acquired exclusive dominion over the Philippines by virtue of discovery and conquest... under the theory of jura regalia, which was introduced into Philippine law upon Spanish conquest in 1521, acquired title to all the lands in the archipelago."
paras.text: "First, according to petitioners, the King of Spain under international law acquired exclusive dominion over the Philippines by virtue of discovery and conquest... under the theory of jura regalia, which was introduced into Philippine law upon Spanish conquest in 1521, acquired title to all the lands in the archipelago."

paras.html: "Second, petitioners and the Solicitor General submit that ancestral lands and ancestral domains are owned by the State... They argue that the Philippine State, as successor to Spain and the United States, is the source of any asserted right of ownership in land."
paras.text: "Second, petitioners and the Solicitor General submit that ancestral lands and ancestral domains are owned by the State... They argue that the Philippine State, as successor to Spain and the United States, is the source of any asserted right of ownership in land."

paras.html: "Third, petitioners and the Solicitor General concede that the Cariño doctrine exists. However, petitioners maintain that the doctrine merely states that title to lands of the public domain may be acquired by prescription. The Solicitor General, for his part, argues that the doctrine applies only to alienable lands of the public domain and, thus, cannot be extended to other lands of the public domain such as forest or timber, mineral lands, and national parks."

paras.html: "Fourth, the Solicitor General asserts that even assuming that native title over ancestral lands and ancestral domains existed by virtue of the Cariño doctrine, such native title was extinguished upon the ratification of the 1935 Constitution."

paras.html: "Fifth, petitioners admit that Congress is mandated under Section 5, Article XII of the Constitution to protect that rights of indigenous peoples to their ancestral lands and ancestral domains. However, they contend that the mandate is subject to Section 2, Article XII and the theory of jura regalia embodied therein."

paras.html: "Finally, on the premise that ancestral lands and ancestral domains are owned by the State, petitioners posit that R.A. 8371 violates Section 2, Article XII of the Constitution which prohibits the alienation of non-agricultural lands of the public domain and other natural resources."

It has been held that the State may impair vested rights through a legitimate exercise of police power... Time-immemorial possession does not create private ownership in cases of natural resources that have been found from generation to generation to be critical to the survival of the Sovereign and its agent, the State."

paras.html: "Generally, under the concept of jura regalia, private title to land must be traced to some grant, express or implied, from the Spanish Crown or its successors, the American Colonial government, and thereafter, the Philippine Republic."
paras.text: "Generally, under the concept of jura regalia, private title to land must be traced to some grant, express or implied, from the Spanish Crown or its successors, the American Colonial government, and thereafter, the Philippine Republic."

paras.html: Cariño (U.S. Supreme Court, reversing the Philippine Supreme Court): "Every presumption is and ought to be taken against the Government in a case like the present. It might, perhaps, be proper and sufficient to say that when, as far back as testimony or memory goes, the land has been held by individuals under a claim of private ownership, it will be presumed to have been held in the same way from before the Spanish conquest, and never to have been public land."

paras.html: "The above ruling institutionalized the recognition of the existence of native title to land, or ownership of land by Filipinos by virtue of possession under a claim of ownership since time immemorial and independent of any grant from the Spanish Crown, as an exception to the theory of jura regalia."

paras.html: Facts of Cariño: Mateo Cariño, an Igorot, applied to register ancestral land in Benguet; he and his ancestors had lived on and cultivated it as far back as they could remember, were recognized as owners, and passed it on by inheritance under native custom, but had no document of title from the Spanish Crown. The government invoked jura regalia; the U.S. Supreme Court held him entitled to registration.

The government invoked jura regalia; the U.S. Supreme Court held him entitled to registration.

paras.html: Cariño (1909) was binding precedent then, and was applied in Oh Cho v. Director of Lands (1946): an exception to the rule that lands not acquired from the Government belong to the public domain is "any land that should have been in the possession of an occupant and of his predecessors in interest since time immemorial, for such possession would justify the presumption that the land had never been part of the public domain or that it had been private property even before the Spanish conquest."

paras.html: "There is no merit in these contentions. A proper reading of Cariño would show that the doctrine enunciated therein applies only to lands which have always been considered as private, and not to lands of the public domain, whether alienable or otherwise."
paras.text: "There is no merit in these contentions. A proper reading of Cariño would show that the doctrine enunciated therein applies only to lands which have always been considered as private, and not to lands of the public domain, whether alienable or otherwise."

paras.html: "A distinction must be made between ownership of land under native title and ownership by acquisitive prescription against the State. Ownership by virtue of native title presupposes that the land has been held by its possessor and his predecessors-in-interest in the concept of an owner since time immemorial. The land is not acquired from the State, that is, Spain or its successors-in-interest, the United States and the Philippine Government. There has been no transfer of title from the State as the land has been regarded as private in character as far back as memory goes."
paras.text: "A distinction must be made between ownership of land under native title and ownership by acquisitive prescription against the State. Ownership by virtue of native title presupposes that the land has been held by its possessor and his predecessors-in-interest in the concept of an owner since time immemorial. The land is not acquired from the State, that is, Spain or its successors-in-interest, the United States and the Philippine Government. There has been no transfer of title from the State as the land has been regarded as private in character as far back as memory goes."

paras.html: "In contrast, ownership of land by acquisitive prescription against the State involves a conversion of the character of the property from alienable public land to private land, which presupposes a transfer of title from the State to a private person."
paras.text: "In contrast, ownership of land by acquisitive prescription against the State involves a conversion of the character of the property from alienable public land to private land, which presupposes a transfer of title from the State to a private person."

paras.html: "Since native title assumes that the property covered by it is private land and is deemed never to have been part of the public domain, the Solicitor General's thesis that native title under Cariño applies only to lands of the public domain is erroneous. Consequently, the classification of lands of the public domain into agricultural, forest or timber, mineral lands, and national parks under the Constitution is irrelevant to the application of the Cariño doctrine because the Regalian doctrine which vests in the State ownership of lands of the public domain does not cover ancestral lands and ancestral domains."

paras.html: Spanish period: Spain acquired sovereignty by discovery and occupation and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), when Asia, the Americas, and Africa were deemed terra nullius. But "Although Spain was deemed to have acquired sovereignty over the Philippines, this did not mean that it acquired title to all lands in the archipelago. By virtue of the colonial laws of Spain, the Spanish Crown was considered to have acquired dominion only over the unoccupied and unclaimed portions of our islands."

paras.html: Philip II instructed Legazpi "to inform the natives that the Spaniards had come to do no harm to their persons or to their property."

paras.html: "Spanish colonial laws recognized and respected Filipino landholdings including native land occupancy. Thus, the Recopilación de Leyes de las Indias expressly conferred ownership of lands already held by the natives."

paras.html: "The royal decrees of 1880 and 1894 did not extinguish native title." The Royal Decree of June 25, 1880 required those in "unlawful possession of royal lands" to legalize their possession through adjustment proceedings; the Maura Law (Feb. 13, 1894) declared unadjusted titles forfeited. "Despite the harsh wording of the Maura Law, it was held in the case of Cariño that the royal decree of 1894 should not be construed as confiscation of title, but merely as the withdrawal of the privilege of registering such title."

paras.html: American period: "Neither was native title disturbed by the Spanish cession of the Philippines to the United States." Under the Treaty of Paris (Dec. 10, 1898), "the cession of the Philippines did not impair any right to property existing at the time." The Philippine Bill of 1902 required property acquired from Spain to be administered for the benefit of Filipinos; it and McKinley's Instructions contained the guarantee that "no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law."

paras.html: "Stated simply, the Solicitor General's argument is that the State, as the source of all titles to land, had the power to re-vest in itself, through the 1935 Constitution, title to all lands, including ancestral lands and ancestral domains."

paras.html: "I cannot agree. The text of the provision of the 1935 Constitution invoked by the Solicitor General, while embodying the theory of jura regalia, is too clear for any misunderstanding. It simply declares that 'all agricultural, timber, and mineral lands of the public domain, waters, minerals, coal, petroleum, and other mineral oils, all forces of potential energy, and other natural resources of the Philippines belong to the State.' Nowhere does it state that certain lands which are 'absolutely necessary for social welfare and existence,' including those which are not part of the public domain, shall thereafter be owned by the State."

paras.html: "Section 1, Article XII of the 1935 Constitution [sic: Art. XIII of the 1935 Constitution, as quoted by Panganiban, J.] cannot be construed to mean that vested right which had existed then were extinguished... On the contrary, said Section restated the fundamental rule against the diminution of existing rights by expressly providing that the ownership of lands of the public domain and other natural resources by the State is 'subject to any existing right, grant, lease, or concessions.' The 'existing rights' that were intended to be protected must, perforce, include the right of ownership by indigenous peoples over their ancestral lands and domains. The words of the law should be given their ordinary or usual meaning, and the term 'existing rights' cannot be assigned an unduly restrictive definition."

paras.html: "It is readily apparent from the constitutional records that the framers of the Constitution did not intend Congress to decide whether ancestral domains shall be public or private property. Rather, they acknowledged that ancestral domains shall be treated as private property, and that customary laws shall merely determine whether such private ownership is by the entire indigenous cultural community, or by individuals, families, or clans within the community."
paras.text: "It is readily apparent from the constitutional records that the framers of the Constitution did not intend Congress to decide whether ancestral domains shall be public or private property. Rather, they acknowledged that ancestral domains shall be treated as private property, and that customary laws shall merely determine whether such private ownership is by the entire indigenous cultural community, or by individuals, families, or clans within the community."

paras.html: ConCom record: Davide — "That is exactly the reason... why we will leave it to Congress to make the necessary exception to the general law on property relations." Bennagen — "There would be ownership based on individuals, on clan or lineage, or on community." Bennagen (to Suarez) — "The concept of customary laws is that it is considered as ownership by private individuals, clans and even communities."

A close perusal of the records of the 1986 Constitutional Commission reveals that the framers of the Constitution inserted the phrase 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution' mainly to prevent the impairment of Torrens titles and other prior rights in the determination of what constitutes ancestral lands and ancestral domains."

Bennagen: prior rights established with due process "have to be respected"; Baguio is ancestral land "in the sense that it belongs to Cordillera... but not in terms of the right of a particular person or particular group to exploit, utilize, or sell it"; prior rights will be respected — "Definitely."

paras.html: Second reason — the Constitution is read as a whole: "The Constitution must be construed as a whole... That construction should be used which would give effect to the entire instrument." The State-ownership provisions "should be read together with the other provisions thereof which firmly recognize the rights of the indigenous peoples": Sec. 22, Art. II; Sec. 5, Art. XII; Sec. 1, Art. XIII; Sec. 6, Art. XIII; Sec. 17, Art. XIV; and Sec. 12, Art. XVI.

paras.html: Third reason — equity and balancing: "the first goal of the national economy is the more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth." "The framers of the Constitution did not, by the phrase 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution and national development policies and programs,' intend to establish a hierarchy of constitutional norms." Davide (to Bishop Bacani): "It is not really a question of which is primary or which is more paramount. The concept introduced here is really the balancing of interests."

paras.html: Re: Sec. 3(a) is definitional
paras.text: Re: Sec. 3(a) is definitional

paras.html: "Section 3(a) merely defines the coverage of ancestral domains, and describes the extent, limit and composition of ancestral domains by setting forth the standards and guidelines in determining whether a particular area is to be considered as part of and within the ancestral domains. In other words, Section 3(a) serves only as a yardstick which points out what properties are within the ancestral domains. It does not confer or recognize any right of ownership over the natural resources to the indigenous peoples. Its purpose is definitional and not declarative of a right or title."
paras.text: "Section 3(a) merely defines the coverage of ancestral domains, and describes the extent, limit and composition of ancestral domains by setting forth the standards and guidelines in determining whether a particular area is to be considered as part of and within the ancestral domains. In other words, Section 3(a) serves only as a yardstick which points out what properties are within the ancestral domains. It does not confer or recognize any right of ownership over the natural resources to the indigenous peoples. Its purpose is definitional and not declarative of a right or title."

paras.html: "The specification of what areas belong to the ancestral domains is... important to ensure that no unnecessary encroachment on private properties outside the ancestral domains will result during the delineation process. The mere fact that Section 3(a) defines ancestral domains to include the natural resources found therein does not ipso facto convert the character of such natural resources as private property of the indigenous peoples."

paras.html: "The phrase 'private but community property' is merely descriptive of the indigenous peoples' concept of ownership as distinguished from that provided in the Civil Code."

paras.html: Civil Code ownership: "independent and general power of a person over a thing," with jus utendi, jus abutendi, jus disponendi, and jus vindicandi [opinion spells it "jus vidicandi"]. "In contrast, the indigenous peoples' concept of ownership emphasizes the importance of communal or group ownership. By virtue of the communal character of ownership, the property held in common "cannot be sold, disposed or destroyed" because it was meant to benefit the whole indigenous community and not merely the individual member."

Fianza: "the Court did not recognize native title to natural resources. Rather, it merely upheld the right of the indigenous peoples to claim ownership of minerals under the Philippine Bill of 1902."

paras.html: Spain asserted ownership of minerals "wherever these may be found, whether in public or private lands," recognizing "the separability of title over lands and that over minerals." The U.S. allowed exploration and mineral patents, but "title in these minerals was in all cases sourced from the State." The 1935 framers kept State ownership "to insure their conservation for future generations of Filipinos, to prevent foreign control of the country through economic domination; and to avoid situations whereby the Philippines would become a source of international conflicts." Reiterated in 1973 and 1987.

paras.html: "In any case, a careful reading of Section 7(b) would reveal that the rights given to the indigenous peoples are duly circumscribed" — to manage and conserve; to benefit and share profits; to negotiate terms for exploration; to informed participation and compensation; and to effective government measures.
paras.text: "In any case, a careful reading of Section 7(b) would reveal that the rights given to the indigenous peoples are duly circumscribed" — to manage and conserve; to benefit and share profits; to negotiate terms for exploration; to informed participation and compensation; and to effective government measures.

paras.html: "It must be noted that the right to negotiate terms and conditions granted under Section 7(b) pertains only to the exploration of natural resources. The term 'exploration' refers only to the search or prospecting of mineral resources... The exploration, which is merely a preliminary activity, cannot be equated with the entire process of 'exploration, development and utilization' of natural resources which under the Constitution belong to the State."

paras.html: Re: Sec. 57 — "priority rights"
paras.text: Re: Sec. 57 — "priority rights"

paras.html: "Section 57... grants the indigenous peoples 'priority rights' in the utilization of natural resources and not absolute ownership thereof. Priority rights does not mean exclusive rights. What is granted is merely the right of preference or first consideration in the award of privileges provided by existing laws and regulations, with due regard to the needs and welfare of indigenous peoples living in the area."
paras.text: "Section 57... grants the indigenous peoples 'priority rights' in the utilization of natural resources and not absolute ownership thereof. Priority rights does not mean exclusive rights. What is granted is merely the right of preference or first consideration in the award of privileges provided by existing laws and regulations, with due regard to the needs and welfare of indigenous peoples living in the area."

paras.html: "There is nothing in the assailed law which implies an automatic or mechanical character in the grant of concessions. Nor does the law negate the exercise of sound discretion by government entities." Factors: extent and nature of utilization; impact on environment and IP way of life; IPs "must show that they live in the area and that they are in the best position to undertake the required utilization."

paras.html: "[T]he grant of said priority rights to indigenous peoples is not a blanket authority to disregard pertinent laws and regulations. The utilization of said natural resources is always subject to compliance by the indigenous peoples with existing laws, such as R.A. 7076 and R.A. 7942 since it is not they but the State, which owns these resources."

paras.html: "[T]he grant of priority rights does not preclude the State from undertaking activities, or entering into co-production, joint venture or production-sharing agreements with private entities... There is no intention, as between the State and the indigenous peoples, to create a hierarchy of values; rather, the object is to balance the interests of the State for national development and those of the indigenous peoples."

To do so would unduly limit the ownership rights of the State over the natural resources."

paras.html: Re: Prior informed consent and Sec. 59
paras.text: Re: Prior informed consent and Sec. 59

paras.html: Sec. 57 recognizes that exploitation "may disrupt the natural environment as well as the traditional activities of the indigenous peoples therein. Hence, the need for the prior informed consent of the indigenous peoples." When the State itself undertakes the activity, it "must, as a matter of policy and law, consult the indigenous peoples," in line with the framers' intent that national plans involve "systematic consultation." For non-members, consent "takes the form of a formal and written agreement." "This requirement is not peculiar to IPRA" (Philippine Environmental Policy, EIS System, Local Government Code, Mining Act).

paras.html: "The fact that the NCIP is composed of members of the indigenous peoples does not mean that it (the NCIP) is incapable, or will appear to be so incapable, of delivering justice to the non-indigenous peoples. A person's possession of the trait of impartiality desirable of a judge has nothing to do with his or her ethnic roots. In this wise, the indigenous peoples are as capable of rendering justice as the non-indigenous peoples for, certainly, the latter have no monopoly of the concept of justice."

paras.html: "The application of customary law is limited to disputes concerning property rights or relations in determining the ownership and extent of the ancestral domains, where all the parties involved are members of indigenous peoples, specifically, of the same indigenous group. It therefore follows that when one of the parties to a dispute is a non-member of an indigenous group, or when the indigenous peoples involved belong to different groups, the application of customary law is not required."

paras.html: Purpose and backdrop: "the interpretation of these provisions should take into account the purpose of the law, which is to give life to the constitutional mandate that the rights of the indigenous peoples be recognized and protected." He cites the Draft UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (1994) and the Martinez Cobo working definition, notes that "Philippine legal history... has not been kind to the indigenous peoples" (calling them "uncivilized," "backward people"), and that "One of every six Filipinos is a member of an indigenous cultural community" (about 12 million in some 110 ICCs).

paras.html: His own recapitulation (verbatim):
paras.text: His own recapitulation (verbatim):

paras.html: "(1) The provisions of the IPRA (specifically Sections 3, paragraphs (a) and (b), 5, 6, 7, and 8) affirming the ownership by the indigenous peoples of their ancestral lands and domains by virtue of native title do not diminish the State's ownership of lands of the public domain, because said ancestral lands and domains are considered as private land, and never to have been part of the public domain, following the doctrine laid down in Cariño vs. Insular Government;"
paras.text: "(1) The provisions of the IPRA (specifically Sections 3, paragraphs (a) and (b), 5, 6, 7, and 8) affirming the ownership by the indigenous peoples of their ancestral lands and domains by virtue of native title do not diminish the State's ownership of lands of the public domain, because said ancestral lands and domains are considered as private land, and never to have been part of the public domain, following the doctrine laid down in Cariño vs. Insular Government;"

paras.html: "(2) The constitutional provision vesting ownership over minerals, mineral lands and other natural resources in the State is not violated by Sections 3, 5, 7, 56, 57, 58 and 59 of the IPRA... The State retains full control over the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources even with the grant of said rights to the indigenous peoples, through the imposition of requirements and conditions for the utilization of natural resources under existing laws, such as the Small-Scale Mining Act of 1991 and the Philippine Mining Act of 1995. Moreover, the rights granted to indigenous peoples for the utilization of natural resources within their ancestral domains merely amplify what has been earlier granted to them under the aforesaid laws;"
paras.text: "(2) The constitutional provision vesting ownership over minerals, mineral lands and other natural resources in the State is not violated by Sections 3, 5, 7, 56, 57, 58 and 59 of the IPRA... The State retains full control over the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources even with the grant of said rights to the indigenous peoples, through the imposition of requirements and conditions for the utilization of natural resources under existing laws, such as the Small-Scale Mining Act of 1991 and the Philippine Mining Act of 1995. Moreover, the rights granted to indigenous peoples for the utilization of natural resources within their ancestral domains merely amplify what has been earlier granted to them under the aforesaid laws;"

paras.html: "(3) While the IPRA recognizes the rights of indigenous peoples with regard to their ancestral lands and domains, it also protects the vested rights of persons, whether indigenous or non-indigenous peoples, who may have acquired rights of ownership lands or rights to explore and exploit natural resources within the ancestral lands and domains;"

paras.html: "(4) The Due Process Clause of the Constitution is not violated by the provisions (Sections 40, 51-54, 62, 63, 65 and 66) of the IPRA... The fact the NCIP is composed wholly of indigenous peoples does not mean that it is incapable of being impartial. Moreover, the use of customary laws is sanctioned by paragraph 2, Section 5 of Article XII of the Constitution; and"
paras.text: "(4) The Due Process Clause of the Constitution is not violated by the provisions (Sections 40, 51-54, 62, 63, 65 and 66) of the IPRA... paras.html: "(5) The provision of the Implementing Rules characterizing the NCIP as an independent agency under the Office of the President does not infringe upon the President's power of control under Section 17, Article VII of the Constitution, since said provision as well as Section 40 of the IPRA expressly places the NCIP under the Office of the President, and therefore under the President's control and supervision with respect to its administrative functions. However, insofar as the decisions of the NCIP in the exercise of its quasi-judicial powers are concerned, the same are reviewable by the Court of Appeals, like those of the NLRC and the SEC."

paras.html: R.A. 8371, the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act of 1997 (IPRA), was enacted "precisely to implement" the constitutional provisions on indigenous peoples (Sec. 22, Art. II; Sec. 5, Art. XII; Secs. 1 and 6, Art. XIII; Sec. 17, Art. XIV; Sec. 12, Art. XVI). It took effect on November 22, 1997 [date per Vitug, J.'s opinion].

paras.html: It "acknowledges a general concept of indigenous property right and recognizes title thereto; and creates the NCIP as an independent agency under the Office of the President."

paras.html: Ancestral lands (Sec. 3[b]): lands occupied by individuals, families, and clans of ICCs, "including residential lots, rice terraces or paddies, private forests, swidden farms and tree lots," "occupied, possessed and utilized" by them or their ancestors "since time immemorial, continuously to the present."

paras.html: Ancestral domains (Sec. 3[a]): areas generally belonging to ICCs, including ancestral lands, forests, pasture, residential and agricultural lands, hunting grounds, worship areas, and lands to which they had traditional access; they "also include inland waters, coastal areas and natural resources therein."

paras.html: "The time-tested standards for the exercise of judicial review are: (1) the existence of an appropriate case; (2) an interest personal and substantial by the party raising the constitutional question; (3) the plea that the function be exercised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) the necessity that the constitutional question be passed upon in order to decide the case." (Dumlao v. COMELEC, citing People v. Vera)
paras.text: "The time-tested standards for the exercise of judicial review are: (1) the existence of an appropriate case; (2) an interest personal and substantial by the party raising the constitutional question; (3) the plea that the function be exercised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) the necessity that the constitutional question be passed upon in order to decide the case." (Dumlao v. COMELEC, citing People v. Vera)

paras.html: "An 'actual case or controversy' means an existing case or controversy which is both ripe for resolution and susceptible of judicial determination, and that which is not conjectural or anticipatory, or that which seeks to resolve hypothetical or feigned constitutional problems. A petition raising a constitutional question does not present an 'actual controversy,' unless it alleges a legal right or power. Moreover, it must show that a conflict of rights exists, for inherent in the term 'controversy' is the presence of opposing views or contentions."

paras.html: "In the case at bar, there exists a live controversy involving a clash of legal rights. A law has been enacted, and the Implementing Rules and Regulations approved. Money has been appropriated and the government agencies concerned have been directed to implement the statute. It cannot be successfully maintained that we should await the adverse consequences of the law in order to consider the controversy actual and ripe for judicial resolution."

paras.html: "It is precisely the contention of the petitioners that the law, on its face, constitutes an unconstitutional abdication of State ownership over lands of the public domain and other natural resources. Moreover, when the State machinery is set into motion to implement an alleged unconstitutional statute, this Court possesses sufficient authority to resolve and prevent imminent injury and violation of the constitutional process."

Governor General [text says "As early as 1910"; fn. 41 cites 16 Phil. 366 (1913)]: "when the question is one of public right and the object of the mandamus is to procure the enforcement of a public duty, the people are regarded as the real party in interest, and the relator at whose instigation the proceedings are instituted need not show that he has any legal or special interest in the result, it being sufficient to show that he is a citizen and as such interested in the execution of the laws."

paras.html: "First, according to petitioners, the King of Spain under international law acquired exclusive dominion over the Philippines by virtue of discovery and conquest... under the theory of jura regalia, which was introduced into Philippine law upon Spanish conquest in 1521, acquired title to all the lands in the archipelago."

paras.html: "Second, petitioners and the Solicitor General submit that ancestral lands and ancestral domains are owned by the State... They argue that the Philippine State, as successor to Spain and the United States, is the source of any asserted right of ownership in land."
paras.text: "Second, petitioners and the Solicitor General submit that ancestral lands and ancestral domains are owned by the State... They argue that the Philippine State, as successor to Spain and the United States, is the source of any asserted right of ownership in land."

paras.html: "Third, petitioners and the Solicitor General concede that the Cariño doctrine exists. However, petitioners maintain that the doctrine merely states that title to lands of the public domain may be acquired by prescription. The Solicitor General, for his part, argues that the doctrine applies only to alienable lands of the public domain and, thus, cannot be extended to other lands of the public domain such as forest or timber, mineral lands, and national parks."

Time-immemorial possession does not create private ownership in cases of natural resources that have been found from generation to generation to be critical to the survival of the Sovereign and its agent, the State."

paras.html: "Generally, under the concept of jura regalia, private title to land must be traced to some grant, express or implied, from the Spanish Crown or its successors, the American Colonial government, and thereafter, the Philippine Republic."
paras.text: "Generally, under the concept of jura regalia, private title to land must be traced to some grant, express or implied, from the Spanish Crown or its successors, the American Colonial government, and thereafter, the Philippine Republic."

paras.html: Cariño (U.S. Supreme Court, reversing the Philippine Supreme Court): "Every presumption is and ought to be taken against the Government in a case like the present. It might, perhaps, be proper and sufficient to say that when, as far back as testimony or memory goes, the land has been held by individuals under a claim of private ownership, it will be presumed to have been held in the same way from before the Spanish conquest, and never to have been public land."

paras.html: "The above ruling institutionalized the recognition of the existence of native title to land, or ownership of land by Filipinos by virtue of possession under a claim of ownership since time immemorial and independent of any grant from the Spanish Crown, as an exception to the theory of jura regalia."

paras.html: Facts of Cariño: Mateo Cariño, an Igorot, applied to register ancestral land in Benguet; he and his ancestors had lived on and cultivated it as far back as they could remember, were recognized as owners, and passed it on by inheritance under native custom, but had no document of title from the Spanish Crown. The government invoked jura regalia; the U.S. Supreme Court held him entitled to registration.

The government invoked jura regalia; the U.S. Supreme Court held him entitled to registration.

paras.html: Cariño (1909) was binding precedent then, and was applied in Oh Cho v. Director of Lands (1946): an exception to the rule that lands not acquired from the Government belong to the public domain is "any land that should have been in the possession of an occupant and of his predecessors in interest since time immemorial, for such possession would justify the presumption that the land had never been part of the public domain or that it had been private property even before the Spanish conquest."

paras.html: "There is no merit in these contentions. A proper reading of Cariño would show that the doctrine enunciated therein applies only to lands which have always been considered as private, and not to lands of the public domain, whether alienable or otherwise."
paras.text: "There is no merit in these contentions. A proper reading of Cariño would show that the doctrine enunciated therein applies only to lands which have always been considered as private, and not to lands of the public domain, whether alienable or otherwise."

paras.html: "A distinction must be made between ownership of land under native title and ownership by acquisitive prescription against the State. Ownership by virtue of native title presupposes that the land has been held by its possessor and his predecessors-in-interest in the concept of an owner since time immemorial. The land is not acquired from the State, that is, Spain or its successors-in-interest, the United States and the Philippine Government. There has been no transfer of title from the State as the land has been regarded as private in character as far back as memory goes."
paras.text: "A distinction must be made between ownership of land under native title and ownership by acquisitive prescription against the State. Ownership by virtue of native title presupposes that the land has been held by its possessor and his predecessors-in-interest in the concept of an owner since time immemorial. The land is not acquired from the State, that is, Spain or its successors-in-interest, the United States and the Philippine Government. There has been no transfer of title from the State as the land has been regarded as private in character as far back as memory goes."

paras.html: "In contrast, ownership of land by acquisitive prescription against the State involves a conversion of the character of the property from alienable public land to private land, which presupposes a transfer of title from the State to a private person."
paras.text: "In contrast, ownership of land by acquisitive prescription against the State involves a conversion of the character of the property from alienable public land to private land, which presupposes a transfer of title from the State to a private person."

paras.html: "Since native title assumes that the property covered by it is private land and is deemed never to have been part of the public domain, the Solicitor General's thesis that native title under Cariño applies only to lands of the public domain is erroneous. Consequently, the classification of lands of the public domain into agricultural, forest or timber, mineral lands, and national parks under the Constitution is irrelevant to the application of the Cariño doctrine because the Regalian doctrine which vests in the State ownership of lands of the public domain does not cover ancestral lands and ancestral domains."

paras.html: Spanish period: Spain acquired sovereignty by discovery and occupation and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), when Asia, the Americas, and Africa were deemed terra nullius. But "Although Spain was deemed to have acquired sovereignty over the Philippines, this did not mean that it acquired title to all lands in the archipelago. By virtue of the colonial laws of Spain, the Spanish Crown was considered to have acquired dominion only over the unoccupied and unclaimed portions of our islands."

By virtue of the colonial laws of Spain, the Spanish Crown was considered to have acquired dominion only over the unoccupied and unclaimed portions of our islands."

paras.html: Philip II instructed Legazpi "to inform the natives that the Spaniards had come to do no harm to their persons or to their property."

paras.html: "Spanish colonial laws recognized and respected Filipino landholdings including native land occupancy. Thus, the Recopilación de Leyes de las Indias expressly conferred ownership of lands already held by the natives."

paras.html: "The royal decrees of 1880 and 1894 did not extinguish native title." The Royal Decree of June 25, 1880 required those in "unlawful possession of royal lands" to legalize their possession through adjustment proceedings; the Maura Law (Feb. 13, 1894) declared unadjusted titles forfeited. "Despite the harsh wording of the Maura Law, it was held in the case of Cariño that the royal decree of 1894 should not be construed as confiscation of title, but merely as the withdrawal of the privilege of registering such title."

"Despite the harsh wording of the Maura Law, it was held in the case of Cariño that the royal decree of 1894 should not be construed as confiscation of title, but merely as the withdrawal of the privilege of registering such title."

paras.html: American period: "Neither was native title disturbed by the Spanish cession of the Philippines to the United States." Under the Treaty of Paris (Dec. 10, 1898), "the cession of the Philippines did not impair any right to property existing at the time." The Philippine Bill of 1902 required property acquired from Spain to be administered for the benefit of Filipinos; it and McKinley's Instructions contained the guarantee that "no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law."

paras.text: Re: The 1935 Constitution did not extinguish native title (answering the OSG)

paras.html: "Stated simply, the Solicitor General's argument is that the State, as the source of all titles to land, had the power to re-vest in itself, through the 1935 Constitution, title to all lands, including ancestral lands and ancestral domains."
paras.text: "Stated simply, the Solicitor General's argument is that the State, as the source of all titles to land, had the power to re-vest in itself, through the 1935 Constitution, title to all lands, including ancestral lands and ancestral domains."

paras.html: "I cannot agree. The text of the provision of the 1935 Constitution invoked by the Solicitor General, while embodying the theory of jura regalia, is too clear for any misunderstanding. It simply declares that 'all agricultural, timber, and mineral lands of the public domain, waters, minerals, coal, petroleum, and other mineral oils, all forces of potential energy, and other natural resources of the Philippines belong to the State.' Nowhere does it state that certain lands which are 'absolutely necessary for social welfare and existence,' including those which are not part of the public domain, shall thereafter be owned by the State."

Nowhere does it state that certain lands which are 'absolutely necessary for social welfare and existence,' including those which are not part of the public domain, shall thereafter be owned by the State."

paras.html: "If there is any room for constitutional construction, the provision should be interpreted in favor of the preservation, rather than impairment or extinguishment, of vested rights."

paras.html: "Section 1, Article XII of the 1935 Constitution [sic: Art. XIII of the 1935 Constitution, as quoted by Panganiban, J.] cannot be construed to mean that vested right which had existed then were extinguished... On the contrary, said Section restated the fundamental rule against the diminution of existing rights by expressly providing that the ownership of lands of the public domain and other natural resources by the State is 'subject to any existing right, grant, lease, or concessions.' The 'existing rights' that were intended to be protected must, perforce, include the right of ownership by indigenous peoples over their ancestral lands and domains. The words of the law should be given their ordinary or usual meaning, and the term 'existing rights' cannot be assigned an unduly restrictive definition."
paras.text: "Section 1, Article XII of the 1935 Constitution [sic: Art. XIII of the 1935 Constitution, as quoted by Panganiban, J.] cannot be construed to mean that vested right which had existed then were extinguished... On the contrary, said Section restated the fundamental rule against the diminution of existing rights by expressly providing that the ownership of lands of the public domain and other natural resources by the State is 'subject to any existing right, grant, lease, or concessions.' The 'existing rights' that were intended to be protected must, perforce, include the right of ownership by indigenous peoples over their ancestral lands and domains. The words of the law should be given their ordinary or usual meaning, and the term 'existing rights' cannot be assigned an unduly restrictive definition."

paras.html: "Section 5, Article XII of the Constitution expresses the sovereign intent to 'protect the rights of indigenous peoples to their ancestral lands.' In its general and ordinary sense, the term "right" refers to any legally enforceable claim... When used in relation to property, 'right' includes any interest in or title to an object, or any just and legal claim to hold, use and enjoy it."

paras.html: "It is readily apparent from the constitutional records that the framers of the Constitution did not intend Congress to decide whether ancestral domains shall be public or private property. Rather, they acknowledged that ancestral domains shall be treated as private property, and that customary laws shall merely determine whether such private ownership is by the entire indigenous cultural community, or by individuals, families, or clans within the community."

paras.html: "Section 3(a) merely defines the coverage of ancestral domains, and describes the extent, limit and composition of ancestral domains by setting forth the standards and guidelines in determining whether a particular area is to be considered as part of and within the ancestral domains. In other words, Section 3(a) serves only as a yardstick which points out what properties are within the ancestral domains. It does not confer or recognize any right of ownership over the natural resources to the indigenous peoples. Its purpose is definitional and not declarative of a right or title."
paras.text: "Section 3(a) merely defines the coverage of ancestral domains, and describes the extent, limit and composition of ancestral domains by setting forth the standards and guidelines in determining whether a particular area is to be considered as part of and within the ancestral domains. In other words, Section 3(a) serves only as a yardstick which points out what properties are within the ancestral domains. It does not confer or recognize any right of ownership over the natural resources to the indigenous peoples. Its purpose is definitional and not declarative of a right or title."

paras.html: "The specification of what areas belong to the ancestral domains is... important to ensure that no unnecessary encroachment on private properties outside the ancestral domains will result during the delineation process. The mere fact that Section 3(a) defines ancestral domains to include the natural resources found therein does not ipso facto convert the character of such natural resources as private property of the indigenous peoples."

paras.html: Civil Code ownership: "independent and general power of a person over a thing," with jus utendi, jus abutendi, jus disponendi, and jus vindicandi [opinion spells it "jus vidicandi"]. "In contrast, the indigenous peoples' concept of ownership emphasizes the importance of communal or group ownership. By virtue of the communal character of ownership, the property held in common "cannot be sold, disposed or destroyed" because it was meant to benefit the whole indigenous community and not merely the individual member."

paras.html: Spain asserted ownership of minerals "wherever these may be found, whether in public or private lands," recognizing "the separability of title over lands and that over minerals." The U.S. allowed exploration and mineral patents, but "title in these minerals was in all cases sourced from the State." The 1935 framers kept State ownership "to insure their conservation for future generations of Filipinos, to prevent foreign control of the country through economic domination; and to avoid situations whereby the Philippines would become a source of international conflicts." Reiterated in 1973 and 1987.

paras.html: Re: IPRA amplifies existing laws
paras.text: Re: IPRA amplifies existing laws

paras.html: "The rights given to the indigenous peoples regarding the exploitation of natural resources under Sections 7(b) and 57 of IPRA amplify what has been granted to them under existing laws." RA 7076 (Small-Scale Mining Act of 1991): IPs get priority in small-scale mining contracts in ancestral land declared a people's small-scale mining area. RA 7942 (Philippine Mining Act of 1995): no ancestral land opened for mining without prior consent of the ICC; royalties paid to them.

paras.html: Re: Sec. 7(b) — rights are circumscribed; "exploration" only
paras.text: Re: Sec. 7(b) — rights are circumscribed; "exploration" only

paras.html: "In any case, a careful reading of Section 7(b) would reveal that the rights given to the indigenous peoples are duly circumscribed" — to manage and conserve; to benefit and share profits; to negotiate terms for exploration; to informed participation and compensation; and to effective government measures.

paras.html: "It must be noted that the right to negotiate terms and conditions granted under Section 7(b) pertains only to the exploration of natural resources. The term 'exploration' refers only to the search or prospecting of mineral resources... The exploration, which is merely a preliminary activity, cannot be equated with the entire process of 'exploration, development and utilization' of natural resources which under the Constitution belong to the State."

paras.html: Re: Sec. 57 — "priority rights"
paras.text: Re: Sec. 57 — "priority rights"

paras.html: "Section 57... grants the indigenous peoples 'priority rights' in the utilization of natural resources and not absolute ownership thereof. Priority rights does not mean exclusive rights. What is granted is merely the right of preference or first consideration in the award of privileges provided by existing laws and regulations, with due regard to the needs and welfare of indigenous peoples living in the area."
paras.text: "Section 57... grants the indigenous peoples 'priority rights' in the utilization of natural resources and not absolute ownership thereof. Priority rights does not mean exclusive rights. What is granted is merely the right of preference or first consideration in the award of privileges provided by existing laws and regulations, with due regard to the needs and welfare of indigenous peoples living in the area."

paras.html: "There is nothing in the assailed law which implies an automatic or mechanical character in the grant of concessions. Nor does the law negate the exercise of sound discretion by government entities." Factors: extent and nature of utilization; impact on environment and IP way of life; IPs "must show that they live in the area and that they are in the best position to undertake the required utilization."

paras.html: "[T]he grant of said priority rights to indigenous peoples is not a blanket authority to disregard pertinent laws and regulations. The utilization of said natural resources is always subject to compliance by the indigenous peoples with existing laws, such as R.A. 7076 and R.A. 7942 since it is not they but the State, which owns these resources."

paras.html: "[T]he grant of priority rights does not preclude the State from undertaking activities, or entering into co-production, joint venture or production-sharing agreements with private entities... There is no intention, as between the State and the indigenous peoples, to create a hierarchy of values; rather, the object is to balance the interests of the State for national development and those of the indigenous peoples."

To do so would unduly limit the ownership rights of the State over the natural resources."

paras.html: Re: Prior informed consent and Sec. 59
paras.text: Re: Prior informed consent and Sec. 59

paras.html: Sec. 57 recognizes that exploitation "may disrupt the natural environment as well as the traditional activities of the indigenous peoples therein. Hence, the need for the prior informed consent of the indigenous peoples." When the State itself undertakes the activity, it "must, as a matter of policy and law, consult the indigenous peoples," in line with the framers' intent that national plans involve "systematic consultation." For non-members, consent "takes the form of a formal and written agreement." "This requirement is not peculiar to IPRA" (Philippine Environmental Policy, EIS System, Local Government Code, Mining Act).

paras.html: "The fact that the NCIP is composed of members of the indigenous peoples does not mean that it (the NCIP) is incapable, or will appear to be so incapable, of delivering justice to the non-indigenous peoples. A person's possession of the trait of impartiality desirable of a judge has nothing to do with his or her ethnic roots. In this wise, the indigenous peoples are as capable of rendering justice as the non-indigenous peoples for, certainly, the latter have no monopoly of the concept of justice."

It therefore follows that when one of the parties to a dispute is a non-member of an indigenous group, or when the indigenous peoples involved belong to different groups, the application of customary law is not required."

paras.html: Purpose and backdrop: "the interpretation of these provisions should take into account the purpose of the law, which is to give life to the constitutional mandate that the rights of the indigenous peoples be recognized and protected." He cites the Draft UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (1994) and the Martinez Cobo working definition, notes that "Philippine legal history... has not been kind to the indigenous peoples" (calling them "uncivilized," "backward people"), and that "One of every six Filipinos is a member of an indigenous cultural community" (about 12 million in some 110 ICCs).

paras.html: His own recapitulation (verbatim):
paras.text: His own recapitulation (verbatim):

paras.html: "(1) The provisions of the IPRA (specifically Sections 3, paragraphs (a) and (b), 5, 6, 7, and 8) affirming the ownership by the indigenous peoples of their ancestral lands and domains by virtue of native title do not diminish the State's ownership of lands of the public domain, because said ancestral lands and domains are considered as private land, and never to have been part of the public domain, following the doctrine laid down in Cariño vs. Insular Government;"
paras.text: "(1) The provisions of the IPRA (specifically Sections 3, paragraphs (a) and (b), 5, 6, 7, and 8) affirming the ownership by the indigenous peoples of their ancestral lands and domains by virtue of native title do not diminish the State's ownership of lands of the public domain, because said ancestral lands and domains are considered as private land, and never to have been part of the public domain, following the doctrine laid down in Cariño vs. Insular Government;"

paras.html: "(2) The constitutional provision vesting ownership over minerals, mineral lands and other natural resources in the State is not violated by Sections 3, 5, 7, 56, 57, 58 and 59 of the IPRA... The State retains full control over the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources even with the grant of said rights to the indigenous peoples, through the imposition of requirements and conditions for the utilization of natural resources under existing laws, such as the Small-Scale Mining Act of 1991 and the Philippine Mining Act of 1995. Moreover, the rights granted to indigenous peoples for the utilization of natural resources within their ancestral domains merely amplify what has been earlier granted to them under the aforesaid laws;"
paras.text: "(2) The constitutional provision vesting ownership over minerals, mineral lands and other natural resources in the State is not violated by Sections 3, 5, 7, 56, 57, 58 and 59 of the IPRA... The State retains full control over the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources even with the grant of said rights to the indigenous peoples, through the imposition of requirements and conditions for the utilization of natural resources under existing laws, such as the Small-Scale Mining Act of 1991 and the Philippine Mining Act of 1995. Moreover, the rights granted to indigenous peoples for the utilization of natural resources within their ancestral domains merely amplify what has been earlier granted to them under the aforesaid laws;"

paras.html: "(3) While the IPRA recognizes the rights of indigenous peoples with regard to their ancestral lands and domains, it also protects the vested rights of persons, whether indigenous or non-indigenous peoples, who may have acquired rights of ownership lands or rights to explore and exploit natural resources within the ancestral lands and domains;"
paras.text: "(3) While the IPRA recognizes the rights of indigenous peoples with regard to their ancestral lands and domains, it also protects the vested rights of persons, whether indigenous or non-indigenous peoples, who may have acquired rights of ownership lands or rights to explore and exploit natural resources within the ancestral lands and domains;"

paras.html: "(4) The Due Process Clause of the Constitution is not violated by the provisions (Sections 40, 51-54, 62, 63, 65 and 66) of the IPRA... The fact the NCIP is composed wholly of indigenous peoples does not mean that it is incapable of being impartial. Moreover, the use of customary laws is sanctioned by paragraph 2, Section 5 of Article XII of the Constitution; and"
paras.text: "(4) The Due Process Clause of the Constitution is not violated by the provisions (Sections 40, 51-54, 62, 63, 65 and 66) of the IPRA... The fact the NCIP is composed wholly of indigenous peoples does not mean that it is incapable of being impartial. Moreover, the use of customary laws is sanctioned by paragraph 2, Section 5 of Article XII of the Constitution; and"

paras.html: "(5) The provision of the Implementing Rules characterizing the NCIP as an independent agency under the Office of the President does not infringe upon the President's power of control under Section 17, Article VII of the Constitution, since said provision as well as Section 40 of the IPRA expressly places the NCIP under the Office of the President, and therefore under the President's control and supervision with respect to its administrative functions. However, insofar as the decisions of the NCIP in the exercise of its quasi-judicial powers are concerned, the same are reviewable by the Court of Appeals, like those of the NLRC and the SEC."

paras.html: IRR Rule III, Part II, Sec. 1 is ultra vires: it gives ownership over "lands, waters, and natural resources"; "the inclusion of 'natural resources'... goes beyond the parameters of Section 7 (b) of the law and is contrary to Section 2, Article XII."

Sec. 57 "is an affirmation of" the Regalian doctrine.

paras.html: Security of tenure in the CES is to rank, not position: "Security of tenure in the career executive service is thus acquired with respect to rank and not to position." It does not extend to the particular positions to which CESOs are appointed (a concept applicable only to first- and second-level employees) but to the rank to which the President appoints them.
paras.text: Security of tenure in the CES is to rank, not position: "Security of tenure in the career executive service is thus acquired with respect to rank and not to position." It does not extend to the particular positions to which CESOs are appointed (a concept applicable only to first- and second-level employees) but to the rank to which the President appoints them.

paras.html: No rank, no permanent appointment: A CESO appointed to a position that requires a higher CES rank than the one he holds is not permanently appointed and can claim no security of tenure in that position; the appointment may be withdrawn at will (Achacoso v. Macaraig).
paras.text: No rank, no permanent appointment: A CESO appointed to a position that requires a higher CES rank than the one he holds is not permanently appointed and can claim no security of tenure in that position; the appointment may be withdrawn at will (Achacoso v. Macaraig).

paras.html: Mobility of CESOs: A CESO may be reassigned or transferred from one position, department, bureau, or office to another provided it is made in the interest of public service and involves no reduction in rank or salary (and not oftener than every two years, with appeal to the President). A transfer to a position matching the CESO's rank is not a demotion and does not violate security of tenure.

paras.html: Petitioners' MR was denied on July 22, 1999. Petitioners filed this petition for review on certiorari (Rule 45), arguing that Bacal's transfer to the Office of the Regional Director was appropriate given her rank as CESO III. Their five assigned errors: (I) Bacal has no vested right to the position; (II) PAO Regional Director carries Rank III, not V, and a Rank III officer is not eligible for a Rank I position; (III) she kept her rank and salary on transfer; (IV) she has no clear right to the office; and (V) she failed to exhaust administrative remedies.

paras.html: Six ranks (CESO I highest to CESO VI lowest). The rank depends on (1) level of managerial responsibility and (2) performance (annual CESPES rating). Rank equivalents: I – Undersecretary; II – Assistant Secretary; III – Bureau Director or Department Regional Director; IV – Assistant Bureau Director, Department Assistant Regional Director, or Department Service Chief; V – Bureau Regional Director; VI – Bureau Assistant Regional Director. A Satisfactory rating → rank equivalent to the level of responsibility; Outstanding → one rank higher.

paras.html: Commission on Reorganization's rationale: the old civil service filled higher posts on considerations other than merit and confined promotion to the "next-in-rank"; career executives are to be selected for high qualifications and to act as catalysts of efficiency and innovation. "The status and salary of the career executives will be based on their rank, and not on the job that they occupy at any given time," similar to commissioned officers of the AFP or members of the Foreign Service; rank classification allows the government to use their talents "wherever they are most needed," since a developing country cannot afford to have scarce executive manpower "pegged to particular positions."

paras.html: IRP par. 5(c) and (e) only show that appointment to a CES rank differs from appointment to a CES position. "Appointments ... on the basis of rank" refers to appointment to rank, not to positions; membership in the CES comes with appointment to a class; salary and status follow rank; an Outstanding CESO may be promoted in rank while staying in the same position; reassignment cannot reduce rank or pay.

paras.html: Conclusion: appointment to rank confers security of tenure in the CES, while a permanent appointment to a CES position with the appropriate eligibility confers security of tenure in that position. Bacal acquired tenure in the CES as CESO III (1995) and tenure as Chief Public Attorney (1998). A contrary rule disrupts careerism in the CES.

paras.html: COA's power to audit is non-exclusive: The COA's power to examine and audit under Sec. 2(1), Art. IX-D is not exclusive, so a government bank may be audited concurrently by a private external auditor. In contrast, its authority under Sec. 2(2) to define the scope of its audit, promulgate accounting and auditing rules, and disallow irregular, unnecessary, excessive, extravagant, or unconscionable expenditures is exclusive.
paras.text: COA's power to audit is non-exclusive: The COA's power to examine and audit under Sec. 2(1), Art. IX-D is not exclusive, so a government bank may be audited concurrently by a private external auditor. In contrast, its authority under Sec. 2(2) to define the scope of its audit, promulgate accounting and auditing rules, and disallow irregular, unnecessary, excessive, extravagant, or unconscionable expenditures is exclusive.

paras.html: COA's audit is preponderant and cannot be taken away: COA's findings and conclusions prevail over those of private auditors "at least insofar as government agencies and officials are concerned," and bind them unless modified or reversed by the courts. Under Sec. 3, Art. IX-D, no law may exempt any government entity from COA's jurisdiction.
paras.text: COA's audit is preponderant and cannot be taken away: COA's findings and conclusions prevail over those of private auditors "at least insofar as government agencies and officials are concerned," and bind them unless modified or reversed by the courts. Under Sec. 3, Art. IX-D, no law may exempt any government entity from COA's jurisdiction.

paras.html: Central Bank supervision: The Central Bank's (now BSP's) constitutional power of supervision over banks includes examination and audit, so it has concurrent jurisdiction with COA to examine and audit government banks and may require them to hire independent auditors. COA's audit still prevails, and only COA may allow or disallow their expenditures.

The next day, he told the CB consultant that COA did not object to the proposed scope of audit services.

paras.html: Jan. 19, 1988: DBP sought reconsideration; no response came until the Aug. 29, 1988 letter-decision of the COA Chairman (first assailed decision), which denied the July 1, 1987 request and advised DBP to (1) desist from Cunanan's audit for the year ending Dec. 31, 1987; (2) refrain from paying for such services, citing Sec. 108, PD 1445 (personal liability for unlawful expenditures); and (3) restitute P513,549.24 within 30 days for the 1986 audit [the restitution figure differs from the P487,321.14 billing stated earlier; the decision does not explain the difference].

paras.html: Sept. 26, 1988: DBP appealed. May 20, 1989: The COA en banc denied the appeal (second assailed decision): CB Circular 1124 cannot bind COA; the Central Bank, not the World Bank, required the private audit; PD 2029 is an "anachronism"; and COA Circular No. 86-254 (Mar. 24, 1986) ordered that GOCC audits be undertaken "solely and exclusively" by COA.

paras.html: Commissioner Guingona proposed adding "exclusive" to par. (1); the ConCom rejected it and he withdrew the proposal.

paras.html: Commissioner Monsod explained: (1) the framers did not want an obstacle to private investment, since some government institutions have private (Filipino and foreign) investors who "require the presence of private auditing firms, not exclusively, but concurrently"; (2) private auditing may be required, e.g., for listing in the stock exchange; and (3) the provision should not obstruct privatization.
paras.text: Commissioner Monsod explained: (1) the framers did not want an obstacle to private investment, since some government institutions have private (Filipino and foreign) investors who "require the presence of private auditing firms, not exclusively, but concurrently"; (2) private auditing may be required, e.g., for listing in the stock exchange; and (3) the provision should not obstruct privatization.

paras.html: Guingona then proposed: "Private auditing firms may not examine or audit accounts ... pertaining to the Government ...," arguing that a private audit is a useless duplication and unnecessary expense. Rejected too.
