paras.html: Monsod: government agencies "sometimes borrow money from abroad"; precluding concurrent auditing would "unnecessarily [tie] their hands." "As long as the COA is there, and the COA's power cannot be eliminated ..., then the government funds are protected." Fees are negotiable, and the government "can always refuse to pay unconscionable fees."

paras.html: Qualified political agency: All executive and administrative organizations are adjuncts of the Executive Department; department heads are assistants and agents of the President, and their acts in the regular course of business are, unless disapproved or reprobated by the President, presumptively the acts of the President. This is a corollary of the power of control (Art. VII, Sec. 17); the President may delegate it to Cabinet members except where the Constitution or the situation requires personal action.

This is a corollary of the power of control (Art. VII, Sec. 17); the President may delegate it to Cabinet members except where the Constitution or the situation requires personal action.

paras.html: Delegated reorganization: The President's continuing authority to reorganize the national government (Sec. 20, Book III, Administrative Code; PD 1416 as amended by PD 1772) may be validly delegated to a Cabinet Secretary exercising control over the department. Thus the DENR Secretary may order the transfer of a regional office; the President's power to reorganize administrative regions under RA 6734 and EO 429 includes determining regional centers.

Torres: under this doctrine, which recognizes a single executive, all executive and administrative organizations are adjuncts of the Executive Department; department heads are assistants and agents of the Chief Executive; and, except where the Constitution or law requires the President to act personally or the exigencies demand it, the acts of the Secretaries in the regular course of business are, unless disapproved or reprobated by the Chief Executive, presumptively the acts of the Chief Executive.

paras.html: Declaring a national emergency vs. exercising emergency powers: The President alone may declare a state of national emergency (Sec. 18, Art. VII), even without a congressional enactment. But "the exercise of emergency powers, such as the taking over of privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest, is a different matter. This requires a delegation from Congress." Sec. 17, Art. XII is read in pari materia with Sec. 23(2), Art. VI, so the "State" in Sec. 17, Art. XII refers to Congress.

But "the exercise of emergency powers, such as the taking over of privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest, is a different matter. This requires a delegation from Congress." Sec. 17, Art. XII is read in pari materia with Sec. 23(2), Art. VI, so the "State" in Sec. 17, Art. XII refers to Congress.

paras.html: The calling-out power is the most benign power and is not martial law: PP 1017 is constitutional only insofar as it calls on the AFP to prevent or suppress lawless violence. The President "cannot invoke a greater power when he wishes to act under a lesser power"; the calling-out power cannot justify warrantless arrests, bans on assemblies, media takeovers or censorship, or the issuance of decrees.

paras.html: Review of the calling-out power: The Court may examine whether the power was exercised within constitutional limits or with grave abuse of discretion, but the standard is arbitrariness, not correctness, and the petitioner must show that the President's decision is "totally bereft of factual basis."

paras.html: On February 24, 2006, as the nation celebrated the 20th anniversary of EDSA People Power I, President Arroyo issued Proclamation No. 1017 (PP 1017) declaring a state of national emergency. Its operative portion reads:
paras.text: On February 24, 2006, as the nation celebrated the 20th anniversary of EDSA People Power I, President Arroyo issued Proclamation No. 1017 (PP 1017) declaring a state of national emergency. Its operative portion reads:

paras.html: "…by virtue of the powers vested upon me by Section 18, Article 7 of the Philippine Constitution… and in my capacity as their Commander-in-Chief, do hereby command the Armed Forces of the Philippines, to maintain law and order throughout the Philippines, prevent or suppress all forms of lawless violence as well as any act of insurrection or rebellion and to enforce obedience to all the laws and to all decrees, orders and regulations promulgated by me personally or upon my direction; and as provided in Section 17, Article 12 of the Constitution do hereby declare a State of National Emergency."
paras.text: "…by virtue of the powers vested upon me by Section 18, Article 7 of the Philippine Constitution… and in my capacity as their Commander-in-Chief, do hereby command the Armed Forces of the Philippines, to maintain law and order throughout the Philippines, prevent or suppress all forms of lawless violence as well as any act of insurrection or rebellion and to enforce obedience to all the laws and to all decrees, orders and regulations promulgated by me personally or upon my direction; and as provided in Section 17, Article 12 of the Constitution do hereby declare a State of National Emergency."

paras.html: The WHEREAS clauses cited a "tactical alliance" among elements of the political opposition, the extreme Left (NDF-CPP-NPA), and the extreme Right (military adventurists) to bring down the government; claims "recklessly magnified by certain segments of the national media"; harm to the economy; and a "clear and present danger" to the State.

paras.html: On the same day, the President issued General Order No. 5 (G.O. No. 5) implementing PP 1017. It called upon the AFP and the PNP "to prevent and suppress acts of terrorism and lawless violence in the country," and directed them "to immediately carry out the necessary and appropriate actions and measures to suppress and prevent acts of terrorism and lawless violence."

paras.html: Re: Standing in public suits
paras.text: Re: Standing in public suits

paras.html: Locus standi is "a right of appearance in a court of justice on a given question." Private suits follow the real-party-in-interest rule (Sec. 2, Rule 3). In public suits, the plaintiff sues as a representative of the public (as a "citizen" or "taxpayer") and must show sufficient interest in vindicating the public order.

paras.html: Re: Backdrop — political theorists on emergency power
paras.text: Re: Backdrop — political theorists on emergency power

paras.html: Locke (prerogative; the only remedy against abuse is "to appeal to Heaven"), Rousseau (temporary "supreme magistracy" of limited tenure), Mill (temporary dictatorship in extreme necessity), Machiavelli (standby emergency powers built into the constitution, with checks), and the "constitutional dictatorship" theorists Watkins, Friedrich, and Rossiter (e.g., the dictator should not decide when the emergency exists or ends).

paras.html: Scott and Cotter rejected "constitutional dictatorship" in favor of McIlwain's "constitutionalism": government should be limited, not weak; its two elements are legal limits to arbitrary power and political responsibility to the governed.

paras.html: The 1987 Constitution follows Justice Jackson's "balanced power structure" (Youngstown): each branch is supreme in its sphere, but none has a monopoly of power in times of emergency. In emergencies, the Constitution reposes faith in the Chief Executive but obliges him to operate within carefully prescribed procedural limitations.

paras.html: First, overbreadth is an analytical tool for testing statutes on their faces in free speech cases (US "First Amendment" cases). PP 1017 is not primarily directed at speech; it is a call on the AFP to suppress lawless violence, which is harmful, constitutionally unprotected conduct (U.S. v. Salerno; Broadrick v. Oklahoma).

paras.html: Second, facial invalidation is "manifestly strong medicine", used sparingly and only as a last resort. Ordinarily a litigant cannot challenge a law on the ground that it may conceivably be applied unconstitutionally to others; overbreadth departs from that rule only because of the chilling effect on third parties' speech (Younger v. Harris).

paras.html: Re 4.2: First provision — the calling-out power (Sec. 18, Art. VII) — VALID; NOT martial law
paras.text: Re 4.2: First provision — the calling-out power (Sec. 18, Art. VII) — VALID; NOT martial law

paras.html: Sanlakas: Sec. 18, Art. VII grants the President a "sequence" of graduated powers, from the most to the least benign: the calling-out power, suspension of the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus, and martial law. Citing IBP v. Zamora, the only criterion for calling out is "whenever it becomes necessary" to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion, or rebellion. Owing to her vast intelligence network, the President is in the best position to determine that necessity.

paras.html: The calling-out power involves ordinary police action. Every act beyond it is ultra vires: "He cannot invoke a greater power when he wishes to act under a lesser power… the greater the power, the greater are the limitations."

paras.html: Distinguished from Sanlakas: the "state of rebellion" there rested on the President's power as Chief Executive and on Sec. 4, Ch. 2, Book II [sic: Book III] of the Administrative Code (proclamations declaring "a status or condition of public moment"), so it was "harmless, without legal significance, and deemed not written." PP 1017 is more than that: it also invokes Sec. 17, Art. XII, an "awesome power" to take over private businesses, so it cannot be deemed harmless.

paras.html: The Court adopted the statement of Justice Vicente V. Mendoza (retired Justice) before the Senate Committee on Justice on March 13, 2006: martial law is the most severe threat to civil liberties and "strong medicine"; PP 1017 is no more than a call to the armed forces; and (a) warrantless arrests and seizures, (b) bans on public assemblies, (c) take-over of news media and press censorship, and (d) issuance of Presidential Decrees can be exercised by the Commander-in-Chief only under a valid declaration of martial law or suspension of the writ.

She cannot issue decrees, which are laws of the same category as statutes issued by Marcos under martial law under the 1973 Constitution.

paras.html: → PP 1017 is unconstitutional insofar as it grants the President authority to promulgate "decrees". Legislative power is peculiarly within the province of the Legislature (Sec. 1, Art. VI); "neither Martial Law nor a state of rebellion nor a state of emergency can justify" the President's exercise of legislative power.

paras.html: Since she cannot enact decrees, they are void and cannot be enforced. As to laws, she can only order the military, under PP 1017, to enforce laws pertinent to its duty to suppress lawless violence — not, e.g., customs laws, laws on family and property relations, or obligations and contracts.

paras.html: Sec. 17, Art. XII: "In times of national emergency, when the public interest so requires, the State may, during the emergency and under reasonable terms prescribed by it, temporarily take over or direct the operation of any privately-owned public utility or business affected with public interest."
paras.text: Sec. 17, Art. XII: "In times of national emergency, when the public interest so requires, the State may, during the emergency and under reasonable terms prescribed by it, temporarily take over or direct the operation of any privately-owned public utility or business affected with public interest."

paras.html: Why invoke it? PP 1017 purports to grant the President, without authority or delegation from Congress, the power to take over or direct private public utilities and businesses. The provision was first introduced in the 1973 Constitution, a product of the "martial law" thinking of the 1971 ConCon; Marcos's LOI No. 2 (1972) had the SND take over Meralco, PLDT, NAWASA, PNR, PAL, and others.

paras.html: A distinction must be drawn between the President's authority to declare "a state of national emergency" and to exercise emergency powers.
paras.text: A distinction must be drawn between the President's authority to declare "a state of national emergency" and to exercise emergency powers.

paras.html: (a) Declaring a state of national emergency — VALID. Sec. 18, Art. VII grants the President this power, so no legitimate objection arises. Sec. 23(2), Art. VI speaks of "war or other national emergency," but if the Framers meant to withhold the declaration of national emergency from the President and give it to Congress (as with the declaration of a state of war under Sec. 23(1)), they would have said so. → The President could validly declare a state of national emergency even without a congressional enactment.

paras.html: (b) Exercising emergency powers, such as the takeover — requires a delegation from Congress.

paras.html: Provisions in pari materia are construed together. Sec. 17, Art. XII and Sec. 23(2), Art. VI both relate to national emergencies.
paras.text: Provisions in pari materia are construed together. Sec. 17, Art. XII and Sec. 23(2), Art. VI both relate to national emergencies.

paras.html: Generally, Congress is the repository of emergency powers; Sec. 23(2) authorizes it to delegate them, and "a body cannot delegate a power not reposed upon it." Conditions for the delegation: (1) a war or other emergency; (2) a limited period only; (3) subject to restrictions Congress prescribes; and (4) exercised to carry out a national policy declared by Congress.

paras.html: Sec. 17, Art. XII is an aspect of the emergency powers clause; the takeover is "just another facet" of emergency powers generally reposed in Congress. → When Sec. 17 says "the State may… under reasonable terms prescribed by it," it refers to Congress, not the President. Whether the President may exercise it depends on a law delegating it and prescribing reasonable terms.

paras.html: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer: the US President's seizure of steel mills could not be sustained under the Commander-in-Chief power or the executive power; seizing private property to keep labor disputes from stopping production "is a job for the Nation's lawmakers, not for its military authorities"; the take-care power "refutes the idea that he is to be a lawmaker."

paras.html: Meaning of "emergency": Cacho-Olivares's view (tsunamis, typhoons) is too limited. "Emergency" connotes conditions suddenly intensifying the danger to life or well-being beyond what is normal, with elements of intensity, variety, and perception. In the US since 1933, emergencies have been economic, natural disaster, and national security. Under our Constitution, it may include rebellion, economic crisis, pestilence or epidemic, typhoon, flood, or other similar catastrophe of nationwide proportions.

paras.html: → PP 1017 does not authorize the President during the emergency to take over or direct private public utilities or businesses without authority from Congress. Without legislation, the President cannot (1) decide whether exceptional circumstances warrant a takeover, (2) determine when they have ceased, or (3) identify the businesses to be taken over. She has "no absolute authority to exercise all the powers of the State under Section 17, Article VII [sic: Art. XII] in the absence of an emergency powers act passed by Congress."

paras.html: Of the seven petitions, three show direct injury: David and Llamas (arrest), Cacho-Olivares/Tribune (raid), and KMU/NAFLU-KMU (dispersal). These injuries resulted from the implementation of PP 1017 pursuant to G.O. No. 5.

paras.html: PP 1017 is not invalidated by abusive implementation. Courts cannot declare statutes invalid merely because they may be abused; validity is judged by the general purpose and efficiency to accomplish the end desired, not by effects in a particular case. Nothing in PP 1017 allows the police, expressly or impliedly, to make illegal arrests or searches. Otherwise, given police blunders, "majority of the provisions of the Revised Penal Code would have been declared unconstitutional a long time ago."

paras.html: G.O. No. 5 is valid, except "acts of terrorism." General orders are "acts and commands of the President in his capacity as Commander-in-Chief," internal rules to subordinates that must be reasonable. G.O. No. 5 provides a valid standard: only "necessary and appropriate actions and measures" to suppress lawless violence.

paras.html: But unlike "lawless violence" (found in statutes and the Constitution), "acts of terrorism" is an amorphous, vague concept; Congress has yet to define and punish it. The international community also lacks an agreed definition ("One country's terrorist is another country's freedom fighter"). The word appears only in PD 1835, repealed by EO 167, and neither defines it.

paras.html: Without a definition, "it is President Arroyo alone… who has the discretion to determine what acts constitute terrorism", which may lead to indiscriminate warrantless arrests, raids, media takeovers, and dispersal of unfriendly assemblies (e.g., arresting people on a drinking spree as terrorists). These go beyond the calling-out power and violate the due process clause → the "acts of terrorism" portion of G.O. No. 5 is unconstitutional and deemed deleted.

paras.html: Sec. 2, Art. III: searches and arrests are normally unreasonable without a warrant. Neither exception in Sec. 5(a) or (b), Rule 113 applies: the arresting officers could only cite rallyists wearing "Oust Gloria Now" shirts and an erroneous belief that David led the rally. The inquest prosecutor released him; David was not even wearing the shirt, and wearing it would not suffice for inciting to sedition.

paras.html: Right to assembly (Sec. 4, Art. III): not to be limited except on a showing of clear and present danger of a substantive evil; not subject to prior restraint; a permit may be required only for the use of a public place, not for the assembly itself. David et al. were committing no crime; the charges were "mere afterthought"; even the SolGen could not justify the arrests. De Jonge v. Oregon: "Peaceable assembly for lawful discussion cannot be made a crime."

paras.html: KMU / NAFLU-KMU (171483) — dispersal and arrests unwarranted. They were dispersed merely on Malacañang's directive cancelling all permits. The wholesale cancellation of permits disregards that "tolerance is the rule and limitation is the exception" and eliminated the distinction between protected and unprotected assemblies; respondents did not show the rallyists committed lawless violence. Under BP 880, LGUs regulate rallies and may revoke permits only after due notice and hearing on clear and present danger; petitioners learned of the revocation only at the dispersal, a fatal defect.

paras.text: Daily Tribune (171409) — illegal search and freedom of the press.

paras.html: Undisputed facts: warrantless search; seizure of materials for publication; done at about 1:00 a.m.; with only the building's security guard present; policemen stationed nearby; followed by official warnings. This violated Rule 126, Secs. 4 (probable cause, one specific offense), 8 (presence of the occupant or two witnesses), and 9 (daytime service).

paras.html: It also violated press freedom. Burgos v. Chief of Staff: padlocking newspapers is prior restraint. Though the Tribune was not padlocked, the seizure of materials, the stationing of policemen, and the "arrogant warning" to media are "plain censorship". The Tribune was targeted for its anti-government stance. The motto should be obsta principiis.

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the Petitions are partly granted. The Court rules that PP 1017 is CONSTITUTIONAL insofar as it constitutes a call by President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo on the AFP to prevent or suppress lawless violence. However, the provisions of PP 1017 commanding the AFP to enforce laws not related to lawless violence, as well as decrees promulgated by the President, are declared UNCONSTITUTIONAL. In addition, the provision in PP 1017 declaring national emergency under Section 17, Article VII [sic: Art. XII] of the Constitution is CONSTITUTIONAL, but such declaration does not authorize the President to take over privately-owned public utility or business affected with public interest without prior legislation.

paras.html: Sec. 17, Art. XII is misplaced as a basis: it sits in the article on National Economy and Patrimony, so it presupposes a national emergency of an economic, not political, nature. "State" and "reasonable terms" can only pertain to Congress; the provision is not self-executing and merely declares an economic policy. A takeover without congressional authority is ultra vires. [This reading of "emergency" is narrower than the ponencia's.]

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to DISMISS ALL the petitions. The majority "has imprudently placed the Court in the business of defanging paper tigers" and ruled on non-justiciable issues based on fears that have not materialized. He agrees that PP 1017 is an exercise of the calling-out power and that declaring an emergency differs from exercising emergency powers.

The majority "has imprudently placed the Court in the business of defanging paper tigers" and ruled on non-justiciable issues based on fears that have not materialized. He agrees that PP 1017 is an exercise of the calling-out power and that declaring an emergency differs from exercising emergency powers.

paras.html: I. PP 1017 has no binding legal effect. Following his own ponencia in Sanlakas, a declaration like PP 1017 is "an utter superfluity" that only gives notice and is "devoid of any legal significance"; it cannot create or suspend rights. The calling-out power cannot vest new powers or authorize anyone to break the law; officers who commit illegal acts in its name may be held liable.

paras.html: The majority "grossly misreads" Sanlakas, which rooted the state-of-rebellion declaration in Secs. 1 and 18, Art. VII, not merely the Administrative Code. The calling out of the police derives from the Chief Executive and control powers, not the Commander-in-Chief clause, so the police may be directed to execute all laws. [sic: the opinion cites Sec. 17 for the Commander-in-Chief clause and Sec. 18 for control, apparently transposed.]

paras.html: Contrast with Marcos's PP 1081: it "placed" the country under martial law and ordered indefinite detention for a wide range of crimes; PP 1017 merely "declares." Calling them equivalent is "a rank insult" to martial-law victims.

paras.html: PP 1017 does not claim a power to issue decrees. Under noscitur a sociis, "laws and decrees" (separated by a comma from "orders and regulations promulgated by me") refers to existing Marcos decrees that still have the force of law. Striking the phrase is "killing a flea with dynamite when insect powder would do."

paras.html: PP 1017 is a valid exercise of inherent prerogatives of the President as head of state and "Chief Defender of the democratic way of life" (bully pulpit; Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation): it informs the people of an armed threat without suspending rights.

paras.html: II. Sec. 17, Art. XII. PP 1017 involved no actual takeover, so the discussion is obiter. He agrees that, as a general rule, takeover requires congressional approval (the provision does not say "by law," per Fr. Bernas; RA 6826 after the 1989 coup was enacted under Sec. 23(2), Art. VI). But the requirement is not absolute: in extreme situations where Congress cannot convene (e.g., bombs falling on Manila), the President may act, subject to judicial review. Araneta is inapplicable because it involved expired delegated powers.

paras.html: III. Vagueness is not limited to free speech cases. Citing his opinion in Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan, void-for-vagueness applies to penal statutes generally; overbreadth may be speech-only. The better ground is that PP 1017 creates no rights or obligations.

paras.html: IV. G.O. No. 5 has no infirmity. "Terrorism" has a widely accepted meaning covering acts already punishable under the RPC (rebellion, coup d'état, murder, arson). The majority's drinking-spree example applies equally to "lawless violence." Striking "terrorism" for vagueness after rejecting vagueness for PP 1017 is an inconsistency that "is breath-taking."

paras.html: V. The Court should not rule on individual grievances. Declaring the arrests and raid illegal makes the Court a trier of facts at first instance, without trial and without impleading the officers; it prejudges future cases and forecloses re-examining Umil v. Ramos (rebellion as a continuing crime). A declaration that PP 1017 cannot justify rights violations would suffice.

paras.html: VI. Conclusion: the decision will be seen as "an extended advisory opinion"; the issuances "are valid on their face, and should result in no constitutional or statutory breaches if applied according to their letter."

paras.html: The 90-day mandate: Sec. 4(1), Art. VIII ("Any vacancy shall be filled within ninety days from the occurrence thereof") imposes an imperative duty on the President; the framers confined Sec. 15 to the Executive Department because the JBC's prior, deliberate vetting eliminates the evils (vote-buying, Aytona-type midnight appointments) Sec. 15 targets.

paras.html: The JBC's duty: The JBC must submit its list before the vacancy so as not to shorten the President's 90 days. Its duty to submit is ministerial; its selection of nominees is discretionary. Only the President appoints the Chief Justice.

paras.html: The compulsory retirement of Chief Justice Reynato Puno on May 17, 2010 falls seven days after the presidential elections of May 10, 2010. Under Sec. 4(1) in relation to Sec. 9, Art. VIII, the vacancy "shall be filled within ninety days" from a JBC list of at least three nominees. Sec. 15, Art. VII, however, bars the President from making appointments "two months immediately before the next presidential elections and up to the end of his term," except temporary appointments to executive positions.

paras.html: Per practice, the JBC automatically considered the five most senior Associate Justices: Carpio, Corona, Carpio Morales, Velasco, and Nachura; Velasco and Nachura declined. paras.html: OSG: the incumbent President may appoint the next Chief Justice: prohibition cannot stop the JBC's principal function; nomination is a continuing process; Soriano misreads "Members of the Supreme Court"; mandamus lies to compel submission (ministerial) but not to dictate nominees (discretionary); Sec. 15 does not apply to the Supreme Court given the 90-day mandate and the framers' silence; even Valenzuela recognized exceptions; and compelling reasons exist (expected political cases; the Court as Presidential Electoral Tribunal; historical practice of immediate appointment).

paras.html: Intervenors-oppositors: Sec. 15 bans all appointments from March 10 to June 30, 2010; Valenzuela's exceptions are obiter; the Court can function without a Chief Justice; an Acting Chief Justice is provided for by Sec. 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948; appointing during the 45-day pre-election period is an election offense under the Omnibus Election Code; no list can be submitted before a vacancy; the JBC's nominating act is ministerial.

paras.html: The framers confined the ban to the Executive Department because they established the JBC, whose "unhurried and deliberate prior process" of screening ensures no midnight appointments to the Judiciary. The JBC's intervention eliminates the danger of vote-buying or partisan appointments; its creation was meant to de-politicize the Judiciary (replacing the CA's role). This insulation was absent in Aytona.

paras.html: The argument that 45 of the 90 days would remain after June 30 focuses only on this vacancy and assumes time will remain. Elections fall on the second Monday of May (May 8 to 14), so the ban lasts 109 to 115 days, longer than 90 days. There are thus at least 19 occasions when an outgoing President could not comply with Sec. 4(1). The framers could not have intended this absurdity; they never discussed Sec. 15 in relation to Sec. 4(1) because they never meant it to apply to the courts.

paras.html: Secs. 8(5) and 9, Art. VIII require the JBC to submit a list of at least three nominees for every vacancy. The 90-day period is directed at the President, not the JBC; hence the JBC should start before the vacancy and must submit the list in time for the President to appoint within 90 days. Submitting after the vacancy would shorten the President's period, which would be "unconscionable."

paras.html: Construction: the ponencia's logic backfires — had the framers meant to exclude the Judiciary, they would have written so in Sec. 15's exception. The ban makes no distinction (ubi lex non distinguit); its single exception is exclusive (expressio unius), reinforced by negative language; exceptions are strictly construed. Regalado's lone view cannot reverse a unanimous en banc Valenzuela; ConCom debates are secondary to the text as the people understood it.

paras.html: The Court can function without an appointed CJ: judicial power is vested in one Supreme Court, not the Chief Justice; 14 members remain, more than a quorum; the Court operates on "one member, one vote"; an Acting CJ is provided by law, tradition, and jurisprudence. The 90-day allowance itself rebuts the need to avoid even a day's vacancy.

paras.html: Mandamus and Sec. 12, Art. VII: Mandamus issues only for a well-defined, clear, and certain legal right and a ministerial duty. Sec. 12, Art. VII ("In case of serious illness of the President, the public shall be informed of the state of his health") does not make disclosure of the President's medical records a ministerial duty: per the ConCom deliberations, the burden is on the Office of the President to choose the appropriate means of releasing the information, and the state of health is "left to the President and his doctor."

VII ("In case of serious illness of the President, the public shall be informed of the state of his health") does not make disclosure of the President's medical records a ministerial duty: per the ConCom deliberations, the burden is on the Office of the President to choose the appropriate means of releasing the information, and the state of health is "left to the President and his doctor."

paras.html: Serious illness must be shown: The duty under Sec. 12 is triggered by serious illness. Claims based on online news articles are hearsay "twice removed" and without probative value; the President's visible performance of duties belies the claim. A petition failing to allege a prima facie case for mandamus may be dismissed outright.

paras.html: Re: Requisites of mandamus
paras.text: Re: Requisites of mandamus

paras.html: Mandamus commands one who (1) unlawfully neglects an act the law specifically enjoins as a duty, or (2) unlawfully excludes another from a right or office, with no other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy. It is an extraordinary remedy issued only in "extreme necessity" (City of Davao v. Olanolan).
paras.text: Mandamus commands one who (1) unlawfully neglects an act the law specifically enjoins as a duty, or (2) unlawfully excludes another from a right or office, with no other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy. It is an extraordinary remedy issued only in "extreme necessity" (City of Davao v. Olanolan).

paras.html: It will not compel anything that is not the official's duty, or give the applicant anything not entitled by law; the right must be "well defined, clear, and certain" (Uy Kiao Eng v. Lee; Pimentel III v. COMELEC).
paras.text: It will not compel anything that is not the official's duty, or give the applicant anything not entitled by law; the right must be "well defined, clear, and certain" (Uy Kiao Eng v. Lee; Pimentel III v. COMELEC).

paras.html: Cause of action: (1) the plaintiff's legal right; (2) the defendant's correlative obligation; and (3) the defendant's act or omission violating the right. It accrues only when the obligated party refuses to comply (PCA v. Primex).

paras.html: The incumbent President is immune from suit during his tenure: the immunity need not be written in the 1987 Constitution or in law; the framers omitted it because it was "understood in present jurisprudence" (Bernas, 1986 ConCom; David v. Macapagal-Arroyo).
paras.text: The incumbent President is immune from suit during his tenure: the immunity need not be written in the 1987 Constitution or in law; the framers omitted it because it was "understood in present jurisprudence" (Bernas, 1986 ConCom; David v. Macapagal-Arroyo).

paras.html: The Philippine immunity is unqualified while he holds office: unlike the US rule, it does not distinguish whether or not the suit pertains to an official act, and it does not hinge on the nature of the suit; it covers a petition for the writ of habeas data, and no balancing of interests applies.
paras.text: The Philippine immunity is unqualified while he holds office: unlike the US rule, it does not distinguish whether or not the suit pertains to an official act, and it does not hinge on the nature of the suit; it covers a petition for the writ of habeas data, and no balancing of interests applies.

paras.html: It attaches to the office and need not be invoked: the Court may dismiss the suit even without the President invoking it. Immunity is not non-accountability: the remedy is to wait until his tenure (not term) ends by resignation or removal through impeachment.

paras.html: Reply: immunity is not absolute; the cases cited for absoluteness (Forbes v. Chuoco Tiaco, Nixon v. Fitzgerald) predate the 1987 Constitution and are inconclusive on the incumbent's immunity. Direct resort to the SC was proper because the President has been collecting data on her and storing it in his office. As an aggrieved party, she deserves a judicial remedy.

paras.html: The immunity of the sitting President is absolute and extends to all suits, including amparo and habeas data petitions.

paras.html: Despite its non-inclusion in the 1987 Constitution, the framers intended the immunity to attach to the incumbent [sic: decision says "Section 17, Article VII of the 1973 Constitution"; the immunity provision it later quotes is Sec. 15, Art. VII].
paras.text: Despite its non-inclusion in the 1987 Constitution, the framers intended the immunity to attach to the incumbent [sic: decision says "Section 17, Article VII of the 1973 Constitution"; the immunity provision it later quotes is Sec. 15, Art. VII].

paras.html: Under David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, the President is immune from any civil or criminal case during his tenure; impeachment is the way to hold him accountable. Absolute immunity rests on public policy, so stare decisis applies absent compelling reasons.

paras.html: This suit is the very distraction immunity prevents; the President is the sole embodiment of the Executive, unlike the collegial Judiciary and Congress.

paras.html: Traced to Imperial Rome (Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis): princeps legibus solutus est (the emperor is not bound by statute) and quod principi placuit legis habet (what pleases the prince is law); revived in feudal Europe, especially England.

paras.html: Prof. Seidman: Roman, Church, customary, and feudal law fused into the maxim "the king can do no wrong," which has meant four things: (1) the King is literally above the law; (2) no remedy for royal wrongdoing through ordinary courts ("procedural" meaning); (3) the King has no capacity to do wrong (its true origin, Henry III being a minor); and (4) the King can do wrong but not lawfully.

paras.html: The US President can be served with judicial process: United States v. Burr (1807, Marshall, C.J.: subpoena duces tecum to Jefferson; the guard against vexatious subpoenas lies in the court's conduct after issuance); United States v. Nixon (1974: Nixon ordered to surrender the Watergate tapes; a general interest in confidentiality could not defeat the subpoena). But there is a dearth of precedent on suing an incumbent US President.

paras.html: By extent: absolute (actions within the scope of duties and discretionary, not ministerial; Butz v. Economou: only if essential to the conduct of public business → attaches to the function, not the office) vs. qualified (good-faith subjective test → Wood v. Strickland added the objective "should have known" test → Harlow v. Fitzgerald dropped the subjective test: (1) was the right clearly established at the time? (2) should the official reasonably have known the act was unlawful?).

paras.html: Security of a completed appointment: Once an appointment is issued and the appointee assumes office under a completed appointment, he acquires a legal, not merely equitable, right protected by statute and the Constitution; it cannot be taken away by revocation or removal except for cause, with previous notice and hearing. An accepted appointment cannot be withdrawn by the appointing authority; only the CSC may recall it, on grounds in its rules.

Abeja of Pagbilao, Quezon appointed 14 municipal employees between June 1 and June 27, 1995 (Registration Officer I, Bookbinder III, Accounting Clerks, Clerks, General Services Officer, Municipal Agriculturist, Bookkeeper II, Agricultural Technologist, Day Care Worker I, Utility Worker II, and Utility Foreman).

Abeja of Pagbilao, Quezon appointed 14 municipal employees between June 1 and June 27, 1995 (Registration Officer I, Bookbinder III, Accounting Clerks, Clerks, General Services Officer, Municipal Agriculturist, Bookkeeper II, Agricultural Technologist, Day Care Worker I, Utility Worker II, and Utility Foreman).

paras.html: Upon assuming office, petitioner Mayor Conrado de Rama issued Office Order No. 95-01 on June 30, 1995, recalling the 14 appointments — admittedly his very first official act, with no prior notice or hearing. By letter dated July 13, 1995, he asked the CSC to recall them, alleging they were "midnight" appointments in violation of Sec. 15, Art. VII.

paras.html: While pending, three employees (Marino, Ayala, and Oriasel) claimed their salaries, which De Rama withheld although CSC Field Director Gulim had declared their appointments permanent. The CSC Legal and Quasi-Judicial Division ordered payment (Rule V, Sec. 10, Omnibus Rules: an appointee who has assumed office is entitled to salary at once).

paras.html: April 30, 1996: The CSC denied the recall: the appointments were issued according to law, effective immediately, and could not be withdrawn by the appointing authority until disapproved by the CSC (Rule V, Secs. 9 and 10). Sec. 15, Art. VII prohibits only appointments by an outgoing President and cannot apply to local elective officials; "the appointing authority can validly issue appointments until his term has expired, as long as the appointee meets the qualification standards." The appointments were approved by the Head of the CSC Field Office in Lucena City, and De Rama presented no evidence warranting recall.

Sec. 15, Art. VII prohibits only appointments by an outgoing President and cannot apply to local elective officials; "the appointing authority can validly issue appointments until his term has expired, as long as the appointee meets the qualification standards." The appointments were approved by the Head of the CSC Field Office in Lucena City, and De Rama presented no evidence warranting recall.

paras.html: De Rama moved for reconsideration, arguing the CSC lacked jurisdiction to refuse the recall or to uphold the appointments, and that they were fraudulently issued. November 21, 1996: the CSC denied it, citing Aquino v. CSC (a completed appointment confers a legal right). He later filed a "supplement" alleging irregularities; the CSC found no new evidence.

They must set forth events that happened after the pleading supplemented; the alleged fraud and irregularities were contemporaneous with the appointments and should have been raised at the first opportunity.

paras.html: Midnight appointments are bad — whether by a President or a mayor — because they are hurried, without due deliberation, on the eve of departure; CSC attestation does not make them less odious. The outgoing executive retains the power to appoint until the last day, but appointments must be "few and so spaced as to afford some assurance of deliberate action" (Aytona).

paras.html: Legislature may abolish inferior courts, if done in good faith: The conceded legislative power of judicial reorganization includes the power to abolish existing inferior courts. "Nothing is better settled in our law than that the abolition of an office within the competence of a legitimate body if done in good faith suffers from no infirmity." As with offices in the other branches, so with the judiciary: "The test remains whether the abolition is in good faith."
paras.text: Legislature may abolish inferior courts, if done in good faith: The conceded legislative power of judicial reorganization includes the power to abolish existing inferior courts. "Nothing is better settled in our law than that the abolition of an office within the competence of a legitimate body if done in good faith suffers from no infirmity." As with offices in the other branches, so with the judiciary: "The test remains whether the abolition is in good faith."

paras.html: Abolition is not removal: "There can be no tenure to a non-existent office." From the standpoint of strict law, valid abolition does not impair the security of tenure of judges (Art. X, Sec. 7). But a mere change of name is not abolition (Brillo v. Enage, distinguished).

paras.html: Harmonizing reorganization with the SC's removal power: Because abolition has the same practical effect on incumbents as removal (a power vested in the SC), in implementing BP 129 "as far as incumbent justices and judges are concerned, this Court be consulted and that its view be accorded the fullest consideration." This is a saving construction in the body of the decision; the fallo only dismisses the petition.

paras.html: Background: the judicial reorganization
paras.text: Background: the judicial reorganization

paras.html: August 7, 1980: The President created the Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization (EO 611; amended by EO 619-A, September 5, 1980). Its task: formulate plans, within 70 days, giving the President "sufficient options for the reorganization of the entire Judiciary," covering all lower courts (CA, CFIs, City and Municipal Courts, all Special Courts) but excluding the Sandiganbayan.
paras.text: August 7, 1980: The President created the Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization (EO 611; amended by EO 619-A, September 5, 1980). Its task: formulate plans, within 70 days, giving the President "sufficient options for the reorganization of the entire Judiciary," covering all lower courts (CA, CFIs, City and Municipal Courts, all Special Courts) but excluding the Sandiganbayan.

paras.html: Membership: Chief Justice Fernando (Chairman), Minister of Justice Ricardo Puno (Co-Chairman), Justices Ramon C. Aquino and Ameurfina Melencio-Herrera, retired Justice Felix Q. Antonio, and Deputy Minister of Justice Jesus Borromeo.

paras.html: October 17, 1980: The Committee submitted its Report ("Proposed Guidelines for Judicial Reorganization"). It cited clogged dockets as a problem "of the utmost gravity" despite the SC's supervision of lower courts since 1973, and said reforms were "both pressing and urgent"; it would be the first major reform since the Judiciary Act took effect on June 16, 1901.

paras.html: Cabinet Bill No. 42 was drafted "substantially in accordance with" the Report's options, though some options were not adopted (e.g., instead of confining the intermediate appellate court to appellate work, its jurisdiction was increased to help the SC).

paras.html: "The provisions of this Act shall be immediately carried out in accordance with an Executive Order to be issued by the President. The Court of Appeals, the Courts of First Instance, [... and the other existing courts] shall continue to function as presently constituted and organized, until the completion of the reorganization provided in this Act as declared by the President. Upon such declaration, the said courts shall be deemed automatically abolished and the incumbents thereof shall cease to hold office." Pending cases, records, and personnel are transferred to the new courts.

paras.html: Petitioners — Judge de la Llana (Presiding Judge, Branch II, City Court of Olongapo) and seven members of the Philippine bar — filed a "Petition for Declaratory Relief and/or for Prohibition" with the SC to enjoin the Minister of the Budget, the COA Chairman, and the Minister of Justice from taking any action implementing BP 129.
paras.text: Petitioners — Judge de la Llana (Presiding Judge, Branch II, City Court of Olongapo) and seven members of the Philippine bar — filed a "Petition for Declaratory Relief and/or for Prohibition" with the SC to enjoin the Minister of the Budget, the COA Chairman, and the Minister of Justice from taking any action implementing BP 129.

paras.html: The Court considered it an action for prohibition. It noted (fn. 4) that declaratory relief should be filed in a CFI and that "there is no such proceeding known in constitutional law to declare an act unconstitutional"; courts declare acts unconstitutional only as an incident of deciding cases.

paras.html: Grounds: (1) BP 129 violates the security of tenure of judges (Art. X, Sec. 7) and judicial independence; (2) it was enacted arbitrarily, without good faith; (3) undue delegation to the President of the power to fix the new judges' compensation and to determine when the reorganization is deemed complete.

paras.html: Proceedings: SG Estelito Mendoza (assisted by ASG Reynato Puno) filed an Answer defending BP 129 as a legitimate exercise of the Batasan's power to reorganize the judiciary. A Supplemental Answer was filed on October 8, 1981, and petitioners' Reply on October 13. The case was heard on October 15, 1981 (morning and afternoon), with amici curiae (Sen. Lorenzo Sumulong, Dean Irene Cortes, the IBP, PBA, women lawyers' groups, the Trial Lawyers Association; memoranda from Sen. Jose W. Diokno and Atty. Ambrosio Padilla).

paras.html: Saving construction: between a construction that saves and one that invalidates a statute, the former is preferred; "the Constitution enters into and forms part of every act." Nuñez v. Sandiganbayan: provisions must be construed "to preclude any possible erosion on the powers vested in this Court by the Constitution." Precedent: PD 537 (Sec. 7) had the SC itself implement the conversion of Municipal Courts into Municipal Circuit Courts; BP 129 has no such provision, but "the spirit that informs it should not be ignored in the Executive Order" under Sec. 44. Tañada v. Cuenco (fn. 82): literal language not controlling if it would raise a constitutional objection.

paras.html: Harmonization: the Batasan is expressly vested with power to reorganize and abolish inferior courts; the practical effect resembles removal, now vested in the SC. "It is of the essence of constitutionalism to assure that neither agency is precluded from acting within the boundaries of its conceded competence." Citing Angara v. Electoral Commission (overlapping functions), Laurel in Planas v. Gil (quoting Holmes: no "watertight compartments"), and Tuason in Arnault v. Pecson. Without harmonization, "there could be a case of power against power. That we should avoid."

Given the presumptions of constitutionality and good faith, the Court can hardly speculate on legislative motives; good faith "must needs be granted." What must be reconciled is the implied power to abolish with the express tenure guaranty.

paras.html: Judges' tenure is broader than that of civil servants because the judiciary is a co-equal branch; the abolition cases (e.g., Manalang v. Quitoriano) involved executive employees. Dean Cortes: wholesale abolition opens the door to each ruling majority periodically reorganizing courts, making the judiciary "a veritable straw in the political wind," and would make every judge the President's appointee.

paras.html: Executive consultation with the SC: The President is under no obligation to consult the SC, and the SC "is not called upon to give legal advice to the President"; it cannot give advisory opinions (Bacolod-Murcia Planters' Asso. v. paras.html: Security of tenure covers the whole Civil Service: Art. XII, Sec. 4 of the 1935 Constitution ("No officer or employee in the Civil Service shall be removed or suspended except for cause as provided by law") protects officers in the unclassified as well as the classified service. Only positions that are policy-determining, primarily confidential, or highly technical are excluded, and appointments to these may be terminated at the will of the appointing officer.

paras.html: "For cause" means legal cause: reasons "which the law and sound public policy recognized as sufficient warrant for removal," relating to the administration of the office and of a substantial nature, not merely causes which the appointing power in the exercise of discretion may deem sufficient. The President's pleasure is not a cause.

paras.html: Quoting Dean Aruego (a Constitutional Convention member), as quoted with approval in *Lacson v. Romero*: the merit system eliminates the political factor in selecting civil employees and treats public office as a career open to all, not party patronage; the U.S. "spoils" system from Andrew Jackson's time undermined moral values and efficiency; the merit system "will be ineffective if no safeguards are placed around the separation and removal of public employees"; removal "for causes and in the manner provided by law" means bona fide reasons and a fair hearing, giving reasonable security of tenure.

Without ruling on the privilege, the petition alleges facts constituting threats: the 19 June 2020 PPOC meeting, where officers under respondent's command allegedly identified him and others, viewed with the killing of some of those identified, may, if true, justify the writ. The attached photos of the meeting and slides created a prima facie link to respondent and his subordinates.

paras.html: Third. Neither mere NGO membership nor inclusion in an order of battle equates to actual threats; what constitutes threats depends on the totality of each petitioner's circumstances.

paras.text: Re: Sec. 13, Art. VII and Civil Liberties Union

paras.html: Sec. 13, Art. VII bars the President, VP, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants from holding any other office during their tenure, unless otherwise provided in the Constitution.
paras.text: Sec. 13, Art. VII bars the President, VP, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants from holding any other office during their tenure, unless otherwise provided in the Constitution.

paras.html: CLU: the prohibition does not apply to posts held without additional compensation in an ex officio capacity as provided by law and as required by primary functions; these are additional duties, not "any other office." But the ex officio position is part of the principal office, so the official has no right to additional compensation; e.g., the Finance Secretary at the Monetary Board may not collect "any extra compensation, whether it be in the form of a per diem or an honorarium or an allowance, or some other such euphemism. By whatever name it is designated, such additional compensation is prohibited by the Constitution."

By whatever name it is designated, such additional compensation is prohibited by the Constitution."

paras.html: Nature and reviewability: Impeachment is a sui generis constitutional process that is primarily legal, with political characteristics (Decision); the Resolution calls it "a legal, political, and constitutional procedure." It is not a purely political proceeding, so the Bill of Rights, especially due process and speedy disposition, applies to the entire process. Constitutional issues involving impeachment may, in proper cases, be judicially reviewed; the Court does not determine when, who, and whether an impeachable officer may be removed.

paras.html: Initiation and the one-year bar (as amplified by the Resolution): The Art. XI, Sec. 3(2) periods (Order of Business within 10 session days; referral within 3 session days) are mandatory and ministerial. For this provision, a session day is a calendar day on which the House holds a plenary session. A first-mode complaint is deemed initiated when (a) referred to the Committee on Justice; (b) properly verified and endorsed but not included in the Order of Business or referred within the constitutional periods; or (c) properly verified and endorsed (or referred) but unacted upon at adjournment sine die. A second-mode complaint is initiated upon valid endorsement by at least one-third. There is no priority between modes, but the second mode is barred if pending first-mode complaints violated the constitutional periods.

A second-mode complaint is initiated upon valid endorsement by at least one-third. There is no priority between modes, but the second mode is barred if pending first-mode complaints violated the constitutional periods.

paras.html: Due process at initiation is sui generis: Sec. 3(4) does not exist in isolation and is subject to due process. Under the Resolution, the draft Articles must be accompanied by evidence meeting the quantum set by the House, made available to all members at plenary, and charge acts in relation to office during the current term; the respondent's full opportunity to be heard is at the Senate trial (relaxing the Decision's pre-transmittal hearing requirement).

paras.html: Charges: misuse of confidential intelligence funds, an assassination threat against President Marcos, Jr., and incitement to insurrection and public disorder.

paras.html: The fourth complaint was read as an Additional Reference of Business (3:37 p.m.) alongside the first three. The 36th session adjourned at 7:27 p.m., to resume June 2, 2025.

paras.html: Reckoning: the Constitution identifies none. Reading it as a whole and by its ordinary meaning (Padilla v. Congress; Francisco: initiation = filing and referral; Gutierrez Resolution: referring a barred complaint is GAD), "The one-year bar should be reckoned from the initiation of the impeachment complaint if unacted upon or when it is dismissed if it has been partially acted upon." It may also start upon a violation of the respondent's fundamental rights that ousts the House or Senate of jurisdiction.

paras.text: Due process safeguards the House must observe:

paras.html: (1) The charged acts must be committed during the term, fall under Art. XI, Sec. 2, and be sufficiently grave: for the President and VP, they must betray the trust of the electorate; for the others, undermine autonomy, independence, and impartiality; members of collegial bodies cannot be impeached for collegial decisions.

paras.html: (3) The respondent must have an opportunity to be heard on the evidence (not ex parte). paras.html: A strict reading would require referral to the Committee on Justice even for second-mode complaints. The Court rejected J. Villanueva's implied rewording (referral only for (a) and (b)). Instead: referral is mandatory for the first mode and optional for the second mode, and only for limited purposes: (1) to ensure the endorsements are verified; (2) to confirm the supporting evidence exists and every endorsing member received the complaint and evidence; (3) to respect the House's prerogative to consolidate complaints so only one is endorsed for transmittal.

paras.html: Nature and reviewability: Impeachment is a sui generis constitutional process that is primarily legal, with political characteristics (Decision); the Resolution calls it "a legal, political, and constitutional procedure." It is not a purely political proceeding, so the Bill of Rights, especially due process and speedy disposition, applies to the entire process. Constitutional issues involving impeachment may, in proper cases, be judicially reviewed; the Court does not determine when, who, and whether an impeachable officer may be removed.

It is not a purely political proceeding, so the Bill of Rights, especially due process and speedy disposition, applies to the entire process. Constitutional issues involving impeachment may, in proper cases, be judicially reviewed; the Court does not determine when, who, and whether an impeachable officer may be removed.

paras.html: Initiation and the one-year bar (as amplified by the Resolution): The Art. XI, Sec. 3(2) periods (Order of Business within 10 session days; referral within 3 session days) are mandatory and ministerial. For this provision, a session day is a calendar day on which the House holds a plenary session. A first-mode complaint is deemed initiated when (a) referred to the Committee on Justice; (b) properly verified and endorsed but not included in the Order of Business or referred within the constitutional periods; or (c) properly verified and endorsed (or referred) but unacted upon at adjournment sine die. A second-mode complaint is initiated upon valid endorsement by at least one-third. There is no priority between modes, but the second mode is barred if pending first-mode complaints violated the constitutional periods.

A first-mode complaint is deemed initiated when (a) referred to the Committee on Justice; (b) properly verified and endorsed but not included in the Order of Business or referred within the constitutional periods; or (c) properly verified and endorsed (or referred) but unacted upon at adjournment sine die. A second-mode complaint is initiated upon valid endorsement by at least one-third. There is no priority between modes, but the second mode is barred if pending first-mode complaints violated the constitutional periods.

paras.html: Due process at initiation is sui generis: Sec. 3(4) does not exist in isolation and is subject to due process. Under the Resolution, the draft Articles must be accompanied by evidence meeting the quantum set by the House, made available to all members at plenary, and charge acts in relation to office during the current term; the respondent's full opportunity to be heard is at the Senate trial (relaxing the Decision's pre-transmittal hearing requirement).

paras.html: (1) The charged acts must be committed during the term, fall under Art. paras.html: A strict reading would require referral to the Committee on Justice even for second-mode complaints. The Court rejected J. Villanueva's implied rewording (referral only for (a) and (b)). Instead: referral is mandatory for the first mode and optional for the second mode, and only for limited purposes: (1) to ensure the endorsements are verified; (2) to confirm the supporting evidence exists and every endorsing member received the complaint and evidence; (3) to respect the House's prerogative to consolidate complaints so only one is endorsed for transmittal.

paras.html: Resignation (Art. VII, Sec. 8): Resignation is a factual question; there must be intent to resign coupled with acts of relinquishment. No formal requirement applies: it may be oral or written, express or implied. Absent a resignation letter, it is determined by the "totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts and circumstantial evidence."

No formal requirement applies: it may be oral or written, express or implied. paras.html: Temporary inability (Art. VII, Sec. 11): Whether the President is unable to discharge his powers is committed to Congress; its recognition of the Vice President as President is a political question the Court cannot review. EDSA I (revolution, extra-constitutional) presented a political question; EDSA II (exercise of speech and assembly, intra-constitutional) presents legal questions.

paras.html: Presidential immunity: Incumbent Presidents are immune from suit during their tenure but not beyond. A non-sitting President enjoys no immunity from criminal prosecution for acts during incumbency (plunder, bribery, graft). Where the impeachment proceedings have become functus officio, conviction by the Senate is not a condition precedent to criminal prosecution.

paras.html: May 11, 1998: Estrada was elected President and Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (GMA) Vice President, for six-year terms beginning June 30, 1998.
paras.text: May 11, 1998: Estrada was elected President and Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (GMA) Vice President, for six-year terms beginning June 30, 1998.

paras.html: Oct. 4, 2000: Ilocos Sur Governor Luis "Chavit" Singson accused Estrada, his family, and friends of receiving millions from jueteng lords. Oct. 5: Senate Minority Leader Guingona delivered his "I Accuse" speech (₱220 million in jueteng money; ₱70 million in tobacco excise taxes for Ilocos Sur); referred to the Senate Blue Ribbon and Justice Committees. The House began investigations and impeachment moves.

paras.html: Calls for resignation followed: Cardinal Sin (Oct. 11), the CBCP (Oct. 13), former Presidents Aquino (Oct. 17) and Ramos. GMA resigned as DSWD Secretary (Oct. 12). Senior economic advisers and DTI Secretary Roxas resigned; Senate President Drilon, Speaker Villar, and 47 representatives left the ruling coalition.

paras.html: Nov. 13, 2000: Speaker Villar transmitted Articles of Impeachment signed by 115 representatives (over one-third) to the Senate. Nov. 20: the Senate impeachment court convened (21 senator-judges, CJ Davide presiding). Dec. 7: trial began. Clarissa Ocampo (Equitable-PCI Bank) testified that Estrada signed as "Jose Velarde" on a ₱500 million investment agreement.

paras.html: Jan. 16, 2001: by an 11–10 vote, the senator-judges refused to open the second envelope allegedly showing a ₱3.3 billion "Jose Velarde" account. Prosecutors walked out; Senate President Pimentel resigned; crowds gathered at the EDSA Shrine. Jan. 17: public prosecutors resigned and withdrew their appearance; the trial was postponed indefinitely.

paras.html: Jan. 19: AFP Chief of Staff Gen. Angelo Reyes withdrew the AFP's support, followed by the PNP; Cabinet officials resigned. Estrada had agreed to a snap presidential election in which he would not run (2:30 p.m.) and later agreed to open the second envelope.

paras.html: Jan. 20: negotiations for a "peaceful and orderly transfer of power" began at 12:20 a.m. at Malacañang (Angara, Bagatsing, et al. for Estrada; de Villa, Romulo, Perez for GMA). At noon, CJ Davide administered the oath to GMA as President at EDSA. At 2:30 p.m., Estrada and his family left Malacañang, issuing a press statement expressing "strong and serious doubts about the legality and constitutionality of her proclamation" but leaving "for the sake of peace and in order to begin the healing process of our nation."

paras.html: Baker v. Carr factors (textual commitment, lack of judicially manageable standards, etc.); Tañada v. Cuenco: political questions are those to be decided by the people in their sovereign capacity, or where full discretionary authority is delegated to the political branches — issues of wisdom, not legality. The 1987 Constitution narrowed the doctrine by expanding judicial review to grave abuse of discretion (Art. VIII, Sec. 1) and, e.g., Art. VII, Sec. 18.

paras.html: Lawyers League v. Aquino and related cases do not apply: the Aquino government came from a successful revolution installed "in defiance of" the 1973 Constitution (Freedom Constitution); its legitimacy was beyond judicial scrutiny. paras.html: Forbes v. Chuoco Tiaco (1910): the Governor-General cannot be personally mulcted in civil damages for official acts within (or honestly believed within) his authority; otherwise, matters of state would be delayed and distrust of government would follow. The 1935 Constitution had no immunity provision. The 1973 Constitution (1981 amendment), Art. VII, Sec. 17 granted immunity during tenure and, thereafter, for official acts, extended to those acting on his orders (Agabin: "absolute immunity defense syndrome").

paras.html: Courts cannot reverse the award of contest judges: "[T]he judiciary has no power to reverse the award of the board of judges of an oratorical contest." Neither would it interfere in literary contests, beauty contests, and similar competitions. Qualifier: this does not apply to activities the Government has chosen to regulate through the Games and Amusements Board (EO 392, s. 1950).

paras.html: No right to the prize before proclamation: A contestant has merely the privilege to compete, which does not ripen into a demandable right unless and until he or she is proclaimed winner by the appointed arbiters, referees, or judges.
paras.text: No right to the prize before proclamation: A contestant has merely the privilege to compete, which does not ripen into a demandable right unless and until he or she is proclaimed winner by the appointed arbiters, referees, or judges.

paras.html: Error is not wrong; damnum absque injuria: "Error and wrong do not mean the same thing." A "wrong" is the deprivation or violation of a right. If fraud or malice were proven, it would be a different proposition, but the action should then be against the individual judge or judges responsible, not the other judges.

paras.html: Elective officials – no exception: No elective official shall be eligible for appointment or designation in any capacity to any public office or position during his tenure. Unlike the second paragraph (appointive officials), the first paragraph of Sec. 7, Art. IX-B admits no exception ("unless otherwise allowed by law or by the primary functions of his position"), except those the Constitution itself recognizes (e.g., the President as head of the economic and planning agency, the VP as Cabinet member, a member of Congress as ex officio JBC member).
paras.text: Elective officials – no exception: No elective official shall be eligible for appointment or designation in any capacity to any public office or position during his tenure. Unlike the second paragraph (appointive officials), the first paragraph of Sec. 7, Art. IX-B admits no exception ("unless otherwise allowed by law or by the primary functions of his position"), except those the Constitution itself recognizes (e.g., the President as head of the economic and planning agency, the VP as Cabinet member, a member of Congress as ex officio JBC member).

paras.html: Power of choice is the heart of appointment: When Congress vests the appointing power in the President, it cannot at the same time limit his choice to only one candidate. Congress may prescribe qualifications, but qualifications that only one person can meet eliminate the President's discretion and are an irregular restriction on the appointing power.
paras.text: Power of choice is the heart of appointment: When Congress vests the appointing power in the President, it cannot at the same time limit his choice to only one candidate. Congress may prescribe qualifications, but qualifications that only one person can meet eliminate the President's discretion and are an irregular restriction on the appointing power.

paras.html: Ineligibility is not forfeiture: An elective official must resign first before he may be appointed. An appointment made while he is an incumbent is void, but he does not automatically forfeit his elective office, and he may be treated as a de facto officer whose acts are upheld and whose emoluments he may retain.

paras.html: Re: Limits on Congress
paras.text: Re: Limits on Congress

paras.html: When Congress clothes the President with the power to appoint an officer, it cannot at the same time limit the choice of the President to only one candidate. The conferment necessarily carries the discretion of whom to appoint.
paras.text: When Congress clothes the President with the power to appoint an officer, it cannot at the same time limit the choice of the President to only one candidate. The conferment necessarily carries the discretion of whom to appoint.

paras.html: Even on the pretext of prescribing qualifications, Congress may not divest the appointing authority, directly or indirectly, of his discretion. When the qualifications prescribed can only be met by one individual, the enactment eliminates the discretion to choose and constitutes an irregular restriction on the power of appointment.
paras.text: Even on the pretext of prescribing qualifications, Congress may not divest the appointing authority, directly or indirectly, of his discretion. paras.html: Distinguished from Sec. 13, Art. paras.html: Gordon remains Mayor of Olongapo City, and his acts as SBMA official are not necessarily null and void. He may be considered a de facto officer: one whose acts the law will hold valid so far as they involve the interest of the public and third persons, where the duties were exercised under color of an appointment void because the officer was not eligible, or under color of an appointment pursuant to a public unconstitutional law before it is adjudged to be such (Luna v. Rodriguez).

paras.html: The President and Congress act in tandem: Under Sec. 18, Art. VII, the President initiates the proclamation of martial law or the suspension of the writ, but only Congress can maintain it. Because congressional review is automatic, the Court must let Congress act first; the validity of the proclamation is "first a political question in the hands of Congress before it becomes a justiciable one in the hands of the Court." The Court steps in as the "final rampart" only when Congress defaults.

paras.html: Lifting before Congress acts moots the case: The withdrawal of Proc. 1959 after eight days, before the joint session could act and before it was meaningfully implemented, was a supervening event that obliterated any justiciable controversy. The exceptions to mootness did not apply, since the proclamation looked "more like saber-rattling than an actual deployment and arbitrary use of political power."

paras.html: The massacre and the state of emergency:
paras.text: The massacre and the state of emergency:

paras.html: On November 23, 2009, heavily armed men, believed led by the ruling Ampatuan family, gunned down 57 civilians on a highway in Ampatuan, Maguindanao, and buried them under shoveled dirt (the "Maguindanao massacre").
paras.text: On November 23, 2009, heavily armed men, believed led by the ruling Ampatuan family, gunned down 57 civilians on a highway in Ampatuan, Maguindanao, and buried them under shoveled dirt (the "Maguindanao massacre").

paras.html: Per the OSG's narration (quoted in J. Carpio's dissent): the convoy carried the wife and female relatives of Buluan Vice Mayor Esmael "Toto" Mangudadatu, lawyers, and media, on the way to file Mangudadatu's certificate of candidacy for Governor at the COMELEC office in Shariff Aguak. Mangudadatu had sent women and media believing they would deter an attack. About 100 armed men stopped the convoy at a PNP checkpoint and brought it to the hills of Brgy. Masalay; soldiers later found the bodies and three graves with a provincial-government backhoe nearby. Twenty-nine of the victims were media personnel; five victims were merely travelling on the same highway.

paras.text: Lifting of martial law:

paras.html: On December 12, 2009, before Congress could act, PGMA issued Proclamation 1963, lifting martial law and restoring the writ in Maguindanao, eight days after Proc. 1959. Its whereas clauses stated that over 600 persons who allegedly rose publicly had surrendered or been arrested, that the areas held by armed groups had been cleared, that the courts and prosecutors' offices of Cotabato City had resumed work, and that the ARMM Vice-Governor had assumed as Acting Governor. Proc. 1946 (state of emergency) remained in force.

paras.html: In Resolutions of December 8 and 15, 2009, the Court consolidated the petitions and required comment. The December 15 Resolution posed six questions: mootness after Proc. 1963; whether "rebellion" in Sec. 18 means Art. 134 RPC rebellion; whether martial law/suspension authorizes warrantless arrests; whether the power is joint and sequential with Congress; which prevails if the Court and Congress conflict; and whether the Court's ruling is essential to related acts during martial law. The OSG also raised standing.

paras.html: Impeachment is not beyond judicial review: Under the expanded judicial power (Sec. 1, Art. VIII), courts may review "questions which are not truly political in nature." The test is "whether there are constitutionally imposed limits on powers or functions conferred upon political bodies"; if there are, the courts are duty-bound to examine whether the branch acted within them. Art. XI, Sec. 3 imposes such limits (manner of filing, required votes, one-year bar). But what constitutes an impeachable offense is a truly political question left to Congress.
paras.text: Impeachment is not beyond judicial review: Under the expanded judicial power (Sec. 1, Art. VIII), courts may review "questions which are not truly political in nature." The test is "whether there are constitutionally imposed limits on powers or functions conferred upon political bodies"; if there are, the courts are duty-bound to examine whether the branch acted within them. Art. XI, Sec. 3 imposes such limits (manner of filing, required votes, one-year bar). But what constitutes an impeachable offense is a truly political question left to Congress.

paras.html: Meaning of "initiate": Under Sec. 3(5), Art. XI, impeachment proceedings are initiated by the filing of the impeachment complaint coupled with Congress' taking initial action on it, i.e., referral to the Committee on Justice (or filing by one-third of the House with the Secretary General). Once initiated, no other complaint may be filed against the same official within one year.

paras.html: Limits on rule-making: Congress' power to promulgate impeachment rules (Sec. 3(8)) is limited "to effectively carry out the purpose of this section"; rules that give "initiate" a different meaning are unconstitutional.

paras.html: November 28, 2001: The 12th Congress adopted new Rules of Procedure in Impeachment Proceedings. Rule V, Sec. 16 provides that proceedings are "deemed initiated": (a) for complaints filed by a Member or by a citizen with a Member's endorsement, on the day the Committee on Justice finds the complaint sufficient in substance, or on the date the House votes to overturn or affirm the Committee's finding of insufficiency; and (b) for complaints or resolutions filed or endorsed by at least one-third of the House, at the time of filing with the Secretary General. Sec. 17 bars another proceeding within one year from the date proceedings are "deemed initiated."

paras.html: Two differences: (1) Judicial review in the US is only impliedly granted and discretionary; ours is express, "not just a power but also a duty," and expanded to grave abuse by any branch. (2) The US Constitution gives the House the "sole power of impeachment" without limitation; ours, though giving the House the exclusive power to initiate, imposes limits in Sec. 3(2)–(5): manner of filing, required vote, and the one-year bar.

paras.html: Bernas: an impeachment proceeding is "a complexus of acts": the beginning (filing and referral to the Committee on Justice), the middle (deliberations), and the end (transmittal to the Senate). Under reddendo singula singulis, Sec. 3(1) concerns "cases" (brought to the Senate by the House's one-third vote), while Sec. 3(5) concerns "proceedings" (begun in the House). Equating the two is a misreading.

paras.html: The Court resolved on the merits only whether the proceedings transgressed the one-year bar; it did not assume jurisdiction where it had none or turn political questions into justiciable ones. The charge of "judicial supremacy" and of closing ranks to protect a brother is "patently without basis": "the fundamental issue is not him but the validity of a government branch's official act." "No one is above the law or the Constitution", but the Chief Justice also does not get "less in law than anybody else."

paras.html: Political question: The House's discretion covers its rules and what constitutes an impeachable offense (the latter bound by ejusdem generis with treason and bribery). But "when constitutional limits or proscriptions are expressed, discretion is effectively withheld"; who is impeachable, the votes needed, and the one-year bar are all reviewable. He cited Nixon (courts may review action transgressing "identifiable textual limits"), J. Souter's separate opinion there, Powell v. McCormack, and Turley.

paras.html: History: British legacy (Edward III, Henry IV); US Convention debates (Virginia Plan, Committee of Eleven, Madison's rejected proposal of SC trial); Nixon (Rehnquist: impeachment is the only check on the judiciary, so judicial review would be "counterintuitive"). Impeachment is dominantly political in England and the US.

Impeachment is dominantly political in England and the US.

paras.html: Philippine setting: impeachment is now a "commixture of political and judicial components", sui generis. Post-EDSA, the Constitution reconfigured impeachment with limits like Sec. 3(5) and expanded judicial power → the petitions concern the non-political aspect; it is a justiciable right of the Chief Justice (Casibang v. Aquino). He cited Angara, Bondoc, Arroyo v. HRET, Tolentino, and Macalintal v. COMELEC.

paras.html: Restraint v. activism: He traced the philosophies (Thayer, Frankfurter, majoritarianism v. minority rights). The 1987 Constitution adopted neither exclusively. The coordinacy theory holds that each branch has an independent duty to interpret the Constitution, so courts "listen to the voice" of the others without abdicating (Marbury).

paras.html: Why defer: (1) the House's "exclusive" and the Senate's "sole" powers are textual; (2) to stop the descent into a constitutional crisis (Alejandrino; Angara); (3) to avoid an "imperial judiciary," since legislators are co-guardians (Cardozo); (4) timing rests on prudence; the wrong timing "can negate the existence of our very jurisdiction." He quoted amicus Salonga: "this Court will eventually have jurisdiction but not yet."

Cruz; Romulo v. Yñiguez; Santiago v. Guingona; Montesclaros; Arroyo v. De Venecia). "[T]he jurisdiction of this Court is over the alleged unconstitutional Rules of the House, not over the impeachment proceedings."

paras.html: JDF and fiscal autonomy: Under PD 1949, the Chief Justice has sole power to disburse the JDF (80% COLA / 20% equipment) and COA, not Congress, audits it; COA had cleared the JDF. Congress' power of the purse cannot impair COA's exclusive audit power (Sec. 2, Art. IX-D) or the judiciary's fiscal autonomy (Sec. 3, Art. VIII; Bengzon v. Drilon).

paras.html: Seasonable but premature as to the Senate. Rejects the amici's exhaustion and primary-jurisdiction suggestions: the House was bent on transmittal; the Senate cannot rule on House rules (co-equal chambers); splitting the issues breeds conflicting decisions; primary jurisdiction attaches only upon transmittal; and no special expertise is needed. An unconstitutional measure "should be slain on sight" (J. I. Cruz in Fernandez v. Torres).
