paras.html: Purpose of Sec. 3(5) (Villacorta–Romulo; Muñoz-Palma): to prevent harassment and to let the legislature legislate. "Deemed initiated" is constructive initiation by legal fiction, whereas the Constitution refers to actual initiation. Subsecs. (1)–(5) apply to the House, (6)–(7) to the Senate, and (8) to both. The Senate is not called upon to review the House, and its action would itself disrupt legislative work.

paras.html: The power to impeach is executive in character, and the power to try is judicial. The 1987 Constitution introduced "conditionalities and limitations theretofore unheard of" which are mandatory (Tañada v. Cuenco). Compliance with constitutional limits on a delegated power is "invariably a justiciable controversy" (Gonzales v. COMELEC; Sanidad v. COMELEC; de Castro v. Committee on Justice (1985) conceded the outcome would differ had the 1973 Constitution laid down the procedure). Nixon is at most persuasive for Senate proceedings.

paras.html: "Initiate": the term first appeared in the 1973 Constitution (unicameral) and was retained "improper[ly]"; Sec. 3(1) "initiate" should be read as "impeach", distinct from Sec. 3(5). The 12th Congress Rules are a radical departure from prior Rules (which copied the Constitution) and allow "an infinite number of complaints", defeating the bar's purposes.

VII ban covers acting designations: The prohibition against Members of the Cabinet, their deputies, and assistants holding any other office applies to all appointments or designations, whether permanent or temporary. paras.html: Exceptions are strictly confined: Officials under Sec. 13 may hold another office only where the Constitution itself so provides (e.g., the VP as a Cabinet member; the SOJ as ex officio JBC member) or in an ex officio capacity (by law, required by the primary functions of the principal office, and without additional compensation). They cannot invoke the broader exceptions of Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B ("unless otherwise allowed by law or the primary functions of his position"). The positions of Secretary of Justice and Solicitor General are not ex officio to each other.

paras.html: Meaning of ex officio (CLU): "from office; by virtue of office"; authority annexed to the official position, exercised "without any other appointment or authority other than that conferred by the office"; an ex officio member serves "without further warrant or appointment." Because the ex officio position is part of the principal office, the official has no right to additional compensation.

paras.html: Because of Sec. 13, Agra did not validly hold the position of Acting SOJ concurrently with Acting SolGen, so he was not a de jure officer for his entire tenure as Acting SOJ. A de jure officer is one deemed in all respects legally appointed and qualified and whose term has not expired (Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: CLU: officials in the questioned positions may be considered de facto officers and are entitled to emoluments for actual services rendered. Where there is no de jure officer, a de facto officer who in good faith possessed the office and discharged its duties may recover its salary, since "it seems unjust that the public should benefit by the services of an officer de facto and then be freed from all liability to pay."

paras.html: A de facto officer derives his appointment from one having colorable authority to appoint, and the appointment is valid on its face (Dimaandal v. COA). He may also be one in possession of an office and discharging its duties under color of authority, i.e., authority from an appointment however irregular or informal, so that he is not a mere volunteer (CSC v. Joson, Jr.).

paras.html: Hence, the acts of a de facto officer are as valid for all purposes as those of a de jure officer, insofar as the public or third persons are concerned (Mechem; Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the Court GRANTS the petition for certiorari and prohibition; ANNULS AND VOIDS the designation of Hon. Alberto C. Agra as the Acting Secretary of Justice in a concurrent capacity with his position as the Acting Solicitor General for being unconstitutional and violative of Section 13, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution; and DECLARES that Hon. Alberto C. Agra was a de facto officer during his tenure as Acting Secretary of Justice. No pronouncement on costs of suit. SO ORDERED.

Alberto C. Agra was a de facto officer during his tenure as Acting Secretary of Justice. No pronouncement on costs of suit. SO ORDERED.

paras.html: The Sec. 13, Art. VII ban covers acting designations: The prohibition against Members of the Cabinet, their deputies, and assistants holding any other office applies to all appointments or designations, whether permanent or temporary. "To hold an office" means to possess or occupy it, which implies the actual discharge of its functions and duties; Sec. 13 makes no reference to the nature of the appointment.
paras.text: The Sec. 13, Art. VII ban covers acting designations: The prohibition against Members of the Cabinet, their deputies, and assistants holding any other office applies to all appointments or designations, whether permanent or temporary. "To hold an office" means to possess or occupy it, which implies the actual discharge of its functions and duties; Sec. 13 makes no reference to the nature of the appointment.

paras.html: Exceptions are strictly confined: Officials under Sec. 13 may hold another office only where the Constitution itself so provides (e.g., the VP as a Cabinet member; the SOJ as ex officio JBC member) or in an ex officio capacity (by law, required by the primary functions of the principal office, and without additional compensation). They cannot invoke the broader exceptions of Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B ("unless otherwise allowed by law or the primary functions of his position"). The positions of Secretary of Justice and Solicitor General are not ex officio to each other.

paras.html: De facto officer doctrine: One whose concurrent designation is void is not a de jure officer, but is a de facto officer whose official acts are valid and binding as to the public and third persons.

Executive Secretary: other appointive officials may hold other offices when allowed by law or their primary functions, but Cabinet members, their deputies, and assistants may do so only when expressly authorized by the Constitution itself. paras.html: Because of Sec. 13, Agra did not validly hold the position of Acting SOJ concurrently with Acting SolGen, so he was not a de jure officer for his entire tenure as Acting SOJ. A de jure officer is one deemed in all respects legally appointed and qualified and whose term has not expired (Topacio v. Ong).
paras.text: Because of Sec. 13, Agra did not validly hold the position of Acting SOJ concurrently with Acting SolGen, so he was not a de jure officer for his entire tenure as Acting SOJ. A de jure officer is one deemed in all respects legally appointed and qualified and whose term has not expired (Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: CLU: officials in the questioned positions may be considered de facto officers and are entitled to emoluments for actual services rendered. Where there is no de jure officer, a de facto officer who in good faith possessed the office and discharged its duties may recover its salary, since "it seems unjust that the public should benefit by the services of an officer de facto and then be freed from all liability to pay."
paras.text: CLU: officials in the questioned positions may be considered de facto officers and are entitled to emoluments for actual services rendered. Where there is no de jure officer, a de facto officer who in good faith possessed the office and discharged its duties may recover its salary, since "it seems unjust that the public should benefit by the services of an officer de facto and then be freed from all liability to pay."

paras.html: A de facto officer derives his appointment from one having colorable authority to appoint, and the appointment is valid on its face (Dimaandal v. COA). He may also be one in possession of an office and discharging its duties under color of authority, i.e., authority from an appointment however irregular or informal, so that he is not a mere volunteer (CSC v. Joson, Jr.).

paras.html: Hence, the acts of a de facto officer are as valid for all purposes as those of a de jure officer, insofar as the public or third persons are concerned (Mechem; Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: Members of the Constitutional Commissions fall under the general rule: Not being Cabinet officials, they are covered by Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B rather than Sec. 13, Art. VII, so they may hold another office or employment if allowed by law or by the primary functions of their position. An ex officio post is valid only if it is derived from the primary functions of the principal office and carries no additional compensation. Hence, Sec. 14, Ch. 3, Title I-A, Book V, EO 292 (CSC Chairman sits on boards of entities affecting the career and welfare of government employees) is constitutional.

paras.html: Jun. 6, 2011: RA 10149 (GOCC Governance Act of 2011) took effect. Sec. 13 maintains the number of directors/trustees under the charters; Sec. 14 allows ex officio members to designate alternates; Sec. 15 requires appointive directors to be appointed by the President from a GCG shortlist; Sec. 17 sets one-year terms and gives incumbent appointive board members a term only until Jun. 30, 2011. paras.html: Sec. 1, Art. IX-A expressly describes the Commissions as "independent." Although their functions are essentially executive, they are not under the control of the President. Each conducts its own proceedings under its own rules and discretion, and its decisions are subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A; Brillantes, Jr. v. Yorac).

Each conducts its own proceedings under its own rules and discretion, and its decisions are subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A; Brillantes, Jr. v. Yorac).

paras.html: To safeguard independence, Sec. 2, Art. IX-A imposes disqualifications on the Chairmen and members: (a) holding any other office or employment during their tenure; (b) practicing any profession; (c) actively managing or controlling a business that may be affected by their functions; and (d) being financially interested in any government contract, franchise, or privilege. This case involves (a).

paras.html: A de jure officer is one deemed in all respects legally appointed and qualified and whose term has not expired (Topacio v. Ong).
paras.text: A de jure officer is one deemed in all respects legally appointed and qualified and whose term has not expired (Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: CLU: officials in the questioned positions may be considered de facto officers entitled to emoluments for actual services rendered; "[a]ny per diem, allowances or other emoluments received . . . by virtue of actual services rendered in the questioned positions may therefore be retained." [Quoted by the Court; the decision does not separately rule on Duque's per diems.]

paras.html: A de facto officer derives his appointment from one with colorable authority and the appointment is valid on its face (Dimaandal v. COA), or possesses the office and discharges its duties under color of authority, so that he is not a mere volunteer (CSC v. Joson, Jr.). His acts are as valid as those of a de jure officer insofar as the public or third persons are concerned (Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the petition is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The Court UPHOLDS THE CONSTITUTIONALITY of Section 14, Chapter 3, Title I-A, Book V of Executive Order No. 292; ANNULS AND VOIDS Executive Order No. 864 dated February 22, 2010 and the designation of Hon. Francisco T. Duque III as a Member of the Board of Directors/Trustees of the Government Service Insurance System; Philippine Health Insurance Corporation; Employees Compensation Commission; and Home Development Mutual Fund in an ex officio capacity in relation to his appointment as Chairman of the Civil Service Commission for being UNCONSTITUTIONAL AND VIOLATIVE of Sections 1 and 2, Article IX-A of the 1987 Constitution; and DECLARES that Hon. Francisco T. Duque III was a de facto officer during his tenure as Director/Trustee of the GSIS, PhilHealth, ECC, and HDMF. No pronouncement on costs of suit. SO ORDERED.

paras.html: Members of the Constitutional Commissions fall under the general rule: Not being Cabinet officials, they are covered by Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B rather than Sec. 13, Art. VII, so they may hold another office or employment if allowed by law or by the primary functions of their position. An ex officio post is valid only if it is derived from the primary functions of the principal office and carries no additional compensation. Hence, Sec. 14, Ch. 3, Title I-A, Book V, EO 292 (CSC Chairman sits on boards of entities affecting the career and welfare of government employees) is constitutional.

paras.html: Sec. 1, Art. IX-A expressly describes the Commissions as "independent." Although their functions are essentially executive, they are not under the control of the President. Each conducts its own proceedings under its own rules and discretion, and its decisions are subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A; Brillantes, Jr. v. Yorac).
paras.text: Sec. 1, Art. IX-A expressly describes the Commissions as "independent." Although their functions are essentially executive, they are not under the control of the President. Each conducts its own proceedings under its own rules and discretion, and its decisions are subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A; Brillantes, Jr. v. Yorac).

paras.html: To safeguard independence, Sec. 2, Art. IX-A imposes disqualifications on the Chairmen and members: (a) holding any other office or employment during their tenure; (b) practicing any profession; (c) actively managing or controlling a business that may be affected by their functions; and (d) being financially interested in any government contract, franchise, or privilege. This case involves (a).

paras.html: The Court also listed, citing Nachura, the other features that ensure independence: constitutional creation (not abolishable by statute); express independence; powers not reducible by statute; removal only by impeachment; seven-year terms; no reappointment or acting appointments; salaries not decreased; fiscal autonomy; own procedural rules; disqualifications; and power to appoint their own personnel.

Sec. 7, Art. IX-B is the general rule; Sec. 13, Art. VII is the exception for the President, VP, Cabinet members, and their deputies and assistants.

paras.html: Ex officio (CLU): "from office; by virtue of office"; authority annexed to the official position; membership "by virtue of his title to a certain office, and without further warrant or appointment". Because the ex officio position is part of the principal office, the official has no right to additional compensation; his services are already paid by the compensation of the principal office.

paras.html: Rufino v. Endriga: every government office must fall under one of the three branches, the independent constitutional bodies, a quasi-judicial body, or an LGU. The President's control applies to all officers of the Executive branch, whoever appointed them; control means the power to revise or reverse their discretionary acts. "The Executive branch is unitary"; an executive office not under the President's control is a "lost command" without legal or constitutional basis.

His acts are as valid as those of a de jure officer insofar as the public or third persons are concerned (Topacio v. Ong).

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the petition is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The Court UPHOLDS THE CONSTITUTIONALITY of Section 14, Chapter 3, Title I-A, Book V of Executive Order No. 292; ANNULS AND VOIDS Executive Order No. 864 dated February 22, 2010 and the designation of Hon. Francisco T. Duque III as a Member of the Board of Directors/Trustees of the Government Service Insurance System; Philippine Health Insurance Corporation; Employees Compensation Commission; and Home Development Mutual Fund in an ex officio capacity in relation to his appointment as Chairman of the Civil Service Commission for being UNCONSTITUTIONAL AND VIOLATIVE of Sections 1 and 2, Article IX-A of the 1987 Constitution; and DECLARES that Hon. Francisco T. Duque III was a de facto officer during his tenure as Director/Trustee of the GSIS, PhilHealth, ECC, and HDMF. No pronouncement on costs of suit. SO ORDERED.

paras.html: COA audit of non-governmental entities is limited: Under Sec. 29(1) of PD 1445 (reproduced in Sec. 14(1), Book V of the Administrative Code), COA's visitorial authority over non-governmental entities "required to pay levies or have government share" pertains only to the audit of "funds . . . coming from or through the government." MECO's verification fees (collected for DOLE) and consular fees (under Sec. 2(6), EO 15) are such funds.

paras.html: Three attributes of a GOCC: (1) organization as a stock or non-stock corporation; (2) public character of its function; and (3) government ownership. Possession of all three is necessary. In a non-stock corporation, government control exists when "at least majority of the members are government officials holding such membership by appointment or designation" (Liban v. Gordon) or there is "substantial participation of the government in the selection" of the governing board (Boy Scouts v. NLRC).

paras.html: Background: One China and the MECO
paras.text: Background: One China and the MECO

paras.html: After the Chinese civil war, two governments claimed sovereignty over China: the communist People's Republic of China (PROC) on the mainland and the nationalist Republic of China (ROC) on Taiwan. After UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 (1971), most states shifted recognition to the PROC.
paras.text: After the Chinese civil war, two governments claimed sovereignty over China: the communist People's Republic of China (PROC) on the mainland and the nationalist Republic of China (ROC) on Taiwan. After UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 (1971), most states shifted recognition to the PROC.

paras.html: On 9 June 1975, the Philippines and the PROC signed the Joint Communiqué. The Philippines recognized the PROC as "the sole legal government of China", respected its position that Taiwan is an integral part of Chinese territory, and undertook to remove all its official representations from Taiwan within one month.
paras.text: On 9 June 1975, the Philippines and the PROC signed the Joint Communiqué. The Philippines recognized the PROC as "the sole legal government of China", respected its position that Taiwan is an integral part of Chinese territory, and undertook to remove all its official representations from Taiwan within one month.

paras.html: The One China commitment did not bar unofficial, "people-to-people" relations with Taiwan, but these had to pass through offices outside the official organs: the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (for Taiwan) and the MECO (for the Philippines).
paras.text: The One China commitment did not bar unofficial, "people-to-people" relations with Taiwan, but these had to pass through offices outside the official organs: the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (for Taiwan) and the MECO (for the Philippines).

paras.html: MECO (originally Asian Exchange Center, Inc.; renamed MECO on 1 January 1993) is a non-stock, non-profit corporation under BP 68 (Corporation Code), incorporated on 16 December 1977. [sic: the Prelude says "16 December 1997"; the Court later says 1977, which fits the 1993 renaming.] Its purposes include developing the commercial and industrial interests of Filipinos, receiving grants and subsidies, and acquiring property.

paras.html: MECO was "entrusted" by the government with fostering "friendly" and "unofficial" relations with the people of Taiwan (trade, investment, culture, science, education), and "authorized" to perform "consular and other functions". Today it oversees OFWs in Taiwan, promotes the Philippines to Taiwanese tourists and investors, and facilitates travel between the two.

paras.html: EO 15, s. 2001 (16 May 2001): Sec. 1 authorizes MECO to assist in investment promotion, export and manpower promotion, negotiation of people-to-people agreements, and cultural exchanges. Sec. 2 authorizes its Taiwan offices to issue visas and passports, authenticate documents, provide translation, assist Filipinos in Taiwan, and collect "reasonable fees" on the first four functions "to defray the cost of its operations" (Sec. 2(6)).

paras.html: Courts decide otherwise moot cases if: (1) there is a grave violation of the Constitution; (2) the situation is exceptional and paramount public interest is involved; (3) the constitutional issue requires formulation of controlling principles to guide the bench, the bar, and the public; and (4) the case is capable of repetition yet evading review.

paras.html: First, the petition makes a serious allegation that COA was remiss in its constitutional or legal duty to audit an otherwise auditable entity.
paras.text: First, the petition makes a serious allegation that COA was remiss in its constitutional or legal duty to audit an otherwise auditable entity.

paras.html: Second, there is paramount public interest in whether COA failed to audit MECO, since it determines whether COA faithfully fulfilled its role as "guardian of the public treasury," in which any citizen has an interest.

paras.html: Third, there is paramount public interest in the legal status of MECO, "a novelty" in jurisprudence, which bears directly on the country's One China commitment. (The Court took its cue from DFA Sec. Del Rosario's 24 May 2011 letter objecting to including MECO as a GICP in the bills that became RA 10149, because official status would contravene MECO's purpose and hurt relations with China and Taiwan.)

paras.html: Government instrumentalities are agencies of the national government that, by reason of some "special function or jurisdiction," are allotted "operational autonomy" and are "not integrated within the department framework" (Sec. 2(10), Introductory Provisions, Administrative Code). They include: (1) regulatory agencies; (2) chartered institutions; (3) government corporate entities or government instrumentalities with corporate powers (GCE/GICP); and (4) GOCCs.
paras.text: Government instrumentalities are agencies of the national government that, by reason of some "special function or jurisdiction," are allotted "operational autonomy" and are "not integrated within the department framework" (Sec. 2(10), Introductory Provisions, Administrative Code). They include: (1) regulatory agencies; (2) chartered institutions; (3) government corporate entities or government instrumentalities with corporate powers (GCE/GICP); and (4) GOCCs.

paras.html: GOCC (Sec. 2(13), Administrative Code; replicated in Sec. 3(o), RA 10149, GOCC Governance Act of 2011): any agency organized as a stock or non-stock corporation, vested with functions relating to public needs, whether governmental or proprietary, and owned by the government directly or through its instrumentalities, wholly or, for stock corporations, to the extent of at least 51% / a majority of the capital stock.
paras.text: GOCC (Sec. 2(13), Administrative Code; replicated in Sec. 3(o), RA 10149, GOCC Governance Act of 2011): any agency organized as a stock or non-stock corporation, vested with functions relating to public needs, whether governmental or proprietary, and owned by the government directly or through its instrumentalities, wholly or, for stock corporations, to the extent of at least 51% / a majority of the capital stock.

IX-D gives COA the "power, authority and duty" to "examine, audit and settle" the "accounts" (revenue, receipts, expenditures, uses of funds and property) of: (1) the government, its subdivisions, agencies and instrumentalities; (2) GOCCs with original charters; (3) GOCCs without original charters; (4) constitutional bodies, commissions and offices with fiscal autonomy; and (5) non-governmental entities receiving subsidy or equity, directly or indirectly, from or through the government, which are required by law or the granting institution to submit to COA audit as a condition of subsidy or equity. [The Court's list omits item (b) of the provision, autonomous state colleges and universities.]

paras.html: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.
paras.text: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.

paras.html: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.
paras.text: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.

paras.html: Meaning of "reappointment." "Reappointment" means a second appointment to one and the same office (Sibal, citing Visarra). J. Dizon, dissenting in Visarra v. Miraflor: the ban refers to a second appointment to the same office; an occupant needs no second appointment unless he ceased to be the legal occupant. → A promotion, albeit entailing a second appointment, involves a different office and is not, strictly, a reappointment. J. Bautista, concurring in Visarra, likewise viewed a promotional appointment as not prohibited under the 1935 Constitution.

paras.html: No textual restriction? The command is that members are appointed "for a term of seven years" and appointment to a vacancy "shall be only for the unexpired portion." The President has two and only two options: a full seven years for a vacancy by expiration, or the unexpired term for a vacancy by death, disability, resignation, or impeachment. Otherwise the President could "trifle with terms of office fixed by the Constitution."

paras.html: Garcia precedent (1959). The promotion of COMELEC Commissioner Garcia to succeed Chairman Carag upon expiration of the latter's term, under the 1935 Constitution, is not a precedent under the 1987 Constitution. That it went uncontested does not matter: "the promotion in question was either legal or it was not. If it were not, no amount of repetitive practices would clear it of invalidating taint."

paras.html: Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D, 1987 Constitution: "The Chairman and Commissioners shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years without reappointment. Of those first appointed, the Chairman shall hold office for seven years, one Commissioner for five years, and the other Commissioner for three years, without reappointment. Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor. In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity." The identical rule governs the CSC and COMELEC.

paras.html: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.
paras.text: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.

paras.html: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.
paras.text: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.

paras.html: Aggregate seven-year limit; Matibag abandoned in part: No one may serve in the Commission, as Chairman, Commissioner, or both, for an aggregate of more than seven years. The fourth situation in Matibag v. Benipayo (barring the reappointment of one who served less than seven years to an unexpired term) is obiter and is abandoned.

paras.html: A case is moot when its purpose has become stale or it ceases to present a justiciable controversy owing to supervening events, so that a resolution would be of no practical value. As a general rule, the Court does not decide moot cases.

paras.html: David v. Macapagal-Arroyo: the Court decides otherwise moot cases if (1) there is a grave violation of the Constitution; (2) the situation is of exceptional character and paramount public interest is involved; (3) the constitutional issue requires formulation of controlling principles to guide the bench, the bar, and the public; and (4) the case is capable of repetition yet evading review.

paras.html: First set of commissioners. Their terms (seven, five, and three years) have expired and matter only in understanding the rotational plan. Gaminde v. COA: their terms start on a common date (Feb. 2, 1987) regardless of the dates of appointment, so the two-year interval recurs regularly; in a belated appointment, the delay is counted against the appointee.

paras.html: Republic v. Imperial: two conditions are indispensable to the rotational plan: (a) the first terms start on a common date; and (b) a vacancy from death, resignation, or disability is filled only for the unexpired balance. Its purpose: to prevent a four-year administration from appointing more than one permanent commissioner, or, per CONCOM Commissioner Monsod, "to prevent one person (the President of the Philippines) from dominating the commissions"; it also ensures continuity and independence.

paras.html: Vacancy by expiration vs. other causes. An appointment to a vacancy from expiration of a term is for seven years. There is an unexpired portion only when, because of death, disability, resignation, or impeachment, a sitting member cannot complete the term. Where the vacancy is from expiration, "there is technically no unexpired portion to speak of."

paras.html: CONCOM deliberations. Commissioner Aquino proposed that "the appointee shall in no case serve an aggregate period of more than seven years," thinking of a commissioner upgraded to chairman; Commissioner Monsod answered "It is covered"; Commissioner Foz explained that under the unexpired-portion clause, "if there is upgrading of position from commissioner to chairman, the appointee can serve only the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor", and "He takes it at his own risk."

paras.html: Meaning of "reappointment." "Reappointment" means a second appointment to one and the same office (Sibal, citing Visarra). J. Dizon, dissenting in Visarra v. Miraflor: the ban refers to a second appointment to the same office; an occupant needs no second appointment unless he ceased to be the legal occupant. → A promotion, albeit entailing a second appointment, involves a different office and is not, strictly, a reappointment. J. Bautista, concurring in Visarra, likewise viewed a promotional appointment as not prohibited under the 1935 Constitution.

paras.html: No textual restriction? The command is that members are appointed "for a term of seven years" and appointment to a vacancy "shall be only for the unexpired portion." The President has two and only two options: a full seven years for a vacancy by expiration, or the unexpired term for a vacancy by death, disability, resignation, or impeachment. Otherwise the President could "trifle with terms of office fixed by the Constitution."

paras.html: Garcia precedent (1959). The promotion of COMELEC Commissioner Garcia to succeed Chairman Carag upon expiration of the latter's term, under the 1935 Constitution, is not a precedent under the 1987 Constitution. That it went uncontested does not matter: "the promotion in question was either legal or it was not. If it were not, no amount of repetitive practices would clear it of invalidating taint."

paras.html: Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D, 1987 Constitution: "The Chairman and Commissioners shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years without reappointment. Of those first appointed, the Chairman shall hold office for seven years, one Commissioner for five years, and the other Commissioner for three years, without reappointment. Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor. In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity." The identical rule governs the CSC and COMELEC.

paras.html: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.
paras.text: Promotion is not a prohibited reappointment: "Reappointment" in Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D means a movement to one and the same office (Commissioner to Commissioner, Chairman to Chairman). A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment, not a barred reappointment, provided (a) the aggregate of the service as Commissioner and the unexpired term as Chairman does not exceed seven years, and (b) the chairmanship became vacant by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.

paras.html: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.
paras.text: Fixed terms; the President cannot split terms: An appointment to a vacancy caused by the expiration of the predecessor's term must always be for a full seven-year term; an appointment for a lesser period is void. An appointment to a vacancy from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment is for the unexpired portion only, but not less than that portion. Hence, a sitting Commissioner cannot be promoted to a chairmanship vacated by expiration of term: seven years would exceed the aggregate limit, and anything less would violate the fixed term.

paras.html: Aggregate seven-year limit; Matibag abandoned in part: No one may serve in the Commission, as Chairman, Commissioner, or both, for an aggregate of more than seven years. The fourth situation in Matibag v. Benipayo (barring the reappointment of one who served less than seven years to an unexpired term) is obiter and is abandoned.

paras.html: A case is moot when its purpose has become stale or it ceases to present a justiciable controversy owing to supervening events, so that a resolution would be of no practical value. As a general rule, the Court does not decide moot cases.

paras.html: David v. Macapagal-Arroyo: the Court decides otherwise moot cases if (1) there is a grave violation of the Constitution; (2) the situation is of exceptional character and paramount public interest is involved; (3) the constitutional issue requires formulation of controlling principles to guide the bench, the bar, and the public; and (4) the case is capable of repetition yet evading review.

paras.html: (1) The rotational plan, or staggering of terms, so that appointments after the first set occur every two years; (2) a fixed maximum term of seven years for members appointed because of the expiration of a term; (3) the prohibition on reappointment of members who served the full seven years, or of the first appointees who served their terms; (4) the limit of a successor's term to the unexpired portion of the predecessor's term; and (5) the ban on temporary or acting appointments or designations.

paras.html: First set of commissioners. Their terms (seven, five, and three years) have expired and matter only in understanding the rotational plan. Gaminde v. COA: their terms start on a common date (Feb. 2, 1987) regardless of the dates of appointment, so the two-year interval recurs regularly; in a belated appointment, the delay is counted against the appointee.

paras.html: Republic v. Imperial: two conditions are indispensable to the rotational plan: (a) the first terms start on a common date; and (b) a vacancy from death, resignation, or disability is filled only for the unexpired balance. Its purpose: to prevent a four-year administration from appointing more than one permanent commissioner, or, per CONCOM Commissioner Monsod, "to prevent one person (the President of the Philippines) from dominating the commissions"; it also ensures continuity and independence.

paras.html: Vacancy by expiration vs. other causes. An appointment to a vacancy from expiration of a term is for seven years. There is an unexpired portion only when, because of death, disability, resignation, or impeachment, a sitting member cannot complete the term. Where the vacancy is from expiration, "there is technically no unexpired portion to speak of."

paras.html: CONCOM deliberations. Commissioner Aquino proposed that "the appointee shall in no case serve an aggregate period of more than seven years," thinking of a commissioner upgraded to chairman; Commissioner Monsod answered "It is covered"; Commissioner Foz explained that under the unexpired-portion clause, "if there is upgrading of position from commissioner to chairman, the appointee can serve only the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor", and "He takes it at his own risk."

paras.html: Meaning of "reappointment." "Reappointment" means a second appointment to one and the same office (Sibal, citing Visarra). J. Dizon, dissenting in Visarra v. Miraflor: the ban refers to a second appointment to the same office; an occupant needs no second appointment unless he ceased to be the legal occupant. → A promotion, albeit entailing a second appointment, involves a different office and is not, strictly, a reappointment. J. Bautista, concurring in Visarra, likewise viewed a promotional appointment as not prohibited under the 1935 Constitution.

Reyes' "stick or carrot" view, the Court found CJ Moran's view in De Vera "just as logically sound and perhaps even more compelling": "Moral character is no doubt the most effective safeguard of independence." With moral integrity, a commissioner is independent with or without the possibility of reappointment.

paras.html: No textual restriction? The command is that members are appointed "for a term of seven years" and appointment to a vacancy "shall be only for the unexpired portion." The President has two and only two options: a full seven years for a vacancy by expiration, or the unexpired term for a vacancy by death, disability, resignation, or impeachment. Otherwise the President could "trifle with terms of office fixed by the Constitution."

paras.html: Garcia precedent (1959). The promotion of COMELEC Commissioner Garcia to succeed Chairman Carag upon expiration of the latter's term, under the 1935 Constitution, is not a precedent under the 1987 Constitution. That it went uncontested does not matter: "the promotion in question was either legal or it was not. If it were not, no amount of repetitive practices would clear it of invalidating taint."

paras.html: Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-D, 1987 Constitution: "The Chairman and Commissioners shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years without reappointment. Of those first appointed, the Chairman shall hold office for seven years, one Commissioner for five years, and the other Commissioner for three years, without reappointment. Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor. In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity." The identical rule governs the CSC and COMELEC.

paras.html: Rotational plan; common starting date: The rotational plan for the Constitutional Commissions requires that the terms of the first appointees start on a common date, irrespective of the variations in the dates of their appointments and qualification, and that any vacancy be filled only for the unexpired balance of the term (Republic v. Imperial). Under the 1987 Constitution, that common date is February 2, 1987, the date of ratification. In case of a belated appointment or qualification, the interval between the start of the term and actual qualification is counted against the appointee.

paras.html: Term vs. tenure: The term is "the time during [which] the officer may claim to hold office as of right," and it fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another; the term is not affected by hold-over. Tenure is the period the incumbent actually holds office and may be shorter than the term. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII (transitory provision) governs the tenure of the incumbent commissioners, not the term under Art. IX.

paras.html: Quoting Topacio Nueno v. Angeles (also citing Alba v. Evangelista, Paredes v. Abad, Aparri v. CA): "The term means the time during the officer may claim to hold office as of right, and fixes the interval after which the several incumbents shall succeed one another. The tenure represents the term during which the incumbent actually holds the office. The term of office is not affected by the hold-over. The tenure may be shorter than the term for reasons within or beyond the power of the incumbent."

paras.html: "Unless" imports an exception to the general rule (Tajanlangit v. Cazeñas). paras.html: "WHEREFORE, we adjudge that the term of office of Ms. Thelma P. Gaminde as Commissioner, Civil Service Commission, under an appointment extended to her by President Fidel V. Ramos on June 11, 1993, expired on February 02, 1999. However, she served as de facto officer in good faith until February 02, 2000, and thus entitled to receive her salary and other emoluments for actual service rendered. Consequently, the Commission on Audit erred in disallowing in audit such salary and other emoluments, including that of her co-terminous staff.
paras.text: "WHEREFORE, we adjudge that the term of office of Ms. Thelma P. Gaminde as Commissioner, Civil Service Commission, under an appointment extended to her by President Fidel V. Ramos on June 11, 1993, expired on February 02, 1999. However, she served as de facto officer in good faith until February 02, 2000, and thus entitled to receive her salary and other emoluments for actual service rendered. Consequently, the Commission on Audit erred in disallowing in audit such salary and other emoluments, including that of her co-terminous staff.

paras.html: Staggering is one of several measures ensuring the Commissions' independence, alongside fiscal autonomy, power to appoint their own personnel, rule-making on pleadings and practice, fixed terms, removal only by impeachment, and salaries that cannot be decreased during tenure.

paras.html: Citing Fr. Bernas: the uneven first terms aim (1) to avoid, as much as possible, members being appointees of the same President, and (2) to ensure continuity within the body. This creates a three-tiered system of succession.

paras.html: Rotational plan; common starting date: The rotational plan for the Constitutional Commissions requires that the terms of the first appointees start on a common date, irrespective of the variations in the dates of their appointments and qualification, and that any vacancy be filled only for the unexpired balance of the term (Republic v. Imperial). Under the 1987 Constitution, that common date is February 2, 1987, the date of ratification. In case of a belated appointment or qualification, the interval between the start of the term and actual qualification is counted against the appointee.

paras.html: Term vs. tenure: The term is "the time during [which] the officer may claim to hold office as of right," and it fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another; the term is not affected by hold-over. Tenure is the period the incumbent actually holds office and may be shorter than the term. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII (transitory provision) governs the tenure of the incumbent commissioners, not the term under Art. IX.

paras.html: Quoting Topacio Nueno v. Angeles (also citing Alba v. Evangelista, Paredes v. Abad, Aparri v. CA): "The term means the time during the officer may claim to hold office as of right, and fixes the interval after which the several incumbents shall succeed one another. The tenure represents the term during which the incumbent actually holds the office. The term of office is not affected by the hold-over. The tenure may be shorter than the term for reasons within or beyond the power of the incumbent."

paras.html: Sec. 15: the incumbent members of the CSC, COMELEC, and COA "shall continue in office for one year after the ratification of this Constitution, unless they are sooner removed for cause or become incapacitated … or appointed to a new term thereunder," and no Member shall serve longer than seven years including pre-ratification service.

paras.html: This provision contemplates "tenure" not "term" of the incumbents.

paras.html: "Unless" imports an exception to the general rule (Tajanlangit v. Cazeñas). The incumbents continue for one year under their existing appointments at the discretion of the appointing power, who may cut their tenure short by (1) removal for cause, (2) incapacity, or (3) appointment to a new term, all of which may happen before the one-year period ends.

paras.html: "WHEREFORE, we adjudge that the term of office of Ms. Thelma P. Gaminde as Commissioner, Civil Service Commission, under an appointment extended to her by President Fidel V. Ramos on June 11, 1993, expired on February 02, 1999. However, she served as de facto officer in good faith until February 02, 2000, and thus entitled to receive her salary and other emoluments for actual service rendered. Consequently, the Commission on Audit erred in disallowing in audit such salary and other emoluments, including that of her co-terminous staff.
paras.text: "WHEREFORE, we adjudge that the term of office of Ms. Thelma P. Gaminde as Commissioner, Civil Service Commission, under an appointment extended to her by President Fidel V. Ramos on June 11, 1993, expired on February 02, 1999. However, she served as de facto officer in good faith until February 02, 2000, and thus entitled to receive her salary and other emoluments for actual service rendered. Consequently, the Commission on Audit erred in disallowing in audit such salary and other emoluments, including that of her co-terminous staff.

paras.html: Staggering is one of several measures ensuring the Commissions' independence, alongside fiscal autonomy, power to appoint their own personnel, rule-making on pleadings and practice, fixed terms, removal only by impeachment, and salaries that cannot be decreased during tenure.

paras.html: Rotational plan; common starting date: The rotational plan for the Constitutional Commissions requires that the terms of the first appointees start on a common date, irrespective of the variations in the dates of their appointments and qualification, and that any vacancy be filled only for the unexpired balance of the term (Republic v. Imperial). Under the 1987 Constitution, that common date is February 2, 1987, the date of ratification. In case of a belated appointment or qualification, the interval between the start of the term and actual qualification is counted against the appointee.
paras.text: Rotational plan; common starting date: The rotational plan for the Constitutional Commissions requires that the terms of the first appointees start on a common date, irrespective of the variations in the dates of their appointments and qualification, and that any vacancy be filled only for the unexpired balance of the term (Republic v. Imperial). Under the 1987 Constitution, that common date is February 2, 1987, the date of ratification. In case of a belated appointment or qualification, the interval between the start of the term and actual qualification is counted against the appointee.

paras.html: Term vs. tenure: The term is "the time during [which] the officer may claim to hold office as of right," and it fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another; the term is not affected by hold-over. Tenure is the period the incumbent actually holds office and may be shorter than the term. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII (transitory provision) governs the tenure of the incumbent commissioners, not the term under Art. IX.

paras.html: De facto officer: An appointee is bound by the term stated in the appointment she accepted; but one who stays beyond that term and serves as a de facto officer in good faith is entitled to her salary and emoluments for actual service rendered.

Imperial (1955): "the operation of the rotational plan requires two conditions, both indispensable to its workability: (1) that the terms of the first three (3) Commissioners should start on a common date, and, (2) that any vacancy due to death, resignation or disability before the expiration of the term should only be filled only for the unexpired balance of the term."

paras.html: Quoting Topacio Nueno v. Angeles (also citing Alba v. Evangelista, Paredes v. Abad, Aparri v. CA): "The term means the time during the officer may claim to hold office as of right, and fixes the interval after which the several incumbents shall succeed one another. The tenure represents the term during which the incumbent actually holds the office. The term of office is not affected by the hold-over. The tenure may be shorter than the term for reasons within or beyond the power of the incumbent."

paras.html: Sec. 15: the incumbent members of the CSC, COMELEC, and COA "shall continue in office for one year after the ratification of this Constitution, unless they are sooner removed for cause or become incapacitated … or appointed to a new term thereunder," and no Member shall serve longer than seven years including pre-ratification service.
paras.text: Sec. 15: the incumbent members of the CSC, COMELEC, and COA "shall continue in office for one year after the ratification of this Constitution, unless they are sooner removed for cause or become incapacitated … or appointed to a new term thereunder," and no Member shall serve longer than seven years including pre-ratification service.

paras.html: "Unless" imports an exception to the general rule (Tajanlangit v. Cazeñas). The incumbents continue for one year under their existing appointments at the discretion of the appointing power, who may cut their tenure short by (1) removal for cause, (2) incapacity, or (3) appointment to a new term, all of which may happen before the one-year period ends.

paras.html: "WHEREFORE, we adjudge that the term of office of Ms. Thelma P. Gaminde as Commissioner, Civil Service Commission, under an appointment extended to her by President Fidel V. Ramos on June 11, 1993, expired on February 02, 1999. However, she served as de facto officer in good faith until February 02, 2000, and thus entitled to receive her salary and other emoluments for actual service rendered. Consequently, the Commission on Audit erred in disallowing in audit such salary and other emoluments, including that of her co-terminous staff.

paras.html: Judges should not assist or be detailed to the DOJ: The Court does not look with favor at the long-standing practice of judges being detailed in the Department of Justice to assist the Secretary, even if it were only in connection with his work of exercising administrative authority over the courts. The line between what a judge may and may not do with the other departments "must always be kept clear and jealously observed, lest the principle of separation of powers… be gradually eroded." No judge, even of the lowest court, should place himself where his actions on matters submitted to him would be subject to review, prior approval, or reversal by any authority other than the CA or the SC. The Court "feels very strongly that it is best that this practice is discontinued." [Stated in the body; the fallo only dismisses the complaint and furnishes the SecJ a copy.]

paras.html: Salary without judicial functions is not dishonesty: After taking his oath and formally assuming office, a judge has a "perfect right to earn the salary of a judge" even if he performs no judicial function, especially when the offices duty-bound to furnish his court's place and facilities fail to do so without any fault on his part.

paras.html: Space: The Calamba mayor promised the west wing of the municipal building once the treasurer's office moved out, but the treasurer and several councilors objected. The mayor asked respondent to look for rental space, with the municipality paying. The Republic Bank negotiations failed when the owner refused to reduce the rent to ₱300 a month. The municipality finally leased the second floor of the Laguna Development Bank on October 26, 1970 after a month of negotiations; another month passed before funds were released to convert the hall into a courtroom and offices (including for the assistant provincial fiscal).

paras.html: Publication in each Congress: under Sec. 21, Art. VI, the Senate may conduct inquiries in aid of legislation only in accordance with its duly published rules of procedure. Following Neri, "It is incumbent upon the Senate to publish the rules for its legislative inquiries in each Congress or otherwise make the published rules clearly state that the same shall be effective in subsequent Congresses or until they are amended or repealed."
paras.text: Publication in each Congress: under Sec. 21, Art. VI, the Senate may conduct inquiries in aid of legislation only in accordance with its duly published rules of procedure. Following Neri, "It is incumbent upon the Senate to publish the rules for its legislative inquiries in each Congress or otherwise make the published rules clearly state that the same shall be effective in subsequent Congresses or until they are amended or repealed."

paras.html: Mode of publication: publication means publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation (Art. 2, Civil Code; Tañada). A free booklet or the Senate website is not sufficient, and the E-Commerce Act does not make the internet a medium for publishing laws and rules.

paras.html: Tapes surfaced containing a wiretapped conversation purportedly between President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and COMELEC Commissioner Virgilio Garcillano, allegedly with instructions to manipulate the 2004 presidential election results in her favor. The controversy put the legitimacy of the administration on the line.

The controversy put the legitimacy of the administration on the line.

paras.html: June 8, 2005: then Minority Floor Leader Francis Escudero delivered the privilege speech "Tale of Two Tapes," which set off a joint inquiry by five House committees (Public Information; Public Order and Safety; National Defense and Security; Information and Communications Technology; Suffrage and Electoral Reforms).
paras.text: June 8, 2005: then Minority Floor Leader Francis Escudero delivered the privilege speech "Tale of Two Tapes," which set off a joint inquiry by five House committees (Public Information; Public Order and Safety; National Defense and Security; Information and Communications Technology; Suffrage and Electoral Reforms).

paras.html: July 5, 2005: NBI Director Reynaldo Wycoco, Atty. Alan Paguia, and the lawyer of former NBI Deputy Director Samuel Ong submitted seven alleged "original" tapes of the supposed three-hour conversation. After debate on admissibility and authenticity, the tapes were played in the House chambers.

paras.html: (2) Institution vs. business: the main Senate Rules continue from Congress to Congress (Sec. 137), which reflects a continuing body. The inquiry Rules are, like the main Rules, not "pending matters and proceedings" that terminate with a Congress; those are unfinished investigations and bills [in one quotation he labels the unfinished-business rule "Sec. 136" under Rule XLIV; the ponencia and his earlier quotation use Sec. 123]. Otherwise, the Senate could choose not to take up its inquiry Rules and be left with none, an absurd result. By contrast, the House is not continuing and adopts its rules each Congress (e.g., the 14th Congress House adopted the 13th Congress rules provisionally on Nov. 20, 2007).

paras.html: (3) Historical and comparative support: the 1935-era Senate Rules had the same structure; Arnault (citing McGrain v. Daugherty) held the Senate continuing; the US Senate's Standing Rules (Rule V(2)) continue from one Congress to the next. The rules reflect, not create, the continuing nature.

paras.html: (4) One-time publication suffices: under Tañada, a single publication in the OG or a newspaper generally suffices; many rules (e.g., the Amparo and Habeas Data Rules) lack "until amended or repealed" language yet remain in force. The Aug. 24, 1995 publication satisfied Sec. 21. The exception is when continuity is interrupted, as with the House at the end of a Congress.

paras.html: Framing: the case is not about balancing privacy against the right to information, nor privacy against the inquiry power. The "bone of contention" is whether the Senate can use inadmissible evidence of an illegally recorded private communication.
paras.text: Framing: the case is not about balancing privacy against the right to information, nor privacy against the inquiry power. The "bone of contention" is whether the Senate can use inadmissible evidence of an illegally recorded private communication.

paras.html: RA 4200: Sec. 1 penalizes secretly recording a private communication and knowingly possessing, replaying, or communicating it; Sec. 3 allows court-ordered wiretaps for listed crimes; Sec. 4 makes illegally obtained communications inadmissible in any judicial, quasi-judicial, legislative, or administrative hearing. A communication is private by its context, not its content (Ramirez v. CA; the Tañada–Diokno exchange on public speeches).

As a general rule, illegally wiretapped material is inadmissible for any purpose (Salcedo-Ortanez; Olivarez), but exceptions should be read in for (a) prosecutions for violations of RA 4200 itself, and (b) legislative inquiries whose purpose is to craft or improve laws on illegal wiretapping.

paras.html: Good moral character is continuing: "the possession of good moral character is both a condition precedent and a continuing requirement" to warrant admission to the bar and to retain membership in the legal profession (Zaguirre v. Castillo). Admission to the Bar does not preclude a subsequent judicial inquiry, upon proper complaint, into the respondent's mental or moral fitness before he became a lawyer; admission creates only a rebuttable presumption of qualification, which may be refuted by clear and convincing evidence.

paras.html: Disbarment is a matter of public interest: laws on double jeopardy or procedure (verification of pleadings, prejudicial questions, prescription of offenses, affidavits of desistance) do not apply in determining a lawyer's qualifications and fitness for membership in the Bar. The complainant is not a direct party; effectively, his or her participation is that of a witness.

paras.html: Disciplinary power and the standard: Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5) makes the Court's disciplinary authority over the Bar "merely incidental" to its exclusive power to admit applicants to the practice of law. Disbarment requires grossly immoral, not simply immoral, conduct: conduct so corrupt as to constitute a criminal act, so unprincipled as to be reprehensible to a high degree, or committed under such scandalous or revolting circumstances as to shock the community's sense of decency.

paras.html: First, admission to the practice of law is a component of the administration of justice and a matter of public interest because it involves service to the public. The admission qualifications are also qualifications for the continued enjoyment of the privilege to practice law.
paras.text: First, admission to the practice of law is a component of the administration of justice and a matter of public interest because it involves service to the public. The admission qualifications are also qualifications for the continued enjoyment of the privilege to practice law.

paras.html: Second, lack of qualifications or violation of the standards for the practice of law, like criminal cases, is a matter of public concern that the State may inquire into through this Court. The complainant is therefore not a direct party whose interest in the outcome is wholly his or her own; effectively, his or her participation is that of a witness who brought the matter to the Court's attention.

paras.html: July 30, 2010: President Benigno Aquino III issued EO 2, "Recalling, Withdrawing, and Revoking Appointments Issued by the Previous Administration in Violation of the Constitutional Ban on Midnight Appointments." Sec. 1 defines midnight appointments as: (a) those made on or after March 11, 2010, including those dated before March 11 where the appointee accepted, took oath, or assumed on or after March 11, except temporary executive appointments; (b) those made before March 11 but to take effect after, or to offices vacant only after that date; and (c) appointments within 45 days before the May 10, 2010 elections in violation of Sec. 261, Omnibus Election Code. Sec. 2 recalls and revokes them and declares the positions vacant.

Macaraig).

paras.html: Staggering aims to minimize the appointing authority's opportunity to appoint a majority and ensure continuity; but it is not a statutory prohibition, direct or indirect, against acting appointments. Binamira v. Garrucho upheld a temporary appointment of the PTA General Manager despite a fixed six-year term and staggered board terms.

paras.html: Staggering does not even guarantee that one President cannot appoint all members; under RA 6975 (effective January 1, 1991), the 1992–1998 President could theoretically appoint all four. And RA 8551 (Sec. 7) dropped the staggering provision, so the argument has no statutory basis as the law now stands.

paras.html: Meaning of "forthwith": In Art. XI, Sec. 3(4), "forthwith" means "within a reasonable time, which may be a longer or shorter period, according to the circumstances of each particular case" (Fischer v. Ambler; Behn, Meyer & Co. v. Antholtz). The Senate's duty to try includes preparatory acts for the trial. Because Sec. 3(4), unlike Sec. 3(2), fixes no period, "it is for the Senate to determine when it will conduct the actual trial," but the Senate "must not unduly delay the conduct of the trial." [Ruled "even on the merits," after the petition was found moot; J. Singh treats this part as obiter.]

paras.html: Feb. 6: SP Escudero announced that the Senate would not hold the impeachment trial during its session break, because it can convene as an impeachment court only in plenary session, and that it would use the recess to review and update its impeachment rules. paras.html: The text is clear: "trial by the Senate shall forthwith proceed." paras.html: The Senate's Rules of Procedure on Impeachment Trials likewise do not require convening as an impeachment court first: the Senate receives the Articles (Rule I); the SP administers the Presiding Officer's oath (Rule II), which precedes the senators' oath (Rule III). (2) No negligence: the Articles arrived the afternoon the Senate adjourned, there was a dilemma whether it could act out of session, and it was preparing (Lihaylihay v. Treasurer Tan). (3) The duty is discretionary: time, place, and manner are left to the Senate, which promulgates its own rules (Art. XI, Sec. 3(8)) (Spouses Espiridion v. CA).

paras.html: Presidential immunity does not cover the acts of subordinates: A petition for prohibition against the DECS Secretary and Regional Director to stop a reassignment is not a suit against the President, because "the questioned acts are those of petitioners and not of the President." Furthermore, presidential decisions may be questioned before the courts where there is grave abuse of discretion or where the President acted without or in excess of jurisdiction (Medrana v. Office of the President).

paras.html: Indefinite reassignment violates security of tenure: A reassignment with no fixed period and no stated objective or purpose from which its temporariness may be inferred is indefinite and violates the employee's security of tenure.
paras.text: Indefinite reassignment violates security of tenure: A reassignment with no fixed period and no stated objective or purpose from which its temporariness may be inferred is indefinite and violates the employee's security of tenure.

paras.html: Unconsented transfers (Bentain v. CA): Security of tenure covers "unconsented transfers which are tantamount to illegal removals." A temporary transfer without consent is permissible, but not when it is a preliminary step toward removal, a scheme to lure the employee away from his permanent position, designed to indirectly terminate his service, or meant to force his resignation.

paras.html: Deportation power not limited to statutory grounds: The deportation of an undesirable alien may be effected (1) by the President, after due investigation, under Sec. 69 of the Revised Administrative Code, or (2) by the Commissioner of Immigration under Sec. 37 of the Immigration Law. Because Sec. 69 and EO 398 do not specify grounds, the Deportation Board may investigate an alien on a ground not enumerated in Sec. 37; the law grants the Chief Executive full discretion to determine whether an alien's residence is so undesirable as to injure the security, welfare, or interest of the State.

paras.html: Inherent power. The State has the inherent power to deport undesirable aliens (Chuoco Tiaco v. Forbes, 228 U.S. 549). The Chief Executive may exercise it "when he deems such action necessary for the peace and domestic tranquility of the nation."

paras.html: Full discretion. As observed by J. Labrador (Tan Tong v. Deportation Board; Tan Sin v. Deportation Board), no legal or constitutional provision defines the power to deport, because the law intends to grant the Chief Executive "full discretion to determine whether an alien's residence in the country is so undesirable as to affect or injure the security, welfare or interest of the state." The adjudication of the facts also devolves on him, and his decision is final and executory.

paras.html: A line item for recall exists in the GAA: The 2014 GAA item for the "Conduct and supervision of elections, referenda, recall votes and plebiscites" is a valid line item appropriation for recall elections. "To be valid, an appropriation must indicate a specific amount and a specific purpose. However, the purpose may be specific even if it is broken down into different related sub-categories of the same nature." "Conduct elections" covers regular, special, and recall elections.
paras.text: A line item for recall exists in the GAA: The 2014 GAA item for the "Conduct and supervision of elections, referenda, recall votes and plebiscites" is a valid line item appropriation for recall elections. "To be valid, an appropriation must indicate a specific amount and a specific purpose. However, the purpose may be specific even if it is broken down into different related sub-categories of the same nature." "Conduct elections" covers regular, special, and recall elections.

paras.html: Augmentation from savings: Where the COMELEC admits that the funds under that item are insufficient, there is an actual deficiency, and the COMELEC Chairman may augment the item from the COMELEC's savings, as authorized by Sec. 25(5), Art. VI and Sec. 67 of the 2014 GAA.
paras.text: Augmentation from savings: Where the COMELEC admits that the funds under that item are insufficient, there is an actual deficiency, and the COMELEC Chairman may augment the item from the COMELEC's savings, as authorized by Sec. 25(5), Art. VI and Sec. 67 of the 2014 GAA.

paras.html: No "contingent fund" requirement: There is no constitutional requirement that the appropriation be lodged in "contingent funds"; Congress has plenary power to lodge it in current operating expenditures. The Constitution requires an appropriation for a specific purpose or program, not for each sub-set of projects or activities.

Bayron, the incumbent Mayor of Puerto Princesa City, for loss of trust and confidence brought about by "gross violation of pertinent provisions of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, gross violation of pertinent provisions of the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials, Incompetence, and other related gross inexcusable negligence/dereliction of duty, intellectual dishonesty and emotional immaturity."

paras.html: Program, not Project: It has a line item for the "Conduct and supervision of elections, referenda, recall votes and plebiscites" under the Program category (₱1,401,501,000), but this is "legally intended to finance the basic continuing staff support and administrative operations" (salaries, office maintenance), not the actual conduct of recall elections. Actual elections were always funded by separate Project line items (2007, 2010, 2013 GAAs). Using Program funds for a Project is illegal except by valid augmentation. Funding recall would violate Sec. 29(1), Art. VI (no money paid out except by appropriation made by law), *Brillantes, Jr. v. COMELEC*, and the Government Auditing Code.

paras.html: Augmentation not possible: It listed three requisites (a law authorizing the Chairman, a deficient existing line item, savings). paras.html: Power to appoint carries the power to remove: “As a general rule, therefore, all officers appointed by the President are also removable by him.” The exception is when the law (or the Consti) expressly vests removal in another office (SC justices, lower-court judges, ConCom members, the Ombudsman). Since the President appoints the Deputies (Sec. 9, Art. XI), Sec. 8(2) of RA 6770 merely laid down in express terms an authority already implied.

paras.html: Concurrent, not exclusive, disciplinary power; independence is political independence: The Ombudsman's disciplinary authority over a Deputy Ombudsman and the Special Prosecutor is not exclusive; the President shares it, but only (1) for the grounds for removing the Ombudsman by impeachment and (2) after due process. The challenge to Sec. 8(2) was DENIED only because the Court was equally divided and no majority voted to invalidate it (Sec. 4(2), Art. VIII).

paras.html: Aug. 23, 2010 – Quirino Grandstand hostage-taking: Dismissed police officer P/S Insp. Rolando Mendoza hijacked a tourist bus in Manila, demanding his reinstatement (signs: “Release final decision”; “Big mistake to correct a big wrong decision”). paras.html: IIRC: The Incident Investigation and Review Committee (chair: Justice Sec. Leila de Lima; vice-chair: DILG Sec. Jesse Robredo) found that Gonzales (with Gutierrez) let the MR “languish for more than nine (9) months” despite the Ombudsman rule to resolve MRs within five days; enforced the dismissal while the MR was pending; showed “undue interest” by motu proprio requesting the case and naming a CIDG officer as nominal complainant; and failed to act decisively during the crisis. Mendoza had earlier accused Gonzales of demanding ₱150,000. [The IIRC report says the Mendoza decision was “duly approved on May 21, 2009”; sic: the decision's own narrative says Feb. 16, 2009.] Gonzales and Gutierrez refused to take part in the IIRC, invoking the Ombudsman's independence. The IIRC recommended referral to the OP.

paras.html: The Ombudsman's administrative power flows from its mandate to protect the people (Sec. 13, Art. XI) and RA 6770, which gives it “full administrative disciplinary power” over all officials (Sec. 21), except those removable only by impeachment, Members of Congress, and the Judiciary. History: the Tanodbayan (1973 Consti) → the 1987 Ombudsman, freed of prosecutorial duties to act “in a quick, inexpensive and effective manner.”

paras.html: But that authority is “by no means exclusive.” Sec. 21 grants the Ombudsman disciplinary authority over all officials; Sec. 8(2) grants the President express power of removal over a Deputy and the Special Prosecutor.

paras.html: Harmonious construction: every part of a statute must be given effect; apparently conflicting provisions must be reconciled as a coordinated whole → Congress intended concurrent disciplinary jurisdiction of the Ombudsman and the President. The sharing “goes into the wisdom of the legislature,” beyond judicial inquiry.

paras.html: Doctrine of implication: the power to appoint carries with it the power to remove (Aguirre v. De Castro) → as a general rule, all officers appointed by the President are removable by him.

paras.html: Exception: when the law expressly vests removal in another authority. paras.html: Plea bargaining (Sec. 2, Rule 116) is allowed when the prosecution lacks sufficient evidence of the crime charged. paras.html: I. Sec. 2, Art. XI empowers Congress
paras.text: I. Sec. 2, Art. XI empowers Congress

paras.html: The second sentence (“All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment”) expressly grants Congress the power to determine the manner, cause, and disciplinary authority for removing non-impeachable officers.
paras.text: The second sentence (“All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment”) expressly grants Congress the power to determine the manner, cause, and disciplinary authority for removing non-impeachable officers.

paras.html: History: Regalado added it to limit Congress — to stop it from making favored officials (e.g., Sandiganbayan justices under PD 1606) removable only by impeachment. [The opinion says “inserting the second sentence in Section 8 (2), Article XI”; sic: should be Sec. 2, Art. XI.]

paras.html: Sec. 8(2) and Sec. 21 → concurrent jurisdiction of the President and the Ombudsman; courts should not casually void acts of the elected legislature absent a clear violation.

paras.html: II. Independence comes in degrees
paras.text: II. Independence comes in degrees

paras.html: Independence is a judicially enforceable norm, but the Consti intended different degrees: for NEDA, BSP, CHR, Congress operationalizes it; for the CSC, COA, COMELEC, legislative power is more limited (fiscal autonomy, rule-making).

paras.html: An independent body has exclusive disciplinary authority only if the Consti expressly says so, as with the Judiciary (Secs. 6 & 11, Art. VIII). Example: the President may remove Monetary Board members (Sec. 10, RA 7653). Reading in exclusivity would be “judicial legislation or a disguised constitutional amendment.”

COMELEC (even congressional review of COMELEC rules is invalid).

XI cover the Deputies too → no sense in insulating their appointment and salary but not their tenure; even filing a case can suspend them; with only one term, a removable Deputy recreates the ineffective Tanodbayan. RA 7653 cannot validate an unsupported provision.
