paras.html: Power to appoint carries the power to remove: “As a general rule, therefore, all officers appointed by the President are also removable by him.” The exception is when the law (or the Consti) expressly vests removal in another office (SC justices, lower-court judges, ConCom members, the Ombudsman). Since the President appoints the Deputies (Sec. 9, Art. XI), Sec. 8(2) of RA 6770 merely laid down in express terms an authority already implied.
paras.text: Power to appoint carries the power to remove: “As a general rule, therefore, all officers appointed by the President are also removable by him.” The exception is when the law (or the Consti) expressly vests removal in another office (SC justices, lower-court judges, ConCom members, the Ombudsman). Since the President appoints the Deputies (Sec. 9, Art. XI), Sec. 8(2) of RA 6770 merely laid down in express terms an authority already implied.

paras.html: Concurrent, not exclusive, disciplinary power; independence is political independence: The Ombudsman's disciplinary authority over a Deputy Ombudsman and the Special Prosecutor is not exclusive; the President shares it, but only (1) for the grounds for removing the Ombudsman by impeachment and (2) after due process. The challenge to Sec. 8(2) was DENIED only because the Court was equally divided and no majority voted to invalidate it (Sec. 4(2), Art. VIII).

paras.html: Betrayal of public trust: Acts that warrant removal “may be less than criminal but must be attended by bad faith and of such gravity and seriousness as the other grounds for impeachment.” Plain errors of judgment and isolated negligence do not qualify.

Rolando Mendoza hijacked a tourist bus in Manila, demanding his reinstatement (signs: “Release final decision”; “Big mistake to correct a big wrong decision”). paras.html: IIRC: The Incident Investigation and Review Committee (chair: Justice Sec. Leila de Lima; vice-chair: DILG Sec. Jesse Robredo) found that Gonzales (with Gutierrez) let the MR “languish for more than nine (9) months” despite the Ombudsman rule to resolve MRs within five days; enforced the dismissal while the MR was pending; showed “undue interest” by motu proprio requesting the case and naming a CIDG officer as nominal complainant; and failed to act decisively during the crisis. Mendoza had earlier accused Gonzales of demanding ₱150,000. [The IIRC report says the Mendoza decision was “duly approved on May 21, 2009”; sic: the decision's own narrative says Feb. 16, 2009.] Gonzales and Gutierrez refused to take part in the IIRC, invoking the Ombudsman's independence. The IIRC recommended referral to the OP.

paras.html: The Ombudsman's administrative power flows from its mandate to protect the people (Sec. 13, Art. XI) and RA 6770, which gives it “full administrative disciplinary power” over all officials (Sec. 21), except those removable only by impeachment, Members of Congress, and the Judiciary. History: the Tanodbayan (1973 Consti) → the 1987 Ombudsman, freed of prosecutorial duties to act “in a quick, inexpensive and effective manner.”

paras.html: But that authority is “by no means exclusive.” Sec. 21 grants the Ombudsman disciplinary authority over all officials; Sec. 8(2) grants the President express power of removal over a Deputy and the Special Prosecutor.

paras.html: Harmonious construction: every part of a statute must be given effect; apparently conflicting provisions must be reconciled as a coordinated whole → Congress intended concurrent disciplinary jurisdiction of the Ombudsman and the President. The sharing “goes into the wisdom of the legislature,” beyond judicial inquiry.

paras.html: I. Sec. 2, Art. XI empowers Congress
paras.text: I. Sec. 2, Art. XI empowers Congress

paras.html: The second sentence (“All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment”) expressly grants Congress the power to determine the manner, cause, and disciplinary authority for removing non-impeachable officers.
paras.text: The second sentence (“All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment”) expressly grants Congress the power to determine the manner, cause, and disciplinary authority for removing non-impeachable officers.

paras.html: History: Regalado added it to limit Congress — to stop it from making favored officials (e.g., Sandiganbayan justices under PD 1606) removable only by impeachment. [The opinion says “inserting the second sentence in Section 8 (2), Article XI”; sic: should be Sec. 2, Art. XI.]

paras.html: II. Independence comes in degrees
paras.text: II. Independence comes in degrees

paras.html: Independence is a judicially enforceable norm, but the Consti intended different degrees: for NEDA, BSP, CHR, Congress operationalizes it; for the CSC, COA, COMELEC, legislative power is more limited (fiscal autonomy, rule-making).

paras.html: An independent body has exclusive disciplinary authority only if the Consti expressly says so, as with the Judiciary (Secs. 6 & 11, Art. VIII). Example: the President may remove Monetary Board members (Sec. 10, RA 7653). Reading in exclusivity would be “judicial legislation or a disguised constitutional amendment.”

paras.html: Independence of the Ombudsman bars presidential discipline of a Deputy Ombudsman: The Ombudsman's independence “cannot be inferior — but is similar in degree and kind” to that of the Constitutional Commissions. Subjecting the Deputy Ombudsman to discipline and removal by the President, “whose own alter egos and officials in the Executive Department are subject to the Ombudsman's disciplinary authority, cannot but seriously place at risk the independence” of the Office → Sec. 8(2), RA 6770 is unconstitutional insofar as the Deputy Ombudsman is concerned (8–7).
paras.text: Independence of the Ombudsman bars presidential discipline of a Deputy Ombudsman: The Ombudsman's independence “cannot be inferior — but is similar in degree and kind” to that of the Constitutional Commissions. Subjecting the Deputy Ombudsman to discipline and removal by the President, “whose own alter egos and officials in the Executive Department are subject to the Ombudsman's disciplinary authority, cannot but seriously place at risk the independence” of the Office → Sec. 8(2), RA 6770 is unconstitutional insofar as the Deputy Ombudsman is concerned (8–7).

paras.html: “As provided by law” is not carte blanche: Congress's power under the second sentence of Sec. 2, Art. XI to fix the manner, cause, and disciplinary authority for removing non-impeachable officers must still respect due process, security of tenure, separation of powers, checks and balances, and the Ombudsman's independence.

paras.html: Pre-1973 presidential Ombudsman-like agencies failed for lack of political independence (and could only fact-find and recommend). The 1973 Consti made the Ombudsman (Tanodbayan) constitutionally mandated; PD 1487, as amended by PD 1607 and PD 1630, created it; in 1979 the Special Prosecutor's powers were transferred to the Tanodbayan himself.
paras.text: Pre-1973 presidential Ombudsman-like agencies failed for lack of political independence (and could only fact-find and recommend). The 1973 Consti made the Ombudsman (Tanodbayan) constitutionally mandated; PD 1487, as amended by PD 1607 and PD 1630, created it; in 1979 the Special Prosecutor's powers were transferred to the Tanodbayan himself.

paras.html: The 1987 Consti created a new Office “by constitutional fiat”, with independence expressly guaranteed, to enforce Sec. 27, Art. II (honesty and integrity; anti-graft) and Sec. 1, Art. XI (public office is a public trust). It is the “protector of the people” (Sec. 12, Art. XI), an “activist watchman”, and “a notch above other grievance-handling investigative bodies” (DOJ v. Liwag). RA 6770 (enacted under Sec. 13(8)) gives it disciplinary authority over all officials, including Cabinet members (Sec. 21).

paras.html: By clear constitutional design, the OSP is separate from the Office of the Ombudsman. Its inclusion in the Office under Sec. 3, RA 6770 does not ipso facto give it constitutional independence; the law merely attaches it. Congress and the President may do so, and presidential removal may serve as a check on the Ombudsman → Sec. 8(2) is valid as to the Special Prosecutor.

Sandiganbayan: control = alter, modify, set aside, substitute judgment; supervision = see that duties are performed).

paras.html: Independence thus means organizational separation, which does not obviate an external disciplining authority under checks and balances, a principle of “functional interrelation,” not total insulation. Congress's plenary power fills the framers' silence → all doubts resolved for constitutionality.

paras.html: Independence of the Ombudsman bars presidential discipline of a Deputy Ombudsman: The Ombudsman's independence “cannot be inferior — but is similar in degree and kind” to that of the Constitutional Commissions. Subjecting the Deputy Ombudsman to discipline and removal by the President, “whose own alter egos and officials in the Executive Department are subject to the Ombudsman's disciplinary authority, cannot but seriously place at risk the independence” of the Office → Sec. 8(2), RA 6770 is unconstitutional insofar as the Deputy Ombudsman is concerned (8–7).
paras.text: Independence of the Ombudsman bars presidential discipline of a Deputy Ombudsman: The Ombudsman's independence “cannot be inferior — but is similar in degree and kind” to that of the Constitutional Commissions. Subjecting the Deputy Ombudsman to discipline and removal by the President, “whose own alter egos and officials in the Executive Department are subject to the Ombudsman's disciplinary authority, cannot but seriously place at risk the independence” of the Office → Sec. 8(2), RA 6770 is unconstitutional insofar as the Deputy Ombudsman is concerned (8–7).

paras.html: “As provided by law” is not carte blanche: Congress's power under the second sentence of Sec. 2, Art. XI to fix the manner, cause, and disciplinary authority for removing non-impeachable officers must still respect due process, security of tenure, separation of powers, checks and balances, and the Ombudsman's independence.

paras.html: YES. A justiciable question is one “inherently susceptible of being decided on grounds recognized by law” (IBP v. Zamora), as where the court finds constitutionally imposed limits on a political branch's powers (citing J. Puno's separate opinion in IBP v. Zamora).

paras.html: The Court does not inquire into the wisdom of Congress's choice to grant concurrent authority; it asks only whether the grant violates the Consti, specifically the independence in Sec. 5, Art. XI.

paras.html: Neither the Executive nor the Legislature can create the power Sec. 8(2) grants where the Consti confers none. When authority is “drawn from a vacuum”, especially one that runs counter to a core constitutional principle, the Court is duty-bound to intervene under Art. VIII.

paras.html: Pre-1973 presidential Ombudsman-like agencies failed for lack of political independence (and could only fact-find and recommend). The 1973 Consti made the Ombudsman (Tanodbayan) constitutionally mandated; PD 1487, as amended by PD 1607 and PD 1630, created it; in 1979 the Special Prosecutor's powers were transferred to the Tanodbayan himself.

The 1973 Consti made the Ombudsman (Tanodbayan) constitutionally mandated; PD 1487, as amended by PD 1607 and PD 1630, created it; in 1979 the Special Prosecutor's powers were transferred to the Tanodbayan himself.

paras.html: The 1987 Consti created a new Office “by constitutional fiat”, with independence expressly guaranteed, to enforce Sec. 27, Art. II (honesty and integrity; anti-graft) and Sec. 1, Art. XI (public office is a public trust). It is the “protector of the people” (Sec. 12, Art. XI), an “activist watchman”, and “a notch above other grievance-handling investigative bodies” (DOJ v. Liwag). RA 6770 (enacted under Sec. 13(8)) gives it disciplinary authority over all officials, including Cabinet members (Sec. 21).

paras.html: By clear constitutional design, the OSP is separate from the Office of the Ombudsman. Its inclusion in the Office under Sec. 3, RA 6770 does not ipso facto give it constitutional independence; the law merely attaches it. Congress and the President may do so, and presidential removal may serve as a check on the Ombudsman → Sec. 8(2) is valid as to the Special Prosecutor.

paras.html: Initiation = filing + referral (Francisco reaffirmed): "The initiation starts with the filing of the complaint which must be accompanied with an action to set the complaint moving." The initial action is the referral of the complaint to the Committee on Justice. Two complaints simultaneously referred initiate only one impeachment proceeding, so there is no violation of the one-year bar.

paras.html: Purpose of the one-year bar: It concerns "the element of time, and not the number of complaints". The officer defends in only one proceeding, and Congress runs only one proceeding, per year: "There is no repeat ride for one full year."

paras.html: "Promulgate" is not "publish": Sec. 3(8), Art. XI uses "promulgate" in its general sense of "to make known"; how to promulgate is for Congress to decide. The impeachment provisions are self-executing; even assuming publication is required, its absence does not nullify proceedings taken in compliance with the self-executing constitutional provisions.

Edre Olalia, Ferdinand Gaite, and James Terry Ridon) filed a second complaint, endorsed by Party-List Reps. Colmenares, Casiño, Mariano, Ilagan, Tinio, and De Jesus. paras.html: Grounds: Both complaints allege betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution. The first cites the low conviction rate since 2008, inaction on the NBN-ZTE deal involving PGMA and her husband, delay in the Ensign Pestaño death probe, upholding the arrest of Rep. Hontiveros-Baraquel, the ₱1-million Le Cirque dinner, delays on public-interest cases, and refusal of access to SALNs. The second cites delay on the Fertilizer Fund Scam, non-prosecution of Gen. Eliseo de la Paz ("Euro General") for undeclared currency, disregard of the Court's directive in Information Technology Foundation v. COMELEC, and violation of Secs. 12–13, Art. XI and Sec. 16, Art. III (speedy disposition).

paras.html: Determining sufficiency is an exponent of the House's rule-making power (Sec. 3(8)); the Constitution itself only requires a "hearing" (Sec. 3(2)). Prudential considerations call for respecting this, "absent any contravention of the minimum constitutional guidelines."

paras.html: "Promulgate" v. "publish": Black's defines promulgate broadly ("to publish; to announce officially; to make public"), but there is a statutory difference in usage. The Constitution uses "promulgate" 12 times. Court rules are published, but judgments are "promulgated" by delivery to the clerk of court. Congress' canvassing rules (Sec. 4, Art. VII) for the May 2010 elections took effect upon adoption without publication. For agencies, publication follows promulgation.

The Constitution grants up to three session days for deliberation before referral → "far from being mechanical."

paras.html: I. Publication and due process. The House must act within constitutional standards (grounds, periods, votes, the one-year bar, promulgation of rules) and respect individual rights → judicial review.
paras.text: I. Publication and due process. The House must act within constitutional standards (grounds, periods, votes, the one-year bar, promulgation of rules) and respect individual rights → judicial review.

paras.html: To "promulgate" means to publish or announce officially. Under Art. 2, Civil Code and Tañada v. Tuvera, laws and rules affecting the public must be published; impeachment rules "fill in the details" (as the ponencia itself says, they "fill the gaps"), are not internal, and gravely affect the officer and the public (any citizen may file).

paras.html: The Rules published Sept. 2 took effect only on Sept. 17, 2010; actual knowledge does not substitute for publication (NASECORE v. ERC).

paras.html: Rebuttals: court judgments bind only parties, while rules bind the public; the House's failure to publish canvassing rules proves nothing; "issue, adopt, set forth, establish" are words that do not imply publication; the ConCom knew Art. 2 and Tañada; and the 15th Congress itself published its rules.

paras.html: Under Neri, each new chamber must publish its rules, so mere adoption of the prior Congress' rules does not suffice. Impeachable officers deserve no less protection than witnesses (they face removal, disqualification, and contempt).

paras.html: On the periods: Art. 2 allows a shorter effectivity period; the 10- and 3-session-day periods are constitutional acts unaffected by the Rules, and only the 60-session-day Committee period is affected. Fifteen calendar days fit within 60 session days, and there is no implied repeal of the publication requirement. The House "chose not to undertake any immediate publication."

paras.html: Revisiting Francisco: it was "eerily silent" on the purposes of Sec. 3(5) (only J. Azcuna's concurrence addressed them). Receipt and referral are mechanical, mandatory acts. The first meaningful, discretionary act is the Committee's determination of sufficiency in form and substance, a test of validity, and only a valid complaint should bar others.

paras.html: Control over a chartered instrumentality's awards: The SBMA Board of Directors and officers are subject to the control and supervision of the Office of the President. Under LOI 620, the President's approval is required for contracts of national government offices, agencies, and instrumentalities (including GOCCs) involving P2,000,000 and above, awarded through public bidding or negotiation. Thus the President "may, within his authority, overturn or reverse any award made by the SBMA Board of Directors for justifiable reasons", and an award not yet so approved is not final and binding and confers no clear and unmistakable right.

paras.html: Calling-out power is reviewable only for grave abuse: The President has full discretion to call out the armed forces "whenever it becomes necessary" to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion or rebellion. Unlike martial law and the suspension of the writ, there is no provision for congressional revocation or SC review of the sufficiency of its factual basis. The Court may only ask whether the power was exercised within constitutional limits or with grave abuse of discretion, and the petitioner must show that the President's decision is "totally bereft of factual basis."

paras.html: In view of the alarming increase in violent crimes in Metro Manila (robberies, kidnappings, carnappings), President Joseph Ejercito Estrada, in a verbal directive, ordered the PNP and the Philippine Marines to conduct joint visibility patrols for crime prevention and suppression.
paras.text: In view of the alarming increase in violent crimes in Metro Manila (robberies, kidnappings, carnappings), President Joseph Ejercito Estrada, in a verbal directive, ordered the PNP and the Philippine Marines to conduct joint visibility patrols for crime prevention and suppression.

paras.html: The Secretary of National Defense, the AFP Chief of Staff, the PNP Chief, and the SILG were tasked to execute and implement the order.
paras.text: The Secretary of National Defense, the AFP Chief of Staff, the PNP Chief, and the SILG were tasked to execute and implement the order.

paras.html: In compliance, the PNP Chief, through Police Chief Superintendent Edgar B. Aglipay, formulated Letter of Instruction (LOI) 02/2000, detailing how the patrols, called Task Force Tulungan, would be conducted. The Task Force was placed under the leadership of the Police Chief of Metro Manila.

paras.html: Memorandum (24 January 2000): The President then confirmed his directive in a Memorandum to the AFP Chief of Staff and the PNP Chief:
paras.text: Memorandum (24 January 2000): The President then confirmed his directive in a Memorandum to the AFP Chief of Staff and the PNP Chief:

paras.html: He wanted to improve peace and order in Metro Manila through a more effective crime prevention program, including increased police patrols; augmentation from the AFP is necessary to heighten police visibility.
paras.text: He wanted to improve peace and order in Metro Manila through a more effective crime prevention program, including increased police patrols; augmentation from the AFP is necessary to heighten police visibility.

paras.html: Invoking his Commander-in-Chief powers under Sec. 18, Art. VII, he directed the AFP Chief of Staff and PNP Chief to coordinate the deployment of the Marines to assist the PNP in preventing or suppressing criminal or lawless violence.
paras.text: Invoking his Commander-in-Chief powers under Sec. 18, Art. VII, he directed the AFP Chief of Staff and PNP Chief to coordinate the deployment of the Marines to assist the PNP in preventing or suppressing criminal or lawless violence.

paras.html: He declared that the Marines' services were merely temporary and for a reasonable period only, until the situation improved.

paras.html: Situation: Crimes in Metro Manila were perpetrated not only by ordinary criminals but by organized syndicates whose members include active and former police/military personnel, whose training, skill, discipline, and firepower are well above the capability of the local police alone.

Cuenco); cf. the Baker v. Carr factors, led by a "textually demonstrable constitutional commitment of the issue to a coordinate political department."

paras.html: When a grant of power is qualified, conditional, or limited, whether the conditions were met is justiciable, the problem being legality, not wisdom (Santiago v. Guingona); the Court has jurisdiction to delimit constitutional boundaries (Bengzon v. Senate Blue Ribbon Committee).

paras.html: When political questions are involved, the Constitution limits the determination to whether there was grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction (Marcos v. Manglapus; Daza v. Singson; Coseteng v. Mitra).

CSC). The Court cannot substitute its judgment (Ledesma v. CA), but a plenary power is no obstacle to inquiry into its abuse (Bondoc v. Pineda).

paras.html: Structure of Sec. 18: Congress may revoke, and the SC may review the sufficiency of the factual basis of, martial law and the suspension of the writ only. There is no equivalent provision for the calling-out power → it is in a different category; otherwise the framers would have lumped the three powers together. Expressio unius est exclusio alterius (Sarmiento v. Mison).

paras.html: ConCom deliberations: Fr. Bernas described a "graduated power": calling out, then suspension, then martial law; the first two greater powers are subject to review, but when the President exercises the "lesser power of calling on the Armed Forces … his judgment cannot be reviewed by anybody." Comm. Regalado: calling out does not require legislative concurrence "nor is it subject to judicial review."

paras.html: Why the difference: calling out is the lesser and more benign power; suspension and martial law curtail basic civil rights and so need congressional safeguards and judicial review.

paras.html: Conditions: Suspension and martial law require that (1) there be an actual invasion or rebellion and (2) public safety requires it. These are not required for calling out; the only criterion is "whenever it becomes necessary."

paras.html: Even in the US, which has a long tradition of hostility to domestic use of the military and whose Constitution, unlike ours, does not expressly provide for the calling-out power, military assistance to civilian law enforcement is allowed in similar circumstances. paras.html: Every successor gets a full seven-year term: Harmonizing Sec. 11, Art. XI with Sec. 8(3) of RA 6770, “in any vacancy for the positions of Ombudsman and the deputies, whether as a result of the expiration of the term or death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the predecessor, the successor shall always be appointed for a full term of seven years.” The term is reckoned from the date of appointment, not from 2 February 1987.
paras.text: Every successor gets a full seven-year term: Harmonizing Sec. 11, Art. XI with Sec. 8(3) of RA 6770, “in any vacancy for the positions of Ombudsman and the deputies, whether as a result of the expiration of the term or death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the predecessor, the successor shall always be appointed for a full term of seven years.” The term is reckoned from the date of appointment, not from 2 February 1987.

paras.html: Rank and salary only: Sec. 10, Art. XI equates the Ombudsman and the Deputies with the Chairman and Members of the Constitutional Commissions only as to rank and salary, not term of office. The Office of the Ombudsman is not a constitutional commission (it is not a collegial body), so the 7-5-3 rotational plan and the Gaminde ruling do not apply to it.

paras.html: Ordinary meaning: “salary” is a recompense for services; “rank” is a designation fixing an officer's relative position in privilege, precedence, command, or pay. Neither includes “term of office”, i.e., the time during which the officer may claim to hold office as of right, which fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another (Fetalino v. COMELEC, citing Nueno v. Angeles).

paras.html: Gaminde v. COA: Gaminde was appointed ad interim CSC Commissioner on 11 June 1993 (assumed 22 June 1993); her appointment paper said her term would expire on 2 February 1999. The COA disallowed her salaries after that date. The SC held her term expired on 2 February 1999: the first appointees' staggered 7-5-3 terms began on 2 February 1987, and any delay in appointment or qualification is counted against the appointee. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII concerns tenure, not term.

paras.html: Every successor gets a full seven-year term: Harmonizing Sec. 11, Art. XI with Sec. 8(3) of RA 6770, “in any vacancy for the positions of Ombudsman and the deputies, whether as a result of the expiration of the term or death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the predecessor, the successor shall always be appointed for a full term of seven years.” The term is reckoned from the date of appointment, not from 2 February 1987.

paras.html: Rank and salary only: Sec. 10, Art. XI equates the Ombudsman and the Deputies with the Chairman and Members of the Constitutional Commissions only as to rank and salary, not term of office. The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall be natural-born citizens of the Philippines, … at least forty years old, of recognized probity and independence, … members of the Philippine Bar … The Ombudsman must have for ten years or more been a judge or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines.
paras.text: Sec. 8. The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall be natural-born citizens of the Philippines, … at least forty years old, of recognized probity and independence, … members of the Philippine Bar … The Ombudsman must have for ten years or more been a judge or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines.

paras.html: Sec. 10. The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall have the rank of Chairman and Members, respectively, of the Constitutional Commissions, and they shall receive the same salary, which shall not be decreased during their term of office.

paras.html: Sec. 11. The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall serve for a term of seven years without reappointment. They shall not be qualified to run for any office in the election immediately succeeding their cessation from office.

paras.html: The framers intended to constitutionalize the Office of the Ombudsman with autonomy and independence equal to the CSC, COMELEC, COA, and CHR: fiscal autonomy, qualifications, manner of appointment, removal, salary, rank, and term (Secs. 5–14, Art. XI).

paras.html: Since the Ombudsman and Deputies have the same status as the constitutional commissions, the latter's term limitations apply to them. Granting a full term to a successor when the vacancy is for a cause other than expiration ignores the framers' intent and Sec. 11.

paras.html: The Ombudsman is not sui generis. A fresh seven-year term for every successor lets an outgoing President divest the next President of the prerogative to appoint; under an unexpired-term policy, every President can appoint one.

paras.html: Ordinary meaning: “salary” is a recompense for services; “rank” is a designation fixing an officer's relative position in privilege, precedence, command, or pay. Neither includes “term of office”, i.e., the time during which the officer may claim to hold office as of right, which fixes the interval after which incumbents succeed one another (Fetalino v. COMELEC, citing Nueno v. Angeles).

paras.html: Canons applied: verba legis (Chavez v. JBC; Saguisag v. Ochoa; Padilla v. Congress): index animi sermo and verba legis non est recedendum; expressio unius est exclusio alterius and expressium facit cessare tacitum (CIR v. Puregold); a law limited to certain matters may not be extended to others (Malinias v. COMELEC); clear law means application, not interpretation (Umali v. JBC); Holmes's “no canon against using common sense.”

De Vera (1949), on the 1935 COMELEC's nine-year term: to place a new member every three years, a successor to one who ceases before the term expires must be appointed only for the unexpired portion; otherwise the appointment “would be offensive to the Constitution.”

paras.html: Republic v. Imperial (1955): the plan aims to keep one seat vacant every three years so that no President can appoint more than one commissioner. It has two indispensable conditions: (1) the first terms start on a common date; and (2) vacancies are filled only for the unexpired balance.

paras.html: The plan was carried into the CSC, COMELEC, and COA under Art. XII of the 1973 Constitution (7-5-3) and Sec. 1(2), Arts. IX-B, IX-C, and IX-D of the 1987 Constitution. The first terms start on a common date, regardless of appointment dates, so that a regular two-year interval recurs.

paras.html: The Ombudsman and Deputies are not collegial, so the rotation is “implausible” for them. If it applied, who among the first Deputies would take the seven-, five-, or three-year term? The Constitution is silent; the Court may not, in the guise of interpretation, enlarge its scope (Kida v. Senate).

paras.html: Acting-capacity argument (raised first in the memorandum): the bar on appointment or designation “in a temporary or acting capacity” is in Art. IX [sic: petitioner and Court cite “Sec. 2 of Art. IX (A), (B), and (C)”; the quoted text is in Sec. 1(2) of Arts. IX-B, C, and D], which refers exclusively to the constitutional commissions. Art. XI has no such prohibition. What does carry over is that the Ombudsman and Deputies are subject to the same disqualifications and prohibitions in Sec. 2, Art. IX-A (no other office, no practice of profession, no financial interest in government contracts).

paras.html: Gaminde v. COA: Gaminde was appointed ad interim CSC Commissioner on 11 June 1993 (assumed 22 June 1993); her appointment paper said her term would expire on 2 February 1999. The COA disallowed her salaries after that date. The SC held her term expired on 2 February 1999: the first appointees' staggered 7-5-3 terms began on 2 February 1987, and any delay in appointment or qualification is counted against the appointee. Sec. 15, Art. XVIII concerns tenure, not term.

paras.html: Supervision over the IBP: The Supreme Court, exercising its power of supervision over the Integrated Bar, may suspend the oath-taking of IBP officers-elect, inquire into the conduct of IBP elections, annul those elections, and amend, modify, or repeal the IBP By-Laws (under Sec. 77, Art. XI of the By-Laws).

paras.html: On June 3, 1989, at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), the House of Delegates (120 chapter presidents or their alternates) elected and proclaimed the IBP's national officers, including: Atty. Violeta Drilon (President), Atty. Bella Tiro (Executive Vice-President), Atty. Salvador Lao (Chairman, House of Delegates), Atty. Renato F. Ronquillo (Secretary), Atty. Teodoro Quicoy (Treasurer), Atty. Oscar Badelles (Sergeant-at-Arms), and the nine regional Governors and Vice-Presidents (Cortes, Atienza, Jalandoni, Grapilon, Almine, Siyangco, Teruel, Tiongco, and Datumanong).

paras.html: The voting and canvassing, conducted by the "IBP Comelec" headed by Justice Reynato Puno of the Court of Appeals, were unanimously adjudged by participants and observers to be above board; Justice Puno devised safeguards against tampering with and marking of ballots.

paras.html: What concerned the Court was instead the electioneering and extravagance of the campaign of the three presidential candidates: Attys. Drilon, Nereo Paculdo, and Ramon Nisce.
paras.text: What concerned the Court was instead the electioneering and extravagance of the campaign of the three presidential candidates: Attys. Drilon, Nereo Paculdo, and Ramon Nisce.

paras.html: Media reports:

paras.html: Columns by Emil Jurado (Manila Standard), Luis Mauricio (Malaya, "The Invertebrated Bar" and "The Disintegrating Bar"), and Teodoro Locsin, Jr. (Philippines Free Press), and a Daily Globe editorial, were unanimously critical of the "vote-buying and pressure tactics" of the three candidates.
paras.text: Columns by Emil Jurado (Manila Standard), Luis Mauricio (Malaya, "The Invertebrated Bar" and "The Disintegrating Bar"), and Teodoro Locsin, Jr. (Philippines Free Press), and a Daily Globe editorial, were unanimously critical of the "vote-buying and pressure tactics" of the three candidates.

paras.html: Jurado reported that Atty. Drilon allegedly used PNB helicopters to visit far-flung chapters on the pretext of distributing Bigay Puso donations; that DOLE regional directors and labor arbiters, granted leave by her husband (the Labor Secretary), campaigned for her; and that members of the U.P. Sigma Rho Fraternity and ACCRA lawyers engaged in vote-buying, with government positions promised by the Labor Secretary's office.

Drilon allegedly used PNB helicopters to visit far-flung chapters on the pretext of distributing Bigay Puso donations; that DOLE regional directors and labor arbiters, granted leave by her husband (the Labor Secretary), campaigned for her; and that members of the U.P. Sigma Rho Fraternity and ACCRA lawyers engaged in vote-buying, with government positions promised by the Labor Secretary's office.

paras.html: Mauricio added that out-of-town delegates were billeted in plush hotels and "wined and dined continuously," with votes priced at P15,000 to P20,000, and some crucial votes rising to P50,000 on election day. He also wrote that a "top official of the judiciary" allegedly closeted himself with campaigners at the PICC during a recess.

paras.html: The officers-elect were set to take their oath before the Court en banc on July 4, 1989. Disturbed by the reports, the Court, exercising its power of supervision over the Integrated Bar, suspended the oath-taking and resolved to inquire into the veracity of the reports.

paras.html: By en banc resolution of June 15, 1989, the Court directed the outgoing and incoming members of the Board of Governors, the principal officers, and the Chairman of the House of Delegates to appear on June 20, 1989 to inform it on the reports and recommend approaches to strengthen adherence to the IBP's fundamental principles. The resolution recalled the IBP's "basic postulate" that it "shall be non-political in character" with no lobbying or campaigning, and that officers would be chosen "on the basis of professional merit and willingness and ability to serve."

paras.html: DENR Secretary Factoran borrowed a PNB plane for Asst. Sec. Antonio Tria's official Bicol trip [the Resolution first calls Tria "Undersecretary," then "Assistant Secretary"]. On May 23, 1989, the Drilon group (Drilon, Tiu, Grapilon, Amy Wong, Tiongco) rode along to Naga, Daet, and Legaspi, met chapter presidents, and asked for support. Except for Tria, all passengers on the manifest were IBP candidates.

paras.html: Sec. 14, IBP By-Laws (Prohibited acts and practices relative to elections): prohibits, whether by a candidate or any other member, directly or indirectly: (a) distribution of campaign material except on election day; (b) election-day distribution of anything other than a one-page legal-size biodata, or distribution by unauthorized persons; (c) campaigning while holding an elective, judicial, quasi-judicial, or prosecutory office; (d) formation of tickets, single slates, or combinations; (e) to induce a vote, paying dues, giving food, drink, entertainment, transportation, or anything of value, or making promises or expenditures. [The Resolution's headings (7) and (8) cite Sec. 14(e) and 14(a); the content of heading (8) tracks Sec. 14(b).]

paras.html: ② The By-Law provisions for direct election by the House of Delegates of the HoD officers, the IBP President, and the EVP (approved in Bar Matter No. 287, resolution of "July 9, 1980" [sic: elsewhere the Resolution dates the BM 287 resolution July 9, 1985]) are repealed.
paras.text: ② The By-Law provisions for direct election by the House of Delegates of the HoD officers, the IBP President, and the EVP (approved in Bar Matter No. 287, resolution of "July 9, 1980" [sic: elsewhere the Resolution dates the BM 287 resolution July 9, 1985]) are repealed.

paras.html: ③ The former system is restored: the President and EVP are elected by the Board of Governors (the nine regional governors) from among themselves (Sec. 47, Art. VII, original By-Laws). The EVP's automatic succession to the presidency, abolished by the July 9, 1985 resolution in BM 287, is restored.

paras.html: ④ At the end of the President's two-year term, the EVP automatically succeeds; the incoming Board elects a new EVP from among themselves. The EVP position rotates among the nine regions; one who has served as president may not run for EVP until the rotation is completed.

paras.html: The Court ORDERS: (1) the IBP elections held on June 3, 1989 are hereby annulled; (2) the By-Law provisions for direct election by the House of Delegates of its officers, the IBP President, and the EVP are repealed; (3)–(4) election of the President and EVP by the Board of Governors from among themselves and the EVP's automatic succession are restored, with rotation among the nine regions; (5)–(11) Secs. 47, 33(b), 37, 39, and 33(a) are amended, Sec. 33(g) repealed, and Sec. 39(a), (b), (1)–(7), Art. VI deleted; (12) special elections for the Board of Governors within three months, the Board electing the President and EVP within 30 days, with the June 3 slate candidates and those connected with the irregularities ineligible; (13) a caretaker board pending the special elections, without prejudice to further measures. SO ORDERED.

VI deleted; (12) special elections for the Board of Governors within three months, the Board electing the President and EVP within 30 days, with the June 3 slate candidates and those connected with the irregularities ineligible; (13) a caretaker board pending the special elections, without prejudice to further measures. SO ORDERED.

paras.html: Confidentiality of deliberations: "[A]ny release of a copy to the public, or to the parties, of an unpromulgated ponencia infringes on the confidential internal deliberations of the Court." A frank exchange of ideas, free from publicity and pressure, is essential to the independence of judicial decision-making. Since even clerks of court are held to this, a higher standard of care applies to magistrates.

paras.html: Retirement does not moot an administrative case: The Court retains jurisdiction to declare a retired official innocent or guilty, because penalties such as disqualification from government office and forfeiture of benefits may still be imposed.

paras.html: Res ipsa loquitur and circumstantial evidence: A justice who was not formally charged may still be disciplined. The doctrine does not dispense with proof of the facts, but when the facts are shown by the record and no credible explanation negates the strong inference of evil intent, no further hearing is needed. Circumstantial evidence may prove both gross negligence and serious misconduct.

paras.html: New Code of Judicial Conduct, Canon 4, Sec. 9: confidential information acquired by judges in their judicial capacity shall not be used or disclosed for purposes unrelated to their judicial duties. The Code of Conduct for Court Personnel, Canon II, Secs. 1 to 4, prohibits disclosure of confidential information, which includes drafts, internal discussions, and records of internal deliberations, and these remain confidential even after the decision is made public.

paras.html: "Ineluctably, any release of a copy to the public, or to the parties, of an unpromulgated ponencia infringes on the confidential internal deliberations of the Court." Internal deliberations are confidential (Chavez v. PCGG). A frank exchange of exploratory ideas, free from publicity and pressure, is essential to protect the independence of decision-making (Chavez v. PEA).

paras.html: Re: Res ipsa loquitur
paras.text: Re: Res ipsa loquitur

paras.html: Under res ipsa loquitur, the Court may impose its authority upon erring judges whose actuations, on their face, would show gross incompetence, ignorance of the law or misconduct (De los Santos v. Mangino; Cruz v. Yaneza; both citing Macalintal v. Teh).

paras.html: Applications cited: People v. Valenzuela (further hearings dispensed with; judge's mere denial not accepted); Cathay Pacific v. Romillo (bad faith from glaring circumstances); Prudential Bank v. Castro (partiality shown by orders and summary judgment); Consolidated Bank v. Capistrano; Cruz v. Yaneza (modus operandi of approving bail beyond territorial jurisdiction); de los Santos v. Magsino [sic: fn. 261 names it De los Santos v. Mangino].

paras.html: Re: Dizon and the "toning down" of the doctrine
paras.text: Re: Dizon and the "toning down" of the doctrine

paras.html: In re Dizon: the doctrine does not dispense with proving the facts on which the inference of evil intent rests. It only means that when the facts are admitted or shown by the record and no credible explanation negating the strong inference of evil intent is forthcoming, no further hearing is needed.
paras.text: In re Dizon: the doctrine does not dispense with proving the facts on which the inference of evil intent rests. It only means that when the facts are admitted or shown by the record and no credible explanation negating the strong inference of evil intent is forthcoming, no further hearing is needed.

paras.html: Louis Vuitton v. Villanueva (doctrine inapplicable to knowingly rendering an unjust judgment; malice must be proven) and Fernandez v. Verzola (an erroneous decision is not itself evidence of corruption) toned the doctrine down. But Dizon's "inference of evil intent" bolstered its application to serious misconduct, not only gross negligence.

paras.html: Habeas corpus has very limited availability as a post-conviction remedy: review of a judgment of conviction via habeas corpus is allowed only when, as a consequence of a judicial proceeding, (a) there has been a deprivation of a constitutional right resulting in the restraint of a person; (b) the court had no jurisdiction to impose the sentence; or (c) an excessive penalty has been imposed, as such sentence is void as to the excess (Feria v. CA).
paras.text: Habeas corpus has very limited availability as a post-conviction remedy: review of a judgment of conviction via habeas corpus is allowed only when, as a consequence of a judicial proceeding, (a) there has been a deprivation of a constitutional right resulting in the restraint of a person; (b) the court had no jurisdiction to impose the sentence; or (c) an excessive penalty has been imposed, as such sentence is void as to the excess (Feria v. CA).

paras.html: Habeas corpus is not a writ of error: it permits a collateral challenge to the jurisdiction of the court, not a review of mere errors of fact or law committed within jurisdiction; "a habeas corpus petition reaches the body, but not the record of the case" (Velasco v. CA). A denial of a constitutional right ousts the court of jurisdiction, so the void judgment may be collaterally attacked through habeas corpus (Chavez v. CA; Gumabon).

paras.html: New trial after finality; DNA evidence: a motion for new trial under Rule 121 is available only before the judgment of conviction becomes final. Post-trial DNA evidence is not "newly discovered evidence" if it could have been discovered and produced at trial with reasonable diligence. Pregnancy is not an element of rape, so paternity is only tangentially related to guilt.

paras.html: In an information dated January 9, 1995, filed with the RTC of Pasig City, Aileen Mendoza charged petitioner Reynaldo de Villa, her uncle by affinity (she was his niece by affinity), with rape. He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment on January 26, 1995.
paras.text: In an information dated January 9, 1995, filed with the RTC of Pasig City, Aileen Mendoza charged petitioner Reynaldo de Villa, her uncle by affinity (she was his niece by affinity), with rape. He pleaded not guilty at his arraignment on January 26, 1995.

paras.html: Prosecution's version: In the third week of April 1994, at about 10:00 a.m., Aileen, then 12 years and ten months old, woke up in her family's rented room in Sagad, Pasig, to find petitioner on top of her. He covered her mouth with a pillow and threatened to kill her, so she could only cry. He inserted his penis into her vagina, made thrusting motions, and ejaculated.

paras.html: Her mother, Leonila Mendoza, noticed Aileen's pregnancy in November 1994. Confronted, Aileen revealed that petitioner had raped her, and her parents filed a complaint at the Pasig Police Station.

paras.html: Dr. Rosaline Cosidon confirmed that Aileen was eight months pregnant and found healed hymenal lacerations at the 5:00 and 8:00 positions. On December 19, 1994, Aileen gave birth to a baby girl, Leahlyn Mendoza.

paras.html: Calvan v. CA: the writ, though not designed to interrupt the orderly administration of justice, may be invoked by a special circumstance requiring immediate action. The inquiry is addressed not to errors within jurisdiction but to whether the proceeding or judgment is a complete nullity, probing the power and authority (an equivalent test of jurisdiction) of the court to render the order. It is the nullity of the judgment that makes it susceptible to collateral attack.

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to dismiss. The DNA evidence here is not material and relevant to the crime of rape: even assuming petitioner is not the father of the child conceived within the period of the rape, that does not prove he could not have committed the crime, so habeas corpus and new trial are unavailing. But the case should not close the door to a convict who, after final judgment, obtains DNA results that exonerate him.

paras.html: Before post-conviction DNA statutes, US courts required the convict to apply for testing; once the result confirmed innocence, they held a motion *in limine* hearing on admissibility or ordered a new trial; the prosecution usually declined to re-try, and the convict was released.

paras.html: Every person has a right to avail of a new technology that irrefutably proves his innocence despite a final conviction, provided the technology was not available during his trial. This is part of the constitutional right to due process, which a convict does not lose.

paras.html: Under Sec. 5(5), Art. VIII (power to promulgate rules for the protection and enhancement of constitutional rights), the Court may, even without a law, order a new trial if post-conviction DNA testing will establish that the convict could not possibly have committed the crime.

paras.html: Judges must not interfere in cases pending elsewhere: Rule 2.04, Canon 2, Code of Judicial Conduct mandates a judge to "refrain from influencing in any manner the outcome of litigation or dispute pending before another court or administrative agency." "The slightest form of interference cannot be countenanced."

paras.html: Appearance of impropriety; conduct off the bench: Magistrates "should avoid not only acts of impropriety, but all appearances of impropriety." A judge's conduct "must be free of even a whiff of impropriety, not only with respect to the performance of his judicial duties, but also his behavior outside the courtroom and as a private individual."

paras.html: 1:30–2:00 p.m.: Justice Demetria, PATAFA President Go Teng Kok, and Atty. Reinerio Paas (Go Teng Kok's lawyer and a close friend of Demetria) went to Formaran's DOJ office, which he shared with SP Albert Fonacier. Demetria apparently did not know Formaran: he greeted Fonacier, "Kamusta ka, Prosecutor Formaran?"

paras.html: Go Teng Kok immediately pleaded with Formaran to withdraw the motion to inhibit Judge Muro, claiming it would delay the case, and feared that a new judge might convict his friend Yu Yuk Lai. Even before 18 July, Go Teng Kok had been asking Formaran to go slow in prosecuting her.

paras.html: Demetria asked about the status of the case. Told that the motion was submitted for resolution and was based partly on the unsigned letter, he opined that it was "a bit dangerous" to anchor a judge's inhibition on an anonymous letter. He told the persistent Go Teng Kok to "keep his cool" and asked Formaran if he could do something to help Go Teng Kok.

paras.html: Formaran at first politely declined, but later, "just to put an end to (the) conversation," said he would bring the matter to CSP Zuño. Demetria replied, "Iyon pala," then stood up and left, followed by Paas and Go Teng Kok.

paras.html: 20 July 2000: The PDI reported that a "Supreme Court Justice . . . and an outspoken sports person and leader" had been exerting "undue pressure" on the DOJ to go slow on the re-arrested Yu Yuk Lai. That afternoon, the names of Demetria and Go Teng Kok were disclosed to the media to clear the Supreme Court Justices affected by the erroneous report. 21 July 2000: several newspapers named them as "drug lawyers."

paras.html: He vehemently denied interceding for Yu Yuk Lai. He admitted visiting the DOJ on 18 July but said he went to "visit old friends"; meeting Go Teng Kok, whom he did not know until then, was purely accidental. Atty. Paas and Go Teng Kok corroborated him.

The "help" could well be "within legal bounds or line of duty."

paras.html: Rule 2.04 requires a judge to "refrain from influencing in any manner the outcome of litigation or dispute pending before another court or administrative agency." "The slightest form of interference cannot be countenanced." Once a judge uses his influence to derail or interfere with a proceeding for the benefit of a party, public confidence in the judicial system "is diminished, if not totally eroded."

paras.html: Magistrates must avoid "not only acts of impropriety, but all appearances of impropriety," and must exercise their influence in society "with utmost prudence and discretion."
paras.text: Magistrates must avoid "not only acts of impropriety, but all appearances of impropriety," and must exercise their influence in society "with utmost prudence and discretion."

paras.html: The conduct of everyone connected with an office dispensing justice "must be characterized with propriety and must be above suspicion" (Jereos, Jr. v. Reblando, Sr.). It "must be free of even a whiff of impropriety, not only with respect to the performance of his judicial duties, but also his behavior outside the courtroom and as a private individual."

paras.html: Compulsory Bar integration is valid: it is a valid exercise of the State's police power and is supported by the SC's "explicit unequivocal grant" of power under Sec. 5(5), Art. X of the 1973 Constitution to promulgate rules on the admission to the practice of law and the integration of the Bar. The practice of law is not a property right but a mere privilege, clothed with public interest.
paras.text: Compulsory Bar integration is valid: it is a valid exercise of the State's police power and is supported by the SC's "explicit unequivocal grant" of power under Sec. 5(5), Art. X of the 1973 Constitution to promulgate rules on the admission to the practice of law and the integration of the Bar. The practice of law is not a property right but a mere privilege, clothed with public interest.

paras.html: Freedom of association is not violated: integration does not make a lawyer a member of any group of which he is not already a member; the only compulsion is the payment of annual dues, a reasonable regulatory fee. Even assuming it compels membership, the compulsion is justified by police power. A penalty enforcing the fee, which may be avoided by payment, is not arbitrary.

paras.html: Disbarment proceedings are sui generis: they are neither purely civil nor purely criminal but an investigation by the Court into the conduct of its officers, whose primary issue is fitness to practice law. Hence, preventive suspension in disbarment proceedings is different in nature from preventive suspension under RA 6770, the RRACCS, and the Labor Code, and the Court may impose it immediately, without waiting for the answer, when the act speaks for itself (res ipsa loquitur), its authorship is undisputed, and delay would render the Court's disciplinary power inefficacious.
paras.text: Disbarment proceedings are sui generis: they are neither purely civil nor purely criminal but an investigation by the Court into the conduct of its officers, whose primary issue is fitness to practice law. Hence, preventive suspension in disbarment proceedings is different in nature from preventive suspension under RA 6770, the RRACCS, and the Labor Code, and the Court may impose it immediately, without waiting for the answer, when the act speaks for itself (res ipsa loquitur), its authorship is undisputed, and delay would render the Court's disciplinary power inefficacious.

paras.html: A lawyer cannot divide his personality: lawyers may be disciplined for conduct in their private capacity if it shows unfitness. Under Sec. 2, Canon II of the CPRA, a lawyer shall not behave in a scandalous manner "whether in public or private life"; Secs. 3 and 4 bar gender-based harassment and require dignified, gender-fair language in all dealings, including social media; and Sec. 36 imposes a duty to understand the risks of social media.

paras.html: Inhibition and contempt: bias and prejudice must be proved by clear and convincing evidence; bare allegations do not suffice. The Court is a collegial body, so a resolution of the Court En Banc does not depend on any one Justice. Unfounded accusations of partiality against Justices in a pleading constitute direct contempt and, under Sec. 14, Canon II of the CPRA, a ground for disciplinary action.

paras.html: Impeachable lawyer-officers cannot be disbarred during incumbency: "A public officer who under the Constitution is required to be a Member of the Philippine Bar as a qualification for the office held by him and who may be removed from office only by impeachment, cannot be charged with disbarment during the incumbency of such public officer."
paras.text: Impeachable lawyer-officers cannot be disbarred during incumbency: "A public officer who under the Constitution is required to be a Member of the Philippine Bar as a qualification for the office held by him and who may be removed from office only by impeachment, cannot be charged with disbarment during the incumbency of such public officer."

paras.html: Nor criminally charged with offenses carrying removal: During incumbency, such officer cannot be charged criminally before the Sandiganbayan or any other court with any offense which carries with it the penalty of removal from office, or any penalty service of which would amount to removal from office.
paras.text: Nor criminally charged with offenses carrying removal: During incumbency, such officer cannot be charged criminally before the Sandiganbayan or any other court with any offense which carries with it the penalty of removal from office, or any penalty service of which would amount to removal from office.

paras.html: Not immunity, but a procedural requirement: The officer must first be removed by impeachment; only then may he be held to answer criminally or administratively (by disbarment). A fiscal or other prosecuting officer should forthwith and motu proprio dismiss charges against a Member of the Court; the remedy of one with a legitimate grievance is impeachment.

paras.html: 17 February 1988: By a per curiam Resolution, the Court dismissed the charges for utter lack of merit and required Cuenco to show cause why he should not be administratively dealt with for making unfounded serious accusations against Justice Fernan.
paras.text: 17 February 1988: By a per curiam Resolution, the Court dismissed the charges for utter lack of merit and required Cuenco to show cause why he should not be administratively dealt with for making unfounded serious accusations against Justice Fernan.

paras.html: The same Resolution gave "another reason" for dismissal: Members of the SC must be members of the Bar and may be removed only by impeachment, so disbarring a sitting Member would circumvent the impeachment mandate (quoted in the ruling below).

paras.html: Judicial privilege (deliberative process privilege): Court records that are "predecisional" and "deliberative" in nature, as well as the Court's deliberations, raffle results, and agenda actions, are privileged and "cannot be the subject of a subpoena if judicial privilege is to be preserved."

paras.html: Internal vs. external matters: Justices, and court officials and employees, may not be compelled to testify on matters that are part of the internal deliberations and actions of the Court in the exercise of their adjudicatory functions and duties, while testimony on matters external to those functions (e.g., bribery) may be compelled.

paras.html: Institutional privilege: The privileges belong to the Supreme Court as an institution, not to any individual justice, judge, or court employee; no sitting or retired justice, not even the Chief Justice, may claim exception without the consent of the Court.

Members of the Court and Court officials and employees may not be compelled to testify on matters that are part of the internal deliberations and actions of the Court in the exercise of their adjudicatory functions, while testimony on matters external to those functions may be compelled.

paras.html: Re: Separation of powers, judicial independence, and comity
paras.text: Re: Separation of powers, judicial independence, and comity

paras.html: The doctrine of separation of powers inures not by express provision but as an underlying principle that is the bedrock of checks and balances (Angara v. Electoral Commission). Each branch is separate, co-equal, coordinate, and supreme within its own sphere.
paras.text: The doctrine of separation of powers inures not by express provision but as an underlying principle that is the bedrock of checks and balances (Angara v. Electoral Commission). Each branch is separate, co-equal, coordinate, and supreme within its own sphere.

paras.html: A lesser-known aspect is comity: the voluntary observance of inter-departmental courtesy for the harmonious working of government. The Judiciary applies it by exercising restraint on political questions; the other branches may apply it by refraining from continuing acts questioned before the courts.

The Judiciary applies it by exercising restraint on political questions; the other branches may apply it by refraining from continuing acts questioned before the courts.

paras.html: In an impeachment, where doubt exists, the standard is "the need to preserve the structure of a democratic and republican government, particularly the check and balance that should prevail."

paras.html: Re: The general rule of transparency and its limits
paras.text: Re: The general rule of transparency and its limits

paras.html: The right to information (Art. III, Sec. 7) is granted "subject to such limitations as may be provided by law" and is not absolute. Private persons have the right to privacy; institutions have their own right to confidentiality, expressed as the need to protect the integrity of their constitutional tasks.

Private persons have the right to privacy; institutions have their own right to confidentiality, expressed as the need to protect the integrity of their constitutional tasks.

paras.html: The Court follows a policy of transparency, embodied in Sec. 11, Rule 136 of the Rules of Court (the clerk shall give certified copies to "any person demanding the same," even a non-party, for the fees). But this grant is subject to the limitations the laws and the Court's own rules provide, chiefly the need to protect the integrity of the adjudicative function.

paras.html: Re: What court records are confidential (IRSC)
paras.text: Re: What court records are confidential (IRSC)

paras.html: Privileges "create a hierarchy of rights that protect certain confidential relationships over and above the public's evidentiary need" (citing Kellogg and US v. Bryan).
paras.text: Privileges "create a hierarchy of rights that protect certain confidential relationships over and above the public's evidentiary need" (citing Kellogg and US v. Bryan).

paras.html: The IRSC prohibits disclosure of: (1) the result of the raffle of cases, available only to the parties and their counsel, and not even to them for bar matters, administrative cases, and criminal cases with a life-imprisonment penalty (Rule 7, Sec. 3); (2) the actions taken by the Court on each case in its agenda, confidential until the resolution embodying the action is officially released (Rule 10, Sec. 2; see Rule 11, Sec. 5); and (3) the deliberations of the Members in court sessions (Rule 10, Sec. 2).

paras.html: Rationale, citing J. Abad's concurring opinion in Arroyo v. De Lima: confidentiality lets Members "freely discuss the issues without fear of criticism for holding unpopular positions" or fear of humiliation; the privilege prevents the "chilling" of deliberative communications.

paras.html: The privilege is not exclusive to the Judiciary. Chavez v. PEA (through J. Carpio): internal deliberations of the SC and other collegiate courts, and executive sessions of either house of Congress, are confidential and "cannot be pried open by a co-equal branch of government". J. Brion's Separate Concurring Opinion in Neri v. Senate Committee notes that all branches are entitled to this treatment.

paras.html: Senate v. Ermita: Members of the SC are exempt from Congress' power of inquiry in aid of legislation; since judicial power is vested in a collegial body, each Member is exempt on the basis of separation of powers, fiscal autonomy, and the constitutional independence of the judiciary. This ruling was dictated by comity: the highest levels of each department are exempt from the compulsory processes of the other departments on matters related to their functions.

paras.html: Witnesses need not be summoned to testify on matters of public record (records a government unit is required by law to keep). paras.html: On Judicial Privilege:
paras.text: On Judicial Privilege:

paras.html: Judicial privilege is implied from Judicial Power, as executive privilege is implied from Executive Power (Chavez v. PEA).
paras.text: Judicial privilege is implied from Judicial Power, as executive privilege is implied from Executive Power (Chavez v. PEA).

paras.html: First limit: it may be invoked only if the information arose from the performance of official adjudicatory functions. Information on crimes, misconduct, violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct or any law, and financial, budgetary, personnel and similar administrative matters is not confidential.
paras.text: First limit: it may be invoked only if the information arose from the performance of official adjudicatory functions. Information on crimes, misconduct, violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct or any law, and financial, budgetary, personnel and similar administrative matters is not confidential.

paras.html: Second limit: being merely implied, it must be weighed against express constitutional rights (freedom of expression and of the press, right to information, full public disclosure under Art. II, Sec. 28); the Judiciary cannot claim confidentiality beyond what is essential and necessary to preserve the exercise of Judicial Power.

II, Sec. 28); the Judiciary cannot claim confidentiality beyond what is essential and necessary to preserve the exercise of Judicial Power.

paras.html: → Information of no or de minimis value, like the date and time the Clerk of Court received a Justice's dissent, is not confidential; it is an official record covered by the right to information, which must prevail here.

paras.html: On the Constitutional Duty to Explain One's Dissent:
paras.text: On the Constitutional Duty to Explain One's Dissent:

paras.html: Art. VIII, Sec. 13: a Member who dissents "must state the reason therefor"; the framers made it mandatory, and violation is a culpable violation of the Constitution.
paras.text: Art. VIII, Sec. 13: a Member who dissents "must state the reason therefor"; the framers made it mandatory, and violation is a culpable violation of the Constitution.

paras.html: Explaining a dissent is both a right (free expression) and a duty → the majority can never suppress a dissent; doing so is itself a culpable violation. The dissent may even include internal deliberations if material to stating its reasons.
paras.text: Explaining a dissent is both a right (free expression) and a duty → the majority can never suppress a dissent; doing so is itself a culpable violation. The dissent may even include internal deliberations if material to stating its reasons.

paras.html: If a dissent breaches judicial privilege, any sanction can come only through impeachment by Congress; any other rule lets the majority "terrorize the minority into acquiescence."
paras.text: If a dissent breaches judicial privilege, any sanction can come only through impeachment by Congress; any other rule lets the majority "terrorize the minority into acquiescence."

paras.html: A dissenting Justice can explain himself only in the dissent, not in the media; dissents often later become the majority rule or are enacted into law → they deserve as much leeway as possible.
paras.text: A dissenting Justice can explain himself only in the dissent, not in the media; dissents often later become the majority rule or are enacted into law → they deserve as much leeway as possible.

paras.text: SERENO, J., Concurring and Dissenting Opinion

paras.html: TLDR: Agrees that judicial privilege can deny access to specific records and bar oral disclosure of specific matters, but holds that it is a qualified privilege that cannot impose a general gag order. She votes to PARTIALLY GRANT the letters and to have court personnel partially comply with the subpoenas, treating administrative and non-adjudicatory records as public, and dissents from three points: (a) regulating the duty to explain dissents, (b) withholding the notarized SPA, and (c) withholding the date and time her dissent was received.

paras.html: Public Accountability and Qualified Judicial Privilege:
paras.text: Public Accountability and Qualified Judicial Privilege:

paras.html: Judicial privilege derives from US practice, where it is qualified. Williams v. Mercer (11th Cir.): in the investigation of Judge Alcee Hastings for bribery, a qualified privilege protects communications between a judge and staff on judicial business, but appointment diaries, schedules, travel itineraries, sign-in sheets, and telephone logs are not privileged, and even privileged matters yield to a demonstrated need (importance of the inquiry, relevance, lack of alternatives).
paras.text: Judicial privilege derives from US practice, where it is qualified. Williams v. Mercer (11th Cir.): in the investigation of Judge Alcee Hastings for bribery, a qualified privilege protects communications between a judge and staff on judicial business, but appointment diaries, schedules, travel itineraries, sign-in sheets, and telephone logs are not privileged, and even privileged matters yield to a demonstrated need (importance of the inquiry, relevance, lack of alternatives).

paras.html: Also cites US v. Nixon (no absolute presidential privilege against a criminal subpoena), Gravel v. US, and Milne (the very author the majority relies on), who concludes that the privilege must yield to significant interests such as an investigation of judicial misconduct.
paras.text: Also cites US v. Nixon (no absolute presidential privilege against a criminal subpoena), Gravel v. US, and Milne (the very author the majority relies on), who concludes that the privilege must yield to significant interests such as an investigation of judicial misconduct.

paras.html: Impeachment of the highest judicial officer is of paramount societal importance; comity behooves the Court to give the Impeachment Court wide latitude. Accountability of public officers (Art. XI) is "absolute and unconditional", unlike the qualified privilege → the Court must justify each withheld item with specific and responsive reasons.

Accountability of public officers (Art. XI) is "absolute and unconditional", unlike the qualified privilege → the Court must justify each withheld item with specific and responsive reasons.

paras.html: Privileges cannot cover crimes or wrongdoing (Neri, where all Justices agreed executive privilege does not guard against disclosure of a crime).
paras.text: Privileges cannot cover crimes or wrongdoing (Neri, where all Justices agreed executive privilege does not guard against disclosure of a crime).

paras.html: Where an article of impeachment is sought to be proven through logbook entries and time stamps, no privilege applies, since these do not touch the mental deliberative process.

paras.text: Requested and Subpoenaed Court Records:

paras.html: All official records, including court records, are subject to the right to information; the Court's own Administrative Circular No. 2-02 sets a presumption in favor of public disclosure → confidentiality, as the exception, is strictly construed.

paras.html: Applies Kellogg's two-step analysis: (1) is the document actually deliberative? (2) balance the interests. Concurs that drafts, research materials, internal memoranda, minutes, agenda, and recommended actions are privileged; but administrative and non-adjudicatory documents must be disclosed.

paras.html: Points of divergence:
paras.text: Points of divergence:

paras.html: First: the penal laws punish only unauthorized, voluntary disclosure, not disclosure compelled by a superior authority like the Impeachment Court; the majority misquoted Sec. 3(k), RA 3019 ("unauthorized persons"); no one claimed the Impeachment Court grants immunity (obedience to a lawful order under Art. 11(6), RPC, was merely discussed as a defense).

paras.html: Second: requiring the Court's approval of every waiver is "rife with dictatorial dangers," especially since the respondent in the impeachment heads the collegial body that decides on the waiver; it preempts the Impeachment Court and constitutes unconstitutional interference.
paras.text: Second: requiring the Court's approval of every waiver is "rife with dictatorial dangers," especially since the respondent in the impeachment heads the collegial body that decides on the waiver; it preempts the Impeachment Court and constitutes unconstitutional interference.

paras.html: Third: privilege for court personnel covers only documents intimately and directly related to adjudication; logbooks, travel orders, time of filing, the Sheriff's Return, and the FMBO certification are administrative and must be produced.

paras.html: The Constitutional Duty to Explain a Dissent:
paras.text: The Constitutional Duty to Explain a Dissent:

paras.html: Traces the duty from the 1934 Convention (Aruego), the 1935 and 1973 texts, to the 1987 change from "shall" to "must" (Regalado–Maambong exchange: failure is a culpable violation).

paras.html: The Annex A reservation on published opinions (Nos. 16–19) amounts to prior censorship and curtails the duty to explain; opinions already promulgated and posted on the Court's website are public records, and how to appreciate them is for the Impeachment Court. Justices have narrated deliberations before without censure (People v. Caruncho; Misolas v. Panga).

paras.html: Supervision over the JBC and review by certiorari: The Court's supervision over the JBC (Sec. 8, Art. VIII) is the power of oversight; it covers the overseeing of compliance with the JBC's rules. Certiorari lies against the JBC under the Court's expanded judicial power (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) for grave abuse of discretion, even if the JBC does not exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions. Mandamus does not lie because the duty to nominate is discretionary.
paras.text: Supervision over the JBC and review by certiorari: The Court's supervision over the JBC (Sec. 8, Art. VIII) is the power of oversight; it covers the overseeing of compliance with the JBC's rules. Certiorari lies against the JBC under the Court's expanded judicial power (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) for grave abuse of discretion, even if the JBC does not exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions. Mandamus does not lie because the duty to nominate is discretionary.

paras.html: "Integrity" under the unanimity rule: Sec. 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 applies only when an applicant's moral fitness is challenged. The act complained of must be, at the least, linked to the moral character of the person and not to his judgment as a professional. A disagreement over legal strategy is not a question of integrity; an alleged extra-marital affair and alleged insider trading are.

paras.html: Due process in JBC proceedings: Though JBC proceedings are sui generis and impressed with discretion, the right to due process is available and demandable as a matter of right when an objection to an applicant is raised. A trial-type hearing is not required, but the applicant must be informed of the objection and given a reasonable opportunity and sufficient time to intelligently muster his response (the minimum set by JBC-010).

paras.html: The vacancy and the nomination:
paras.text: The vacancy and the nomination:

paras.html: Associate Justice Roberto Abad compulsorily retired on May 22, 2014. On March 6, 2014, the JBC announced the opening for application or recommendation for his position.
paras.text: Associate Justice Roberto Abad compulsorily retired on May 22, 2014. On March 6, 2014, the JBC announced the opening for application or recommendation for his position.

paras.html: On March 14, 2014, the JBC received a letter from UP Dean Danilo Concepcion nominating Jardeleza, then the incumbent Solicitor General. Jardeleza accepted, was included among the candidates, and was interviewed on May 29, 2014.
paras.text: On March 14, 2014, the JBC received a letter from UP Dean Danilo Concepcion nominating Jardeleza, then the incumbent Solicitor General. Jardeleza accepted, was included among the candidates, and was interviewed on May 29, 2014.

paras.html: The official list of candidates was published in The Philippine Star on April 26, 2014; the 10-day period under JBC-010 for filing complaints or oppositions ended on May 6, 2014 (fn. 51). No complaint or opposition was filed against Jardeleza in that period, and none was raised in his public interview (per Jardeleza's account, quoted in Leonen's dissent).

paras.text: The invocation of the unanimity rule:

paras.html: Sec. 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 provides:
paras.text: Sec. 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 provides:

paras.html: "SEC. 2. Votes required when integrity of a qualified applicant is challenged. — In every case where the integrity of an applicant who is not otherwise disqualified for nomination is raised or challenged, the affirmative vote of all the Members of the Council must be obtained for the favorable consideration of his nomination."

Votes required when integrity of a qualified applicant is challenged. — In every case where the integrity of an applicant who is not otherwise disqualified for nomination is raised or challenged, the affirmative vote of all the Members of the Council must be obtained for the favorable consideration of his nomination."

paras.html: The general rule (Sec. 1, Rule 10) requires the affirmative vote of at least a majority of all the Members of the Council.
paras.text: The general rule (Sec. 1, Rule 10) requires the affirmative vote of at least a majority of all the Members of the Council.

paras.html: At the June 5, 2014 JBC executive session, Chief Justice Sereno (JBC ex officio Chairperson) manifested that Jardeleza lacked the integrity required of a member of the Court and that she would invoke Sec. 2, Rule 10 against him. The ground was his manner of handling an international arbitration case for the government, shown in a confidential legal memorandum, which she said could have been detrimental to the national interest. She reiterated the invocation at the June 16, 2014 session.

She reiterated the invocation at the June 16, 2014 session.

paras.html: The ponencia keeps the case confidential. Leonen's dissent, quoting the JBC's Supplemental Comment-Reply, identifies it as Republic of the Philippines v. People's Republic of China (UNCLOS arbitration), where Jardeleza, as agent, allegedly sought the exclusion of a 14-paragraph discussion of Itu Aba from the Philippine Memorial. The CJ viewed this as "disloyal"; Sec. De Lima said it was a collective strategy of the legal team.

paras.html: On June 16 and 17, 2014, JBC member Justice Aurora Santiago Lagman called Jardeleza by telephone, told him of the CJ's invocation, and directed him to "make himself available" on June 30, 2014, when he would be informed of the objections to his integrity.

paras.text: The letter-petition:

paras.html: On June 25, 2014, Jardeleza filed a letter-petition (A.M. No. 14-07-01-SC-JBC) asking the Court, under its supervision over the JBC, to order the JBC to: (1) give him at least five working days' written notice of any hearing, with the sworn specifications of the charges, sworn statements of witnesses, and supporting documents, all made part of the public record; (2) allow him to cross-examine his oppositors in public; (3) reset the June 30 hearing; and (4) disallow the CJ from voting on the nominees.

paras.html: The letter-petition was raffled only on July 1, 2014, a day after the JBC vote. Jardeleza attributed the delay to the CJ.
