paras.html: The June 30, 2014 meeting:
paras.text: The June 30, 2014 meeting:

paras.html: Without Jardeleza present, Associate Justice Carpio appeared as a resource person to explain a classified legal memorandum supporting the CJ's objection. Sec. De Lima then briefed Jardeleza in an ante-room. He was summoned at around 2:00 p.m.
paras.text: Without Jardeleza present, Associate Justice Carpio appeared as a resource person to explain a classified legal memorandum supporting the CJ's objection. Sec. De Lima then briefed Jardeleza in an ante-room. He was summoned at around 2:00 p.m.

paras.html: The CJ told him the Council wished to ask about three issues: (1) his actuations in handling an international arbitration case not compatible with public interest; (2) reports of an extra-marital affair in SMC; and (3) alleged insider trading that led to a "show cause" order from the Philippine Stock Exchange. Issues (2) and (3) were raised for the first time at this meeting; they originated from newspaper reports that the CJ might raise "immorality" issues, which she deduced referred to his time as General Counsel of San Miguel Corporation.

Issues (2) and (3) were raised for the first time at this meeting; they originated from newspaper reports that the CJ might raise "immorality" issues, which she deduced referred to his time as General Counsel of San Miguel Corporation.

paras.html: Asked whether he wanted to defend himself, Jardeleza said he would if due process were observed: he demanded that the CJ execute a sworn statement of her objections and that he be allowed to cross-examine her in a public hearing, with the same required of Justice Carpio. Rep. Niel Tupas Jr. wanted to hear his explanation, but Jardeleza refused, as he would not be "lulled into waiving his rights". He put a written statement on record and asked the JBC to defer its meeting because the Court en banc would act on his letter-petition the next day. He was then excused.

paras.html: Jardeleza filed a petition for certiorari and mandamus under Rule 65 with prayer for a TRO, seeking to compel the JBC to include him in the shortlist, on the ground that the JBC and the CJ gravely abused their discretion in excluding him despite his sufficient number of votes.

paras.html: The JBC filed its Comment on August 11, 2014. The Executive Secretary's Comment raised the possible unconstitutionality of Sec. 2, Rule 10 and prayed for Jardeleza's inclusion. Jardeleza replied on August 15, 2014. Minutes before closing that day, the JBC filed a Supplemental Comment-Reply attaching the minutes of its meetings and a "Statement of the Chief Justice on the Integrity Objection."

The disbarment complaint was re-docketed as a separate administrative case.

paras.html: Disagreement in legal opinion is a normal, even essential, part of the legal community. A lawyer has complete discretion on what legal strategy to employ (Mattus v. Villaseca), provided he serves his client with competence and diligence within the bounds of law; a lawyer is not an insurer of victory. "Stripped of a clear showing of gross neglect, iniquity, or immoral purpose, a strategy of a legal mind remains a legal tactic acceptable to some and deplorable to others. It has no direct bearing on his moral choices."

paras.html: Extra-marital affair: bears a candid relation to moral character. A lawyer's deliberate participation in extra-marital affairs is a disgraceful stain on ethical and moral principles (Guevarra v. Eala; Samaniego v. Ferrer). Even relationships that never became physical may be immoral if more than professional or friendly (Geroy v. Calderon). Immorality is not confined to sexual matters (Sealana-Abbu v. Laurenciana-Huraño). Moral character is objective; good reputation alone is not enough (Tolentino v. Mendoza; Garrido v. Garrido).

Gacott) → yet, "notwithstanding being 'a class of its own,' the right to be heard and to explain one's self is availing."

paras.html: Due process neither negates nor renders illusory the JBC's duty to recommend and is no encroachment on its discretion; it supports and enriches the exercise of its discretion, giving the JBC a clearer understanding and guarding it from unsound, capricious assessments. The JBC need not strictly apply the rules of evidence, but "the only test that an exercise of discretion must surmount is that of soundness."

paras.html: JBC-010 ("Rule to Further Promote Public Awareness of and Accessibility to the Proceedings of the JBC," effective October 1, 2002) shows the JBC's deference to the applicant's right to be informed and to be heard: any complaint or opposition may be filed within 10 days of publication; it shall be in writing, under oath, in 10 copies; the Secretary shall furnish the candidate a copy; the candidate has 5 days to comment; and the candidate can be made to explain it in the interview.

paras.html: JBC-010 bears great weight because: (1) it covers "any" complaint or opposition; (2) it uses the mandatory "shall"; and (3) it speaks of the very essence of due process. It does not require a trial-type hearing, but it gives the applicant the right to answer → the minimum requirements of due process.

paras.html: Although he was verbally informed and later asked to explain, the JBC treated JBC-010 with indifference. Even granting ex argumenti that the 10-day period applies only to the public and not to JBC members, the June 5 invocation should have raised procedural issues; several members wanted to hear him, but JBC-010 was never on the agenda. Only on June 16 did the Council agree to invite him, by telephone.

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to DISMISS the petition. The Court's supervision over the JBC is merely administrative; neither certiorari nor mandamus lies; the JBC's interpretation of its own rules was reasonable and collegial; Jardeleza has no vested right to a nomination and was given the chance to be heard but refused; and any relief would prejudice the four nominees, who were not impleaded.

paras.html: The petition, "in the guise of an invocation of due process," tempts the Court to reach beyond its duties and order the JBC to amend a list that was unanimously signed by all JBC members and validly transmitted; none dissented to nominating only four. The Court should exercise judicial restraint; doubts should be resolved in deference to co-equal constitutional organs.

He later admitted being informed of the integrity issue at least right after the executive session but never explained its substance.

paras.html: I. Supervision over the JBC is mainly administrative
paras.text: I. Supervision over the JBC is mainly administrative

paras.html: The JBC is a fully independent constitutional body that checks the President's appointing power (Chavez v. JBC). Supervision is manifested in composition (CJ as chair, Clerk of Court as secretary), budget, and emoluments; nothing in the Constitution allows the Court to interfere with the JBC's discretion. Cites J. Brion's separate opinion in De Castro v. JBC: the Court cannot intervene in the JBC's principal function.

The JBC does not adjudicate rights; its process is "loosely akin to a 'job interview,'" and its request for Jardeleza to appear was an extension of its discreet background check.

paras.html: The lack of a definition of integrity is not unconstitutional; integrity is malleable and may differ per candidate. For the government's principal counsel in the maritime arbitration, lack of integrity can mean unexplained decisions that put the initiative in peril. A qualified vote is not strange (the Constitution uses them, e.g., Art. XVIII), and giving integrity primacy is not arbitrary.

paras.html: Natural-born requirement for SC Members: "No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court ... unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines" (Sec. 7(1), Art. VIII). One who became a Filipino through his father's naturalization while a minor is a naturalized, not a natural-born, citizen. Until he proves otherwise in appropriate adversarial court proceedings and corrects his records, he cannot accept an appointment to the Court and may be enjoined from doing so.
paras.text: Natural-born requirement for SC Members: "No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court ... unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines" (Sec. 7(1), Art. VIII). One who became a Filipino through his father's naturalization while a minor is a naturalized, not a natural-born, citizen. Until he proves otherwise in appropriate adversarial court proceedings and corrects his records, he cannot accept an appointment to the Court and may be enjoined from doing so.

paras.html: Citizenship entries can be changed only judicially: a change in citizenship is a substantial change in the civil register; it requires a judicial order in an adversarial Rule 108 proceeding. Summary administrative correction under RA 9048 does not apply to nationality, and BI/DOJ recognition of natural-born status cannot amend a final naturalization decision.

paras.html: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).
paras.text: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).

paras.html: Parameters: There must be (1) actual rebellion or invasion (rebellion as defined in Art. 134, RPC) and (2) a public safety requirement, concurring. The President needs only probable cause to believe rebellion exists. Review covers only facts known to the President at the time of the proclamation (in the Proclamation and the Report), taken in totality, for sufficiency, not accuracy; the Court does not calibrate the President's choice among his graduated powers.

paras.html: Territorial scope: The Constitution leaves to the President whether to place "the Philippines or any part thereof" under martial law. Because rebellion "cannot be confined a priori within predetermined bounds", martial law over the whole of Mindanao was upheld. Terrorism neither negates nor absorbs rebellion.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: A government operation to capture Isnilon Hapilon (ASG leader) and Maute Group leaders Abdullah and Omarkhayam Maute met armed resistance that escalated into open hostility in Marawi City. Per the President's Report: at 2:00 PM, the Maute Group and ASG attacked government and private facilities; at 4:00 PM, about 50 armed men assaulted the Marawi City Jail and freed at least 68 inmates; power was cut citywide; the Marawi Police Station was ambushed and burned; three bridges fell under their control; checkpoints were set up at the Iligan–Marawi junction; Dansalan College, the Cathedral of Maria Auxiliadora, and other buildings were burned and hostages taken; the Maute Group reportedly took over Amai Pakpak Hospital and hoisted the DAESH/ISIS flag; about 75% of Marawi was reportedly infiltrated; 11 soldiers and police were killed and 35 wounded.

paras.html: "WHEREAS, today 23 May 2017, the same Maute terrorist group has taken over a hospital in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, established several checkpoints within the City, burned down certain government and private facilities and inflicted casualties on the part of Government forces, and started flying the flag of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) in several areas, thereby openly attempting to remove from the allegiance to the Philippine Government this part of Mindanao and deprive the Chief Executive of his powers and prerogatives . . . constituting the crime of rebellion; and WHEREAS, this recent attack shows the capability of the Maute group and other rebel groups to sow terror, and cause death and damage to property not only in Lanao del Sur but also in other parts of Mindanao."

paras.html: May 25, 2017: The President submitted a written Report to Congress: Mindanao as a "hotbed of violent extremism" (Zamboanga siege, Davao bombing, Mamasapano, bombings in Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Basilan); the ASG and the ISIS-backed Maute Group (263 members) aiming to establish a DAESH wilayat in Mindanao; Marawi's strategic location; and that public safety required martial law "in the whole of Mindanao until such time that the rebellion is completely quelled."

paras.html: After briefings, the Senate adopted P.S. Resolution No. 388 (Proclamation "satisfactory, constitutional and in accordance with the law"; "no compelling reason to revoke"), and the House adopted House Resolution No. 1050 (full support; "no reason to revoke").

paras.html: Jun. 5, 2017 – G.R. No. 231658 (Lagman): Five Representatives filed a petition under the third paragraph of Sec. 18, Art. VII, arguing: (1) no rebellion, only terrorism; the Maute Group is a "private militia"; the ISIS flag is propaganda; the conflict was precipitated by the government's bid to capture Hapilon, so at most there is an "imminent danger" of rebellion, no longer a ground; (2) the Report contained "false, inaccurate, contrived and hyperbolic accounts" (Amai Pakpak Hospital, Landbank, schools, police chief beheading, city hall); (3) it included old, resolved events (Butig, the 2016 jailbreak, Zamboanga, Davao, Mamasapano); (4) the President acted alone without consulting the military; and (5) the military had pre-empted the plan; no MILF hostility; foreign fighters "undetermined."

"Rebellion" has its technical meaning under Art. 134, RPC (Regalado in the CONCOM): (1) a public uprising and taking arms against the Government; and (2) the purpose of removing from allegiance any part of the territory or armed forces, or depriving the Chief Executive or Congress of their powers or prerogatives.

paras.html: Rebellion is a crime of masses that "cannot be confined a priori, within predetermined bounds" (People v. Lovedioro). Padre Faura illustration: rebels seizing the Court's compound and raising the ISIS flag could have comrades lurking in the PGH or Manila Science High School; the President need not wait for an uprising in Quezon City before covering it.

paras.html: Public safety is abstract and has no physical metes and bounds. Under the absorption doctrine (Hernandez, Dasig), crimes committed elsewhere in furtherance of rebellion (e.g., a murder in Makati) are part of the rebellion → territorial scope cannot be fixed in proportion to the "range" of rebellion. Limiting martial law to the place of actual fighting would let rebels escape and keep their supply lines.

No evidence of rebellion in Camiguin, Dinagat, Bukidnon, and elsewhere.

Public safety was not shown: no civilian government failed to function, and respondents did not show what martial law would add to the calling-out power.

paras.html: Vagueness: a declaration must articulate the powers to be exercised; otherwise it is unconstitutionally vague. General Order No. 1 and the AFP's Operational Directive expanded it to all lawless violence, the NPA, drug syndicates, and "peace spoilers"; the AFP even defined martial law as military takeover of civilian government.

paras.html: BERSAMIN, J.: The 1987 Constitution reverts to the traditional, theater-of-war concept of martial law (Ex parte Milligan; Duncan v. Kahanamoku). Agrees the proceeding is sui generis and the Court acts as a trier of facts; requiring grave abuse could void a proclamation with nine false bases out of ten despite one true basis. The burden is on petitioners (presumptions of constitutionality and good faith), but suggests that specific denials could shift the burden of evidence to the Government. Upholds coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: VELASCO, J.: Martial law is the law of necessity, akin to self-defense; probable cause is the measure, judged on facts presented to the President at the time; later-discovered falsity does not invalidate the act at inception. Quotes Bernas's amicus brief in Fortun that public safety adds a forward-looking nuance to rebellion. Necessity also limits martial law powers (J. Teehankee): intrusions must be proportional, and officers are personally liable for ultra vires acts, the "ultimate safeguard"; discusses warrantless arrests, custodial rights, and IHL.

paras.html: LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.: Concurs on grounds deviating in part from the majority: a certiorari or prohibition petition is not barred as a vehicle (the Fortun opinions tacitly admitted it); "probable cause," "reasonableness," and absence of arbitrariness are practically the same standard, and what matters is how it is applied (J. Muñoz Palma in Aquino v. Ponce Enrile); the Court may relax the burden-of-proof rules, as its closed-door briefing was "judicial activism consistent with" Sec. 18. ISIS-linked groups' unification under an emir justified coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: PERALTA, J.: Recounts congressional action. Rebellion is a continuing crime: acts in different places with the same purpose (Lagman conceded this in Peralta's interpellation). ASG, Maute, AKP, and BIFF are linked toward a wilayah, so the danger stretches across Mindanao; the Constitution must adapt (e.g., checkpoint searches against car bombs).

paras.html: JARDELEZA, J.: Sufficiency of factual basis is distinct from grave abuse. Proposes a standard of reasonableness ("such evidence that is adequate to satisfy a reasonable mind") because probable cause, a criminal-process standard, cannot measure public safety. As a sui generis proceeding, the Court cannot indulge the presumption of regularity; the Government should first present its facts, and attaching declassified proof to the Report is advisable. Finds public safety reasonably required martial law in all Mindanao (Hapilon as emir, the wilayat plan, the Davao attack).

paras.html: MENDOZA, J.: The proceeding is sui generis; the burden of proof is on the Government, since petitioners lack access to intelligence (exception for negative facts). Shares J. Perlas-Bernabe's view that the threshold is reasonableness, neither probable cause nor arbitrariness. Territorial coverage is the President's discretion; confining martial law to Marawi is "unrealistic and impractical."

paras.html: PERLAS-BERNABE, J. (concurring in the result): The proceeding is sui generis (closer to a special proceeding than an action); "sufficient factual basis" means adequate proof, rejecting both probable cause and the Lansang arbitrariness test. The Government bears the burden of proving compliance; executive information enjoys a presumption of regularity as to facts only, not conclusions of law, so the petitioner carries the burden of evidence to debunk it. The Court must ask whether the territorial extent is rationally commensurate to the exigencies; here it was.

paras.html: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).
paras.text: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).

paras.html: Parameters: There must be (1) actual rebellion or invasion (rebellion as defined in Art. 134, RPC) and (2) a public safety requirement, concurring. The President needs only probable cause to believe rebellion exists. Review covers only facts known to the President at the time of the proclamation (in the Proclamation and the Report), taken in totality, for sufficiency, not accuracy; the Court does not calibrate the President's choice among his graduated powers.

paras.html: Territorial scope: The Constitution leaves to the President whether to place "the Philippines or any part thereof" under martial law. Because rebellion "cannot be confined a priori within predetermined bounds", martial law over the whole of Mindanao was upheld. Terrorism neither negates nor absorbs rebellion.

paras.html: Sep. 4, 2016: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 55, declaring a state of national emergency on account of lawless violence in Mindanao.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: A government operation to capture Isnilon Hapilon (ASG leader) and Maute Group leaders Abdullah and Omarkhayam Maute met armed resistance that escalated into open hostility in Marawi City. Per the President's Report: at 2:00 PM, the Maute Group and ASG attacked government and private facilities; at 4:00 PM, about 50 armed men assaulted the Marawi City Jail and freed at least 68 inmates; power was cut citywide; the Marawi Police Station was ambushed and burned; three bridges fell under their control; checkpoints were set up at the Iligan–Marawi junction; Dansalan College, the Cathedral of Maria Auxiliadora, and other buildings were burned and hostages taken; the Maute Group reportedly took over Amai Pakpak Hospital and hoisted the DAESH/ISIS flag; about 75% of Marawi was reportedly infiltrated; 11 soldiers and police were killed and 35 wounded.

paras.text: May 23, 2017: Proclamation No. 216 declared martial law and suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the "Mindanao group of islands" for not more than 60 days. It was "DONE in the Russian Federation." Its key Whereas clauses:

paras.html: "WHEREAS, today 23 May 2017, the same Maute terrorist group has taken over a hospital in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, established several checkpoints within the City, burned down certain government and private facilities and inflicted casualties on the part of Government forces, and started flying the flag of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) in several areas, thereby openly attempting to remove from the allegiance to the Philippine Government this part of Mindanao and deprive the Chief Executive of his powers and prerogatives . . . constituting the crime of rebellion; and WHEREAS, this recent attack shows the capability of the Maute group and other rebel groups to sow terror, and cause death and damage to property not only in Lanao del Sur but also in other parts of Mindanao."

paras.html: May 25, 2017: The President submitted a written Report to Congress: Mindanao as a "hotbed of violent extremism" (Zamboanga siege, Davao bombing, Mamasapano, bombings in Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Basilan); the ASG and the ISIS-backed Maute Group (263 members) aiming to establish a DAESH wilayat in Mindanao; Marawi's strategic location; and that public safety required martial law "in the whole of Mindanao until such time that the rebellion is completely quelled."

VII, arguing: (1) no rebellion, only terrorism; the Maute Group is a "private militia"; the ISIS flag is propaganda; the conflict was precipitated by the government's bid to capture Hapilon, so at most there is an "imminent danger" of rebellion, no longer a ground; (2) the Report contained "false, inaccurate, contrived and hyperbolic accounts" (Amai Pakpak Hospital, Landbank, schools, police chief beheading, city hall); (3) it included old, resolved events (Butig, the 2016 jailbreak, Zamboanga, Davao, Mamasapano); (4) the President acted alone without consulting the military; and (5) the military had pre-empted the plan; no MILF hostility; foreign fighters "undetermined."

paras.html: Lansang (1935 Constitution) applied a "prudentially narrow test of arbitrariness." The 1987 Constitution, by providing for review of sufficiency of the factual bases, "has in fact done away with the test of arbitrariness". Under contemporaneous construction, "sufficiency of factual basis" is the only test: the Court need not be satisfied that the decision is correct, only that it had sufficient factual bases.

Padre Faura illustration: rebels seizing the Court's compound and raising the ISIS flag could have comrades lurking in the PGH or Manila Science High School; the President need not wait for an uprising in Quezon City before covering it.

paras.html: Public safety is abstract and has no physical metes and bounds. Under the absorption doctrine (Hernandez, Dasig), crimes committed elsewhere in furtherance of rebellion (e.g., a murder in Makati) are part of the rebellion → territorial scope cannot be fixed in proportion to the "range" of rebellion. Limiting martial law to the place of actual fighting would let rebels escape and keep their supply lines.

paras.html: Points of disagreement: the necessity inquiry requires proportionality (greater powers only when less intrusive ones fail) and defining the metes and bounds of martial law; it is feasible (e.g., by province); doing so does not substitute the Court's wisdom. Excessive leeway led to "the absurdity of martial law in places as terrorism and rebellion-free as Dinagat Islands or Camiguin."

paras.html: Probable cause existed for actual rebellion in Marawi (adopting the CJ's findings), but there was insufficient showing that public safety required martial law over all Mindanao: no armed uprising in eastern Mindanao; fleeing rebels may be pursued under the continuing-crime doctrine without martial law, which itself cannot extend actual rebellion wherever offenders go (J. Feliciano in Lacson v. Perez). The SolGen's answer ("political judgment") showed martial law was at most "beneficial" or "preferable," not required.

paras.html: Vagueness: a declaration must articulate the powers to be exercised; otherwise it is unconstitutionally vague. General Order No. 1 and the AFP's Operational Directive expanded it to all lawless violence, the NPA, drug syndicates, and "peace spoilers"; the AFP even defined martial law as military takeover of civilian government.

paras.html: BERSAMIN, J.: The 1987 Constitution reverts to the traditional, theater-of-war concept of martial law (Ex parte Milligan; Duncan v. Kahanamoku). Agrees the proceeding is sui generis and the Court acts as a trier of facts; requiring grave abuse could void a proclamation with nine false bases out of ten despite one true basis. The burden is on petitioners (presumptions of constitutionality and good faith), but suggests that specific denials could shift the burden of evidence to the Government. Upholds coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: VELASCO, J.: Martial law is the law of necessity, akin to self-defense; probable cause is the measure, judged on facts presented to the President at the time; later-discovered falsity does not invalidate the act at inception. Quotes Bernas's amicus brief in Fortun that public safety adds a forward-looking nuance to rebellion. Necessity also limits martial law powers (J. Teehankee): intrusions must be proportional, and officers are personally liable for ultra vires acts, the "ultimate safeguard"; discusses warrantless arrests, custodial rights, and IHL.

paras.html: LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.: Concurs on grounds deviating in part from the majority: a certiorari or prohibition petition is not barred as a vehicle (the Fortun opinions tacitly admitted it); "probable cause," "reasonableness," and absence of arbitrariness are practically the same standard, and what matters is how it is applied (J. Muñoz Palma in Aquino v. Ponce Enrile); the Court may relax the burden-of-proof rules, as its closed-door briefing was "judicial activism consistent with" Sec. 18. ISIS-linked groups' unification under an emir justified coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: PERALTA, J.: Recounts congressional action. Rebellion is a continuing crime: acts in different places with the same purpose (Lagman conceded this in Peralta's interpellation). ASG, Maute, AKP, and BIFF are linked toward a wilayah, so the danger stretches across Mindanao; the Constitution must adapt (e.g., checkpoint searches against car bombs).

paras.html: JARDELEZA, J.: Sufficiency of factual basis is distinct from grave abuse. Proposes a standard of reasonableness ("such evidence that is adequate to satisfy a reasonable mind") because probable cause, a criminal-process standard, cannot measure public safety. As a sui generis proceeding, the Court cannot indulge the presumption of regularity; the Government should first present its facts, and attaching declassified proof to the Report is advisable. Finds public safety reasonably required martial law in all Mindanao (Hapilon as emir, the wilayat plan, the Davao attack).

paras.html: MENDOZA, J.: The proceeding is sui generis; the burden of proof is on the Government, since petitioners lack access to intelligence (exception for negative facts). Shares J. Perlas-Bernabe's view that the threshold is reasonableness, neither probable cause nor arbitrariness. Territorial coverage is the President's discretion; confining martial law to Marawi is "unrealistic and impractical."

paras.html: PERLAS-BERNABE, J. (concurring in the result): The proceeding is sui generis (closer to a special proceeding than an action); "sufficient factual basis" means adequate proof, rejecting both probable cause and the Lansang arbitrariness test. The Government bears the burden of proving compliance; executive information enjoys a presumption of regularity as to facts only, not conclusions of law, so the petitioner carries the burden of evidence to debunk it. The Court must ask whether the territorial extent is rationally commensurate to the exigencies; here it was.

Petitioners bear the burden; probable cause existed; the entire Mindanao coverage had sufficient basis.

paras.html: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).
paras.text: Sui generis review: The "appropriate proceeding" under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII is any action by a citizen questioning the sufficiency of the factual basis of martial law or the suspension of the writ. It is not a certiorari petition, and the test is sufficiency of factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion or arbitrariness. The Court's review is independent of Congress's power to revoke (Fortun set aside).

paras.html: Parameters: There must be (1) actual rebellion or invasion (rebellion as defined in Art. 134, RPC) and (2) a public safety requirement, concurring. The President needs only probable cause to believe rebellion exists. Review covers only facts known to the President at the time of the proclamation (in the Proclamation and the Report), taken in totality, for sufficiency, not accuracy; the Court does not calibrate the President's choice among his graduated powers.

paras.html: Territorial scope: The Constitution leaves to the President whether to place "the Philippines or any part thereof" under martial law. Because rebellion "cannot be confined a priori within predetermined bounds", martial law over the whole of Mindanao was upheld. Terrorism neither negates nor absorbs rebellion.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: A government operation to capture Isnilon Hapilon (ASG leader) and Maute Group leaders Abdullah and Omarkhayam Maute met armed resistance that escalated into open hostility in Marawi City. Per the President's Report: at 2:00 PM, the Maute Group and ASG attacked government and private facilities; at 4:00 PM, about 50 armed men assaulted the Marawi City Jail and freed at least 68 inmates; power was cut citywide; the Marawi Police Station was ambushed and burned; three bridges fell under their control; checkpoints were set up at the Iligan–Marawi junction; Dansalan College, the Cathedral of Maria Auxiliadora, and other buildings were burned and hostages taken; the Maute Group reportedly took over Amai Pakpak Hospital and hoisted the DAESH/ISIS flag; about 75% of Marawi was reportedly infiltrated; 11 soldiers and police were killed and 35 wounded.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: Proclamation No. 216 declared martial law and suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the "Mindanao group of islands" for not more than 60 days. It was "DONE in the Russian Federation." Its key Whereas clauses:
paras.text: May 23, 2017: Proclamation No. 216 declared martial law and suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the "Mindanao group of islands" for not more than 60 days. It was "DONE in the Russian Federation." Its key Whereas clauses:

paras.html: "WHEREAS, today 23 May 2017, the same Maute terrorist group has taken over a hospital in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, established several checkpoints within the City, burned down certain government and private facilities and inflicted casualties on the part of Government forces, and started flying the flag of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) in several areas, thereby openly attempting to remove from the allegiance to the Philippine Government this part of Mindanao and deprive the Chief Executive of his powers and prerogatives . . . constituting the crime of rebellion; and WHEREAS, this recent attack shows the capability of the Maute group and other rebel groups to sow terror, and cause death and damage to property not only in Lanao del Sur but also in other parts of Mindanao."

paras.html: May 25, 2017: The President submitted a written Report to Congress: Mindanao as a "hotbed of violent extremism" (Zamboanga siege, Davao bombing, Mamasapano, bombings in Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Basilan); the ASG and the ISIS-backed Maute Group (263 members) aiming to establish a DAESH wilayat in Mindanao; Marawi's strategic location; and that public safety required martial law "in the whole of Mindanao until such time that the rebellion is completely quelled."

paras.html: Jun. 5, 2017 – G.R. No. 231658 (Lagman): Five Representatives filed a petition under the third paragraph of Sec. 18, Art. VII, arguing: (1) no rebellion, only terrorism; the Maute Group is a "private militia"; the ISIS flag is propaganda; the conflict was precipitated by the government's bid to capture Hapilon, so at most there is an "imminent danger" of rebellion, no longer a ground; (2) the Report contained "false, inaccurate, contrived and hyperbolic accounts" (Amai Pakpak Hospital, Landbank, schools, police chief beheading, city hall); (3) it included old, resolved events (Butig, the 2016 jailbreak, Zamboanga, Davao, Mamasapano); (4) the President acted alone without consulting the military; and (5) the military had pre-empted the plan; no MILF hostility; foreign fighters "undetermined."

paras.html: Lansang (1935 Constitution) applied a "prudentially narrow test of arbitrariness." The 1987 Constitution, by providing for review of sufficiency of the factual bases, "has in fact done away with the test of arbitrariness". Under contemporaneous construction, "sufficiency of factual basis" is the only test: the Court need not be satisfied that the decision is correct, only that it had sufficient factual bases.

paras.html: Actual rebellion only in Marawi: the 400–500 armed Maute-Hapilon fighters' uprising in Marawi is indisputable rebellion, but the Proclamation itself speaks of removing "this part of Mindanao", and the Report calls Marawi a "precedent" to spreading control: an admission that the rebellion had yet to spread. No evidence of rebellion in Camiguin, Dinagat, Bukidnon, and elsewhere.

paras.html: Capability is not a ground: the fear of spread is a threat, not even imminent; allowing martial law on it reinstates "imminent danger," which the framers removed.

paras.html: "Predetermined bounds" misread: Lovedioro refers to the crimes absorbed in rebellion, not geographic boundaries. Escaping rebels can be arrested anywhere with or without warrant, since rebellion is a continuing crime (Umil v. Ramos). Sporadic bombings elsewhere are terrorism, not rebellion.

paras.html: BERSAMIN, J.: The 1987 Constitution reverts to the traditional, theater-of-war concept of martial law (Ex parte Milligan; Duncan v. Kahanamoku). Agrees the proceeding is sui generis and the Court acts as a trier of facts; requiring grave abuse could void a proclamation with nine false bases out of ten despite one true basis. The burden is on petitioners (presumptions of constitutionality and good faith), but suggests that specific denials could shift the burden of evidence to the Government. Upholds coverage of all Mindanao.

The burden is on petitioners (presumptions of constitutionality and good faith), but suggests that specific denials could shift the burden of evidence to the Government. paras.html: VELASCO, J.: Martial law is the law of necessity, akin to self-defense; probable cause is the measure, judged on facts presented to the President at the time; later-discovered falsity does not invalidate the act at inception. Quotes Bernas's amicus brief in Fortun that public safety adds a forward-looking nuance to rebellion. Necessity also limits martial law powers (J. Teehankee): intrusions must be proportional, and officers are personally liable for ultra vires acts, the "ultimate safeguard"; discusses warrantless arrests, custodial rights, and IHL.

paras.html: LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.: Concurs on grounds deviating in part from the majority: a certiorari or prohibition petition is not barred as a vehicle (the Fortun opinions tacitly admitted it); "probable cause," "reasonableness," and absence of arbitrariness are practically the same standard, and what matters is how it is applied (J. Muñoz Palma in Aquino v. Ponce Enrile); the Court may relax the burden-of-proof rules, as its closed-door briefing was "judicial activism consistent with" Sec. 18. ISIS-linked groups' unification under an emir justified coverage of all Mindanao.

paras.html: PERALTA, J.: Recounts congressional action. Rebellion is a continuing crime: acts in different places with the same purpose (Lagman conceded this in Peralta's interpellation). ASG, Maute, AKP, and BIFF are linked toward a wilayah, so the danger stretches across Mindanao; the Constitution must adapt (e.g., checkpoint searches against car bombs).

paras.html: JARDELEZA, J.: Sufficiency of factual basis is distinct from grave abuse. Proposes a standard of reasonableness ("such evidence that is adequate to satisfy a reasonable mind") because probable cause, a criminal-process standard, cannot measure public safety. As a sui generis proceeding, the Court cannot indulge the presumption of regularity; the Government should first present its facts, and attaching declassified proof to the Report is advisable. Finds public safety reasonably required martial law in all Mindanao (Hapilon as emir, the wilayat plan, the Davao attack).

Territorial coverage is the President's discretion; confining martial law to Marawi is "unrealistic and impractical."

paras.html: PERLAS-BERNABE, J. (concurring in the result): The proceeding is sui generis (closer to a special proceeding than an action); "sufficient factual basis" means adequate proof, rejecting both probable cause and the Lansang arbitrariness test. The Government bears the burden of proving compliance; executive information enjoys a presumption of regularity as to facts only, not conclusions of law, so the petitioner carries the burden of evidence to debunk it. The Court must ask whether the territorial extent is rationally commensurate to the exigencies; here it was.

paras.html: Sufficiency, not accuracy: Sec. 18, Art. VII requires the Court to determine only the sufficiency of the factual basis, not its accuracy, which is a higher standard. The Court looks at the totality of the facts in the President's possession prior to and at the time of the declaration; subsequent events have no bearing, and inaccuracies in some facts do not invalidate the declaration as long as other facts support the existence of actual rebellion or invasion and the public-safety requirement.
paras.text: Sufficiency, not accuracy: Sec. 18, Art. VII requires the Court to determine only the sufficiency of the factual basis, not its accuracy, which is a higher standard. The Court looks at the totality of the facts in the President's possession prior to and at the time of the declaration; subsequent events have no bearing, and inaccuracies in some facts do not invalidate the declaration as long as other facts support the existence of actual rebellion or invasion and the public-safety requirement.

paras.html: Martial law has a "time fuse": The President's declaration lasts at most 60 days and automatically terminates. Its extension, though initiated by the President, is approved by Congress and is a distinct and separate joint executive-legislative act (RBH No. 11). The expiry of Proclamation No. 216 rendered the challenge to its sufficiency moot, and the Court has no jurisdiction to review the extension in petitions that assail only the proclamation.

paras.html: Leeway is not surrender: The leeway given to the Executive does not concede the judicial power to review; it rests on the requirement of actual (not imminent) rebellion or invasion, which makes time of the essence, and on the President's access to confidential information.

paras.html: Territorial scope is fixed by the Constitution. Sec. 18 requires (1) actual rebellion or invasion and (2) public safety. Actual rebellion, as defined by the RPC (public uprising and taking up arms, with the purpose of removing territory or forces from allegiance or depriving the Chief Executive or Congress of powers; Ladlad v. Velasco), must exist in the particular territory before martial law may be declared there.

paras.html: No rebellion outside Marawi. The Proclamation itself refers only to "this part of Mindanao," meaning Marawi City; the Report names no other place with a similar uprising.

paras.html: History. The Jones Law (1916), the 1935 Constitution, and the 1973 Constitution allowed martial law for rebellion "or imminent danger thereof" → placing the whole country under martial law for a local rebellion was then justified by the danger of spread. The 1987 Constitution intentionally removed "imminent danger."
paras.text: History. The Jones Law (1916), the 1935 Constitution, and the 1973 Constitution allowed martial law for rebellion "or imminent danger thereof" → placing the whole country under martial law for a local rebellion was then justified by the danger of spread. paras.html: Spill-over = imminent danger. Upholding martial law outside Marawi because of a possible "spill-over of hostilities" or escape of rebels would unlawfully reinstate the deleted ground. The President may choose between calling out the armed forces and declaring martial law, but has no wide leeway on territorial scope.

paras.html: Sec. 18 is a neutral, straightforward fact-checking mechanism. It does not assign blame or ascribe grave abuse, so a finding of insufficiency exposes the Executive to no liability.

paras.html: Accuracy is inextricably linked to sufficiency. Sufficient factual basis necessarily means "sufficient truthful, accurate, or at the very least, credible" basis. The Court's judgment is not temporally bound to the date of the proclamation: per the Bernas–Bengzon exchange in the ConCom, the Court's judgment is "transitory" because facts change → the Court may nullify if the facts are shown false or no longer obtaining during review (or uphold if facts later become sufficient).

paras.html: "False dichotomy." Evidence is the means of ascertaining the truth (Rule 128, Sec. 1); accepting false facts makes the quantum of evidence illusory. The Executive's superior data-gathering apparatus should raise the bar, not lower it; otherwise the finding rests on bare allegations, akin to relying on presumptions of regularity, which amounts to judicial rubber-stamping.

paras.html: Standard of review under Sec. 18, Art. VII: The standard is sufficiency of the factual basis, not grave abuse of discretion. The Court need not make an independent determination of the facts; it evaluates the reports of the implementing agencies in their totality, not piecemeal, giving due regard to those "not palpably false, contrived and untrue." "The test of sufficiency is not accuracy nor preciseness but reasonableness of the factual basis."

paras.html: May 23, 2017: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for not more than 60 days, to address the rebellion of the Maute Group and the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG). Its whereas clauses cited the Maute group's takeover of a hospital in Marawi City, its checkpoints, the burning of facilities, and the flying of the ISIS flag, "thereby openly attempting to remove from the allegiance to the Philippine Government this part of Mindanao."

Its whereas clauses cited the Maute group's takeover of a hospital in Marawi City, its checkpoints, the burning of facilities, and the flying of the ISIS flag, "thereby openly attempting to remove from the allegiance to the Philippine Government this part of Mindanao."

paras.html: May 25, 2017: Within 48 hours, the President submitted his written Report to Congress. The Senate (P.S. Res. No. 388) and the House (H. Res. No. 1050) expressed support and found no cause to revoke.

paras.html: Because the Court determines the sufficiency of the factual basis, "the standard of review under Section 18, Article VII is not grave abuse of discretion."

paras.html: Sufficiency is determined from the facts in the President's request, supported by the reports of his alter egos to Congress – the same bases on which Congress granted the extension. The Court cannot expect exactitude; inadequacies in some facts are not reason enough to invalidate "as long as there are other related and relevant circumstances" supporting the finding.

paras.html: Responding to Monsod: The Court need not make an independent determination of the factual basis. It "needs only to assess and evaluate the written reports of the government agencies."

paras.html: Elements of rebellion under Art. 134, RPC (as applied in Lagman v. Medialdea and Lagman v. Pimentel III): (1) (a) public uprising and (b) taking arms against the Government; (2) purpose of removing from allegiance territory or armed forces, or depriving the Chief Executive or Congress of their powers. Its gravamen is an armed public uprising, a "crime of masses" that "cannot be confined a priori, within predetermined bounds."

paras.html: Rebellion, "within the context of the situation in Mindanao, encompasses no definite time nor particular locality of actual war and continues even when actual fighting has ceased." It results from "a series or combination of acts and events, past, present and future."

paras.html: The country faces rebellion on several fronts, each a sufficient basis for martial law. The President need not wait until a city is overrun: the Constitution "does not demand that a city be first taken over or people get killed"; it asks only that there be an actual, existing rebellion in the territory. The basis must not be arbitrary, but it need not be "so accurate that there is no room for changes or correction."

paras.html: The Sec. 18 safeguards (a)–(n), quoted from Lagman v. Pimentel III: actual invasion/rebellion plus public safety; 60-day limit; report within 48 hours; revocation by majority of Congress voting jointly, which the President cannot set aside; extension only on Congress's approval upon the President's initiative; SC review within 30 days; martial law does not suspend the Constitution or supplant civil courts; suspension of the writ applies only to those judicially charged for rebellion or offenses connected with invasion; detainees must be charged within three days or released.

paras.html: Actual rebellion required. The 1987 Constitution deliberately deleted "imminent danger"; rebellion means the crime under Art. 134, RPC, as held in Lagman v. Medialdea and as Proclamation No. 216 itself cited.

paras.html: Same rebellion only. Congress may extend only "if the ... rebellion shall persist" – the same rebellion in the initial proclamation, which named only the Maute group. That rebellion ended with Hapilon's death and Marawi's liberation; the President himself declared Marawi liberated (Oct. 17, 2017). At the oral arguments, Maj. Gen. Lorenzo admitted there is no ongoing armed rebellion in Marawi.

paras.html: Against the ponencia: (I) accuracy is required – "how can something that is inaccurate and untrue be considered sufficient?"; (II) false dichotomy: on review, probable cause must rest on substantial evidence; (III) the ponencia "finds a forest where there is not a single tree"; (IV) Montenegro rests on Barcelon v. Baker, which treated the matter as a political question; (V) rebellion is not broader than the RPC definition [Caguioa quotes ponencia language on rebellion's "expansive scope" that does not appear in the ponencia as promulgated]; (VI)–(VII) continuing-crime and "consistent pattern" reasoning do not dispense with proof of overt act plus political purpose; (VIII) public clamor is irrelevant to a Sec. 18 review.

paras.html: Congress may extend more than once, for the period it fixes: "Section 18, Article VII is clear that the only limitations to the exercise of the congressional authority to extend such proclamation or suspension are that the extension should be upon the President's initiative; that it should be grounded on the persistence of the invasion or rebellion and the demands of public safety; and that it is subject to the Court's review of the sufficiency of its factual basis upon the petition of any citizen." The "same manner" clause refers to the mode of voting, not to a 60-day period.
paras.text: Congress may extend more than once, for the period it fixes: "Section 18, Article VII is clear that the only limitations to the exercise of the congressional authority to extend such proclamation or suspension are that the extension should be upon the President's initiative; that it should be grounded on the persistence of the invasion or rebellion and the demands of public safety; and that it is subject to the Court's review of the sufficiency of its factual basis upon the petition of any citizen." The "same manner" clause refers to the mode of voting, not to a 60-day period.

paras.html: Scope of the Court's review: Under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII, the Court's review of Congress' extension is limited to the sufficiency of the factual basis; a certiorari petition invoking expanded jurisdiction (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) is not the proper remedy. Because the Court's judgment is "transitory," a ruling on the original proclamation does not bar review of the persistence of the rebellion.
paras.text: Scope of the Court's review: Under Sec. 18(3), Art. VII, the Court's review of Congress' extension is limited to the sufficiency of the factual basis; a certiorari petition invoking expanded jurisdiction (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) is not the proper remedy. Because the Court's judgment is "transitory," a ruling on the original proclamation does not bar review of the persistence of the rebellion.

paras.html: Persistence of rebellion and public safety: Rebellion is a continuing crime; the end of armed combat in one place does not end it, nor does it cease "by estoppel" on account of official pronouncements. Public safety requires the extension when present and past acts of the actual rebellion "endanger and will endanger public safety"; the Constitution sets no threshold that government must first be unable to function.

paras.html: May 23, 2017: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for not more than 60 days, to address the rebellion of the Maute Group and the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG).
paras.text: May 23, 2017: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for not more than 60 days, to address the rebellion of the Maute Group and the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG).

paras.html: May 25, 2017: Within the 48-hour period, the President submitted his written Report to Congress. The Senate (P.S. Res. No. 388) and the House (H. Res. No. 1050) expressed full support and found no cause to revoke.

paras.html: July 18 and 22, 2017: On the President's request, Congress, in a Special Joint Session, adopted Resolution of Both Houses (RBH) No. 2, extending Proc. 216 until December 31, 2017 (first extension).

paras.html: Including the NPA "will not render it void." The NPA (communist rule) and the DAESH/ISIS-inspired rebels differ in ideology but share the purpose of overthrowing the duly constituted government, and the NPA's violence hardly distinguishes it from the architects of the Marawi siege.

paras.html: The NPA was not included in Proc. 216 because of ongoing peace negotiations ("not explicitly included" as a matter of comity, per the OSG). It would make no sense to exclude a communist rebellion that persists in the same region.

paras.html: Reliance on the Executive's facts: the President may rely on intelligence reports and classified documents (Lagman). The request was based on AFP and PNP assessments, a "careful personal evaluation" of reports (ES Medialdea), and the President's personal knowledge. The AFP briefed both Houses on December 12; resource persons answered interpellations at the joint session; Rep. Papandayan confirmed remnants' recruitment in Lanao del Sur. Since the facts are with the Executive, "the Court will have to rely on the fact-finding capabilities of the [E]xecutive [D]epartment; in turn, the Executive Department will have to open its findings to the scrutiny of the Court." It did so at oral arguments, with NICA-vetted data whose reliability was not challenged.

paras.html: Martial law is a law of necessity ("Necessity creates the conditions for martial law and at the same time limits the scope of martial law"). When the need ends, the President may lift it before the year ends, and Congress may pre-terminate the extension, since the power to fix the period includes the power to shorten it. Because the Court's judgment is transitory, any citizen may again petition for review if they fail to lift it.

paras.html: The doctrine of necessity: The ponencia sets no parameters for either requirement and no limits on the length or number of extensions. Tracing American cases (Luther v. Borden, Ex parte Milligan, Moyer v. Peabody, Sterling v. Constantin, Duncan v. Kahanamoku), martial law is "the law of necessity in national emergency"; under the 1987 Constitution, necessity is expressed in "public safety requires it."

Borden, Ex parte Milligan, Moyer v. Peabody, Sterling v. Constantin, Duncan v. Kahanamoku), martial law is "the law of necessity in national emergency"; under the 1987 Constitution, necessity is expressed in "public safety requires it."

paras.html: Calibration and proportionality: Following Sterling, the Court must weigh the gravity of the situation against martial law; the danger must arise in a state of significant armed conflict. The Court must also calibrate the territorial coverage and, for extensions, whether the danger is commensurate with the period (as in Lansang v. Garcia).

paras.html: No operational necessity shown: Her exchange with Gen. Guerrero yielded only that martial law is partly "psychological," projects "a strong authority," and eases coordination, an "undocumented experiential claim" against documented claims of abuses.

paras.html: Period of extension: Congress has final say but not unbridled discretion: the period must be definite and reasonable (a rational match with the two requisites), fixed through Congress' independent evaluation; the Court's review covers the sufficiency of the factual basis of the period too.

paras.html: Merits: Recruitment, bombing plans, and "serious security concern" show at most imminent danger of an uprising, a ground deleted by the framers. BIFF and ASG incidents lacked particularity and may have been counted before. The NPA rebellion was not a basis of Proc. 216 as reviewed in Lagman; adding a new actor to show that rebellion "persists" is "self-contradictory."

paras.html: Preliminary: Rejects petitioners' reliance on Ex parte Milligan (martial law as military jurisdiction over civilians in a theater of war); it conflicts with Sec. 18(4), Art. VII, under which the Constitution and civil courts continue to operate.

paras.html: First, the Maute rebellion ceased. "Persist" means the continued existence of the same rebellion cited in the initial proclamation. Proc. 216 and the Report identified the Maute Group. The President's October 17, 2017 declaration of Marawi's liberation, Sec. Lorenzana's announcement ending combat operations, and Col. Brawner's statement confirm that actual rebellion no longer persisted; no evidence of Maute rebellion elsewhere.

paras.html: Second, remnants' capability is not rebellion. "Capability to rebel, absent an actual rebellion or invasion, is not a ground"; allowing it would reinstate "imminent danger," which was intentionally removed.

paras.html: Third, the NPA rebellion cannot justify the extension. Lagman upheld Proc. 216 solely on the Maute rebellion. Citing the NPA bypasses the mandatory 60-day period for an initial declaration; the government may proclaim martial law over the NPA rebellion, but must observe the 60 days before seeking extension. Congress' concurrence cannot cure this.

paras.html: Votes to dismiss. The parameters of review are the same as in Lagman (including whether territorial extent is rationally commensurate), but the object is Congress' extension. The Constitution limits neither the number nor the length of extensions; Congress is not bound by the President's recommendation.

paras.html: A rebellion "survives in legal existence" until the movement stops; a showing of substantial inactivity or loss of capability suffices to end it. No such showing here; rebels regrouped. Supervening activities of other groups (BIFF, Turaifie, NPA) may be considered; nothing requires an extension to relate solely to the same group. Public safety is a more malleable concept deserving deference, circumscribed by truth and reason.

paras.html: Heightened scrutiny: Sec. 18 requires stricter review than past Constitutions (tracing Barcelon, Montenegro, Lansang, Aquino v. Enrile, Parong) and includes review for grave abuse. The majority's deferential review is "a reincarnation of the political question doctrine."

paras.html: Undefined powers and targets: There can be no rational review when the powers to be exercised under martial law are not defined; the request was a "carte blanche." The government gave no targets beyond "to quell the rebellion," and Gen. Guerrero cited mainly a "psychological advantage." Rehabilitation and economic goals are not grounds.

paras.html: Evidence: Letters and briefings are allegations (factum probandum versus factum probans); intelligence must be shown to have undergone rigorous analysis. Recruitment motives (clan, revenge, money) do not show rebellion; 537 rebels against more than 100,000 AFP personnel; no basis for covering all of Mindanao; no basis for one year.

paras.html: NPA and terrorism: The NPA's "surreptitious insertion" was not a basis of Proc. 216; its attacks targeted private entities. Terrorism differs from rebellion and calls for counter-violent-extremism programs (citing the UK's CONTEST), not military rule.

Only 7 BIFF and 5 ASG incidents occurred between Marawi's liberation and December 13, 2017; data were generic, mistimed, or irrelevant. Recruits' motives (clan, revenge, money) are not the political purposes in Art. 134.

paras.html: Votes to dismiss all petitions (per the Chief Justice's certification). Drop the President as respondent. Extension is a joint executive-legislative act; the President and Congress need only be convinced of probable cause that rebellion persists. Duration is for Congress; there is no one-time limit. "Remnants" may be as dangerous as the original fighters. Congress' rules cannot be assailed in a Sec. 18 proceeding. Fears of a Marcos-type regime are speculative given the 1987 safeguards.

paras.html: Power to remove is limited by security of tenure: a presidential appointee comes under the President's direct disciplining authority, since "the power to remove is inherent in the power to appoint" (Sec. 16, Art. VII). But this power "is not an absolute one": a presidential appointee who is also a career service officer enjoys security of tenure and "may only be removed for a cause and in accordance with procedural due process."

paras.html: Effect of acquittal on an administrative case: as a rule, administrative and criminal cases are independent. However, where "the very basis of the administrative case ... is his conviction in the criminal action which was later on set aside ... upon a categorical and clear finding that the acts for which he was administratively held liable are not unlawful and irregular," the acquittal necessarily entails the dismissal of the administrative action.

paras.html: Reorganization must be in good faith: the President has the power to reorganize, but "reorganization is regarded as valid provided it is pursued in good faith" (Dario v. Mison). The circumstances in Sec. 2 of RA 6656 (e.g., significant increase in positions; abolition of an office and creation of another performing substantially the same functions) are evidence of bad faith.

paras.html: Re: The rule and the exception
paras.text: Re: The rule and the exception

paras.html: Rule: administrative cases are independent from criminal actions for the same act; dismissal or acquittal of the criminal charge does not foreclose administrative action or relieve administrative liability (Police Commission v. Lood; OCA v. Enriquez).
paras.text: Rule: administrative cases are independent from criminal actions for the same act; dismissal or acquittal of the criminal charge does not foreclose administrative action or relieve administrative liability (Police Commission v. Lood; OCA v. Enriquez).

paras.html: Exception: the case's "circumstantial setting ... sets it miles apart" from the rule. Where the very basis of the administrative case is the conviction, later set aside upon a categorical and clear finding that the acts are not unlawful and irregular, the acquittal necessarily entails the dismissal of the administrative action, because there is no more basis nor justifiable reason to maintain it.

paras.html: Dario v. Mison (1989): a reorganization is in good faith if for economy or efficiency; then no dismissal occurs because the position ceases to exist, and security of tenure is not "a Chinese wall." But if abolition is done for political reasons, to defeat security of tenure, or otherwise not in good faith, it is void ab initio, as where there is merely a change of nomenclature or claims of economy are belied by ample funds.

paras.html: Four votes are needed to grant an MR: The COMELEC en banc decides by a majority vote of all its members (Sec. 7, Art. IX-A), i.e., four. The movant carries the burden of convincing four commissioners that the division committed reversible error. If the en banc fails to muster four votes on the MR even after rehearing, the MR is denied and the division's ruling stands affirmed; the case is not dismissed. This modifies the doctrine in Mendoza v. COMELEC (2010).

paras.html: An MR before the en banc is an "incidental matter": Under Sec. 6, Rule 18 of the COMELEC Rules, a pending MR of a division ruling falls under the third effect (petition or motion denied), not the first (dismissal of an action "originally commenced in the Commission") or the second (affirmance in "appealed cases").

paras.html: On May 14, 2013, Legaspi filed a Petition for Disqualification against Germar and Santos, alleging that from May 11, 2013 until election day they engaged in massive vote-buying, using their political leaders as conduits.

paras.html: Per witness accounts, the political leaders, camped inside the North Hills Village Homeowners Association office in Brgy. Bitungol, distributed to voters envelopes containing ₱500.00 each and a sample ballot bearing the respondents' names.

paras.html: Military efforts foiled the vote-buying, and the office was padlocked. The newly installed Chief of Police, P/Supt. Dale Soliba, and his subordinates then tried to force open the office and retrieve four boxes of undistributed envelopes (about ₱800,000.00), but concerned citizens thwarted them in flagrante delicto and intercepted the evidence.

paras.html: Evidence offered (fn. 5): sworn statements of eyewitnesses; P/Supt. Soliba's turn-over report of the confiscated items; photos; police blotter entries; sworn statements of 194 voters who were offered or given ₱250.00–₱500.00 each for their votes and issued yellow stubs; statements that respondents' team promised ₱500.00–₱1,000.00 to voters who would not vote and would have their fingers inked; and BEI minutes of Cluster Precinct No. 60 allowing three voters to vote after verifying the ink on their fingers was not COMELEC's indelible ink.

paras.html: Sept. 1, 2015 Decision: the Court DISMISSED the petition, applying Mendoza v. COMELEC (Mar. 25, 2010). It classified SPA No. 13-323 (DC) as an action "originally commenced in the Commission," so the en banc's failure to reach a majority required dismissal of the entire case, regardless of the Division's ruling. It also held that an MR before the en banc is not an "action or proceeding," a phrase limited to Part V of the COMELEC Rules (Rules 20–34). paras.html: Mendoza (as summarized): Mendoza won the 2007 Bulacan gubernatorial race; the COMELEC Second Division granted Pagdanganan's election protest and annulled his proclamation. paras.html: The PET is constitutional: it is authorized by the last paragraph of Sec. 4, Art. VII, "as supported by the discussions of the Members of the Constitutional Commission." The 1987 Constitution "constitutionalized what was statutory" before it, and under the doctrine of necessary implication the grant of jurisdiction "includes the means necessary to carry it into effect."
paras.text: The PET is constitutional: it is authorized by the last paragraph of Sec. 4, Art. VII, "as supported by the discussions of the Members of the Constitutional Commission." The 1987 Constitution "constitutionalized what was statutory" before it, and under the doctrine of necessary implication the grant of jurisdiction "includes the means necessary to carry it into effect."

paras.html: The PET exercises judicial, not quasi-judicial, power: it is "an institution independent, but not separate, from the judicial department." The Justices constituting it do not violate Sec. 12, Art. VIII, because the Constitution itself (Sec. 4, Art. VII) exempts them, just as Sec. 17, Art. VI exempts the Justices sitting in the SET and HRET.

paras.html: Bernas: election contests are by nature judicial and cognizable only by courts. The background is Roxas v. Before that law, no one had jurisdiction over P/VP contests → "What we have done is to constitutionalize what was statutory", and it is not an infringement on separation of powers because the power given is judicial.

paras.html: SC's exclusive administrative supervision: Art. VIII, Sec. 6 exclusively vests in the SC administrative supervision over all courts and court personnel, from the Presiding Justice of the CA down to the lowest municipal trial court clerk. Only the SC can oversee their compliance with all laws and take the proper administrative action against them; no other branch may intrude into this power without running afoul of the doctrine of separation of powers.

paras.html: Only the first group needs confirmation: Under Sec. 16, Art. VII, only presidential appointments belonging to the first group require CA confirmation. Congress cannot by law expand the CA's confirmation power to officials not mentioned in the first sentence (Tarrosa v. Singson); thus Secs. 26 and 31 of RA 6975, insofar as they require CA confirmation of PNP officers, are unconstitutional — but being severable, the rest of RA 6975 stands.
paras.text: Only the first group needs confirmation: Under Sec. 16, Art. VII, only presidential appointments belonging to the first group require CA confirmation. Singson); thus Secs. 26 and 31 of RA 6975, insofar as they require CA confirmation of PNP officers, are unconstitutional — but being severable, the rest of RA 6975 stands.

paras.html: The PNP is not the AFP: The Constitution distinguishes the armed forces (Sec. 4, Art. XVI) from one police force, national in scope and civilian in character (Sec. 6, Art. XVI). PNP directors and chief superintendents are not "officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain."

paras.html: Sec. 31: appointments are made as follows: (a) Police Officer I to Senior Police Officer IV — by the PNP regional director or the Chief, attested by the CSC; (b) Inspector to Superintendent — by the Chief, attested by the CSC; (c) Senior Superintendent to Deputy Director General — by the President upon the Chief's recommendation, with the CSC Chairman's endorsement, and "subject to confirmation by the Commission on Appointments"; and (d) Director General — by the President, subject to CA confirmation.

paras.html: Sarmiento III v. Mison: Sec. 16 contemplates a system of checks and balances between the executive and legislative branches. Under the 1935 Constitution, when almost all appointments needed CA consent, the CA became a venue of "horse-trading"; under the 1973 Constitution, the President's absolute appointing power with hardly any check led to abuse. Hence the "middle ground": certain high positions are subject to confirmation, the rest left to the President.

Under the 1935 Constitution, when almost all appointments needed CA consent, the CA became a venue of "horse-trading"; under the 1973 Constitution, the President's absolute appointing power with hardly any check led to abuse. Hence the "middle ground": certain high positions are subject to confirmation, the rest left to the President.

paras.html: As consistently ruled in Mison, Bautista v. Salonga, Quintos-Deles, and Calderon v. Carale, there are four groups of presidential appointees: (1) department heads, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, AFP officers from colonel or naval captain, and officers whose appointments are vested in the President by the Constitution; (2) officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by law; (3) those the President may be authorized by law to appoint; and (4) lower-ranked officers whose appointments Congress may vest in the President alone.

paras.html: Separate judgment in a forfeiture case: Summary judgment on the Swiss deposits (Republic v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 152154) does not bar a subsequent partial summary judgment on other assets expressly sought to be forfeited in the same petition (Civil Case No. 0141). The Sandiganbayan's ruling is a separate judgment under Sec. 5, Rule 36.
paras.text: Separate judgment in a forfeiture case: Summary judgment on the Swiss deposits (Republic v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 152154) does not bar a subsequent partial summary judgment on other assets expressly sought to be forfeited in the same petition (Civil Case No. 0141). The Sandiganbayan's ruling is a separate judgment under Sec. 5, Rule 36.

paras.html: Jurisdiction over a res abroad: Forfeiture proceedings are in the nature of proceedings in rem or quasi in rem. Jurisdiction over the res is acquired by seizure or by institution of legal proceedings; potential custody suffices (Perkins v. Dizon). That the Arelma assets are held in the US does not deprive the Sandiganbayan of authority.

paras.html: Judgment vs. execution: Execution is merely the ministerial phase of adjudication; the authority to rule on whether assets are ill-gotten cannot be conflated with concerns over how the ruling may be enforced.

paras.text: Background:

paras.html: Civil Case No. 0141, the Republic's petition for forfeiture under RA 1379 before the Sandiganbayan, sought to recover all the Marcos assets enumerated in it, including a corporate entity "Arelma, Inc." that maintained an account and portfolio with Merrill Lynch, New York, allegedly organized to hide ill-gotten wealth. Other listed assets: holding companies and investments; landholdings, buildings, condominium units, mansions; New York properties; bills (₱27,744,535), time deposits (₱46.4 million), foreign currencies, and jewelry seized by US customs in Honolulu; US$30 million in Central Bank dollar-denominated Treasury Bills; shares of stock, private vehicles, and US real estate.

Other listed assets: holding companies and investments; landholdings, buildings, condominium units, mansions; New York properties; bills (₱27,744,535), time deposits (₱46.4 million), foreign currencies, and jewelry seized by US customs in Honolulu; US$30 million in Central Bank dollar-denominated Treasury Bills; shares of stock, private vehicles, and US real estate.

paras.html: The Sandiganbayan's ruling is a separate judgment under Sec. 5, Rule 36: when more than one claim is presented, the court may at any stage render a separate judgment on one claim; it terminates the action only as to that claim, and the action proceeds on the rest.

paras.html: The theory fails to distinguish the issuance of a judgment from its execution. "[T]he execution of a Court's judgment is merely a ministerial phase of adjudication" (Far Eastern Surety v. De Hernandez). The Sandiganbayan's authority to rule on the character of the assets as ill-gotten "cannot be conflated" with concerns about enforcement.

paras.html: Re: Potential jurisdiction over the res
paras.text: Re: Potential jurisdiction over the res

paras.html: Granting partial summary judgment despite the assets being abroad was not error; ruling otherwise "contravenes the intent of the forfeiture law, and indirectly privileges violators who are able to hide public assets abroad."
paras.text: Granting partial summary judgment despite the assets being abroad was not error; ruling otherwise "contravenes the intent of the forfeiture law, and indirectly privileges violators who are able to hide public assets abroad."

paras.html: Forfeiture proceedings are "in the nature of proceedings in rem or quasi in rem": jurisdiction over the res is acquired "(a) by the seizure of the property under legal process… or (b) as a result of the institution of legal proceedings"; in the latter case the property, though within the court's potential power, need not be in its actual custody (Macahilig v. Heirs of Magalit).
paras.text: Forfeiture proceedings are "in the nature of proceedings in rem or quasi in rem": jurisdiction over the res is acquired "(a) by the seizure of the property under legal process… or (b) as a result of the institution of legal proceedings"; in the latter case the property, though within the court's potential power, need not be in its actual custody (Macahilig v. Heirs of Magalit).

paras.html: Potential jurisdiction is not new: Perkins v. Dizon (citing El Banco Español-Filipino v. Palanca) held that "potential custody" suffices when, from the nature of the action, the court's power over the property is impliedly recognized by law.

paras.html: Specificity: An election protest must clearly and specifically allege, and then prove, the irregularities, specifying the precincts where each violation occurred and how it transpired. "When the protestant fails to meet the strict requirement of specificity and established rules on evidence to support the allegations of election irregularities, the election protest must be dismissed." (PET Rules, Rule 17(C)(d) and Rule 21.)

"When the protestant fails to meet the strict requirement of specificity and established rules on evidence to support the allegations of election irregularities, the election protest must be dismissed." (PET Rules, Rule 17(C)(d) and Rule 21.)

paras.html: Pilot provinces (Rule 65): "In election protests before this Tribunal, the mandatory ceiling in designating pilot provinces is three. Failure to show substantial recovery of votes in these pilot provinces entails the protest's dismissal." The pilot provinces must cover all causes of action; if the protestant fails in them, the protest is dismissed forthwith "without further consideration of the other provinces mentioned in the protest," including a separate cause of action for annulment of elections.

paras.html: Annulment of election results vs. failure of elections: Electoral tribunals (including the PET) may annul election results as an incident of their judicial function and an indispensable consequence of their constitutional mandate, but only for the contested position and without special elections. The power to declare a failure of elections, and consequently to conduct special elections, "is lodged exclusively with the Commission on Elections." Both hinge on the same grounds and quantum of evidence.

paras.html: Protestant Ferdinand "Bongbong" R. Marcos, Jr. and protestee Maria Leonor "Leni" G. Robredo were two of six candidates for vice president in the May 9, 2016 national and local elections.
paras.text: Protestant Ferdinand "Bongbong" R. Marcos, Jr. and protestee Maria Leonor "Leni" G. Robredo were two of six candidates for vice president in the May 9, 2016 national and local elections.

paras.html: Robredo garnered 14,418,817 votes; Marcos garnered 14,155,344 votes, a slim margin of 263,473 votes.
paras.text: Robredo garnered 14,418,817 votes; Marcos garnered 14,155,344 votes, a slim margin of 263,473 votes.

paras.html: On May 30, 2016, Congress issued Resolution of Both Houses No. 1, which recognized the canvass results and proclaimed Robredo as the duly elected Vice President.

paras.html: The Protest and the Counter-Protest:
paras.text: The Protest and the Counter-Protest:

paras.html: On June 29, 2016, Marcos filed this Election Protest with the PET on two causes of action: (A) Robredo's proclamation is null and void because the Certificates of Canvass generated by the Consolidation and Canvass System are not authentic; and (B) massive electoral fraud, anomalies, and irregularities (terrorism, violence, intimidation, pre-shading of ballots, vote-buying, substitution of voters, flying voters, pre-loaded SD cards, misreading and improper rejection of ballots, malfunctioning VCMs, and abnormally high undervotes) in the protested precincts.

paras.html: The irregularities allegedly occurred in 39,221 clustered precincts in about 27 provinces and cities. Marcos prayed for annulment of elections in 2,756 clustered precincts and judicial revision in the remaining 36,465.
