paras.html: July 12, 2016: The PET issued a Precautionary Protection Order directing COMELEC to safeguard the ballot boxes and election paraphernalia in the 92,509 clustered precincts covered by the Protest.
paras.text: July 12, 2016: The PET issued a Precautionary Protection Order directing COMELEC to safeguard the ballot boxes and election paraphernalia in the 92,509 clustered precincts covered by the Protest.

paras.html: Robredo filed a Verified Answer with Special and Affirmative Defenses and Counter-Protest. She argued that the Protest failed to specify the acts or omissions constituting fraud and that it was really a pre-proclamation controversy for the National Board of Canvassers. Her Counter-Protest contested 7,547 clustered precincts in 13 provinces (vote-buying, intimidation, substitution). She prayed for a preliminary hearing, dismissal for lack of jurisdiction and insufficiency, and affirmance of her proclamation.

paras.html: January 24, 2017 Resolution: The PET confirmed its jurisdiction under Art. VII, Sec. 4 ("sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of the President or Vice-President"), found the Protest sufficient in form and substance, and denied Robredo's motion to dismiss and her request for a preliminary hearing on her affirmative defenses. Robredo moved for reconsideration (February 27, 2017); resolution was deferred until after the preliminary conference (June 6, 2017).

paras.html: At the July 11, 2017 preliminary conference, with Marcos's consent, the PET recast his claims into three causes of action:

paras.html: First – Annulment of Proclamation: the COCs are not authentic and cannot be the basis of the vote count;
paras.text: First – Annulment of Proclamation: the COCs are not authentic and cannot be the basis of the vote count;

paras.html: Second – Revision and Recount: revision and recount of paper ballots and/or ballot images, and examination of voters' receipts, election returns, audit logs, voters' lists, VCMs, SD cards, etc., in all 36,465 protested clustered precincts (Rules 38–45, 2010 PET Rules);

paras.html: Third – Annulment of Elections: annulment of the vice-presidential results in Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, and Basilan for terrorism, intimidation, harassment of voters, and pre-shading of ballots in all 2,756 protested clustered precincts there.

paras.html: August 29, 2017 Resolution: The PET dismissed the first cause of action. The authenticity of the COCs could only be tested by a manual recount of all votes in all precincts, and since Marcos limited the recount to his second and third causes of action, resolving the first would have no practical effect. It also denied Robredo's motion for reconsideration and reiterated that the Protest was sufficient in form and substance.

Under Rule 65, Marcos designated Camarines Sur, Iloilo, and Negros Oriental as his pilot provinces; their results would determine whether the Tribunal would proceed with the rest. Witnesses were limited to three per clustered precinct, on pain of waiver. Action on the technical-examination motion was deferred as premature.

paras.html: COMELEC's Compliance: Eight petitions to declare failure of elections were filed in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao (none in Basilan); all were dismissed and the rulings became final; no special elections were held. Hataman* was dismissed for mootness, not on the merits.

paras.html: The three vehicles for challenging election results are (1) failure of election cases; (2) pre-proclamation controversies; and (3) election contests (election protest or quo warranto). What remains consistent across all modalities is the requirement of specificity.
paras.text: The three vehicles for challenging election results are (1) failure of election cases; (2) pre-proclamation controversies; and (3) election contests (election protest or quo warranto). What remains consistent across all modalities is the requirement of specificity.

paras.html: Failure of elections (OEC Sec. 6) requires that the illegality affect more than 50% of the votes cast; the petition must specifically allege the essential grounds (*Pasandalan v. COMELEC*).
paras.text: Failure of elections (OEC Sec. 6) requires that the illegality affect more than 50% of the votes cast; the petition must specifically allege the essential grounds (*Pasandalan v. COMELEC*).

paras.html: Pre-proclamation controversies are limited to the exclusive list in OEC Sec. 243; under the AES, only the illegal composition or proceedings of the Board of Canvassers; they require "specific verbal objections subsequently reduced to writing" (*Macabago v. COMELEC*).
paras.text: Pre-proclamation controversies are limited to the exclusive list in OEC Sec. 243; under the AES, only the illegal composition or proceedings of the Board of Canvassers; they require "specific verbal objections subsequently reduced to writing" (*Macabago v. COMELEC*).

paras.html: An election protest is a contest between the defeated and winning candidates on grounds of fraud or irregularities in the casting and counting of ballots or preparation of returns; it centers on who validly obtained the plurality. Quo warranto questions election on grounds of disloyalty or ineligibility (*Samad v. COMELEC*; *Tecson v. COMELEC*).

Practically, recounts demand significant time and resources.

paras.html: Rule 65, 2010 PET Rules: "The Tribunal may require the protestant or counter-protestant to indicate … the province or provinces numbering not more than three, best exemplifying the frauds or irregularities … If upon examination of such ballots and proof, and after making reasonable allowances, the Tribunal is convinced that … the protestant … will most probably fail to make out his case, the protest may forthwith be dismissed, without further consideration of the other provinces mentioned in the protest."

paras.html: History: COMELEC has held the power to declare failure of elections since RA 6388 (1971 Election Code; the SC only confirmed the date of special elections), through the 1978 Election Code, BP 881 (OEC; motu proprio), the 1988 COMELEC Rules, and RA 7056 / RA 7166 (postponement, failure, and special elections "shall be decided only by the [COMELEC] sitting en banc by a majority vote").

paras.html: The 1973 Constitution impliedly repealed RA 1793 by removing direct popular election of the president (giving it to the National Assembly); the vice-presidency was "constitutionally non-existent." VII, Sec. 4, par. 7 (*Macalintal v. PET*).

paras.html: Residual executive power: Although the 1987 Constitution limits specific presidential powers, it "maintains intact what is traditionally considered as within the scope of 'executive power.'" Executive power is "more than the sum of specific powers so enumerated." The President has residual, unstated powers implicit in and correlative to the paramount duty to safeguard the general welfare, including the power, as protector of the peace, to bar the return of the Marcoses.

paras.html: Right to return: The right to return to one's country is distinct from the right to travel and liberty of abode. It is not in the Bill of Rights but is part of the law of the land as a generally accepted principle of international law (Art. II, Sec. 2), protected against arbitrary deprivation (ICCPR Art. 12(4)).

paras.html: In February 1986, Ferdinand Marcos was deposed by the non-violent "people power" revolution and forced into exile; Corazon Aquino was declared President under a revolutionary government. The 1987 Constitution reinforced her presidency.
paras.text: In February 1986, Ferdinand Marcos was deposed by the non-violent "people power" revolution and forced into exile; Corazon Aquino was declared President under a revolutionary government. The 1987 Constitution reinforced her presidency.

paras.html: Challenges followed: the failed Manila Hotel coup (1986) by Marcos's political leaders; the takeover of Channel 7 by rebel troops supported by "Marcos loyalists"; the Marcos spouses' plot to return from Hawaii with mercenaries on an aircraft chartered by a Lebanese arms dealer; and the bloody Aug. 28, 1987 coup led by Col. Gregorio Honasan. The country also faced the communist insurgency and the secessionist movement in Mindanao, a devastated economy, foreign debt, and the elusive recovery of ill-gotten wealth.

paras.html: The right of the Marcoses to return is guaranteed by the Bill of Rights: Sec. 1, Art. III (due process, equal protection) and Sec. 6, Art. III (liberty of abode may be impaired only "upon lawful order of the court"; the right to travel only in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health "as may be provided by law"). There must be legislation before any authority may impair the right to travel.

paras.html: Under international law, the right to return is guaranteed: UDHR Art. 13 and ICCPR Art. 12 ("No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of the right to enter his own country").

paras.html: The President has only enumerated powers; "what is not enumerated is impliedly denied to her" (inclusio unius est exclusio alterius). Petitioners framed sub-issues on whether the President found a clear and present danger, whether due process (notice and hearing) was observed, and whether respondents proved the danger.

paras.html: The issue is a political question. Properly framed, it is whether the Marcoses may return "in the face of the determination by the President that such return… will endanger national security and public safety." Whether such danger exists "falls within the exclusive authority and competence of the President."

paras.html: The right involved is not the right to travel from the Philippines to other countries or within the Philippines. It is the right to return to one's country, "a totally distinct right under international law, independent from although related to the right to travel."

paras.html: The UDHR treats movement and residence within a state (Art. 13(1)) separately from the right to leave and return (Art. 13(2)). The ICCPR treats liberty of movement (Art. 12(1)) and the right to leave (Art. 12(2)), restrictable by law for national security and similar grounds (Art. 12(3)), separately from the right to enter one's own country, of which no one may be "arbitrarily deprived" (Art. 12(4)). So the limits on the right to return cannot be construed like those on abode and travel.

II is "the most loosely drawn chapter"; Schlesinger) and Philippine constitutional history, the Court held that executive power is not merely enforcing the laws: the President is head of state and head of government, and whatever powers inhere in those positions pertain to the office unless the Constitution withholds them; some powers, like foreign relations, do not involve executing any law.

paras.html: "[A]lthough the 1987 Constitution imposes limitations on the exercise of specific powers of the President, it maintains intact what is traditionally considered as within the scope of 'executive power.' Corollarily, the powers of the President cannot be said to be limited only to the specific powers enumerated in the Constitution. In other words, executive power is more than the sum of specific powers so enumerated."

II: "The prime duty of the Government is to serve and protect the people" (Sec. 4); peace and order and the general welfare are essential (Sec. 5); sovereignty resides in the people (Sec. 1). paras.html: The problem is balancing the general welfare against individual rights. The rights invoked are not absolute (cf. Zaldivar v. Sandiganbayan). "The power involved is the President's residual power to protect the general welfare of the people." It is founded on the President's duty as steward of the people (paraphrasing Theodore Roosevelt: to do anything not forbidden by the Constitution or laws that the nation's needs demand), on the oath, and on the duty to take care that the laws are faithfully executed.

paras.html: NO. The question is "whether or not there exist factual bases for the President to conclude that it was in the national interest to bar the return of the Marcoses." If they exist, she did not act arbitrarily.
paras.text: NO. The question is "whether or not there exist factual bases for the President to conclude that it was in the national interest to bar the return of the Marcoses." If they exist, she did not act arbitrarily.

paras.html: From the pleadings, oral arguments, and the briefing in chambers, factual bases exist. The country is besieged by a communist insurgency, a separatist movement, rightist conspiracies, urban terrorism, and the murder of soldiers, police, and officials. The documented efforts of the Marcoses and their followers to destabilize the country support the conclusion that their return would "exacerbate and intensify the violence".

paras.html: Double sale of immovables (Art. 1544) requires good faith in both acquisition and recording: the second buyer must prove prior registration and good faith, i.e., purchase without knowledge or notice of the prior sale. The presence of occupants other than the vendors puts the buyer on inquiry; relying on the vendor's assurance instead of asking the occupant is not good faith. A sale of realty must be in writing to be enforceable, but it need not be notarized.

paras.html: Assignments I and II attack the findings of fact affirmed by the CA. As a rule, only questions of law are raised under Rule 45, but review is allowed under the recognized exceptions, among them: (a) speculation, surmises, or conjectures; (b) manifestly mistaken, absurd, or impossible inference; (c) grave abuse of discretion; (d) misapprehension of facts; (e) conflicting findings; (f) the CA went beyond the issues, contrary to both parties' admissions; (g) CA contrary to the trial court; (h) conclusions without citation of specific evidence; (i) facts in the petition and briefs undisputed by respondents; (j) finding premised on absence of evidence but contradicted by the record; and (k) the CA manifestly overlooked relevant, undisputed facts that would justify a different conclusion (Lacanilao v. CA; Philippine Home Assurance v. CA; Floro v. Llenado).

paras.text: Re: The rule on double sale (Art. 1544)

paras.html: The CA treated Reynaldo's reliance on Godofredo's assurance as good faith. But this is a double sale: ownership of an immovable passes (1) to the one who in good faith first recorded it; (2) failing that, to the one who in good faith was first in possession; (3) failing that, to the one with the oldest title (Balatbat v. CA).

CA).

paras.html: Where title is registered, the requirement is two-fold: acquisition in good faith and recording in good faith. To get priority, the second buyer must prove both prior recording and good faith, i.e., without knowledge or notice of a prior sale. Good faith is judged from the circumstances surrounding the purchase (Bautista v. CA).

paras.html: Requisites for treating a sale with right to repurchase as an equitable mortgage: (1) a contract denominated as a sale; and (2) an intention to secure an existing debt by way of mortgage (Matanguihan).

paras.html: Presumption (Art. 1602): a sale with right to repurchase is presumed an equitable mortgage when (1) the price is unusually inadequate; (2) the vendor remains in possession as lessee or otherwise; (3) a new instrument extends or grants a new redemption period; (4) the purchaser retains part of the price; (5) the vendor binds himself to pay the taxes; or (6) in any other case where the real intention may fairly be inferred to be security for a debt or obligation. In case of doubt, it is construed as an equitable mortgage (Art. 1603).

In case of doubt, it is construed as an equitable mortgage (Art. 1603).

paras.html: Circumstances showing a mortgage here: (1) the Veneracions never took actual possession of the three lots; (2) the De la Pazes remained in possession of the Melencio lot, which they co-owned and lived on; (3) between the first and second sales, the Veneracions made no effort to take possession; and (4) when the redemption period expired and the De la Pazes announced they were selling to another for P200,000, the Veneracions did not object; instead, they offered to buy the two lots for P180,000, matching Mr. Tecson.

paras.html: An ad interim appointment is permanent, not temporary: it takes effect immediately and can no longer be withdrawn by the President once the appointee has qualified into office. Being subject to confirmation does not alter its permanent character; it ends only upon the two resolutory conditions in Sec. 16, Art. VII: disapproval by the Commission on Appointments or the next adjournment of Congress. It is therefore not the temporary or acting appointment prohibited by Sec. 1(2), Art. IX-C.

paras.html: Renewal of a by-passed ad interim appointment is not a reappointment: "A reappointment presupposes a previous confirmed appointment." A by-passed appointment may be renewed because there is no final disapproval, and the renewal does not let the appointee serve beyond the fixed seven-year term (here, so long as the terms still expire on February 2, 2008).

paras.html: Re: Disapproved vs. by-passed appointments
paras.text: Re: Disapproved vs. by-passed appointments

paras.html: Disapproved: a disapproval is a final decision on the merits, a refusal to consent after deliberating on qualifications; with no appeal provided, it binds the appointee and the President. The President cannot renew it "not because of the constitutional prohibition on reappointment, but because of a final decision" of the CA.
paras.text: Disapproved: a disapproval is a final decision on the merits, a refusal to consent after deliberating on qualifications; with no appeal provided, it binds the appointee and the President. The President cannot renew it "not because of the constitutional prohibition on reappointment, but because of a final decision" of the CA.

paras.html: By-passed: an appointment not finally acted upon on the merits at the close of the session (for lack of time or failure of the CA to organize). There is no final decision → the President is free to renew it. Recognized in Sec. 17 of the CA Rules: unacted appointments are returned to the President and "unless new nominations or appointments are made, shall not again be considered."
paras.text: By-passed: an appointment not finally acted upon on the merits at the close of the session (for lack of time or failure of the CA to organize). paras.html: J. Concepcion, Jr. in Guevara v. Inocentes: the appointment ceases upon adjournment not because of implied disapproval, for the CA may affect ad interim appointments "only by action, never by omission", but because the President is then free to make new appointments or reappointments. Sec. 16 was lifted verbatim from Sec. 10(4), Art. VII of the 1935 Constitution, so this jurisprudence applies; the practice was interrupted only by the 1973 Constitution, which had no CA.

paras.html: Re: The four situations where the reappointment ban applies
paras.text: Re: The four situations where the reappointment ban applies

paras.html: (1) A confirmed appointee who serves the full seven years; (2) a confirmed appointee who serves part and resigns, who cannot be reappointed to a vacancy from retirement; (3) one confirmed to an unexpired term who completes it; and (4) one who previously served a term of less than seven years, who cannot be reappointed even to an unexpired term from death or resignation, similar to the first appointees under the second sentence of Sec. 1(2). None applies to Benipayo, Borra, or Tuason.

paras.html: "[A]n ad interim appointment that has lapsed by inaction of the Commission on Appointments does not constitute a term of office." paras.html: Act No. 1446 granted a franchise to Charles M. Swift "to construct, maintain, and operate an electric railway, and to construct, maintain, and operate an electric light, heat, and power system from a point in the City of Manila in an easterly direction to the town of Pasig, in the Province of Rizal."

Swift "to construct, maintain, and operate an electric railway, and to construct, maintain, and operate an electric light, heat, and power system from a point in the City of Manila in an easterly direction to the town of Pasig, in the Province of Rizal."

paras.html: Section 11 of the Act provides:
paras.text: Section 11 of the Act provides:

paras.html: "Whenever any franchise or right of way is granted to any other person or corporation, now or hereafter in existence, over portions of the lines and tracks of the grantee herein, the terms on which said other person or corporation shall use such right of way, and the compensation to be paid to the grantee herein by such other person or corporation for said use, shall be fixed by the members of the Supreme Court, sitting as a board of arbitrators, the decision of a majority of whom shall be final."

paras.html: Pardon does not ipso facto restore a forfeited public office: An absolute pardon granted after conviction frees the individual from all the penalties and legal disabilities and restores his civil rights, and it restores his eligibility for appointment to the office forfeited by the conviction. But it does not ipso facto restore him to that office; he must reapply and undergo the usual procedure for a new appointment, and the appointing power may weigh the facts of the offense.

paras.html: Pardon implies guilt: "Pardon implies guilt. It does not erase the fact of the commission of the crime and the conviction thereof. It does not wash out the moral stain. It involves forgiveness and not forgetfulness." Unless expressly grounded on innocence, it cannot restore lost reputation. It looks to the future and is not retrospective, so it gives no right to backpay.

paras.html: Definition (United States v. Wilson): "an act of grace, proceeding from the power entrusted with the execution of the laws, which exempts the individual, on whom it is bestowed, from the punishment the law inflicts for a crime he has committed." A pardon is a deed, to the validity of which delivery is essential, and delivery is not complete without acceptance.

paras.html: Pelobello v. Palatino (72 Phil. 441), adopting the broad view in Cristobal v. Labrador (1940): subject to constitutional limits, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action; an absolute pardon "not only blots out the crime committed but removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction"; the Chief Executive should be at liberty to relieve the party completely "from the accessory and resultant disabilities of criminal conviction."

paras.html: These cases and others (In re Lontok, Pendon v. Diasnes, Mijares v. Custorio) show the unmistakable application of the doctrinal case of Ex parte Garland, whose "sweeping generalizations" still hold sway here even though later American decisions downplayed much of its relevance.

paras.html: The Court's "vital point": the Court concedes that pardon may remit all the penal consequences of a criminal indictment, to give meaning to the principle that a pardon, being a presidential prerogative, should not be circumscribed by legislative action. But it rejects the "fictitious belief" that pardon blots out guilt and that the pardoned person must be treated as innocent; pardon cannot produce such "moral changes" as to equate a pardoned convict with a constantly law-abiding citizen.

paras.html: Pardon does not ipso facto restore a forfeited public office: An absolute pardon granted after conviction frees the individual from all the penalties and legal disabilities and restores his civil rights, and it restores his eligibility for appointment to the office forfeited by the conviction. But it does not ipso facto restore him to that office; he must reapply and undergo the usual procedure for a new appointment, and the appointing power may weigh the facts of the offense.
paras.text: Pardon does not ipso facto restore a forfeited public office: An absolute pardon granted after conviction frees the individual from all the penalties and legal disabilities and restores his civil rights, and it restores his eligibility for appointment to the office forfeited by the conviction. But it does not ipso facto restore him to that office; he must reapply and undergo the usual procedure for a new appointment, and the appointing power may weigh the facts of the offense.

paras.html: Pardon implies guilt: "Pardon implies guilt. It does not erase the fact of the commission of the crime and the conviction thereof. It does not wash out the moral stain. It involves forgiveness and not forgetfulness." Unless expressly grounded on innocence, it cannot restore lost reputation. It looks to the future and is not retrospective, so it gives no right to backpay.

paras.html: Pardon is of British origin, "conceived to temper the gravity of the King's wrath," but Philippine jurisprudence on it is largely influenced by American case law.

paras.html: Definition (United States v. Wilson): "an act of grace, proceeding from the power entrusted with the execution of the laws, which exempts the individual, on whom it is bestowed, from the punishment the law inflicts for a crime he has committed." It is a private, though official, act of the executive, not communicated officially to the Court. A pardon is a deed, to the validity of which delivery is essential, and delivery is not complete without acceptance.

paras.html: Pelobello v. Palatino (72 Phil. 441), adopting the broad view in Cristobal v. Labrador (1940): subject to constitutional limits, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action; an absolute pardon "not only blots out the crime committed but removes all disabilities resulting from the conviction"; the Chief Executive should be at liberty to relieve the party completely "from the accessory and resultant disabilities of criminal conviction."

paras.html: These cases and others (In re Lontok, Pendon v. Diasnes, Mijares v. Custorio) show the unmistakable application of the doctrinal case of Ex parte Garland, whose "sweeping generalizations" still hold sway here even though later American decisions downplayed much of its relevance.

paras.html: The Court's "vital point": the Court concedes that pardon may remit all the penal consequences of a criminal indictment, to give meaning to the principle that a pardon, being a presidential prerogative, should not be circumscribed by legislative action. But it rejects the "fictitious belief" that pardon blots out guilt and that the pardoned person must be treated as innocent; pardon cannot produce such "moral changes" as to equate a pardoned convict with a constantly law-abiding citizen.

paras.html: Power of control: All executive departments, bureaus, and offices are under the President's control (Sec. 17, Art. VII). The power extends to all executive employees from Cabinet Secretary to the lowliest clerk; its constitutional vesture is self-executing, does not require statutory implementation, and may not be limited, much less withdrawn, by the legislature. There is only one Chief Executive, and subordinate officials must implement his directives in good faith.

The power extends to all executive employees from Cabinet Secretary to the lowliest clerk; its constitutional vesture is self-executing, does not require statutory implementation, and may not be limited, much less withdrawn, by the legislature. There is only one Chief Executive, and subordinate officials must implement his directives in good faith.

paras.html: Appropriation is not authority to disburse: The GAA is not self-executory. Personal Services appropriations are not itemized; spending requires a Presidentially approved itemization and expenditure program, and no salary increase may be paid unless specifically authorized by law or appropriate budget circular (Secs. 23 and 34, Book IV; Sec. 60, Book VI, Administrative Code).

paras.html: COA's power: Under the 1987 Constitution, the COA may determine whether government entities comply with laws and regulations in disbursing funds and disallow illegal or irregular disbursements; Guevara v. Gimenez (limiting audit to whether an appropriation exists) has been overturned by Caltex v. COA.

paras.html: The budget process is a cycle with four phases — Budget Preparation, Budget Authorization, Budget Execution, and Budget Accountability (DBM Budget Operations Manual). paras.html: Caltex Philippines v. COA held that Guevara and Ramos v. Aquino were decided under the 1935 Constitution and are no longer controlling. Citing Fr. Bernas: under the 1935 Constitution the Auditor General could only bring irregular expenditures to the attention of the proper officer; under the 1973 and 1987 Constitutions the COA can promulgate rules "for the prevention and disallowance of irregular, unnecessary, excessive, extravagant, or unconscionable expenditures," so non-compliance can be a ground for disapproving payment.

paras.html: Representatives of ex officio members: Representatives of Cabinet members sitting ex officio are covered by both constitutional prohibitions. Under Sec. 7(2), Art. IX-B, no law or administrative order created a new office or authorized extra pay, and the representatives were merely designated, not appointed; designation does not entitle one to the salary of a position. Under Sec. 13, Art. VII (as construed in CLU), the ex officio members cannot receive per diems or honoraria, and "[t]he agent, alternate or representative cannot have a better right than his principal."

paras.html: The representatives assumed their duties by mere designation from the ex officio members (themselves designated), not by appointment. Appointment is selection to exercise the functions of an office; designation merely imposes additional duties on one already in the service. Designation does not entitle the officer to the salary of the position; the basis for claiming salary is a duly approved appointment (Dimaandal v. COA; Santiago v. COA).

paras.html: Presidential communications privilege: presidential communications are presumptively privileged. Elements: (1) the communication relates to a "quintessential and non-delegable presidential power"; (2) it is authored or "solicited and received" by the President or a close advisor in "operational proximity"; and (3) it remains a qualified privilege, overcome only by a showing of adequate (compelling) need and unavailability of the information elsewhere. The power to enter into an executive agreement is quintessential and non-delegable.

The power to enter into an executive agreement is quintessential and non-delegable.

paras.html: Burden and standard (Resolution): the presumption puts the burden on the Senate committees to show that the information is critical to their legislative functions; the bare "pertinency" standard of Arnault "cannot be lightly applied" to a clash between co-equal branches. Senate v. Ermita's "presumption ... against executive secrecy" refers to presumptive authorization of subordinates, not to the President's own claim.

paras.html: Contempt and publication: a contempt order requires a vote of a majority of all members of the committee after deliberation. The Senate is a continuing institution, but its business ends with each Congress; it must publish its inquiry rules in each Congress or make them state that they continue in force. Only orders and proceedings violating the rights of witnesses are void for non-publication (Resolution).

paras.html: U.S. v. Nixon: presidential communications are "presumptively privileged," founded on the President's "generalized interest in confidentiality" and the need for candor of advisors.
paras.text: U.S. v. Nixon: presidential communications are "presumptively privileged," founded on the President's "generalized interest in confidentiality" and the need for candor of advisors.

paras.html: In re Sealed Case: two kinds. The presidential communications privilege covers presidential decision-making, is rooted in separation of powers, and covers entire documents including final and post-decisional materials. The deliberative process privilege covers decision-making of executive officials and rests on common law. Negating the former "is always subject to greater scrutiny." It is confined to staff with "operational proximity" to presidential decision-making on "quintessential and non-delegable Presidential power" (commander-in-chief, appointment and removal, pardon, receiving ambassadors, treaty negotiation). Judicial Watch v. DOJ applied an organizational test: the Pardon Attorney was too remote.
paras.text: In re Sealed Case: two kinds. The presidential communications privilege covers presidential decision-making, is rooted in separation of powers, and covers entire documents including final and post-decisional materials. The deliberative process privilege covers decision-making of executive officials and rests on common law. Negating the former "is always subject to greater scrutiny." It is confined to staff with "operational proximity" to presidential decision-making on "quintessential and non-delegable Presidential power" (commander-in-chief, appointment and removal, pardon, receiving ambassadors, treaty negotiation). Judicial Watch v. DOJ applied an organizational test: the Pardon Attorney was too remote.

paras.html: Older categories: military or state secrets, informers' identities, pending investigations, and especially foreign relations (U.S. v. Curtiss-Wright: "the nature of foreign negotiations requires caution"). Philippine cases: Chavez v. PCGG (state secrets), Chavez v. PEA (presidential conversations, closed-door Cabinet meetings), Senate v. Ermita. The privilege is "highly recognized" where the subject relates to a power textually committed to the President, such as military and foreign relations.

PEA (presidential conversations, closed-door Cabinet meetings), Senate v. Ermita. The privilege is "highly recognized" where the subject relates to a power textually committed to the President, such as military and foreign relations.

paras.html: Elements (from Nixon, In re Sealed Case, Judicial Watch): (1) the communication relates to a "quintessential and non-delegable presidential power"; (2) it is authored or "solicited and received" by a close advisor in "operational proximity" or the President; and (3) the privilege is qualified and may be overcome by a showing of adequate need and unavailability elsewhere.

paras.html: U.S. v. Nixon: confidentiality is not absolute and must be balanced; Nixon v. Sirica: the presumption can be overcome by a showing of public need. But "the record is bereft of any categorical explanation from respondent Committees to show a compelling or critical need for the answers ... in the enactment of a law." The questions "veer more towards the exercise of the legislative oversight function under Section 22" than Sec. 21; the line is hard to draw and depends on the questions and manner of the inquiry.

paras.html: Wrongdoing: the Court agreed that privilege does not guard against disclosure of a crime, but distinguished Nixon: there, a pending criminal proceeding and due process required disclosure, and Nixon expressly did not address congressional demands; here, the setting is a legislative inquiry, and the claim is grounded on presidential communications and diplomatic secrets.

paras.html: Caution on impeachment: the committees should tread carefully on matters that may later be the subject of impeachment. In Senate Select Committee v. Nixon, the Senate committee's need gave way to the House Judiciary Committee's impeachment inquiry; the showing required turned "not on the nature of the presidential conduct that the subpoenaed material might reveal, but ... on the nature and appropriateness of the function"; legislative judgments depend more on predicted consequences than on precise reconstruction of past events.

III, Sec. 7 is "subject to such limitations as may be provided by law": Sec. 7, RA 6713; Art. 229, RPC; Sec. 3(k), RA 3019; Sec. 24(e), Rule 130; plus what jurisprudence and the Constitution treat as confidential.

The right to information "must be balanced with and should give way in appropriate cases" to executive-legislative constitutional precepts.

paras.html: A proper claim requires "a formal claim of privilege, lodged by the head of the department which has control over the matter" and "precise and certain" reasons. Ermita's letter [dated "November 17, 2007" in this part; elsewhere Nov. 15] is the formal claim: "this Office is constrained to invoke the settled doctrine of executive privilege," meaning the Office of the President. "That is more than enough compliance."

paras.html: Second: the committees did not comply with Senate v. Ermita's requirement that invitations contain the "possible needed statute which prompted the need for the inquiry" and the subject and questions. Compliance is imperative under both Secs. 21 and 22 to respect the rights of persons appearing. They never sent the advance list of questions Neri repeatedly requested.

paras.html: Third: only a minority of the Blue Ribbon Committee was present at the Jan. 30, 2008 deliberation. Sec. 18 of the Rules requires "a vote of majority of all its members"; members who did not participate were apparently made to sign → "a cloud of doubt" on the order. The transcript shows Sen. Cayetano acknowledging that only seven were present and that signatures would be gathered afterward ("following the Sabio v. Gordon rule"), while Sen. Pimentel argued the lead committee should simply enforce its decision.

paras.html: Fifth: the order was arbitrary and precipitate: the committees did not first rule on the privilege claim and inform Neri; they "curtly dismissed" his explanation and simultaneously ordered his arrest; they disregarded his motion for reconsideration and his request for advance questions. paras.html: Presidential communications – function impairment test: the privilege attaches to the Office, for the public's benefit. Senate v. Ermita gave it a qualified presumption (so the burden argument of the committees fails), but its strength varies: the more the power is shared, the weaker the presumption. The power to contract foreign loans is shared with the Monetary Board (Art. VII, Sec. 20; Sumulong's ConCom explanation), which weakens it; other factors include timing, detail, audience, certainty, frequency, and form of disclosure.

paras.html: Publication: the Senate under the 1987 Constitution is no longer a continuing body: only 12 of 24 Senators continue, less than a majority (quorum), unlike the 1935 Senate's two-thirds (Arnault). The Rules must be republished each time 12 terms expire; website and pamphlet publication fail Tañada, and the Rules themselves require two newspapers. Because the Rules put liberty at risk, the arrest order is void for lack of published rules [he cites "Section 22, Article VI" as the publication requirement]. The majority of regular members did vote for contempt.

paras.html: Clarification of Senate v. Ermita: its statement that "the presumption inclines heavily against executive secrecy" refers to the exemption claimed by officials in Sec. 2(b) of EO 464 by virtue of their positions, i.e., there is no presumptive authorization from the President to subordinates. That defect is absent here: the President herself, through Ermita, invoked the privilege on a specific matter involving an executive agreement with China. Reading it otherwise makes Senate v. Ermita "engage in self-contradiction."

VII, Sec. 20) "does not make such power less executive", just as the President's veto does not make lawmaking less legislative. The power to enter into an executive agreement is in essence executive, and the final decision remains with the President.

paras.html: Burden on the committees: Nixon involved a court's need for facts in a criminal case; here, the Senate seeks to intrude into the President's sphere, so the burden is on the committees. Per Senate Select Committee v. Nixon, legislative judgments depend more on predicted consequences than on reconstructing past events; "the bare standard of 'pertinency' set in Arnault cannot be lightly applied" to a conflict between co-equal branches. Even CJ Puno's dissent concedes the presumption.

paras.html: Publication – clarification on the "continuing body": the Senate as an institution is continuing, but "in the conduct of its day-to-day business the Senate of each Congress acts separately and independently". Sec. 123, Rule XLIV: all pending matters, including legislative investigations, terminate upon the expiration of one Congress and may be taken up "as if presented for the first time." The main Rules (Sec. 137) stay in force "until they are amended or repealed", but the inquiry Rules only take effect seven days after publication in two newspapers → they cannot be presumed to continue. The Senate must "publish the rules for its legislative inquiries in each Congress or otherwise make the published rules clearly state that the same shall be effective in subsequent Congresses or until they are amended or repealed."

paras.html: Publication is a due process requirement (Tañada), and the Senate validly chose one-time publication in two newspapers (Aug. 21, 1995). The Senate is a continuing body: ConCom deliberations, the framers' design for stability (Federalist papers), McGrain, and Arnault; a "mathematical calculation of a quorum" cannot subvert that design. Under U.S. v. Ballin and Defensor-Santiago v. Guingona, the Court should defer to the Senate's rule-making where private rights are not infringed. The Senate has not re-adopted even its main rules in a decade; holding otherwise would put its acts in doubt.

The privilege may be overcome by adequate, compelling need for important evidence unavailable elsewhere to an appropriate investigating authority.

paras.html: Legislative inquiry and contempt: Congress may compel testimony in inquiries in aid of legislation under Art. VI, Sec. 21, subject to duly published rules and respect for witness rights. paras.html: On April 21, 2007, DOTC entered into a US$329,481,290 contract, approximately P16 billion, with ZTE for the supply of equipment and services for the National Broadband Network project. Financing was to come from the People’s Republic of China. Neri was NEDA Director General during negotiation and signing, and later became CHED Chairman.
paras.text: On April 21, 2007, DOTC entered into a US$329,481,290 contract, approximately P16 billion, with ZTE for the supply of equipment and services for the National Broadband Network project. Financing was to come from the People’s Republic of China. Neri was NEDA Director General during negotiation and signing, and later became CHED Chairman.

paras.html: The project was initially conceived as a Build-Operate-Transfer arrangement. The record described an initial presidential preference for no government loan or guarantee. On March 29, 2007, NEDA acquiesced in conversion into a government-to-government project financed through a Chinese loan. Allegations of influence, bribery and irregular approval prompted the Senate investigation.

On March 29, 2007, NEDA acquiesced in conversion into a government-to-government project financed through a Chinese loan. Allegations of influence, bribery and irregular approval prompted the Senate investigation.

paras.html: Four Senate resolutions supplied the inquiry’s stated subjects: P.S. Res. 127 on approval, responsible officials, anomalies and gaps in BOT and related laws; Res. 129 on national-security implications; Res. 136 on legal and economic justification; and Res. 144 urging cancellation of the ZTE contract.

paras.html: Neri attended the September 26, 2007 hearing, which lasted about eleven hours. He testified that COMELEC Chairman Benjamin Abalos offered him P200 million for approval of the NBN project. paras.html: The Committees issued a November 13, 2007 subpoena requiring Neri to return on November 20. paras.html: Neri did not attend on November 20. The Committees’ November 22 show-cause letter required him to explain why he should not be cited in contempt. In his November 29 reply, he denied intending to snub the Senate, pointed to his extensive prior testimony, and stated that he believed only the three privileged questions remained. He offered to testify on new matters and requested advance notice of what he needed to clarify. Counsel’s accompanying letter referred to presidential instructions and claimed sensitive diplomatic, national-security and related concerns.

paras.html: On December 7, 2007, according to the ponencia, Neri filed a Rule 65 petition for certiorari against the show-cause letter. Without answering his request for advance questions, the Committees issued the January 30, 2008 order citing him in contempt and directing arrest and detention in the Senate Sergeant-at-Arms’ office until he appeared and testified. The order also referred to his absences on September 18, September 20 and October 25, 2007. Neri sought reconsideration the same day.

paras.html: At oral argument on March 4, 2008, the Court identified privilege coverage, the proper procedure for invoking it, and grave abuse in ordering arrest as the questions for resolution. paras.html: Confidentiality protects the public interest in candid, objective, even blunt advice. Advisers must be able to explore policy alternatives privately without continually tempering their views for public appearances. The privilege protects governmental decision-making, not the personal convenience of an officeholder.

paras.html: Re: Presidential communications and deliberative process are distinct
paras.text: Re: Presidential communications and deliberative process are distinct

paras.html: Drawing from In re Sealed Case, the Court distinguished presidential communications privilege, rooted in the Constitution and covering presidential decision-making, from deliberative process privilege, rooted in common law and covering executive officials’ policy deliberations. The former receives greater protection and scrutiny before denial.

The former receives greater protection and scrutiny before denial.

paras.html: Presidential communications privilege may cover pre-decisional, final and post-decisional materials and documents in their entirety; it is not limited to unfinished agency deliberations. The Court cited Judicial Watch v. Department of Justice to show limits on extending the privilege to officials too remote from the President.

paras.text: Re: Three elements and their application

paras.html: 1. Subject matter: The protected communication must relate to a quintessential and non-delegable presidential power. Here, it concerned the President’s power to enter an executive agreement with another country. Philippine jurisprudence traditionally recognizes executive agreements without legislative concurrence.

paras.html: 2. Proximity: The communication must be authored or solicited and received by the President or a close adviser in operational proximity to presidential decision-making. Neri, a Cabinet member communicating directly with PGMA, was a close adviser.

paras.html: 3. Qualification and need: The privilege remains qualified. It may yield to adequate need for likely important evidence unavailable elsewhere to the appropriate investigating authority. Here, the Committees failed to show a compelling or critical legislative need for the three answers or that the information could not be obtained elsewhere.

paras.html: Art. VI, Sec. 21 seeks information for legislation and permits compulsory attendance, including executive officials, subject to valid privilege and other constitutional limits. Sec. 22 concerns the question hour, in which department heads appear with presidential consent or upon a House’s request to give information about their departments. Congress cannot compel that appearance merely to perform oversight. Compulsion is available only insofar as the oversight inquiry is pursued in aid of legislation. The two provisions are complementary but concern distinct powers.

paras.html: Disclosure and secrecy in a democracy: The 1987 Constitution expressly emphasizes information, full disclosure and public accountability, unlike the sparse U.S. constitutional text. Executive privilege serves the public and the institution of the Presidency, not the incumbent’s private protection.

Executive privilege serves the public and the institution of the Presidency, not the incumbent’s private protection.

paras.html: Legislative investigation: Under Arnault, questions must be pertinent to the subject of a lawful inquiry; every answer need not be directly material to a particular bill. Legislative purpose was evident from the resolutions and three pending bills. Improper motives do not invalidate an otherwise authorized inquiry serving a legislative purpose.

paras.html: Different privileges require separate analysis: Diplomatic, military or state-secrets claims require circumstances allowing the Court to assess a reasonable danger from disclosure. Ermita’s bare assertion was insufficient. Neri and his private lawyer could not enlarge the President’s stated grounds by adding military or national-security claims.

paras.html: Function impairment test: Weigh impairment of the President’s constitutional functions from disclosure against impairment of the Senate’s functions from nondisclosure. The strength of presumptive confidentiality varies with the power involved and the timing, detail, audience, frequency, certainty and form of disclosure.

paras.html: Application: The foreign-loan power is shared with the Monetary Board under Art. VII, Sec. 20, weakening the presumption. The questions concerned why a no-loan BOT project became a China-financed undertaking despite a reported bribe. Only Neri could give an effective account of his own presidential conversations. Denial deprived remedial procurement and ODA legislation of a factual basis; counsel’s concern about criticism and political harm did not show significant institutional impairment.

paras.html: YES. The President’s foreign-loan or executive-agreement power remains executive although Art. VII, Sec. 20 requires Monetary Board concurrence and reporting to Congress. Checks and balances do not transform one branch’s power into another branch’s power. By analogy, presidential approval or veto does not make Congress’s lawmaking power executive. The final executive decision remains with the President.

paras.html: The Senate continues as an institution and is not dissolved at every election. Its day-to-day business, however, is conducted independently by each Congress. Under then Senate Rule XLIV, Sec. 123, pending bills and investigations terminate at a Congress’s expiration; the next Congress may revive them as if first presented.

paras.html: The Senate’s main rules expressly remained effective until amendment or repeal. The distinct inquiry rules merely provided effectivity seven days after publication in two newspapers; they lacked the same express continuing-effectivity clause. Continuation could not simply be presumed.

paras.html: Qualified publication rule: The Senate must publish the inquiry rules in each Congress OR clearly provide in the published rules that they continue into later Congresses or until amended or repealed. This qualifies the Decision’s unqualified-sounding republication formulation; it is not a holding that unchanged rules must always be republished regardless of their express terms.

paras.html: Qualified effect of nonpublication: The Court expressly refused to invalidate every order or proceeding under those rules. Only those resulting in violation of witness rights are null and void; otherwise, proceedings remain valid and effective. Publication protects witnesses, and that rationale controls the consequence.

paras.html: Continuing Senate: Constitutional Commission deliberations expressly linked staggered senatorial terms to a continuing Senate, institutional stability and memory. This does not depend on a permanent quorum made up only of holdover members. Outgoing terms end as incoming terms begin; the quorum counts both remaining and newly qualified senators. Death or resignation could defeat an actual quorum even under the 1935 structure, without changing the institution’s nature.

paras.html: Sec. 25, Art. XVIII requires recognition, not identical domestic processes: The VFA complies because it was concurred in by the Philippine Senate and recognized as a treaty by the US. Texas (US Supreme Court, March 25, 2008), which held that non-self-executing treaties are not US domestic law without implementing legislation; (2) whether the VFA is enforceable in the US as domestic law, either because it is self-executing or because implementing legislation exists; and (3) whether the RP-US Mutual Defense Treaty of August 30, 1951 was concurred in by the US Senate, and if so, whether there is proof of the advice-and-consent resolution.

paras.html: VFA Art. V, par. 6: custody of US personnel over whom the Philippines exercises jurisdiction "shall immediately reside with United States military authorities, if they so request," from the commission of the offense until completion of all judicial proceedings. The US must make them available for investigative and judicial proceedings. In extraordinary cases, the Philippines may present its position on custody, which the US "shall take into full account." If proceedings are not completed within one year (excluding appeal and US-caused delays), the US is relieved of its obligations under the paragraph.

paras.text: Examination of Medellin v. Texas:

paras.html: A Mexican national convicted of capital murder in Texas invoked the Vienna Convention and the ICJ's Avena judgment (and President Bush's Memorandum directing state courts to give it effect) to obtain a new trial. The US Supreme Court held that neither Avena nor the Memorandum is directly enforceable federal law.

The US Supreme Court held that neither Avena nor the Memorandum is directly enforceable federal law.

paras.html: Rule: a treaty may be an international commitment but is not binding domestic law unless Congress enacts implementing statutes or the treaty itself conveys an intention that it be self-executing and is ratified on that basis. Self-execution is determined by a textual approach; Art. 94 of the UN Charter ("undertakes to comply") is a commitment of the political branches, and the sole remedy (Security Council) is diplomatic.

paras.html: (1) The VFA's self-executing character must be clear from its text (a "clear statement requirement"); nothing in the VFA's text satisfies it.

paras.html: (2) Recognition by the US President through the former Ambassador is insufficient to make the VFA executory in the US. The VFA is a sole executive agreement: not one pursuant to a treaty (the MDT does not authorize the President to conclude implementing agreements), and not a congressional-executive agreement. It falls in Youngstown's third category, where presidential power is at its lowest ebb.

It falls in Youngstown's third category, where presidential power is at its lowest ebb.

paras.html: (3) A congressional act is necessary to transform the VFA's obligations into US domestic law; Bayan erred in holding it "inconsequential" whether the US treats the VFA as only an executive agreement, because binding effect internationally is distinct from domestic enforceability.

The decisive mark of recognition as a treaty is whether the agreement has obligatory effects and may be a source of rights enforceable in the other State's domestic sphere.

paras.html: Intent of the framers controls: "The primary task in constitutional construction is to ascertain and thereafter assure the realization of the purpose of the framers and of the people in the adoption of the Constitution." The Court may rely on the Constitutional Commission's deliberations, since "the people in ratifying the Constitution were guided mainly by the explanation offered by the framers."

paras.html: Comm. Aquino objected that exempting judges' salaries violates the principle of uniformity of taxation and the equal protection clause; tax is levied on combined income, not on the salary, so why give justices special privileges?
paras.text: Comm. Aquino objected that exempting judges' salaries violates the principle of uniformity of taxation and the equal protection clause; tax is levied on combined income, not on the salary, so why give justices special privileges?

paras.html: Comm. Concepcion (sponsor) answered that the reason is judicial independence: taxing the salary is "an indirect way of decreasing their salary and affecting the independence of the judges." Aquino replied that respecting tenure is fine, but the special tax privilege still violates uniformity and equal protection.
paras.text: Comm. Concepcion (sponsor) answered that the reason is judicial independence: taxing the salary is "an indirect way of decreasing their salary and affecting the independence of the judges." Aquino replied that respecting tenure is fine, but the special tax privilege still violates uniformity and equal protection.

paras.html: Comm. Ople shared the concern for judicial independence but warned that, in erecting a "bastion of justice," the Commission might end up with a "fortress of privileges, an island of extra territoriality"; the income tax exemption is "a kind of economic immunity" denied to the entire executive and legislative departments.

paras.html: Constitutional period and judicial conduct: Under the 1987 Constitution, trial judges must decide and resolve cases within 90 days from submission for decision or resolution. Corollary to this, Sec. 5, Canon 6 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct requires judges to perform all judicial duties efficiently, fairly, and with reasonable promptness. The mandate also covers motions and interlocutory matters.
paras.text: Constitutional period and judicial conduct: Under the 1987 Constitution, trial judges must decide and resolve cases within 90 days from submission for decision or resolution. Corollary to this, Sec. 5, Canon 6 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct requires judges to perform all judicial duties efficiently, fairly, and with reasonable promptness. The mandate also covers motions and interlocutory matters.

paras.html: No self-chosen deadlines: A judge cannot choose his deadline for deciding cases. Without an extension granted by the Court, the failure to decide even a single case within the required period constitutes gross inefficiency (OCA v. Javellana). The Court is sympathetic only to seasonably filed requests for extension.
paras.text: No self-chosen deadlines: A judge cannot choose his deadline for deciding cases. Without an extension granted by the Court, the failure to decide even a single case within the required period constitutes gross inefficiency (OCA v. Javellana). paras.html: Penalty: Inexcusable failure to decide within 90 days warrants suspension without pay or a fine (Sec. 9(1), Rule 140). The fine depends chiefly on the number of cases undecided and on aggravating or mitigating circumstances, damage to the parties, the judge's health and age, and analogous circumstances.

paras.html: Power to abolish includes the lesser power to reorganize (prevailing opinion of 4 Justices): If Congress can abolish courts inferior to the SC, "it can do the lesser thing of reducing the number or changing the category of judges presiding over such courts." A judge "may hold office during good behavior only as long as his position lasts." Abolition is not removal, because "a removal implies that the office exists after the ouster." Qualifier: the Court said it was not dealing with judges "singled out for elimination," nor with a reorganization used "to cloak an unconstitutional and evil purpose."

paras.html: Votes needed to invalidate a statute: Although 7 of 11 Justices believed Sec. 3 of RA 1186 unconstitutional, the petition was denied "due to insufficient votes to invalidate" it. The 4-Justice view prevails, and the opinions of the seven "are in fact dissenting opinions" (J. Bengzon, fn. 1).

paras.html: The seven Justices' position (not the ruling): Congress cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly. Abolishing judges' positions while abolishing no court and increasing the number of judges is an indirect removal that violates Sec. 9, Art. VIII.

paras.html: On tenure, sides with J. Bengzon: fixed tenure during good behavior is a constitutional ban on Congress. "For how could there be a fixed tenure if the office may at any time be abolished?" The implied power to abolish courts "must be deemed withheld where its exercise would bring about what is prohibited"; what cannot be done directly cannot be done by indirection.

Pivotal point: RA 1186 abolished no court yet abolished judges' offices, and increased the number of judges by seven.

paras.html: No military trial of civilians while civil courts function: A military commission or tribunal cannot try and exercise jurisdiction, even during the period of martial law, over civilians for offenses allegedly committed by them as long as the civil courts are open and functioning, and any judgment it renders relating to a civilian is null and void for lack of jurisdiction. Aquino, Jr. v. Military Commission No. 2 (1975) and the cases affirming it are abandoned insofar as inconsistent.

Aquino, Jr. v. Military Commission No. 2 (1975) and the cases affirming it are abandoned insofar as inconsistent.

paras.html: Ouster of jurisdiction: Once a deprivation of a constitutional right is shown to exist, the tribunal that rendered the judgment is deemed ousted of jurisdiction (Gumabon v. Director of Prisons).

paras.html: On December 24, 1979, petitioners Olaguer, Othoniel Jimenez, Ester Misa-Jimenez, Lazaro, Reynaldo Maclang, Magdalena de los Santos-Maclang, Diesmos, Marciano, de Ocampo, and Amado were arrested by the military authorities.
paras.text: On December 24, 1979, petitioners Olaguer, Othoniel Jimenez, Ester Misa-Jimenez, Lazaro, Reynaldo Maclang, Magdalena de los Santos-Maclang, Diesmos, Marciano, de Ocampo, and Amado were arrested by the military authorities.

paras.html: They were first detained at Camp Crame, Quezon City, and later transferred to the detention center at Camp Bagong Diwa, Bicutan, except Olaguer, who stayed at Camp Crame.
paras.text: They were first detained at Camp Crame, Quezon City, and later transferred to the detention center at Camp Bagong Diwa, Bicutan, except Olaguer, who stayed at Camp Crame.

paras.html: Petitioner Mac Aceron voluntarily surrendered sometime in June 1980 and was also incarcerated at Camp Bagong Diwa.
paras.text: Petitioner Mac Aceron voluntarily surrendered sometime in June 1980 and was also incarcerated at Camp Bagong Diwa.

paras.html: All of the petitioners are civilians.

paras.html: Charges and creation of Military Commission No. 34:
paras.text: Charges and creation of Military Commission No. 34:

paras.html: On May 30, 1980, petitioners were charged with subversion (violation of PD 885, the Revised Anti-Subversion Law, as amended by BP 31) upon the recommendation of the Judge Advocate General (Gen. Hamilton Dimaya) and the approval of the Minister of National Defense (Juan Ponce Enrile). The case was docketed as Criminal Case No. MC-34-1.
paras.text: On May 30, 1980, petitioners were charged with subversion (violation of PD 885, the Revised Anti-Subversion Law, as amended by BP 31) upon the recommendation of the Judge Advocate General (Gen. Hamilton Dimaya) and the approval of the Minister of National Defense (Juan Ponce Enrile). The case was docketed as Criminal Case No. MC-34-1.

paras.html: On June 13, 1980, the AFP Chief of Staff (Gen. Romeo Espino) created Military Commission No. 34 to try the case. It was composed of Brig. Gen. Emilio P. Melendres (President), Col. Marciano I. Bacalla (Law Member), and five colonels as members.
paras.text: On June 13, 1980, the AFP Chief of Staff (Gen. Romeo Espino) created Military Commission No. 34 to try the case. It was composed of Brig. Gen. Emilio P. Melendres (President), Col. Marciano I. Bacalla (Law Member), and five colonels as members.

paras.html: On July 30, 1980, an amended charge sheet was filed for seven offenses:
paras.text: On July 30, 1980, an amended charge sheet was filed for seven offenses:

paras.html: (1) unlawful possession of explosives and incendiary devices; (2) conspiracy to assassinate President and Mrs. Marcos; (3) conspiracy to assassinate cabinet members Enrile, Tatad, and Paterno; (4) conspiracy to assassinate Tangco, Roño, and Corpus; (5) arson of nine buildings; (6) attempted murder of Perez, Valencia, and Generals Espino and Ver; and (7) conspiracy and proposal to commit rebellion, and inciting to rebellion.

paras.html: On August 19, 1980, during trial, petitioners filed with the SC a petition for prohibition and habeas corpus to enjoin MC 34 from proceeding and to secure their release. They argued that (a) military commissions have no jurisdiction to try civilians for offenses allegedly committed during martial law, and (b) the proceedings grossly violated their right to due process.
paras.text: On August 19, 1980, during trial, petitioners filed with the SC a petition for prohibition and habeas corpus to enjoin MC 34 from proceeding and to secure their release. They argued that (a) military commissions have no jurisdiction to try civilians for offenses allegedly committed during martial law, and (b) the proceedings grossly violated their right to due process.

paras.html: The OSG filed respondents' Answer on September 23, 1980; petitioners replied on November 20, 1980; respondents filed a Rejoinder on August 31, 1984.

paras.html: Lifting of martial law:
paras.text: Lifting of martial law:

paras.html: On January 17, 1981, President Marcos issued Proclamation No. 2045, officially lifting martial law. It revoked General Order No. 8 (which created the military tribunals) and directed that the military tribunals "are hereby dissolved upon final determination of cases pending therein which may not be transferred to the civil courts without irreparable prejudice to the state in view of the rules on double jeopardy, or other circumstances which render prosecution of the cases difficult, if not impossible."

It revoked General Order No. 8 (which created the military tribunals) and directed that the military tribunals "are hereby dissolved upon final determination of cases pending therein which may not be transferred to the civil courts without irreparable prejudice to the state in view of the rules on double jeopardy, or other circumstances which render prosecution of the cases difficult, if not impossible."

paras.html: Petitioners asked the prosecution (which performed the functions of clerk of court) for copies of the complete record of trial to prepare their defense, but the prosecution dilly-dallied; only a few days before December 4, 1984 did it furnish incomplete transcripts.
paras.text: Petitioners asked the prosecution (which performed the functions of clerk of court) for copies of the complete record of trial to prepare their defense, but the prosecution dilly-dallied; only a few days before December 4, 1984 did it furnish incomplete transcripts.

paras.html: Othoniel Jimenez was scheduled to start presenting evidence on December 4, 1984, but his first witness, whom he asked to be subpoenaed, was never served a subpoena. The other petitioners were, as agreed, to present evidence only after Jimenez.

paras.html: On December 4, 1984, the Commission asked each petitioner if he was ready, rejected their explanations, deemed them to have waived the presentation of evidence, and considered the case submitted.

paras.html: After a recess of only 25 minutes, it found petitioners guilty of all charges and sentenced them to death by electrocution.

Roxas; Scoty's Department Store v. Micaller).

paras.html: Toth v. Quarles (U.S.): "the assertion of military authority over civilians cannot rest on the President's power as Commander-in-Chief or on any theory of martial law." The presiding officer of a court-martial is not a judge protected by tenure and undiminished salary; different rules of evidence and procedure apply; and the convening officer, who selects members and counsel and commands them, can influence the outcome.

paras.html: Proclamation No. 2045 (Jan. 17, 1981), which lifted martial law and abolished the military tribunals created under the emergency, effectively divests MC 34 (and all military tribunals) of its supposed authority to try civilians.

paras.html: The main opinion in Aquino, Jr. rests on the theory that military tribunals have jurisdiction over civilians only as long as the national emergency lasts. Proclamation No. 2045 is the Executive's acknowledgment that the emergency no longer exists → following Aquino, Jr.'s own theory, all military tribunals are functus officio in relation to civilians.

paras.html: WHEREFORE, the Petitions for habeas corpus are DISMISSED for having become moot and academic. The Petitions for certiorari and prohibition are hereby GRANTED. The creation of respondent Military Commission No. 34 to try civilians like the petitioners is hereby declared unconstitutional and all its proceedings are deemed null and void. The temporary restraining order enjoining respondents from executing the Decision of MC 34 is made permanent, and respondents are permanently prohibited from further pursuing Criminal Case No. MC-34-1 against petitioners. The sentence imposing the death penalty on petitioners is vacated for being null and void, and all items or properties taken from petitioners in relation to the case shall be returned to them immediately. No pronouncement as to costs.

paras.html: TLDR: Joins the unanimous judgment vacating the death sentence for lack of military jurisdiction over civilians and expressly overturning Aquino, Jr., which was issued during "the darkest chapter of our history" when doctrines on due process "shrivelled in the effulgence of the overpowering rays of martial rule." Upholds the supremacy of the Constitution, the Rule of Law, and civilian authority over the military.

paras.html: 1. Denial of an impartial tribunal
paras.text: 1. Denial of an impartial tribunal

paras.html: Apart from the right to trial by judicial process, petitioners were denied an impartial trial from the start: the President (Commander-in-Chief) and the Defense Minister, the supposed targets of the conspiracy, were the very authorities who approved the charges and referred them to MC 34.
paras.text: Apart from the right to trial by judicial process, petitioners were denied an impartial trial from the start: the President (Commander-in-Chief) and the Defense Minister, the supposed targets of the conspiracy, were the very authorities who approved the charges and referred them to MC 34.

paras.html: As reviewing authorities, they could reverse or modify any judgment, even an acquittal, and could substitute commission members at pleasure, assign them to hazardous duties, and promote them or block their promotion. Members could hardly go against their superiors' declaration of "overwhelming" evidence.

paras.html: Quotes his own Aquino, Jr. dissent: Marcos publicly declared the evidence against Aquino "not only strong (but) overwhelming" at the August 24, 1971 press conference after the Plaza Miranda bombing; due process requires "the cold neutrality of an independent, wholly free, disinterested and impartial tribunal." Marcos himself had said that "if it were not for the judicial process, I would not be President," yet denied Aquino that process.

paras.html: 3. Reinstatement of the ouster-of-jurisdiction rule
paras.text: 3. Reinstatement of the ouster-of-jurisdiction rule

paras.html: Hails the reinstatement of the rule, "greatly eroded" under martial law, that disregard of an accused's constitutional rights ousts the tribunal of jurisdiction, and habeas corpus is the appropriate remedy (Gumabon). Persons denied a speedy trial should be freed (Conde v. Diaz); indefinite detention without charges becomes punitive and entitles detainees to freedom.

paras.html: 4. Sec. 18, Art. VII, 1987 Constitution – checks on martial law
paras.text: 4. Sec. 18, Art. VII, 1987 Constitution – checks on martial law

paras.html: Lists the changes summarized by former C.J. Roberto Concepcion in his last public address, including: martial law does not suspend the Constitution, supplant civil courts, or confer jurisdiction on military courts over civilians where civil courts function; it does not automatically suspend the privilege of the writ; it cannot be declared on mere imminent danger; the President must report to Congress within 48 hours; Congress may revoke by a majority vote of all its members, which the President cannot set aside; it may not exceed 60 days without Congress's concurrence; the SC may review the sufficiency of its factual basis in a proceeding filed by any citizen and must decide within 30 days; a simple majority now suffices to declare a law unconstitutional; and a detainee must be released unless judicially charged within three days.
paras.text: Lists the changes summarized by former C.J. Roberto Concepcion in his last public address, including: martial law does not suspend the Constitution, supplant civil courts, or confer jurisdiction on military courts over civilians where civil courts function; it does not automatically suspend the privilege of the writ; it cannot be declared on mere imminent danger; the President must report to Congress within 48 hours; Congress may revoke by a majority vote of all its members, which the President cannot set aside; it may not exceed 60 days without Congress's concurrence; the SC may review the sufficiency of its factual basis in a proceeding filed by any citizen and must decide within 30 days; a simple majority now suffices to declare a law unconstitutional; and a detainee must be released unless judicially charged within three days.

paras.html: Contempt for false or evasive testimony requires due process: a legislative contempt for testifying falsely or evasively is "essentially criminal or punitive in nature"; though sui generis, it "must similarly observe the minimum requirements of due process." At the very least, the witness must be given a chance to explain why his or her testimony is not false or evasive before being cited and arrested. Inconsistent or incomplete answers do not by themselves show evasiveness, i.e., a refusal or unwillingness to testify.
paras.text: Contempt for false or evasive testimony requires due process: a legislative contempt for testifying falsely or evasively is "essentially criminal or punitive in nature"; though sui generis, it "must similarly observe the minimum requirements of due process." At the very least, the witness must be given a chance to explain why his or her testimony is not false or evasive before being cited and arrested. Inconsistent or incomplete answers do not by themselves show evasiveness, i.e., a refusal or unwillingness to testify.

paras.html: The standard is valid: the phrase "testifies falsely or evasively" (Sec. 18, Senate Rules of Procedure Governing Inquiries; Sec. 6, Art. 6, Blue Ribbon Rules) is not vague, and the Legislature may itself determine whether a witness so testified (Arnault: obviously false or evasive testimony is equivalent to a refusal to testify). The Court intervenes only if the finding is "evidently without basis."

paras.html: Arrest and publication: the power to arrest a witness is inherent in the power of inquiry and contempt and "need not find textual basis" in the Senate Rules. Rules that state they "shall remain in force until amended or repealed" remain effective in later Congresses without republication (distinguishing Neri).

paras.html: The questioning: Sen. Lacson asked repeatedly about Yang's role beyond introducing four Chinese suppliers; Ong eventually said Yang guaranteed payments to suppliers, but could not recall the form or terms of their written agreement and would "look for it." He called supplier prices a "trade secret." Sen. Drilon pointed out that Pharmally had only ₱625,000 paid-up capital at the start of 2020 yet paid an initial ₱54 million order, and declared Ong "clearly lying"; Ong said the funds came from incorporators' savings and loans from friends, and offered to cooperate with the AMLC.

paras.html: Inquiry: broad, encompassing "everything that concerns the administration of existing laws as well as proposed or possibly needed statutes"; implied under the 1935 Constitution (Arnault) and explicit under the 1973 and 1987 Constitutions; upheld in Majaducom, Ermita, Sabio, Standard Chartered, Neri, and Romero II; available to committees.

paras.html: Contempt: not expressly granted, but inherent and implied; anchored on self-preservation; sui generis, attaching to the Legislature's character as a coordinate branch.

paras.html: Arrest: the Senate Rules expressly mention only detention, but "an arrest is necessary to carry out the coercive process of compelling attendance, testimony, and production of documents." As long as a resource person's testimony is primordial, Congress or its committees may compel appearance by arrest; this power "need not find textual basis" in the Rules. "Necessarily, compelled testimony connotes truthful declaration." [The OSG's argument that contempt excludes arrest is thus rejected.]

paras.html: The rights at stake are due process and freedom from unreasonable seizures (Art. III, Secs. 1 and 2), violated through the contempt power over "testifying falsely or evasively." Sec. 18 (as amended) lets "[t]he Chairman with the concurrence of at least one (1) member" cite a witness who "testifies falsely or evasively"; Sec. 6, Art. 6 of the Blue Ribbon Rules is quoted as requiring "a vote of a majority of all its members" [J. Lazaro-Javier quotes Sec. 6 as also using the Chairman-plus-one-member formula].

paras.html: Yang: citing J. Leonen, the Committee equated inconsistent answers with "testifying evasively". Whether a witness genuinely did not know or was evasive is "largely a matter of judgment" requiring "an assessment of the totality of the evidence," which could not be made on the Sept. 10 testimony alone. "Inconsistent or incomplete answers ... [do] not conclusively establish that he was evasive within the context of contempt, that is, there was refusal or unwillingness to testify"; Yang eventually admitted introducing the suppliers.

paras.html: Nature of the contempt: under Bro. Oca v. Custodio, contempt is civil (to compel) or criminal (to punish), determined by its dominant purpose. "A legislative contempt is essentially criminal or punitive in nature": false testimony is criminally defined (Art. 183, RPC: false testimony and perjury), and the Committee treated it as criminal by ordering arrests and transferring Ong to the Pasay City Jail.

paras.html: Legislative inquiries aim to aid legislation, "not to conduct a trial or make an adjudication", and "cannot be punitive." So legislative contempt, "albeit sui generis in character, must similarly observe the minimum requirements of due process." Quoting CJ Gesmundo's separate opinion: witnesses charged with false or evasive testimony must get stricter due process, at least "a chance to explain why his or her testimony is not false or evasive."
