paras.html: Implicit in the power to punish recalcitrant witnesses is the power to determine whether the witness is contumacious; the Legislature's power is meant to be complete without resort to courts. The Court will not prevent the Legislature from acting just because courts may also punish false testimony; it may find the Legislature arbitrary only "if its finding that a witness testified falsely or evasively is evidently without basis."

paras.html: A law is vague when persons of common intelligence must guess at its meaning; it then violates due process (no fair notice) and gives unbridled discretion. But the doctrine requires only "a reasonable degree of certainty," not mathematical exactitude.

paras.html: "False": false testimony is defined in the RPC (denying the truth or saying something contrary to it under oath); a false statement is known or believed to be untrue, made to deceive or mislead, or made recklessly. "Evasive": a response that does not directly answer the question, or a refusal to admit or deny directly a matter one is presumed to know.

paras.html: No grave abuse: the TSN shows Ong answered "in a roundabout manner" despite repeated questions, and Yang gave shifting answers despite an interpreter. The ponencia glosses over petitioners' earlier refusal to appear despite subpoenas until the Sept. 7 order; together with "purposeful stonewalling," this negates capriciousness. Ong was given many chances on Sept. 10 and after (e.g., the "Brother Tiger" supplier exchange on Sept. 13), was arrested only 11 days later, and Yang evaded arrest.

paras.html: The procedure is void: Sec. 18 and Sec. 6 let the Chairperson with the concurrence of one member cite and punish for contempt [she quotes Sec. 6 with this formula]. For "testifying falsely or evasively," which is "highly contextual" (false only if contrary to the truth; evasive only if a direct answer was available), this "concurrence method" gives no hearing, no notice of the cause, no reasons. A hearing, even by written submissions, is required; its content is for the Senate to set. → Sec. 6, Art. 6 of the Blue Ribbon Rules is contrary to the Constitution.

paras.html: Witness, not accused: a resource person in a legislative inquiry cannot altogether decline to appear or testify; the right against self-incrimination "may only be invoked in legislative inquiry when a specific question implicating such right is propounded" (Sabio; Standard Chartered Bank).

paras.html: No custodial-investigation rights: a legislative inquiry is not a custodial investigation. The right to counsel "can only be invoked by a person under custodial investigation suspected for the commission of a crime", so resource persons cannot invoke it (Philcomsat Holdings v. Senate); the right to remain silent likewise does not apply.

paras.html: The SC, CA, and RTC have concurrent original jurisdiction over certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto, and habeas corpus, but parties must, as a rule, file with the lower-ranked court; failure is sufficient cause for dismissal (GIOS-SAMAR v. DOTC).
paras.text: The SC, CA, and RTC have concurrent original jurisdiction over certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto, and habeas corpus, but parties must, as a rule, file with the lower-ranked court; failure is sufficient cause for dismissal (GIOS-SAMAR v. DOTC).

paras.html: Eight recognized exceptions (GIOS-SAMAR, citing Diocese of Bacolod v. COMELEC): (1) genuine constitutional issues needing immediate resolution; (2) transcendental importance; (3) first impression; (4) constitutional issues better decided by the SC; (5) exigency; (6) review of acts of a constitutional organ; (7) no other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy (in the freedom-of-expression context); (8) public welfare, public policy, broader interest of justice, patent nullity, or appeal clearly inappropriate.

paras.html: Standard Chartered Bank v. Senate Committee on Banks: resource persons are not accused. An accused may refuse to take the witness stand altogether; an ordinary witness must claim the privilege as each incriminating question is asked. The privilege extends to proceedings analogous to criminal cases or where punishment is sought, but witnesses who are neither accused nor penalized for their testimony "cannot altogether decline appearing".

paras.html: No automatic joint session: “The Congress is not constitutionally mandated to convene in joint session except to vote jointly to revoke the President's declaration or suspension.” The phrase “voting jointly” in Art. VII, Sec. 18 explicitly applies only to revocation. But if either House, or both, resolves to revoke, Congress must convene in joint session to vote jointly on the revocation.
paras.text: No automatic joint session: “The Congress is not constitutionally mandated to convene in joint session except to vote jointly to revoke the President's declaration or suspension.” The phrase “voting jointly” in Art. VII, Sec. 18 explicitly applies only to revocation. But if either House, or both, resolves to revoke, Congress must convene in joint session to vote jointly on the revocation.

paras.html: Concurrence is left to each House: The Constitution does not provide for the manner by which Congress expresses concurrence (prior or subsequent) in a proclamation or suspension; the Houses have the discretion to adopt rules of procedure for that purpose (Art. VI, Sec. 16[3]). This does not place the rules of the Houses above the Constitution.

paras.html: Mandamus requires a clear ministerial duty: Mandamus will not issue to compel Congress to convene jointly absent a clear ministerial duty under the Constitution. Praying for mandamus and certiorari over the very same act is contradictory.

paras.text: Proclamation No. 216:

paras.html: May 23, 2017 – President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring a state of martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for a period not exceeding 60 days, on the grounds of rebellion and the necessity of public safety under Art. VII, Sec. 18.
paras.text: May 23, 2017 – President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 216, declaring a state of martial law and suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the whole of Mindanao for a period not exceeding 60 days, on the grounds of rebellion and the necessity of public safety under Art. VII, Sec. 18.

paras.html: Basis (per the Proclamation and the Report): a series of armed attacks and atrocities by the Abu Sayyaf and Maute terrorist groups, with local and foreign affiliates who pledged allegiance to ISIS, aimed at establishing a DAESH wilayah (Islamic Province) in Mindanao.

paras.html: May 31, 2017 – The Committee of the Whole was briefed in a closed-door session (about 6 hours) by ES Medialdea, Sec. Lorenzana, and other security officials. A proposal to call a joint session was debated and rejected.

paras.html: Actual case/ripeness: The separate resolutions of support injure their right “to a proper [and] mandatory legislative review of the declaration of martial law”; the continuing failure to convene jointly is a continuing injury (Padilla). The refusal deprived legislators of a venue to move for revocation or extension, and the public of the chance to be informed of the bases of martial law (Tañada).

The Tañada petitioners ask for liberality because the question is one of first impression and paramount importance.

paras.html: No standing: Generalized interests do not confer standing; petitioners show no direct and personal interest. A taxpayer's suit lies only against the exercise of the spending or taxing power, and martial law is being funded from funds already appropriated. Sen. De Lima suffers no prejudice where Congress's powers are not impaired; and even assuming they were, she has not shown she has been allowed to participate in Senate sessions during her incarceration, so she has no direct injury.

paras.html: Locus standi = a personal and substantial interest such that the party has sustained or will sustain direct injury; the test is a personal stake that assures concrete adverseness (Purisima v. Lazatin, citing Galicto v. Aquino). “Petitioners satisfy these standards.”

paras.html: Citizens: Every citizen has the right, if not the duty, to see that a public grievance is remedied (David v. Macapagal-Arroyo). A citizen asserting a public right represents the public at large; it is enough that he shows he is entitled to relief in the vindication of a public right (De Castro v. JBC). His personal interest lies in being a member of the public in whom the right is vested (Legaspi v. CSC) and in his interest and duty to ensure the proper execution of the law (Tañada v. Tuvera).

paras.html: Plain text: Art. VII, Sec. 18 requires Congress to convene in joint session, deliberate, and vote as a single deliberative body; this is mandatory, not discretionary.

paras.html: “May” qualifies only the power to revoke, not the obligation to convene jointly and vote. Requiring a joint session only when Congress will revoke is absurd, because without convening jointly, Congress cannot know beforehand whether a majority for revocation exists.

paras.html: Framers' intent: The joint session was designed to compel Congress to review the President's action and to contain martial law within a democratic framework. The Tañada petitioners add that “voting jointly” was meant as a procedural requirement for Congress to revoke, affirm, or extend, whether or not Congress is in session or intends to revoke.

paras.html: 24-hour clause: If Congress not in session must convene within 24 hours, then all the more must it convene immediately when in session.

paras.html: Deliberation, transparency, accountability: Separate briefings in executive sessions deprive lawmakers of a deliberative and interrogatory process and the public of transparent proceedings; legislators who wish to revoke should be able to put that vote on record, and the public should know each legislator's position. A regular session is preferable to a briefing so that officials testify under oath.

paras.html: Prior concurrence of Congress is not required for the effectivity of the proclamation; the framers intended to let the President act for up to 60 days without it. Nothing mandates a joint session merely to discuss or review the proclamation. When Congress is not in session, it convenes “in accordance with its rules,” not in joint session.

They show two intentions:

paras.html: (a) Remove prior concurrence. The draft required the concurrence of a majority of all Members for the suspension. Natividad, Padilla, and Monsod argued that in actual invasion or rebellion the President must act fast, concurrence may be impractical, the proclamation has a 60-day “time fuse,” and the SC can review the factual basis; Suarez warned of another Marcos. Vote: 28–12 to delete prior concurrence.

paras.html: (b) Discretionary power to revoke by joint vote. The debate was whether the Houses vote jointly or separately — always for the purpose of revocation. Bernas proposed joint voting as a conscious exception so that it is easier for Congress to revoke and to avoid a deadlock; Monsod agreed (Senators would participate in discussions and lend persuasive weight); Rodrigo and Ople objected that the Senate would be absorbed by the House. Vote: 24–13 for “voting jointly.”

paras.html: Rodrigo's later amendment to give the power to the House alone was rejected 5–25. Rodrigo expressly observed that the provision “does not call for a joint session.”

A joint session can only be inferred from the argument that Representatives would benefit from the Senators' advice → “far from a clear mandate” to automatically convene jointly under all circumstances, even when Congress does not intend to revoke.

paras.html: “Practice and logic dictate” that a collegial body first meets among its own members to reach a stance before convening with another body — exactly what the Houses did. Each House took prompt action: received and assessed the Report, interpellated executive officials, deliberated, then voted to support the proclamation and against a joint session. They placed the proclamation under serious review.

No concurrent resolution was adopted → no joint session could be had.

paras.html: Art. VI, Sec. 16(3) (“Each House shall determine the rules of its proceedings”) is a grant of full discretionary authority generally exempt from judicial interference (Dela Paz v. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations); legislative acts following long-settled practice carry an “armor of constitutionality” (McGillicuddy, a U.S. state case). Qualifier: “Nothing in this Decision should be presumed to give precedence to the rules of the Houses of the Congress over the provisions of the Constitution.” The Court holds only that, since the Constitution does not regulate the manner of concurrence, the Houses may adopt rules for it.

paras.html: Convening jointly does not require discretion; it is a purely ministerial duty compellable by mandamus (Padilla). Mandamus is the proper recourse to enforce a public right; and while mandamus generally does not lie against a coordinate branch or to compel discretion, exceptions exist for gross abuse of discretion, manifest injustice, or palpable excess of authority with no other adequate remedy (Tañada).

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to DISMISS, but only because the petitions are moot and academic (the 60-day period lapsed and Congress has since convened jointly to extend). He dissents from the doctrine: the power to revoke intrinsically and logically includes the duty to deliberate on whether to revoke. Immediately after a proclamation or suspension, Congress must convene as a whole, deliberate jointly in one forum, and then vote.

paras.html: Deferring to the Houses' practice “grant[s] the veneer of constitutionality” and makes the provision unworkable: two forums instead of one; the minority of one chamber goes unheard in the other; executive and military officials are pulled from the field to present twice or more; one chamber may treat information as confidential while the other treats it as public.

Of the four permutations of Senate/House votes, two lead to a constitutional crisis under the ponencia's reading. All of this must happen within 60 days.

The Philippine Bill of 1902 required the Philippine Commission's approval for suspension; the Jones Law (1916) introduced martial law and required notice to the U.S. President; the 1935 and 1973 Constitutions left Congress's role practically nil (1973 required Batasan consent only for an Acting President).

Unlike the Court, which acts only upon a citizen's petition, Congress convenes automatically, and its review has a wider latitude limited only by arbitrariness.

paras.html: No automatic joint session: "The Congress is not constitutionally mandated to convene in joint session except to vote jointly to revoke the President's declaration or suspension." Art. VII, Sec. 18 grants a discretionary power to revoke ("may revoke") and prescribes how to exercise it (voting jointly, by a majority of all Members); it does not even mention a "joint session."
paras.text: No automatic joint session: "The Congress is not constitutionally mandated to convene in joint session except to vote jointly to revoke the President's declaration or suspension." Art. VII, Sec. 18 grants a discretionary power to revoke ("may revoke") and prescribes how to exercise it (voting jointly, by a majority of all Members); it does not even mention a "joint session."

paras.html: Concurrence is for Congress to decide: the Constitution does not regulate how Congress expresses concurrence in a proclamation, so each House may act separately under its own rules (Art. VI, Sec. 16(3)). But if either House, or both, resolves to revoke, Congress "must convene in joint session to vote jointly on the revocation."
paras.text: Concurrence is for Congress to decide: the Constitution does not regulate how Congress expresses concurrence in a proclamation, so each House may act separately under its own rules (Art. VI, Sec. 16(3)). But if either House, or both, resolves to revoke, Congress "must convene in joint session to vote jointly on the revocation."

paras.html: No mandamus or certiorari: absent a clear ministerial duty, mandamus will not issue to compel Congress to convene jointly; and where both Houses decided against a joint session after deliberation and voting under their rules, there is no grave abuse of discretion.

paras.html: Padilla: the plain text, the framers' intent, Fortun v. Macapagal-Arroyo (which called the duty "automatic"), and the 2009 Maguindanao precedent require Congress to convene in joint session, deliberate, and vote as a single body; this is a ministerial duty compellable by mandamus. "May revoke" is discretionary only as to revoking, not as to convening and voting; without a joint session, Congress cannot know whether a majority exists. Standing: citizens and taxpayers; Sen. De Lima as a legislator denied the chance to deliberate.

paras.html: Tañada: a joint session is mandatory "whether or not the Congress is in session or there is intent to revoke"; failure deprives legislators of a deliberative forum and the public of transparent proceedings (briefings in executive session are not enough); legislators should be able to put revocation votes on record.

paras.html: There is no mandatory duty to "vote jointly" except to revoke or extend; hence no actual case. Political question. No standing (generalized interest; no spending; De Lima not shown to have participated while detained). The right to information yields to national security.

paras.html: Art. VII, Sec. 18 does not use the words "joint session"; prior concurrence is not required; the framers deliberately let the President act for 60 days without concurrence. If Congress is not in session, it must convene "in accordance with its rules," not in joint session. Fortun's statement is obiter, and its facts differ. No grave abuse: each House passed its own resolution. The Court cannot direct Congress how to work (separation of powers).

paras.html: YES. Separation of powers (Belgica; Angara) does not bar review because the principal issue is the proper interpretation of Art. VII, Sec. 18, and it is the Judiciary's prerogative to declare "what the law is." When it allocates constitutional boundaries, the Court asserts no superiority.

VIII, Sec. 1; Diocese of Bacolod), the Court reviews the legality, not the wisdom, of how a constitutional duty is exercised; courts "cannot hereafter evade the duty" by calling a matter political (AMCOW, citing Concepcion).

paras.html: Actual case: there are opposing claims (mandatory vs. discretionary duty). An alleged omission constituting neglect of constitutional duty makes out a prima facie case for mandamus; whether petitioners are ultimately entitled to relief is for the merits.

paras.html: Transcendental importance: under the 1935 Constitution, martial law powers were seemingly limitless; the 1987 Constitution made them subject to legislative and judicial review. Congress's role in this check is of paramount public interest.

paras.html: Mootness: the main relief was arguably mooted by (a) the lapse of the 60 days, (b) the July 22 joint-session extension, and (c) Lagman v. Medialdea (sufficiency of factual basis). But under David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, the Court decided because of transcendental significance and novelty, the need to guide the bench, bar, and public, and to clarify congressional conduct "in the event of a repetition."

paras.html: Where the provision is clear, it is applied, not interpreted (Funa v. Villar; J.M. Tuason). The provision grants the power to revoke and prescribes how. "May" is permissive, conferring discretion on whether to revoke; but to revoke, a majority voting jointly is required. The provision "does not actually refer to a 'joint session'"; even conceding that "voting jointly" implies a joint session, it "explicitly applies only to the situation when the Congress revokes."

paras.html: Rules of joint sessions: by parliamentary practice, a joint session requires a concurrent resolution by both Houses; rules for joint sessions are adopted ad hoc (e.g., 2016 canvass; 2009 Proc. 1959). No concurrent resolution, no joint session. Under Art. VI, Sec. 16(3), the Court respects each House's rules; legislative acts following long practice are clothed with an "armor of constitutionality." This does not place House rules above the Constitution.

paras.html: Congress deliberated, albeit separately, and the right to information on national security matters is not absolute. House Rule XI (Secs. 82–83) and Senate Rule XLVII (Secs. 126–128) allow executive sessions when state security is involved, with secrecy obligations (and RA 6713). Martial law's factual basis involves intelligence and military tactics; forcing public discussion would breach confidentiality. Under the Senate's inquiry rules, testimony in executive sessions is under oath anyway.

paras.html: Mandamus (Rule 65, Sec. 3) requires a ministerial duty and a clear legal right; it "never issues in doubtful cases." The Court has no authority to compel a joint session absent a clear ministerial duty and in disregard of the Houses' separate actions and votes not to hold one.

paras.html: Certiorari: praying for both writs against the same non-convening is "contradictory" (mandamus presumes no discretion; certiorari presumes discretion abused). In any case, the Houses decided against a joint session "only after deliberations among their Members and putting the same to vote" → no grave abuse.

paras.html: Unworkability of separate deliberations: two forums mean minorities in each House go unheard by the other; the same information may be confidential in one chamber and public in the other; AFP and PNP officials are pulled from the field to brief twice; results may differ, requiring a bicameral committee, all within 60 days. Of the four permutations (both not revoke; Senate not / House revoke; Senate revoke / House not; both revoke), two lead to deadlock. A joint vote after separate debates becomes "a mere ceremony"; a single filibuster can negate Congress's power.

The 1987 Constitution, reacting to Marcos, gave Congress and the Courts review powers; Monsod's joint-voting proposal aimed to make revocation easier and let Senators "participate fully in the discussions."

The 24-hour convening clause signals urgency and that Congress may use all its powers (legislation, appropriations) to address the crisis; the extension clause ("in the same manner") shows that joint action applies to deliberation too, otherwise extension would also require layered separate deliberations within the same 60 days.

paras.html: Standing in quo warranto: Quo warranto is an action by the Government against individuals (Sec. 1, Rule 66). The sole exception is an individual suing in his own name who claims to be entitled to the office usurped (Sec. 5, Rule 66). To challenge the President, the petitioner "must have been a candidate who ran for the presidential post… and lost to respondent"; a candidate disqualified as a nuisance has no factual basis for a personal claim.
paras.text: Standing in quo warranto: Quo warranto is an action by the Government against individuals (Sec. 1, Rule 66). The sole exception is an individual suing in his own name who claims to be entitled to the office usurped (Sec. 5, Rule 66). To challenge the President, the petitioner "must have been a candidate who ran for the presidential post… and lost to respondent"; a candidate disqualified as a nuisance has no factual basis for a personal claim.

paras.html: One-year prescriptive period: An action for ouster of a public officer must be filed within one year after the cause of ouster, or the petitioner's right to the office, arose (Sec. 11, Rule 66). This period is a condition precedent to the cause of action, and inaction is a waiver (Bumanglag v. Fernandez). The Government's imprescriptible quo warranto (Republic v. Sereno) does not apply to private individuals asserting their own right to the office.

paras.html: A litigant must substantiate a personal stake in the outcome. He must not bring the suit out of "a generic interest or a blanket conviction, however deeply-seated", but where he stands to personally lose or gain depending on the ruling. This concretizes the adverseness of the issues and sharpens their presentation (Lozano v. Nograles, citing Kilosbayan v. Morato).

paras.html: Quo warranto is by nature an action by the Government against individuals. Sec. 1, Rule 66: a verified petition in the name of the Republic against (a) a person who usurps, intrudes into, or unlawfully holds or exercises a public office, position, or franchise; (b) a public officer who does or suffers an act constituting a ground for forfeiture; or (c) an association acting as a corporation without being legally incorporated or without lawful authority.

paras.html: Sole exception to the rule that only the Government may sue: an individual in his own name with "an uncontroverted claim to the position from which ouster is sought". Sec. 5, Rule 66: "A person claiming to be entitled to a public office or position usurped or unlawfully held or exercised by another may bring an action therefor in his own name."

paras.html: Presidential withdrawal from treaties is not absolute: As primary architect of foreign policy, the President enjoys a degree of leeway to withdraw from treaties bona fide deemed contrary to the Constitution or our laws. But the President cannot unilaterally withdraw (a) from treaties entered into pursuant to legislative intent manifested in prior laws, or subsequently affirmed by succeeding laws; or (b) where the Senate's concurrence was expressly premised on the same concurrence for withdrawal (imposed piecemeal per treaty, or through a law, a joint resolution, or a comprehensive Senate resolution). Withdrawal is reviewable for grave abuse of discretion, but only in a justiciable case. [These are laid down "as guide for future cases"; the fallo only dismisses for mootness.]
paras.text: Presidential withdrawal from treaties is not absolute: As primary architect of foreign policy, the President enjoys a degree of leeway to withdraw from treaties bona fide deemed contrary to the Constitution or our laws. But the President cannot unilaterally withdraw (a) from treaties entered into pursuant to legislative intent manifested in prior laws, or subsequently affirmed by succeeding laws; or (b) where the Senate's concurrence was expressly premised on the same concurrence for withdrawal (imposed piecemeal per treaty, or through a law, a joint resolution, or a comprehensive Senate resolution). Withdrawal is reviewable for grave abuse of discretion, but only in a justiciable case. [These are laid down "as guide for future cases"; the fallo only dismisses for mootness.]

paras.html: Statutes prevail over treaties: A treaty concurred in by the Senate has the force and effect of law, but "[i]n case of conflict between a law and a treaty, it is the statute that must prevail", because statutes pass through both chambers while the Senate may only concur. Lantion's statement that "a treaty may repeal a statute" is misplaced obiter.

paras.html: Justiciability: A petition to annul a withdrawal already completed under the treaty's own terms is moot. Individual senators retain standing, but their suit is premature where the Senate as a collegial body has not asserted its prerogative (no constitutional impasse).

paras.html: The Rome Statute is a multilateral treaty that created the International Criminal Court (ICC), with jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression. ICC jurisdiction is complementary to national jurisdictions: it acts only when domestic courts are "unwilling or unable" to prosecute (Art. 17).

ICC jurisdiction is complementary to national jurisdictions: it acts only when domestic courts are "unwilling or unable" to prosecute (Art. 17).

paras.html: 1996 onward (Ramos): The Philippines took part in establishing the ICC as a member of the Drafting Committee. On March 24, 1998, President Ramos issued AO 387 creating a task force on the proposed ICC (DFA chair, DOJ co-chair, OSG, OES, DILG, and UP College of Law).

paras.html: June 15 – July 17, 1998: At the Rome Conference, the Philippines (Head of Delegation Usec. Lauro Baja; Alternate Head Franklin Ebdalin) voted to adopt the Statute, which was adopted by 120 states on July 17, 1998.

paras.html: December 28, 2000: The Philippines, through President Estrada, signed the Rome Statute, subject to ratification and to Senate concurrence under Sec. 21, Art. VII.

paras.html: Sen. Pimentel, Rep. Rosales, the Philippine Coalition for the Establishment of the ICC, and others sought mandamus to compel the Executive to transmit the signed Statute to the Senate. In Pimentel, Jr. v. Executive Secretary, the Court dismissed the petition: ratification is within the President's discretion and cannot be compelled by mandamus.

paras.html: March 16, 2018: Permanent Representative Enrique Manalo deposited the Note Verbale (notice of withdrawal) with the Chef de Cabinet of UN Secretary-General Guterres. [The decision later calls it "[t]he March 15, 2018 Note Verbale" (Part XVII).] The notice affirmed the government's commitment to fight impunity, noting that the Philippines has national legislation punishing atrocity crimes, and called the withdrawal a "principled stand against those who politicize and weaponize human rights."

paras.html: March 17, 2018: The UN Secretary-General received the notification. March 20, 2018: The ICC issued a statement noting the deposit; withdrawal is a sovereign decision with no impact on pending proceedings. The ICC expressed no reservation on the withdrawal's efficacy.

paras.html: Judicial power covers (1) settling actual controversies involving legally demandable rights, and (2) determining grave abuse of discretion by any branch (Sec. 1, Art. VIII). Angara: when the judiciary allocates constitutional boundaries, it asserts no superiority; it only determines conflicting claims in an actual controversy.

paras.html: The expanded certiorari jurisdiction (Tañada v. Angara; Francisco) still requires a prima facie showing of grave abuse, which is in essence the actual case. "[T]he requirement of an actual case or controversy is not dispensed with" (Falcis). No advisory opinions (PBOAP v. DOLE).

Desierto, Demetria v. Alba, and Ashwander v. TVA). The Court must exercise restraint "in the face of political posturing": petitioners "want a different political result."

paras.html: Even before the petitions were filed, the President had completed the irreversible act of withdrawal. Art. 127(1) requires only a written notification to the UN Secretary-General; the withdrawal takes effect one year after receipt. The notice was submitted on March 16 and received on March 17, 2018. "[T]he Philippines had, by then, completed all the requisite acts of withdrawal" → fait accompli.

paras.html: The ICC acknowledged the notice (March 20, 2018) without reservation, and the ASP President announced the departure effective March 17, 2019. This "settles any doubt" on lingering factual occurrences; any discussion of the withdrawal "is, at this juncture, merely a matter of theory."

paras.html: Ruling otherwise would impose the Court's will not only on the Executive but on the ICC itself. The Rome Statute has no proviso for reversing a withdrawal; the Court cannot revoke it "without writing new terms into the Rome Statute."

paras.html: The one-year period pertains only to effectivity, i.e., when the legal consequences take effect, not to approval or finality. Nor does it diminish the ICC's power to continue a probe begun while the state was a party.

Powell's concurring opinion, a dispute between Congress and the President is not ripe "until the political branches reach a constitutional impasse"; "[i]f the Congress chooses not to confront the President, it is not our task to do so." → This Court should likewise stay its hand.

The IBP and PCICC gave no special reason why injured members could not sue themselves; "[a]dvocating human rights as an institution is insufficient." PCICC members who joined also showed no injury.

paras.html: "It is wrong to state that matters of foreign relations are political questions, and thus, beyond the judiciary's reach." The Constitution expressly lets the Court review the constitutionality of "any treaty, international or executive agreement" (Sec. 5(2)(a), Art. VIII).

paras.html: Still, foreign relations generally pertain to the President as "sole organ" (Bayan v. Zamora); political questions concern wisdom, not legality (IBP v. Zamora, citing Baker v. Carr; Tañada v. Cuenco). The Court acts only on grave abuse of discretion.

paras.html: The withdrawal followed the mechanism in the treaty itself; alleged political motives "remain just that: suggestions and suppositions." Grave abuse could be appreciated if the President ran afoul of procedure, disregarded declared periods or terms, or acted out of vindictiveness or personal motives; none was shown.

paras.html: Certiorari: Rule 65 certiorari lies only against tribunals, boards, or officers exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions (Galicto v. Aquino); grave abuse means capricious and whimsical judgment (Sinon v. CSC). The withdrawal "by any stretch of the imagination" is not such an act. Expanded certiorari (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) is distinct, though the Court has allowed Rule 65 as its vehicle; either way, the requisites of justiciability remain.

paras.html: Mandamus: It lies only for a ministerial duty and a clear legal right (Lihaylihay v. Treasurer). No law imposes a duty to retract the withdrawal; it was discretionary. Moreover, it would be "ineffectual and futile": a writ would not restore ICC membership, and the UN Secretary-General may not assent. "This Court is not an international court."

paras.html: Treaties are international agreements requiring legislative concurrence after executive ratification (EO 459). Executive agreements do not need concurrence because they implement existing policy: to adjust treaty details, pursuant to a law, or under the President's independent powers (Saguisag v. Ochoa; China National Machinery v. Santamaria).

Executive agreements do not need concurrence because they implement existing policy: to adjust treaty details, pursuant to a law, or under the President's independent powers (Saguisag v. Ochoa; China National Machinery v. Santamaria).

paras.html: Per Saguisag (quoted): executive agreements must be traceable to express or implied authorization; treaties are superior to executive agreements and "on the same level as a statute." [The quoted Saguisag passage adds that a later law or treaty prevails over a prior one; this sits in tension with the Court's own holding below that statutes prevail.]

paras.html: Incorporation v. transformation: Sec. 2, Art. II incorporates generally accepted principles of international law (custom and general principles of law) as part of the law of the land with no further act. Sec. 21, Art. VII transforms treaties: they become valid and effective only upon two-thirds Senate concurrence, after which they have "the force and effect of a statute" (David v. SET, quoting Pharmaceutical & Health Care Ass'n v. Duque).

paras.html: Youngstown framework (J. Jackson's concurrence in Youngstown v. Sawyer): (1) acting with congressional authorization → power at maximum; (2) acting without grant or denial → "zone of twilight"; (3) acting against the will of Congress → "lowest ebb." It was used in Medellin v. Texas (discussed in CJ Puno's dissent in Nicolas v. Romulo), in J. Brion's opinion in Saguisag, in Gonzales v. Marcos (Fernando, J.: congressional silence as "silence meaning consent"), and in CJ Puno's dissents in Bayan v. Zamora and Akbayan v. Aquino.

paras.html: First: the President "enjoys some leeway in withdrawing from agreements which he or she determines to be contrary to the Constitution or statutes", as part of the duty to faithfully execute the laws (Sec. 17, Art. VII).

paras.html: SC's constitutional power to change venue: Sec. 5(4), Art. X of the (1973) Constitution "expressly empowers" the Court to "order a change of venue or place of trial to avoid a miscarriage of justice."

paras.html: Ground – hostile sentiment and the accused's safety: "Present hostile sentiment against the accused at the place of trial is a justification for transfer of venue." Where the accused's personal safety (not merely a miscarriage of justice) is at stake, it would be "absurd to compel him to undergo trial in a place where his life would be imperilled."

paras.html: Change of venue to avoid a miscarriage of justice: The SC may order "a change of venue or place of trial to avoid a miscarriage of justice" (Art. X, Sec. 5(4), 1973 Consti), a power that incorporated People v. Gutierrez. Although fear may, objectively viewed, be "less than terrifying" to some, "the question must always be the effect it has on the witnesses who will testify." In case of doubt, it should be resolved in favor of a change of venue.

paras.html: Bail in capital offenses: Bail granted without giving the prosecution the opportunity to prove that the evidence of guilt is strong violates procedural due process and is void (People v. San Diego). Searching questions by the judge do not cure this infirmity of a jurisdictional character.

paras.html: Under Art. IV, Sec. 18 of the 1973 Constitution, all persons are bailable before conviction except those charged with capital offenses when evidence of guilt is strong.

paras.html: Granting bail without hearing the prosecution disregards the "authoritative doctrine" in People v. San Diego (Capistrano, J.): whether the motion for bail is resolved in a summary proceeding or in the course of a regular trial, "the prosecution must be given an opportunity to present, within a reasonable time, all the evidence that it may desire to introduce" before the court resolves it. Denying that opportunity is a violation of procedural due process, and the order granting bail "should be considered void on that ground."

Denying that opportunity is a violation of procedural due process, and the order granting bail "should be considered void on that ground."

paras.html: Congress may prescribe how an appropriation is spent. An appropriate provision, directly related to and confined to its appropriation, cannot be vetoed separately while the item is retained. An inappropriate provision—one extending beyond the item, amending other laws, or itself unconstitutional—may be treated as an item and separately vetoed. Thus, the debt-service veto was valid only in part; the road-maintenance ratio and AFP-medicines vetoes were void. Individual legislators have standing to resist an alleged impairment of congressional powers. Padilla disagreed with the inappropriate-provision doctrine. The 1994 CDF holding is historical and was later partially abandoned in Belgica (see separate update).

The decision begins with the four requisites for judicial review: (1) actual and appropriate case; (2) personal and substantial interest; (3) constitutional challenge raised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) constitutional question as the lis mota. The actual preliminary dispute here is legislator standing—not a separate analysis finding every other requisite absent or disputed.

sections.label: Institutional standing is not the only route. In Gonzales v. Macaraig, the entire 23-member Senate sued under an enabling Senate resolution. question.html: W/N the 1994 CDF provision allowing legislators to propose and identify projects unconstitutionally intrudes into executive implementation?
question.text: W/N the 1994 CDF provision allowing legislators to propose and identify projects unconstitutionally intrudes into executive implementation?

sections.label: PETITIONERS' ARGUMENT: Identifying particular projects after enactment is implementation, not making, repealing or amending laws. Congress thereby enters the Executive's domain. [3]
sections.labelHtml: PETITIONERS' ARGUMENT: Identifying particular projects after enactment is implementation, not making, repealing or amending laws. Congress thereby enters the Executive's domain. [3]

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: NO, under the majority's construction in 1994. The power of the purse belongs to Congress, subject to presidential veto. Although the President proposes the budget, Congress makes the final appropriation decision. The power to appropriate includes specifying the activities and projects to be funded, as broadly or particularly as Congress chooses.

sections.label: Congress itself had stated the statutory purposes. Article XLI limited the fund to infrastructure, ambulances, computers, other priority activities and qualified credit facilities. The CDF sought more equal allocations and recognized members' familiarity with their constituents' needs and priorities.

question.text: W/N the provision on members' operating-expense realignment violates Art. VI, Sec. 25(5)?

sections.label: PETITIONERS' ARGUMENT: Only the Senate President and House Speaker—not individual members—are constitutionally authorized to augment their respective appropriations from savings. [4]
sections.labelHtml: PETITIONERS' ARGUMENT: Only the Senate President and House Speaker—not individual members—are constitutionally authorized to augment their respective appropriations from savings. [4]

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: NO, as construed by the Court. Each House's operating appropriation is divided into expense items, with each member allotted a proportionate operating share. Unspent amounts in one category may be proposed for realignment to meet a deficiency in another.
sections.labelHtml: NO, as construed by the Court. Each House's operating appropriation is divided into expense items, with each member allotted a proportionate operating share. Unspent amounts in one category may be proposed for realignment to meet a deficiency in another.

sections.label: General rule → exception: transfers of appropriations are prohibited. The constitutional exception permits specified heads, when authorized by law, to augment items for their own offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations.

sections.label: Statutory authorization: Sec. 16 of the GAA's General Provisions prohibited changes in expenditure items except congressional action or augmentation from savings authorized under Art. VI, Sec. 25(5). The special provision had to operate within that framework.
sections.labelHtml: Statutory authorization: Sec. 16 of the GAA's General Provisions prohibited changes in expenditure items except congressional action or augmentation from savings authorized under Art. VI, Sec. 25(5). The special provision had to operate within that framework.

question.html: W/N debt service is unconstitutional merely because its allocation exceeds the DECS allocation despite education's highest budgetary priority?
question.text: W/N debt service is unconstitutional merely because its allocation exceeds the DECS allocation despite education's highest budgetary priority?

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: NO. Petitioners invoked Art. XIV, Sec. 5(5) against the approximately P86.323-billion debt-service allocation, since DECS received only P37.78045 billion. The Court followed Guingona, Jr. v. Carague and described the educational-priority provision as directory. [5]
sections.labelHtml: NO. Petitioners invoked Art. XIV, Sec. 5(5) against the approximately P86.323-billion debt-service allocation, since DECS received only P37.78045 billion. The Court followed Guingona, Jr. v. Carague and described the educational-priority provision as directory. [5]

sections.label: Meaning of Guingona: the education mandate does not deprive Congress of its ability to respond to national-interest imperatives and other state objectives. In that earlier case, education had the highest allocation among department budgets; improvements to facilities and teacher compensation illustrated compliance.
sections.labelHtml: Meaning of Guingona: the education mandate does not deprive Congress of its ability to respond to national-interest imperatives and other state objectives. In that earlier case, education had the highest allocation among department budgets; improvements to facilities and teacher compensation illustrated compliance.

sections.label: Do not mix the figures: Guingona's quoted P29.740611-billion education allocation and observations on increased teacher compensation refer to that earlier budget, not to independently established 1994 figures.
sections.labelHtml: Do not mix the figures: Guingona's quoted P29.740611-billion education allocation and observations on increased teacher compensation refer to that earlier budget, not to independently established 1994 figures.

sections.label: Why debt service can be larger: Congress could reasonably provide for the enormous inherited debt to protect national honor and creditworthiness and, especially, the economy's survival. The education mandate does not impose an absolute numerical ceiling on debt-service payments.
sections.labelHtml: Why debt service can be larger: Congress could reasonably provide for the enormous inherited debt to protect national honor and creditworthiness and, especially, the economy's survival. The education mandate does not impose an absolute numerical ceiling on debt-service payments.

sections.label: Consequence: the larger debt-service allocation could not be annulled on that comparison alone. The decision does not announce that Congress may disregard education entirely.

question.html: W/N the President could veto the debt-service special provision while retaining the monetary appropriation?
question.text: W/N the President could veto the debt-service special provision while retaining the monetary appropriation?

sections.label: PETITIONERS' ARGUMENTS: An item veto cannot be used to delete a provision while retaining the entire appropriation. Conditions and restrictions belong to Congress's power of the purse; deleting them would rewrite Congress's enactment. [6]
sections.labelHtml: PETITIONERS' ARGUMENTS: An item veto cannot be used to delete a provision while retaining the entire appropriation. Conditions and restrictions belong to Congress's power of the purse; deleting them would rewrite Congress's enactment. [6]

sections.label: RESPONDENTS' ARGUMENT: The challenged restriction did not relate to the debt-service item in the required budgetary sense and could therefore be separately vetoed. The President maintained that changing automatic debt-payment policy required substantive legislation, not a GAA insertion. [6]
sections.labelHtml: RESPONDENTS' ARGUMENT: The challenged restriction did not relate to the debt-service item in the required budgetary sense and could therefore be separately vetoed. The President maintained that changing automatic debt-payment policy required substantive legislation, not a GAA insertion. [6]

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: A. General rule: item veto is not an unrestricted power to edit conditions.
sections.labelHtml: A. General rule: item veto is not an unrestricted power to edit conditions.

sections.label: Under the general veto, the President vetoes the entire bill. The item-veto exception permits rejection of a particular appropriation item, but the entire item must be vetoed. An appropriation item consists of a specified sum dedicated to a specified purpose or distinct fiscal unit.
sections.labelHtml: Under the general veto, the President vetoes the entire bill. The item-veto exception permits rejection of a particular appropriation item, but the entire item must be vetoed. An appropriation item consists of a specified sum dedicated to a specified purpose or distinct fiscal unit.

sections.label: Congress can attach conditions that genuinely control the use of the item. The President cannot retain the money but remove an inseparable, appropriate restriction merely because he prefers another policy.
sections.labelHtml: Congress can attach conditions that genuinely control the use of the item. The President cannot retain the money but remove an inseparable, appropriate restriction merely because he prefers another policy.

sections.label: B. The Gonzales qualification: inappropriate provisions may be separately vetoed.
sections.labelHtml: B. The Gonzales qualification: inappropriate provisions may be separately vetoed.

sections.label: Gonzales v. Macaraig had already rejected the claim that every provision is categorically outside item-veto authority. Art. VI, Sec. 25(2) itself restricts what may be placed in a GAB: a provision must relate specifically to a particular appropriation and operate only on it.

sections.label: The Court identifies as inappropriate provisions:
sections.labelHtml: The Court identifies as inappropriate provisions:

sections.label: Those not related to a particular appropriation item.
sections.labelHtml: Those not related to a particular appropriation item.

sections.label: Those extending in operation beyond the item.
sections.labelHtml: Those extending in operation beyond the item.

sections.label: Unconstitutional provisions.
sections.labelHtml: Unconstitutional provisions.

sections.label: Provisions intended to amend other laws—matters of general legislation requiring separate enactments.
sections.labelHtml: Provisions intended to amend other laws—matters of general legislation requiring separate enactments.

sections.label: Constitutional history: the item veto entered Philippine law through the 1916 Organic Act. The 1935 Constitution expressly linked a veto of a provision affecting an item with veto of the affected item. Although the 1987 Constitution omitted that sentence, Gonzales did not read the omission as eliminating all vetoes of provisions; it applied the specific-relatedness and limited-operation requirements now found in Sec. 25(2).

Although the 1987 Constitution omitted that sentence, Gonzales did not read the omission as eliminating all vetoes of provisions; it applied the specific-relatedness and limited-operation requirements now found in Sec. 25(2).

sections.label: Why the qualification exists: otherwise Congress could insert general legislation or riders in an indispensable appropriation, forcing the President to accept objectionable substantive law or veto essential spending. The Court adopted Henry v. Edwards's protection of both branches: neither executive item-veto power nor legislative appropriation power may be used to defeat the other's constitutional role.

sections.label: Presumption of validity: a veto is part of the legislative process, although exercised by the President. Its placement in Article VI reflects that character. The Court therefore presumes its constitutionality, with the challenger bearing the burden to establish invalidity. This presumption did not save the vetoes of appropriate provisions below.

sections.label: C. Apply separately to the three components of the debt provision.
sections.labelHtml: C. Apply separately to the three components of the debt provision.

sections.label: Excess-payment concurrence requirement → veto VALID. Congress required presidential approval with congressional concurrence for debt payments beyond the amount appropriated in the GAA. This operated on funds outside the particular item, making it inappropriate under Sec. 25(2).
sections.labelHtml: Excess-payment concurrence requirement → veto VALID. Congress required presidential approval with congressional concurrence for debt payments beyond the amount appropriated in the GAA. This operated on funds outside the particular item, making it inappropriate under Sec. 25(2).

sections.label: It also attempted to alter the automatic-appropriation regime under P.D. No. 1177 and E.O. No. 292 and reverse existing debt-payment policy. The Foreign Borrowing Act was also invoked in the Veto Message. Such a change had to be made by separate substantive legislation.

sections.label: The surviving annual appropriation therefore did not become a ceiling overriding the other existing automatic-appropriation laws.
sections.labelHtml: The surviving annual appropriation therefore did not become a ceiling overriding the other existing automatic-appropriation laws.

sections.label: Use for principal and interest of foreign/domestic debt → veto VOID. This tells the Executive how the appropriated money is to be used. It is germane to the very debt-service item.
sections.labelHtml: Use for principal and interest of foreign/domestic debt → veto VOID. This tells the Executive how the appropriated money is to be used. It is germane to the very debt-service item.

sections.label: No payment of Central Bank Board of Liquidators liabilities from this fund → veto VOID. This likewise restricts the use of the particular appropriation. It is an appropriate condition; retaining the item while deleting this limitation exceeds the item-veto power.
sections.labelHtml: No payment of Central Bank Board of Liquidators liabilities from this fund → veto VOID. This likewise restricts the use of the particular appropriation. It is an appropriate condition; retaining the item while deleting this limitation exceeds the item-veto power.

sections.label: Court's express distinction: “These provisos are germane to and have a direct connection with the item on debt service.” It immediately explains: “Inherent in the power of appropriation is the power to specify how the money shall be spent”. [6, PDF p. 15; second sentence quotes the Court's formulation citing Henry]

sections.label: Petitioners alternatively argued that even a valid veto did not allow the President to disregard conditions under R.A. No. 4860, as amended by P.D. No. 81, P.D. No. 1177, the Administrative Code, and P.D. No. 1967. [6, PDF p. 15]

question.html: W/N the veto of SUC use-of-income and revolving-fund provisions was invalid or unduly discriminatory?
question.text: W/N the veto of SUC use-of-income and revolving-fund provisions was invalid or unduly discriminatory?

sections.label: PROVISIONS AND ARGUMENTS: West Visayas State University's income would be shared equally with its hospital. Leyte State College's LSC House/HRDC income would form a revolving fund for those services, with year-end net income remitted to the Treasury. General SUC provisions allowed extension-service income for faculty development, instructional materials and work-study programs, and special-account treatment/use of tuition and other income, subject to stated controls. Petitioners contrasted the veto with permission granted to agencies such as the National Stud Farm. [7]
sections.labelHtml: PROVISIONS AND ARGUMENTS: West Visayas State University's income would be shared equally with its hospital. Leyte State College's LSC House/HRDC income would form a revolving fund for those services, with year-end net income remitted to the Treasury. General SUC provisions allowed extension-service income for faculty development, instructional materials and work-study programs, and special-account treatment/use of tuition and other income, subject to stated controls. Petitioners contrasted the veto with permission granted to agencies such as the National Stud Farm. [7]

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: Veto upheld; no undue discrimination. The relevant distinction was pre-existing authority under special substantive laws, not simple similarity in the agencies' desire to retain income.
sections.labelHtml: Veto upheld; no undue discrimination. The relevant distinction was pre-existing authority under special substantive laws, not simple similarity in the agencies' desire to retain income.

sections.label: President's stated budget rationale: under the one-fund policy, government income accrues to the General Fund; creation of revolving funds requires substantive legal authority. The revenues had already been counted in financing the National Expenditure Program. Fresh authorizations to spend that income on top of appropriations would both reduce available financing and increase agency expenditures, enlarging the deficit.
sections.labelHtml: President's stated budget rationale: under the one-fund policy, government income accrues to the General Fund; creation of revolving funds requires substantive legal authority. The revenues had already been counted in financing the National Expenditure Program. Fresh authorizations to spend that income on top of appropriations would both reduce available financing and increase agency expenditures, enlarging the deficit.

sections.label: Court's answer to unequal-treatment argument: agencies permitted to continue using income already enjoyed statutory exceptions: R.A. No. 4618 for the National Stud Farm, P.D. No. 902-A for the SEC, and E.O. No. 359 for DBM's Procurement Service. They were not situated like agencies receiving new privileges through these GAA provisions.

sections.label: The decision therefore rejected the claim that allowing established revolving funds necessarily made these vetoes arbitrary. The President's fiscal explanation and the Court's legal distinction should not be confused with a finding that all revolving funds are prohibited.

question.html: W/N the President validly vetoed the maximum 30% contracting-out limit for national-road and bridge maintenance?
question.text: W/N the President validly vetoed the maximum 30% contracting-out limit for national-road and bridge maintenance?

sections.label: PETITIONERS' POSITION: This was a condition on how the very road-maintenance appropriation was to be spent. EXECUTIVE POSITION: infrastructure studies favored 70% contracting and 30% force account; maximizing contract maintenance was also a covenant of ADB, OECF and World Bank loans. The Solicitor General relied on the established government policy favoring contracting. [8]
sections.labelHtml: PETITIONERS' POSITION: This was a condition on how the very road-maintenance appropriation was to be spent. EXECUTIVE POSITION: infrastructure studies favored 70% contracting and 30% force account; maximizing contract maintenance was also a covenant of ADB, OECF and World Bank loans. The Solicitor General relied on the established government policy favoring contracting. [8]

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: NO. The second paragraph of DPWH Special Provision No. 2 was appropriate. It capped contracted maintenance at 30%; the balance would be performed by force account (administrative execution). It directly determined the mode of expenditure of the particular maintenance fund.
sections.labelHtml: NO. The second paragraph of DPWH Special Provision No. 2 was appropriate. It capped contracted maintenance at 30%; the balance would be performed by force account (administrative execution). It directly determined the mode of expenditure of the particular maintenance fund.

sections.label: The policy disagreement did not transform it into a rider. Congress preferred at least 70% administrative maintenance; the President believed 70% contracting would be more efficient, practical and economical. A different executive preference—even one supported by a study and references to loan covenants—did not permit deletion of this appropriate condition alone.
sections.labelHtml: The policy disagreement did not transform it into a rider. Congress preferred at least 70% administrative maintenance; the President believed 70% contracting would be more efficient, practical and economical. A different executive preference—even one supported by a study and references to loan covenants—did not permit deletion of this appropriate condition alone.

sections.label: The Solicitor General's argument that Congress reversed an entrenched practice was therefore insufficient. The power of appropriation includes specifying how the fund is spent.
sections.labelHtml: The Solicitor General's argument that Congress reversed an entrenched practice was therefore insufficient. The power of appropriation includes specifying how the fund is spent.

sections.label: Result: veto unconstitutional. The paragraph remained operative. This was not an adjudication that contracting out is inherently bad, or that 70% contracting is always unlawful; it enforced the choice embodied in this appropriation.
sections.labelHtml: Result: veto unconstitutional. The paragraph remained operative. This was not an adjudication that contracting out is inherently bad, or that 70% contracting is always unlawful; it enforced the choice embodied in this appropriation.

question.html: W/N the President could separately veto the AFP requirement to follow the National Drug Policy formulary?
question.text: W/N the President could separately veto the AFP requirement to follow the National Drug Policy formulary?

sections.label: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI
sections.labelHtml: RULING and RATIO DECIDENDI

sections.label: AFP Special Provision No. 12 required all AFP units, hospitals and clinics purchasing medicines to comply strictly with the formulary in DOH's National Drug Policy. The President preferred a transition period for smooth adoption, invoking the educational approach reflected in the Generics Act. [9]
sections.labelHtml: AFP Special Provision No. 12 required all AFP units, hospitals and clinics purchasing medicines to comply strictly with the formulary in DOH's National Drug Policy. paras.html: Supervision, not control: The Constitution vests the President with the power of general supervision, not control, over LGUs (Sec. 4, Art. X). Supervising officials merely see to it that the rules are followed; they do not lay down, modify, or replace the rules (Drilon v. Lim). The President may issue advisories and seek LGUs' cooperation, but "may not withhold or alter any authority or power given them by the Constitution and the law."
paras.text: Supervision, not control: The Constitution vests the President with the power of general supervision, not control, over LGUs (Sec. 4, Art. X). Supervising officials merely see to it that the rules are followed; they do not lay down, modify, or replace the rules (Drilon v. Lim). The President may issue advisories and seek LGUs' cooperation, but "may not withhold or alter any authority or power given them by the Constitution and the law."

paras.html: Automatic release of IRA: LGUs' share in national taxes "shall be automatically released" (Sec. 6, Art. X) and "shall not be subject to any lien or holdback . . . for whatever purpose" (Sec. 286, LGC). Even a temporary withholding is a prohibited holdback. The President may adjust the IRA only under Sec. 284, LGC: an unmanaged public sector deficit, consultation with the presiding officers of Congress and the presidents of the leagues, the recommendation of the Secretaries of Finance, DILG, and DBM, and never below 30% of national internal revenue collections of the third preceding fiscal year.

paras.html: Sec. 4, Art. X: "The President of the Philippines shall exercise general supervision over local governments." This has been interpreted to exclude the power of control.
paras.text: Sec. 4, Art. X: "The President of the Philippines shall exercise general supervision over local governments." This has been interpreted to exclude the power of control.

paras.html: Mondano v. Silvosa: supervision is "overseeing or the power or authority of an officer to see that subordinate officers perform their duties"; if they fail, the superior may take such action as prescribed by law to make them perform. Control is the power "to alter or modify or nullify or set aside" what a subordinate has done and substitute one's judgment.
paras.text: Mondano v. Silvosa: supervision is "overseeing or the power or authority of an officer to see that subordinate officers perform their duties"; if they fail, the superior may take such action as prescribed by law to make them perform. Control is the power "to alter or modify or nullify or set aside" what a subordinate has done and substitute one's judgment.

paras.html: Taule v. Santos: the Chief Executive may only check whether local governments perform their duties under the law; he cannot interfere so long as they act within their authority. Supervision is "the power of mere oversight over an inferior body; it does not include any restraining authority."
paras.text: Taule v. Santos: the Chief Executive may only check whether local governments perform their duties under the law; he cannot interfere so long as they act within their authority. Supervision is "the power of mere oversight over an inferior body; it does not include any restraining authority."

paras.html: Drilon v. Lim: officers in control lay down the rules and may order acts undone or redone, or do them themselves. Supervising officers merely see to it that the rules are followed; they do not lay down, modify, or replace the rules, and may order work redone only to conform to the rules.
paras.text: Drilon v. Lim: officers in control lay down the rules and may order acts undone or redone, or do them themselves. Supervising officers merely see to it that the rules are followed; they do not lay down, modify, or replace the rules, and may order work redone only to conform to the rules.

paras.html: Cabinet members and other executive officials are alter egos under the President's control. Heads of political subdivisions are elected by the people, directly accountable to them, and subject only to supervision so long as they act within their legitimate powers. "By the same token, the President may not withhold or alter any authority or power given them by the Constitution and the law."

paras.html: Re: Extent of local autonomy
paras.text: Re: Extent of local autonomy

paras.html: State policy ensures local autonomy (Sec. 25, Art. II; Sec. 2, Art. X). Ganzon v. CA: autonomy means a more responsive and accountable local government through decentralization; it breaks up the national monopoly over local affairs but does not end the partnership and interdependence with the central government.
paras.text: State policy ensures local autonomy (Sec. 25, Art. II; Sec. 2, Art. X). Ganzon v. CA: autonomy means a more responsive and accountable local government through decentralization; it breaks up the national monopoly over local affairs but does not end the partnership and interdependence with the central government.

paras.html: Limbona v. Mangelin: decentralization of administration (delegating administrative powers, with the President exercising general supervision only to ensure local affairs are administered according to law) vs. decentralization of power (abdication of political power to autonomous units accountable only to their constituents). The Philippine concept is decentralization of administration, not power; policy-setting for the whole country remains with the President and Congress. LGUs are still agents of the national government (Magtajas v. Pryce Properties).

paras.html: Re: Fiscal autonomy and the nature of AO 372
paras.text: Re: Fiscal autonomy and the nature of AO 372

paras.html: AO 372 is a "cash management measure" to match expenditures with resources depleted by the peso depreciation.
paras.text: AO 372 is a "cash management measure" to match expenditures with resources depleted by the peso depreciation.

paras.html: LGUs enjoy fiscal autonomy: the power to create their own sources of revenue in addition to their equitable share in national taxes, and to allocate their resources according to their own priorities, including the preparation of their own budgets, which are not formulated at the national level and imposed on them (citing San Juan v. CSC).

CSC).

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy does not rule out national intervention by way of supervision to keep local programs consistent with national goals. The President heads the economic and planning agency (Sec. 9, Art. XII), but policies are subject to "consultations with . . . local government units"; he cannot act unilaterally.

paras.html: Sec. 284, LGC requisites before the President may interfere in local fiscal matters: (1) an unmanaged public sector deficit of the national government; (2) consultations with the presiding officers of the Senate and the House and the presidents of the leagues; (3) the recommendation of the Secretaries of Finance, DILG, and DBM; and any adjustment may in no case go below 30% of national internal revenue collections of the third preceding fiscal year.

paras.html: A basic feature of local fiscal autonomy is the automatic release of LGUs' shares in national revenue, mandated by Sec. 6, Art. X ("just share . . . which shall be automatically released to them").
paras.text: A basic feature of local fiscal autonomy is the automatic release of LGUs' shares in national revenue, mandated by Sec. 6, Art. X ("just share . . . which shall be automatically released to them").

paras.html: Sec. 286(a), LGC: the share shall be released "without need of any further action, directly to the . . . treasurer . . . within five (5) days after the end of each quarter, and which shall not be subject to any lien or holdback that may be imposed by the national government for whatever purpose." "Shall" is a word of command → the provision is imperative.

paras.html: Sec. 4 withholds 10% of the IRA pending the DBCC's assessment. "Although temporary, it is equivalent to a holdback," which means "something held back or withheld, often temporarily." "Hence, the 'temporary' nature of the retention by the national government does not matter. Any retention is prohibited."

paras.html: Sec. 4 "effectively encroaches on the fiscal autonomy of local governments." The President was well-intentioned, but "the rule of law requires that even the best intentions must be carried out within the parameters of the Constitution and the law. Verily, laudable purposes must be carried out by legal methods."

paras.html: The President as chief fiscal officer
paras.text: The President as chief fiscal officer

paras.html: The President is ultimately responsible for collecting and distributing public money: through the DBM, he prepares and executes the budget; he may fix tariffs within statutory limits, create appropriation reserves, suspend expenditure appropriations, and institute cost-reduction schemes. He supervises fiscal development in LGUs and may set aside tax ordinances contrary to the LGC (Drilon v. Lim). Local plans and budgets must hew to national policies.

paras.html: Under Sec. 284, LGC, in an unmanageable deficit, the President may reduce the IRA from 40% to not less than 30%. By necessary implication, the power to adjust includes the lesser power to withhold temporarily until the fiscal situation is determined ("the exercise of a more absolute power necessarily includes the lesser power"); otherwise the money would be gone before a crisis is confirmed.

paras.html: The "no lien or holdback" phrase is not in the Constitution, which requires only a just share "as determined by law." The LGC IRR (Art. 384) and other laws allow deductions (GSIS premiums, foreign-assisted loans, devolution costs, debt relief under Sec. 531). Sec. 286 does not fix the amount; it requires release of what LGUs are legally entitled to, which may be 30% after adjustment.

paras.html: Acting appointments while Congress is in session: The President may appoint department secretaries in an acting capacity without CA consent even while Congress is in session. An acting appointment is a temporary, stop-gap measure; since a secretary is the President's alter ego, the acting appointee must be a person of her choice and confidence. Sec. 17, Chapter 5, Title I, Book III of the Administrative Code allows her to designate any "competent person," for no more than one year.
paras.text: Acting appointments while Congress is in session: The President may appoint department secretaries in an acting capacity without CA consent even while Congress is in session. An acting appointment is a temporary, stop-gap measure; since a secretary is the President's alter ego, the acting appointee must be a person of her choice and confidence. Sec. 17, Chapter 5, Title I, Book III of the Administrative Code allows her to designate any "competent person," for no more than one year.

paras.html: Limits on Congress: The appointing power is essentially executive; the legislature may interfere only where the Constitution expressly allows, and its role is limited to prescribing qualifications. Congress cannot impose on the President who her alter ego should be (e.g., the undersecretary automatically).
paras.text: Limits on Congress: The appointing power is essentially executive; the legislature may interfere only where the Constitution expressly allows, and its role is limited to prescribing qualifications. Congress cannot impose on the President who her alter ego should be (e.g., the undersecretary automatically).

paras.html: Acting vs. ad interim: Ad interim appointments are made only during a recess and are submitted to the CA; acting appointments may be made whenever there is a vacancy and are not submitted. The one-year limit guards against using acting appointments to circumvent confirmation.

paras.text: Re: Nature of the CA (relevant to standing)

paras.html: Though composed of members of Congress, the CA exercises executive, not legislative, power: it does not legislate when it gives or withholds consent. Cunanan v. Tan, Jr.: the CA is a creature of the Constitution, independent of Congress; its powers emanate directly from the Constitution; it is not an agent of Congress; its functions are "purely executive in nature" (but see J. Concepcion's concurring opinion in Guevara v. Inocentes, fn. 9).

paras.html: The power to appoint is essentially executive; the legislature may not interfere except where the Constitution expressly allows. Limitations on it are construed strictly against the legislature (Sarmiento III v. Mison).

paras.html: The legislature's interference is limited to prescribing qualifications to an appointive office. Congress cannot appoint a person in the guise of prescribing qualifications, nor impose on the President the duty to appoint any particular person (Manalang v. Quitoriano; Flores v. Drilon).

paras.text: Re: Acting appointments and the alter ego

paras.html: "The essence of an appointment in an acting capacity is its temporary nature": a stop-gap measure to fill an office until a permanent occupant is appointed (Marohombsar v. Alonto).

paras.html: When the office of an alter ego such as a department secretary falls vacant, the President must necessarily appoint an alter ego of her choice as acting secretary before her permanent appointee can assume.

paras.html: "Congress, through a law, cannot impose on the President the obligation to appoint automatically the undersecretary as her temporary alter ego." An alter ego, temporary or permanent, holds a position of great trust and confidence; Congress, in the guise of prescribing qualifications, cannot impose who it should be.

paras.html: Sec. 17, Chapter 5, Title I, Book III, EO 292: the President may temporarily designate an officer already in government service "or any other competent person" to perform the functions of an executive office when the regular officer cannot perform his duties or there is a vacancy; compensation rules apply; and "[i]n no case shall a temporary designation exceed one (1) year."

paras.html: Ratification is executive: "under our Constitution, the power to ratify is vested in the President, subject to the concurrence of the Senate. The role of the Senate, however, is limited only to giving or withholding its consent, or concurrence, to the ratification." Signing and ratification are "two separate and distinct steps": signature authenticates the instrument and shows good faith; ratification is the formal act by which the state accepts the treaty.
paras.text: Ratification is executive: "under our Constitution, the power to ratify is vested in the President, subject to the concurrence of the Senate. The role of the Senate, however, is limited only to giving or withholding its consent, or concurrence, to the ratification." Signing and ratification are "two separate and distinct steps": signature authenticates the instrument and shows good faith; ratification is the formal act by which the state accepts the treaty.

paras.html: No duty to ratify or transmit: the President has discretion, even after signing by a Philippine representative, whether or not to ratify; a state has no legal or even moral duty to ratify a treaty signed by its plenipotentiaries (though refusal should rest on substantial grounds). It is "within the authority of the President to refuse to submit a treaty to the Senate or, having secured its consent for its ratification, refuse to ratify it"; the Court cannot compel this by mandamus.

paras.html: The Rome Statute established the International Criminal Court (ICC), with jurisdiction over persons for "the most serious crimes of international concern": genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and aggression; it is "complementary to the national criminal jurisdictions." It was opened for signature in Rome on July 17, 1998 and remained open until Dec. 31, 2000 at UN Headquarters.

It was opened for signature in Rome on July 17, 1998 and remained open until Dec. 31, 2000 at UN Headquarters.

paras.html: Dec. 28, 2000: the Philippines signed the Statute through Chargé d'Affaires Enrique A. Manalo of the Philippine Mission to the UN. The Statute requires that signature be subject to ratification, acceptance, or approval by signatory states [fn. 4 cites Article 25 of the Rome Statute for this; the signature and ratification clause is Article 125].

paras.html: Rule: mandamus lies when a respondent unlawfully neglects an act the law specifically enjoins as a duty (Rule 65, Sec. 3). The petitioner must be an aggrieved party with "a clear legal right to be enforced and a direct interest in the duty or act to be performed" (Legaspi v. CSC). Standing requires a personal and substantial interest and direct injury; "interest" means material interest, not mere interest in the question or an incidental interest (Joya v. PCGG; Gonzales v. Narvasa).
