paras.html: Re: The President in foreign relations; the Senate's check
paras.text: Re: The President in foreign relations; the Senate's check

paras.html: The President, as head of state, is "the sole organ and authority in external relations" and the country's sole representative with foreign nations: the chief architect of foreign policy, with authority to deal with foreign states, extend or withhold recognition, maintain diplomatic relations, and enter into treaties. "In the realm of treaty-making, the President has the sole authority to negotiate with other states."
paras.text: The President, as head of state, is "the sole organ and authority in external relations" and the country's sole representative with foreign nations: the chief architect of foreign policy, with authority to deal with foreign states, extend or withhold recognition, maintain diplomatic relations, and enter into treaties. "In the realm of treaty-making, the President has the sole authority to negotiate with other states."

paras.html: Limit: Sec. 21, Art. VII: "no treaty or international agreement shall be valid and effective unless concurred in by at least two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate." Earlier charters also required legislative concurrence: 1935 (Art. VII, Sec. 10(7): two-thirds of the Senate) and 1973 (Art. VIII, Sec. 14(1): a majority of the Batasang Pambansa). Legislative participation is a check on the Executive in foreign relations (BAYAN v. Zamora).

paras.html: Re: 2.1 – Ratification belongs to the President, not the Senate
paras.text: Re: 2.1 – Ratification belongs to the President, not the Senate

paras.html: Treaty-making steps (Cruz, International Law): negotiation, signature, ratification, and exchange of instruments of ratification (then optional registration and publication under the UN Charter). Negotiators carry full powers. Signature is "primarily intended as a means of authenticating the instrument and for the purpose of symbolizing the good faith of the parties", and does not indicate final consent where ratification is required. Ratification is "the formal act by which a state confirms and accepts the provisions of a treaty"; it lets states examine the treaty and refuse to be bound if inimical.

paras.html: Petitioners equate signing with ratification, but they are "two separate and distinct steps." Ratification is "generally held to be an executive act, undertaken by the head of the state or of the government" (BAYAN v. Zamora).

paras.html: "The signature does not signify the final consent of the state to the treaty. It is the ratification that binds the state." The Rome Statute itself makes signature subject to ratification.

paras.html: After signing, the President, "being accountable to the people", must study the treaty to ensure it is not inimical to the State → the President has the discretion even after signing whether or not to ratify. The Vienna Convention does not restrain this power; otherwise ratification "would be pointless and futile." A state has "no legal or even moral duty to ratify" a treaty signed by its plenipotentiaries (Salonga & Yap), though refusal must rest on substantial, not superficial or whimsical, grounds, or the other state may take offense.

paras.html: "The power to ratify is vested in the President, subject to the concurrence of the Senate. The role of the Senate ... is limited only to giving or withholding its consent, or concurrence, to the ratification." Hence the President may refuse to submit a treaty to the Senate or, having secured its consent, refuse to ratify it.

The role of the Senate ... is limited only to giving or withholding its consent, or concurrence, to the ratification." Hence the President may refuse to submit a treaty to the Senate or, having secured its consent, refuse to ratify it.

paras.html: Refusing to ratify a signed treaty "is a serious step that should not be taken lightly," but it is "within the competence of the President alone, which cannot be encroached by this Court via a writ of mandamus." The Court "has no jurisdiction over actions seeking to enjoin the President in the performance of his official duties" (Severino v. Governor-General) → it cannot compel the Executive to transmit the signed text to the Senate.

paras.html: Session vs. term: Sec. 15, Art. VI "does not pertain to the term of Congress, but to its regular annual legislative sessions and the mandatory 30-days recess". The adjournment sine die of the last regular session on June 11, 2004 did not end the Twelfth Congress, whose members' terms run until noon of June 30 (Art. VI, Secs. 4 and 7).

paras.html: Non-legislative function continues: the legislative functions may close upon final adjournment, "but this does not affect its non-legislative functions, such as that of being the National Board of Canvassers." The joint public session under Sec. 4, Art. VII "has not, and cannot, adjourn sine die until it has accomplished its constitutionally mandated tasks"; a board of canvassers becomes functus officio only when its functions are complete.

paras.html: Sen. Aquilino Pimentel, Jr. filed a petition for prohibition to declare null and void the Joint Committee's continued existence after the adjournment, and to direct it to cease and desist from further proceedings.

paras.html: Petitioner's position: with the adjournment sine die, the Twelfth Congress's term "terminated and expired ... and [it] passed out of legal existence"; henceforth, "all pending matters and proceedings terminate upon the expiration of ... Congress." He relied on "legislative procedure, precedent or practice [as] borne [out] by the rules of both Houses of Congress" and on Sec. 15, Art. VI, arguing the Joint Committee's existence and proceedings became "invalid, illegal and unconstitutional".

paras.text: Re: The rules and precedents contradict petitioner

paras.html: Sec. 42, Rule XIV of the Senate Rules, adopted by the Senate of which petitioner is an incumbent member, provides that the Senate "shall convene in joint session during any voluntary or compulsory recess to canvass the votes for President and Vice President" not later than thirty days after the elections, in accordance with Sec. 4, Art. VII. This "directly contradict[s]" petitioner's claim of legislative procedure, precedent, or practice.

VII. This "directly contradict[s]" petitioner's claim of legislative procedure, precedent, or practice.

paras.html: 1992 and 1998 precedents (cited by the Senate Panel and the OSG, with Salonga's observations): in 1992, both Houses adjourned sine die on May 25, 1992; the Joint Committee finished tallying on June 16; the Eighth Congress convened as National Board of Canvassers and proclaimed Ramos and Estrada on June 22, 1992. In 1998, both Houses adjourned sine die on May 25, 1998; the Joint Committee completed counting on May 27; the Tenth Congress convened on May 29, 1998 and proclaimed Estrada and Arroyo [the Resolution says "Joseph Ejercito Estrada as President and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo as President and Vice-President"].

paras.html: Sec. 15, Art. VI (Congress convenes on the fourth Monday of July and stays in session until thirty days before the next regular session; the President may call a special session) "does not pertain to the term of Congress, but to its regular annual legislative sessions and the mandatory 30-days recess."

paras.html: Terms of office: Senators serve six years from noon of June 30 next following their election, and Representatives three years from noon of June 30 [the Resolution cites "Section 4 of Article VIII" and "Section 7 of the same Article"; the provisions are Art. VI, Secs. 4 and 7]. There being no law to the contrary, until June 30, 2004, the Twelfth Congress "cannot be said to have 'passed out of legal existence.'"

paras.html: The joint public session convened by express directive of Sec. 4, Art. VII "has not, and cannot, adjourn sine die until it has accomplished its constitutionally mandated tasks." A board of canvassers is rendered functus officio only when it has completed its functions; "Its membership may change, but it retains its authority as a board until it has accomplished its purposes" (Pelayo v. COMELEC, citing Bautista v. Fugoso and Aquino v. COMELEC).

paras.html: The Court's rule-making power covers the practice of law, not the study of law: The Court has no primary and direct jurisdiction over legal education; its supervision and regulation is an Executive function. "The definition of the practice of law, no matter how broad, cannot be further enlarged as to cover the study of law."

paras.html: A law on legal education is void insofar as it reaches into the Court's exclusive domain: provisions that, by their plain language, go beyond legal education into the training of lawyers, the requirements for taking the Bar, the Integrated Bar, or legal assistance to the underprivileged encroach upon Sec. 5(5), Art. VIII (Secs. 3[a][2], 7[g], 7[h], and the "continuing legal education" clause of Sec. 2, par. 2 of RA 7662).

paras.html: Background on RA 7662 and the LEB:
paras.text: Background on RA 7662 and the LEB:

paras.html: Prompted by the poor performance of law students and law schools in the bar examinations, Congress passed RA 7662 (Legal Education Reform Act of 1993) on December 23, 1993. Sec. 2 declares the policy to uplift the standards of legal education and, towards this end, to "undertake appropriate reforms in the legal education system, require proper selection of law students, maintain quality among law schools, and require legal apprenticeship and continuing legal education."
paras.text: Prompted by the poor performance of law students and law schools in the bar examinations, Congress passed RA 7662 (Legal Education Reform Act of 1993) on December 23, 1993. Sec. 2 declares the policy to uplift the standards of legal education and, towards this end, to "undertake appropriate reforms in the legal education system, require proper selection of law students, maintain quality among law schools, and require legal apprenticeship and continuing legal education."

paras.html: RA 7662 created the LEB, an executive agency separate from the DECS but attached to it solely for budgetary purposes and administrative support. Its Chair and members are appointed by the President for five years without reappointment, from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the JBC with prior authorization from the Court.

paras.html: Under Sec. 1, Art. VIII, judicial power includes the duty to determine whether there has been grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government. Because of the common ground of "grave abuse of discretion," a Rule 65 petition has been allowed as the procedural vehicle for the expanded jurisdiction. Grave abuse exists when an act is done contrary to the Constitution, the law, or jurisprudence.

paras.html: Ripeness has two aspects: (1) fitness of the issues for decision (purely legal; "final agency action"); and (2) hardship to the parties if review is withheld (effects felt in a concrete way). A question is ripe when the challenged act has a direct and existing adverse effect on the challenger.

The word did not change the texture of police power; it only emphasized that supervision cannot amount to control.

paras.html: (a) "Law admission" means admission to legal education, not to the practice of law. Read in context with the policy to uplift legal education and the LEB's powers to administer, supervise, and accredit law schools, Sec. 7(e) is limited to those seeking enrollment in a law school.

paras.html: (b) Sec. 7(e) is reasonable supervision and regulation. It authorizes only minimum standards, not control; it did not impose an exclusionary and qualifying exam nor prevent schools from imposing their own requirements. paras.html: (c) The LEB may administer an aptitude test. Senate deliberations (Sen. Tolentino on unfit students; Sen. Shahani: an aptitude exam "will have to be specially designed"; Sen. Angara: the board "may very well decide to prescribe such a test, although it is not mandatory") show legislative intent. The Court itself supported an aptitude exam when it approved the CLEBM's proposed amendment ("including a system of law aptitude examination") and in B.M. No. 1161, where it referred a proposed law entrance exam to the LEB. The presumption that the legislature intended a valid law "has not been successfully challenged."

paras.html: (d) The PhiLSAT is reasonably related to improving legal education. Test: concurrence of lawful subject and lawful means (Lupangco: rules must be reasonable and fairly adapted to the end). Petitioners' grounds (not conclusive of aptitude; exam and travel costs; burdensome exemption process; redundant to school exams; no scientific study) are conclusions of fact that beg evidence and go into the wisdom of the PhiLSAT, "an excursion into the policy behind the examinations — a function which is administrative rather than judicial." The subject (improving legal education) is within police power; the PhiLSAT as an aptitude test is the means.

paras.html: Pars. 7, 9, 11, and 15 of LEBMO No. 7-2016 exclude and disqualify those who fail to reach the passing score from being admitted to any law school. By mandating a 55% cut-off, the PhiLSAT "usurps the right and duty of the law school to determine for itself the criteria for the admission of students" and to apply them case by case; it forces absolute rejection of applicants below the cut-off or with expired eligibility.

paras.html: Academic freedom comes into play "only after the applicants had been 'pre-selected' without the school's participation"; schools may only add requirements, making their preference "merely secondary or supplemental to that of the State", which is antithetical to reasonable supervision. Schools must surrender their discretion to a State-determined pool under pain of sanctions and fines → "transfers complete control over admission policies from the law schools to the LEB." Garcia: schools are not "public utilities devoid of any discretion as to whom to admit or reject."

paras.html: Balancing and calibrated approach: the PhiLSAT as an aptitude test is reasonably related to the State's "unimpeachable interest" in improving legal education, but it should not be exclusionary; schools decide how much weight to give its results, provided their discretion is not gravely abused, arbitrary, whimsical, or discriminatory. The Court does not strike down the PhiLSAT entirely; it partially nullifies LEBMO No. 7-2016 insofar as it absolutely prescribes passing the PhiLSAT, and taking it within two years, as a prerequisite for admission to any law school. The rest remains effective under the separability clause.

paras.html: RA 7662 in general does not encroach on the Court's rule-making power; legal education is within the State's police power. "[I]n judicial humility," the Court affirms that supervision of legal education is a political exercise where judges may participate "not as an independent branch of government, but as part of the sovereign people." The PhiLSAT, when used to exclude, qualify, and restrict admissions, is unconstitutional; when administered as a guide for law schools, it is a valid minimum standard. The Court urges consultative summits to improve legal education and screening tools.

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to GRANT the petitions and declare the entire RA 7662 unconstitutional. Agrees the PhiLSAT's passing score violates academic freedom, but holds that any State-sponsored admission test, mandatory or not, and the whole concept of the LEB violate academic freedom; would overturn Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego.

Agrees the PhiLSAT's passing score violates academic freedom, but holds that any State-sponsored admission test, mandatory or not, and the whole concept of the LEB violate academic freedom; would overturn Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego.

paras.html: I. Agreement with the majority: Academic freedom (Garcia; Tangonan v. Paño; Ateneo v. Capulong; Miriam College; Cudia) includes the institution's right to determine who to admit. Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego involved students asserting a right to their chosen course; institutional academic freedom was not raised there. Agrees the PhiLSAT, unlike the NMAT (percentile ranks evaluated against each school's own cut-off), employs a "totalitarian scheme."
paras.text: I. Agreement with the majority: Academic freedom (Garcia; Tangonan v. Paño; Ateneo v. Capulong; Miriam College; Cudia) includes the institution's right to determine who to admit. Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego involved students asserting a right to their chosen course; institutional academic freedom was not raised there. Agrees the PhiLSAT, unlike the NMAT (percentile ranks evaluated against each school's own cut-off), employs a "totalitarian scheme."

paras.html: II. Even a non-mandatory national test infringes academic freedom: academic freedom is a cognate of free expression, so State intrusion must be treated as suspect. Admission policy and the quality of instruction are different standards ("non-sequitur"). The LEB did no specific study; admission tests measure only correlation with first-year grades. Government appointees may lack academic credentials and are prone to influence. The US LSAT is run by a private nonprofit of law schools and is voluntary.

Admission policy and the quality of instruction are different standards ("non-sequitur"). The LEB did no specific study; admission tests measure only correlation with first-year grades. Government appointees may lack academic credentials and are prone to influence. The US LSAT is run by a private nonprofit of law schools and is voluntary.

paras.html: III. Due process: the PhiLSAT is arbitrary because it was not based on scientific research. At oral arguments, LEB Chair Aquende admitted "We have none" (no Philippine study), relying on the US LSAT study; he had taught in only two of 122 law schools. A single written exam as the sole criterion is unreasonable (contrast the holistic review in Grutter v. Bollinger). It infringes life and liberty (right to pursue education) and property (testing fees, travel, opportunity cost).

paras.html: IV. Meritocracy: standardized tests favor the economically privileged; costs make even a non-exclusionary exam exclusionary; ranked results stigmatize low scorers; a national test hides the defects of weak schools ("we incentivize sloth among law schools"). Cites J. Thomas' dissent in Grutter.

paras.html: V. On the majority's ruling: the school's right to determine who to admit is "absolute"; removing the PhiLSAT's mandatory character but retaining it still perpetuates stigma and State control. Teaching law as an academic degree (Sec. 5[2], Art. XIV; Sec. 4, Art. III) differs from licensing (Sec. 5[3], Art. XIV; Sec. 5[5], Art. VIII); a statutory board of political appointees supervising postgraduate legal education is what Sec. 5(2) proscribes.

paras.html: Concurs: the LEB orders and circular making the PhiLSAT mandatory and exclusionary are unconstitutional: (1) the LEB pre-selects the pool; (2) no justification for the 55% score or format (studies were foreign, for other professions); (3) schools face sanctions (closure, phase-out, ₱10,000 fines). PhiLSAT differs from the NMAT (percentile scores, no pass/fail) and the LSAT (run by the LSAC of law schools; not an absolute requirement). Concurs that Sec. 7(h) is unconstitutional and that Sec. 7(e) is constitutional; the LEB keeps its accreditation powers.

paras.html: Dissents (1): it should not be the LEB that leads and controls the admission exam. Models: US LSAT (LSAC), UK LNAT (university consortium), India's CLAT. The LEB's power is supervision, not control (it sees that rules are followed but does not lay them down). The test should not be the sole basis for admission and should be studied for effectiveness.

Dissents from the partial nullification of LEBMO No. 7-2015 [sic: the opinion says "7-2015"; the assailed order is LEBMO No. 7-2016].

paras.html: I. Academic freedom misplaced: it applies differently depending on who invokes it; for individuals it is tied to free expression (traces Adler, Wieman, Sweezy, Barenblatt, Keyishian). Except St. Thomas More, petitioners are individuals who did not claim any infringement of their free expression; of St. Thomas More's six causes of action, only one invokes academic freedom. Academic freedom is not absolute; a minimum PhiLSAT score also discourages the "great evil" of money-making, non-performing law schools (Act No. 3162 survey; Dean Candelaria's 2019 report). Minimum admission standards are no different from standards on tuition increases, buildings, libraries, and teacher qualifications.

paras.html: II. A standardized exclusionary State exam is valid police power (Tablarin). His own research shows the NMAT is also exclusionary: MECS Order No. 52-1985 required it to be "successfully hurdled"; a 45th-percentile cut-off was set in 1987; CHED Memorandum Order No. 18-2016 imposes at least a 40th-percentile cut-off for all medical schools. No reason to treat the NMAT and PhiLSAT differently.

paras.html: III. Reasonableness is a question of fact: the Court is not a trier of facts (Gios-Samar v. DOTC); challenges to reasonableness should go to trial. The presumption of constitutionality prevails absent a factual foundation of record (Ermita-Malate, citing O'Gorman & Young v. Hartford).

paras.html: Issue 1 — jurisdiction: the Court has no primary and direct jurisdiction (textual, historical, impracticable, and legal reasons: Sec. 12, Art. VIII; Meralco v. Pasay), but may intervene in justiciable controversies or when its bar-admission power is infringed.

paras.html: Issue 2 — Sec. 7(e) and LEBMO No. 7: applies a proportionality test (pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportional effects; transparency and intelligibility; range of acceptable outcomes). The PhiLSAT tests basic skills only; 55% is minimal; harms are speculative (passing rates: 81.43% in April 2017, 57.76% in Sept. 2017, 61.39% in April 2018, 56.78% in Sept. 2018). The Decision "takes with its left hand what it gives with the right": it is contradictory to call the PhiLSAT a valid regulation yet allow schools to ignore it.

VIII (Secs. 3[a][2], 7[g], 7[h], and the "continuing legal education" clause of Sec. 2, par. 2 of RA 7662).

paras.html: Background on RA 7662 and the LEB:
paras.text: Background on RA 7662 and the LEB:

paras.html: Prompted by the poor performance of law students and law schools in the bar examinations, Congress passed RA 7662 (Legal Education Reform Act of 1993) on December 23, 1993. Sec. 2 declares the policy to uplift the standards of legal education and, towards this end, to "undertake appropriate reforms in the legal education system, require proper selection of law students, maintain quality among law schools, and require legal apprenticeship and continuing legal education."

Sec. 2 declares the policy to uplift the standards of legal education and, towards this end, to "undertake appropriate reforms in the legal education system, require proper selection of law students, maintain quality among law schools, and require legal apprenticeship and continuing legal education."

paras.html: RA 7662 created the LEB, an executive agency separate from the DECS but attached to it solely for budgetary purposes and administrative support. Its Chair and members are appointed by the President for five years without reappointment, from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the JBC with prior authorization from the Court.

paras.html: "Reasonable": must comply with substantive due process — lawful subject + lawful method (Social Justice Society v. Atienza; PASEI v. Drilon). Per Council of Teachers, the Framers added "reasonable" because of an obiter in PACU (1955) that the Constitution provides for State control of education; supervision refers to external governance and "does not include the right to manage, dictate, overrule and prohibit." The word did not change the texture of police power; it only emphasized that supervision cannot amount to control.

TIP; Non v. Dames; Malabanan v. Ramento; Guzman v. National University) and to the institution itself (Garcia v. Faculty Admission Committee, Loyola School of Theology: the school "decides for itself its aims and objectives and how best to attain them," with a wide sphere of autonomy "certainly extending to the choice of students").

paras.html: Two normative elements: protect and promote quality education, and take appropriate steps to make it accessible. What constitutes quality education is "best left with the political departments" (Council of Teachers). Accessibility means equal opportunity regardless of social and economic differences (Gascon deliberations; ICESCR Art. 13: non-discrimination, physical, and economic accessibility).

paras.html: (a) "Law admission" means admission to legal education, not to the practice of law. Read in context with the policy to uplift legal education and the LEB's powers to administer, supervise, and accredit law schools, Sec. 7(e) is limited to those seeking enrollment in a law school.

paras.html: Contemporaneous interpretation: Sec. 1, Art. VIII of DECS Order No. 27-1989 (precursor) uses admission requirements for enrollment in the law course — this "suffice[s] in itself." paras.html: (b) Sec. 7(e) is reasonable supervision and regulation. It authorizes only minimum standards, not control; it did not impose an exclusionary and qualifying exam nor prevent schools from imposing their own requirements. paras.html: (c) The LEB may administer an aptitude test. Senate deliberations (Sen. Tolentino on unfit students; Sen. Shahani: an aptitude exam "will have to be specially designed"; Sen. Angara: the board "may very well decide to prescribe such a test, although it is not mandatory") show legislative intent. The Court itself supported an aptitude exam when it approved the CLEBM's proposed amendment ("including a system of law aptitude examination") and in B.M. No. 1161, where it referred a proposed law entrance exam to the LEB. The presumption that the legislature intended a valid law "has not been successfully challenged."

paras.html: (d) The PhiLSAT is reasonably related to improving legal education. Test: concurrence of lawful subject and lawful means (Lupangco: rules must be reasonable and fairly adapted to the end). Petitioners' grounds (not conclusive of aptitude; exam and travel costs; burdensome exemption process; redundant to school exams; no scientific study) are conclusions of fact that beg evidence and go into the wisdom of the PhiLSAT, "an excursion into the policy behind the examinations — a function which is administrative rather than judicial." The subject (improving legal education) is within police power; the PhiLSAT as an aptitude test is the means.

paras.text: Re: 6.1 — PhiLSAT as an exclusionary requirement (YES)

paras.html: Pars. 7, 9, 11, and 15 of LEBMO No. 7-2016 exclude and disqualify those who fail to reach the passing score from being admitted to any law school. By mandating a 55% cut-off, the PhiLSAT "usurps the right and duty of the law school to determine for itself the criteria for the admission of students" and to apply them case by case; it forces absolute rejection of applicants below the cut-off or with expired eligibility.

paras.html: Academic freedom comes into play "only after the applicants had been 'pre-selected' without the school's participation"; schools may only add requirements, making their preference "merely secondary or supplemental to that of the State", which is antithetical to reasonable supervision. Schools must surrender their discretion to a State-determined pool under pain of sanctions and fines → "transfers complete control over admission policies from the law schools to the LEB." Garcia: schools are not "public utilities devoid of any discretion as to whom to admit or reject."

Medical schools are not sanctioned for admitting under their own policies; at one point there was no prescribed cut-off; issuance of certificates of eligibility was transferred to the schools.

paras.html: Balancing and calibrated approach: the PhiLSAT as an aptitude test is reasonably related to the State's "unimpeachable interest" in improving legal education, but it should not be exclusionary; schools decide how much weight to give its results, provided their discretion is not gravely abused, arbitrary, whimsical, or discriminatory. The Court does not strike down the PhiLSAT entirely; it partially nullifies LEBMO No. 7-2016 insofar as it absolutely prescribes passing the PhiLSAT, and taking it within two years, as a prerequisite for admission to any law school. The rest remains effective under the separability clause.

paras.html: RA 7662 in general does not encroach on the Court's rule-making power; legal education is within the State's police power. "[I]n judicial humility," the Court affirms that supervision of legal education is a political exercise where judges may participate "not as an independent branch of government, but as part of the sovereign people." The PhiLSAT, when used to exclude, qualify, and restrict admissions, is unconstitutional; when administered as a guide for law schools, it is a valid minimum standard. The Court urges consultative summits to improve legal education and screening tools.

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to GRANT the petitions and declare the entire RA 7662 unconstitutional. Agrees the PhiLSAT's passing score violates academic freedom, but holds that any State-sponsored admission test, mandatory or not, and the whole concept of the LEB violate academic freedom; would overturn Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego.
paras.text: TLDR: Votes to GRANT the petitions and declare the entire RA 7662 unconstitutional. Agrees the PhiLSAT's passing score violates academic freedom, but holds that any State-sponsored admission test, mandatory or not, and the whole concept of the LEB violate academic freedom; would overturn Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego.

paras.html: I. Agreement with the majority: Academic freedom (Garcia; Tangonan v. Paño; Ateneo v. Capulong; Miriam College; Cudia) includes the institution's right to determine who to admit. Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego involved students asserting a right to their chosen course; institutional academic freedom was not raised there. Agrees the PhiLSAT, unlike the NMAT (percentile ranks evaluated against each school's own cut-off), employs a "totalitarian scheme."
paras.text: I. Agreement with the majority: Academic freedom (Garcia; Tangonan v. Paño; Ateneo v. Capulong; Miriam College; Cudia) includes the institution's right to determine who to admit. Tablarin and DECS v. San Diego involved students asserting a right to their chosen course; institutional academic freedom was not raised there. Agrees the PhiLSAT, unlike the NMAT (percentile ranks evaluated against each school's own cut-off), employs a "totalitarian scheme."

paras.html: II. Even a non-mandatory national test infringes academic freedom: academic freedom is a cognate of free expression, so State intrusion must be treated as suspect. Admission policy and the quality of instruction are different standards ("non-sequitur"). The LEB did no specific study; admission tests measure only correlation with first-year grades. Government appointees may lack academic credentials and are prone to influence. The US LSAT is run by a private nonprofit of law schools and is voluntary.

Admission policy and the quality of instruction are different standards ("non-sequitur"). The LEB did no specific study; admission tests measure only correlation with first-year grades. Government appointees may lack academic credentials and are prone to influence. The US LSAT is run by a private nonprofit of law schools and is voluntary.

paras.html: III. Due process: the PhiLSAT is arbitrary because it was not based on scientific research. At oral arguments, LEB Chair Aquende admitted "We have none" (no Philippine study), relying on the US LSAT study; he had taught in only two of 122 law schools. A single written exam as the sole criterion is unreasonable (contrast the holistic review in Grutter v. Bollinger). It infringes life and liberty (right to pursue education) and property (testing fees, travel, opportunity cost).

paras.html: IV. Meritocracy: standardized tests favor the economically privileged; costs make even a non-exclusionary exam exclusionary; ranked results stigmatize low scorers; a national test hides the defects of weak schools ("we incentivize sloth among law schools"). Cites J. Thomas' dissent in Grutter.

paras.html: V. On the majority's ruling: the school's right to determine who to admit is "absolute"; removing the PhiLSAT's mandatory character but retaining it still perpetuates stigma and State control. Teaching law as an academic degree (Sec. 5[2], Art. XIV; Sec. 4, Art. III) differs from licensing (Sec. 5[3], Art. XIV; Sec. 5[5], Art. VIII); a statutory board of political appointees supervising postgraduate legal education is what Sec. 5(2) proscribes.

paras.html: Concurs: the LEB orders and circular making the PhiLSAT mandatory and exclusionary are unconstitutional: (1) the LEB pre-selects the pool; (2) no justification for the 55% score or format (studies were foreign, for other professions); (3) schools face sanctions (closure, phase-out, ₱10,000 fines). PhiLSAT differs from the NMAT (percentile scores, no pass/fail) and the LSAT (run by the LSAC of law schools; not an absolute requirement). Concurs that Sec. 7(h) is unconstitutional and that Sec. 7(e) is constitutional; the LEB keeps its accreditation powers.

paras.html: Dissents (1): it should not be the LEB that leads and controls the admission exam. Models: US LSAT (LSAC), UK LNAT (university consortium), India's CLAT. The LEB's power is supervision, not control (it sees that rules are followed but does not lay them down). The test should not be the sole basis for admission and should be studied for effectiveness.

Dissents from the partial nullification of LEBMO No. 7-2015 [sic: the opinion says "7-2015"; the assailed order is LEBMO No. 7-2016].
paras.text: TLDR: Votes to DISMISS the petition. Concurs that the Court has no jurisdiction over legal education and that its regulation, including admissions, is within police power. Dissents from the partial nullification of LEBMO No. 7-2015 [sic: the opinion says "7-2015"; the assailed order is LEBMO No. 7-2016].

paras.html: I. Academic freedom misplaced: it applies differently depending on who invokes it; for individuals it is tied to free expression (traces Adler, Wieman, Sweezy, Barenblatt, Keyishian). Except St. Thomas More, petitioners are individuals who did not claim any infringement of their free expression; of St. Thomas More's six causes of action, only one invokes academic freedom. Academic freedom is not absolute; a minimum PhiLSAT score also discourages the "great evil" of money-making, non-performing law schools (Act No. 3162 survey; Dean Candelaria's 2019 report). Minimum admission standards are no different from standards on tuition increases, buildings, libraries, and teacher qualifications.

paras.html: II. A standardized exclusionary State exam is valid police power (Tablarin). His own research shows the NMAT is also exclusionary: MECS Order No. 52-1985 required it to be "successfully hurdled"; a 45th-percentile cut-off was set in 1987; CHED Memorandum Order No. 18-2016 imposes at least a 40th-percentile cut-off for all medical schools. No reason to treat the NMAT and PhiLSAT differently.

paras.html: III. Reasonableness is a question of fact: the Court is not a trier of facts (Gios-Samar v. DOTC); challenges to reasonableness should go to trial. The presumption of constitutionality prevails absent a factual foundation of record (Ermita-Malate, citing O'Gorman & Young v. Hartford).

paras.html: TLDR: Accepts that Congress and the LEB have primary and direct jurisdiction over legal education. Votes to affirm the constitutionality in full of Sec. 7(e) and LEBMO No. 7-2016 and of Secs. 7(g) and 7(h) (read as requiring the Court's vetting).

paras.html: Framework: the State, the citizen, and the institution have intersecting rights; none is superior. "Exclusion necessarily comes with quality." Disagrees that the State's power over higher education is merely "auxiliary" (parental-delegation idea fits only young children, not professional education).

paras.html: Issue 1 — jurisdiction: the Court has no primary and direct jurisdiction (textual, historical, impracticable, and legal reasons: Sec. 12, Art. VIII; Meralco v. Pasay), but may intervene in justiciable controversies or when its bar-admission power is infringed.

paras.html: Issue 2 — Sec. 7(e) and LEBMO No. 7: applies a proportionality test (pressing and substantial objective; rational connection; minimal impairment; proportional effects; transparency and intelligibility; range of acceptable outcomes). The PhiLSAT tests basic skills only; 55% is minimal; harms are speculative (passing rates: 81.43% in April 2017, 57.76% in Sept. 2017, 61.39% in April 2018, 56.78% in Sept. 2018). The Decision "takes with its left hand what it gives with the right": it is contradictory to call the PhiLSAT a valid regulation yet allow schools to ignore it.

paras.html: No actual case, no judicial review: The existence of an actual case or controversy is an essential requisite for the exercise of judicial review. The Court "is not empowered to decide moot questions or abstract propositions, or to declare principles or rules of law which cannot affect the result as to the thing in issue," and will refuse to make a "grand pronouncement" that would amount to a "non-binding opinion."
paras.text: No actual case, no judicial review: The existence of an actual case or controversy is an essential requisite for the exercise of judicial review. The Court "is not empowered to decide moot questions or abstract propositions, or to declare principles or rules of law which cannot affect the result as to the thing in issue," and will refuse to make a "grand pronouncement" that would amount to a "non-binding opinion."

paras.html: Mootness: An action is moot when it no longer presents a justiciable controversy because the issues have become academic or dead, or the dispute has already been resolved, so that no one is entitled to judicial intervention unless the issue is likely to be raised again between the parties. Because the "any reelection" question is premised on a person's second election as President (whether immediate or not), and Estrada lost in 2010, the question became hypothetical.

paras.html: Exception not met (fn. 11): "Capable of repetition yet evading review" applies only where both concur: (1) the challenged action is too short in duration to be fully litigated before it ends, and (2) there is a reasonable expectation that the same complaining party would be subjected to the same action again. The second requisite was absent.

paras.html: Re: Mootness
paras.text: Re: Mootness

paras.html: As a rule, the Court may only adjudicate actual, ongoing controversies (Honig v. Doe). It is not empowered to decide moot questions or abstract propositions, or to declare principles or rules of law which cannot affect the result as to the thing in issue.

paras.html: When a case is moot, it becomes non-justiciable.
paras.text: When a case is moot, it becomes non-justiciable.

paras.html: An action is "moot" when it "no longer presents a justiciable controversy because the issues involved have become academic or dead", or when the matter in dispute has already been resolved, so that one is not entitled to judicial intervention unless the issue is likely to be raised again between the parties. There is nothing to resolve because the determination "has been overtaken by subsequent events" (Santiago v. CA).
paras.text: An action is "moot" when it "no longer presents a justiciable controversy because the issues involved have become academic or dead", or when the matter in dispute has already been resolved, so that one is not entitled to judicial intervention unless the issue is likely to be raised again between the parties. There is nothing to resolve because the determination "has been overtaken by subsequent events" (Santiago v. CA).

paras.html: Even assuming an actual case or controversy existed before the proclamation of the President duly elected in the May 10, 2010 elections, "the same is no longer true today". Any discussion of Estrada's "reelection" would be "hypothetical and speculative" and "will serve no useful or practical purpose."

paras.html: Peace power and its limit: The President's power to conduct peace negotiations is implicitly included in her powers as Chief Executive and Commander-in-Chief (citing Sanlakas and Marcos v. Manglapus on residual powers). She may consider and even recommend solutions requiring constitutional amendments to Congress or the people, but may not guarantee them. A clause making such changes a certainty (a term, not a condition) usurps the constituent power of Congress, a constitutional convention, or the people, and is grave abuse of discretion.

paras.html: Right to information and consultation: The right to information (Art. III, Sec. 7) and the policy of full public disclosure (Art. II, Sec. 28) are in "splendid symmetry"; both are self-executory and cover negotiations leading to the consummation of an agreement. EO 3, the LGC, and the IPRA require consultation; the PAPP's "furtive process" was grave abuse of discretion.

International law recognizes only internal self-determination for peoples within a state, absent extreme cases.

paras.html: Background of the GRP–MILF peace process:
paras.text: Background of the GRP–MILF peace process:

paras.html: The MILF, which split from the MNLF in 1984 under Salamat Hashim, engaged the GRP in peace talks beginning 1996 (Agreement on General Cessation of Hostilities, 1997; General Framework of Agreement of Intent, 1998). After MILF attacks in 1999–2000, President Estrada waged "all-out war." President Arroyo resumed talks with Malaysia as facilitator (Kuala Lumpur, Mar. 24, 2001).

paras.html: June 2001: the GRP-MILF Tripoli Agreement on Peace of 2001 covered the Security, Rehabilitation, and Ancestral Domain aspects; on ancestral domain the parties agreed only to discuss it further. Implementing guidelines followed on security (Aug. 2001) and humanitarian/rehabilitation aspects (May 2002). Exploratory talks from 2005 led to the MOA-AD in final form.

paras.html: Concepts and principles: it is the "birthright of all Moros and all Indigenous peoples of Mindanao" to be accepted as "Bangsamoros" (natives of Mindanao, Palawan, and Sulu at conquest, their descendants, and spouses); the Bangsamoro homeland is owned exclusively by them; ancestral domain is not part of the public domain; their right to self-governance is rooted in the past sultanates; they are the "First Nation"; and the Bangsamoro Juridical Entity (BJE) has authority over the ancestral domain.

paras.html: Territory: the homeland covers land, maritime, fluvial, aerial, and atmospheric domains of the Mindanao-Sulu-Palawan region. The BJE core is the present ARMM plus six Lanao del Norte municipalities that voted for ARMM inclusion in 2001, without a new plebiscite; Category A areas to vote within 12 months of signing; Category B areas 25 years after the Comprehensive Compact. BJE "internal waters" extend 15 km; its "territorial waters" up to the RP baselines are under joint jurisdiction.

paras.html: Resources: the BJE may enter into economic and trade relations with foreign countries and open trade missions; the Central Government handles external defense and must ensure BJE participation in ASEAN and UN meetings; the BJE controls energy resources (subject to emergency takeover); total production is shared 75:25 in favor of the BJE; the BJE may modify or cancel existing concessions and permits.

paras.html: Governance: a multinational third party monitors implementation; the relationship between the Central Government and the BJE is "associative", characterized by shared authority; the BJE may build its own civil service, electoral, financial, legal, police and internal security force, judicial system, and other institutions. Par. 7: provisions "requiring amendments to the existing legal framework shall come into force upon signing of a Comprehensive Compact and upon effecting the necessary changes to the legal framework… within the stipulated timeframe."

paras.html: David: courts decide otherwise moot cases if (a) there is a grave violation of the Constitution; (b) the situation is exceptional and paramount public interest is involved; (c) the issue requires controlling principles to guide the bench, the bar, and the public; and (d) it is capable of repetition yet evading review. paras.html: Sec. 28, Art. II (full public disclosure) is in "splendid symmetry" with Sec. 7, Art. III: the right to information lets people demand information; Sec. 28 is the duty of officialdom to give it "even if nobody demands." Per the Ople–Davide exchange, Sec. 28 takes effect immediately; Congress may only provide "reasonable safeguards" and cannot revoke it. Respondents cannot cite the absence of implementing law. Feedback mechanisms (Rosario Braid–Ople) are corollary.

paras.html: Re: The concept of association
paras.text: Re: The concept of association

paras.html: The MOA-AD uses "association" (Territory ¶3; Resources ¶11; Governance ¶4: the relationship "shall be associative characterized by shared authority and responsibility"). In international law, association is formed when two states of unequal power establish durable links, the associate delegating some responsibilities while maintaining its international status as a state (Keitner and Reisman); e.g., the Marshall Islands and FSM with the US. It has usually been "a transitional device of former colonies on their way to full independence."

paras.html: Re: International law
paras.text: Re: International law

paras.html: Under Art. II, Sec. 2, international law is part of the law of the land (Mejoff; Agustin v. Edu). The right of peoples to self-determination is a general principle (ICCPR/ICESCR Art. 1), but Reference re Secession of Quebec: it is normally fulfilled internally, within an existing state; external self-determination (secession) arises only in extreme cases (colonial rule, foreign domination, perhaps denial of internal self-determination). The Aaland Islands jurists: disposing of territory is an attribute of state sovereignty.

The Aaland Islands jurists: disposing of territory is an attribute of state sovereignty.

paras.html: Indigenous peoples likewise have no general right to secession, only internal self-determination. The UN DRIP (2007), even if customary law (not decided), does not require granting the BJE's particular powers (e.g., its own police, aerial domain) and expressly bars impairing territorial integrity (Art. 46). It cannot validate the MOA-AD.

She may suggest them to the people for their independent consideration, but further involvement would vitiate a genuine people's initiative (Lambino v. COMELEC). Her oath is to preserve and defend the Constitution, not change it.

Under international law (Vienna Convention Art. 12(2)(a)), initialing authenticates text and constitutes signature only if so agreed, which was not the case.

paras.html: In any event, the MOA-AD is incongruous with the Constitution: the BJE is not a recognized subdivision and exceeds Art. X powers (courts beyond personal/family/property law; own civil service and elections, contrary to the CSC and COMELEC; natural resources reserved to the State; foreign relations reserved to the President).

paras.html: By long-standing tradition, retiring Justices of the SC and the appellate courts purchase, for sentimental reasons, the government properties they used during their tenure. The practice is recognized as a privilege and a benefit, partly to reward long and faithful service.

paras.html: On March 23, 2004, the Court En Banc issued a Resolution in A.M. No. 03-12-01 (Guidelines on the Purchase of Judiciary Properties by Retiring Members of the Supreme Court and Appellate Courts). Drilon and state that the privilege needs regulation so that respect for a retiring Justice's sentiments is consistent with restraint in disposing of government resources.

paras.html: Independence exists so that power is not concentrated in one branch. Divided power must be wielded by co-equal branches equally capable of independent action; without independence, one branch cannot check the arbitrary or self-interested assertions of another.
paras.text: Independence exists so that power is not concentrated in one branch. Divided power must be wielded by co-equal branches equally capable of independent action; without independence, one branch cannot check the arbitrary or self-interested assertions of another.

paras.html: For the Judiciary, independence means that individual judges freely resolve justiciable disputes, while the branch as a whole works free of restraint and influence from the other branches, save only those imposed by the Constitution itself.
paras.text: For the Judiciary, independence means that individual judges freely resolve justiciable disputes, while the branch as a whole works free of restraint and influence from the other branches, save only those imposed by the Constitution itself.

paras.html: Two concepts (citing Hood and Chan): decisional independence (a judge decides free from political or popular influence, based solely on the facts and the law) and institutional independence (the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive and Legislative; the collective independence of the Judiciary as a body).

paras.html: In re Macasaet (2008): individual judicial independence protects each judge's ability to decide with autonomy; institutional judicial independence protects judges as a class. A truly independent judiciary is possible only when both are preserved and public confidence in the Judiciary is maintained.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy is "one of the most important aspects of judicial independence." Just as the Executive cannot physically stop a court from holding hearings and the Legislature cannot remove all jurisdiction from courts (U.S. v. Klein), courts may not be obstructed in their freedom to use or dispose of their funds for purposes germane to judicial functions.

Just as the Executive cannot physically stop a court from holding hearings and the Legislature cannot remove all jurisdiction from courts (U.S. v. Klein), courts may not be obstructed in their freedom to use or dispose of their funds for purposes germane to judicial functions.

paras.html: Although legislative control of the purse is generally unquestioned, any form of interference by the Legislative or the Executive on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy amounts to an improper check on a co-equal branch. To adjudicate, the Judiciary must be able to command adequate resources.

To adjudicate, the Judiciary must be able to command adequate resources.

paras.html: Sec. 3, Art. VIII: the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy; its appropriations may not be reduced below the previous year's, and once approved shall be automatically and regularly released.
paras.text: Sec. 3, Art. VIII: the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy; its appropriations may not be reduced below the previous year's, and once approved shall be automatically and regularly released.

paras.html: Bengzon v. Drilon (1992): fiscal autonomy is a guarantee of "full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require"; it includes the power to levy, assess, and collect fees, fix compensation, and allocate and disburse funds. "Fiscal autonomy means freedom from outside control." If the SC says it needs 100 typewriters and DBM says only 10, autonomy becomes an "empty and illusory platitude."

paras.html: Background: the retirement privilege
paras.text: Background: the retirement privilege

paras.html: By long-standing tradition, retiring Justices of the SC and the appellate courts purchase, for sentimental reasons, the government properties they used during their tenure. The practice is recognized as a privilege and a benefit, partly to reward long and faithful service.
paras.text: By long-standing tradition, retiring Justices of the SC and the appellate courts purchase, for sentimental reasons, the government properties they used during their tenure. The practice is recognized as a privilege and a benefit, partly to reward long and faithful service.

paras.html: On March 23, 2004, the Court En Banc issued a Resolution in A.M. No. 03-12-01 (Guidelines on the Purchase of Judiciary Properties by Retiring Members of the Supreme Court and Appellate Courts). Its whereas clauses rest the privilege on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy as defined in Bengzon v. Drilon and state that the privilege needs regulation so that respect for a retiring Justice's sentiments is consistent with restraint in disposing of government resources.

paras.text: Re: Separation of powers and judicial independence

paras.html: Angara v. Electoral Commission: separation of powers obtains by actual division in the Constitution; each department has exclusive cognizance of matters within its jurisdiction and is supreme in its own sphere, but a system of checks and balances secures coordination, with the Judiciary as final arbiter determining the law.

Electoral Commission: separation of powers obtains by actual division in the Constitution; each department has exclusive cognizance of matters within its jurisdiction and is supreme in its own sphere, but a system of checks and balances secures coordination, with the Judiciary as final arbiter determining the law.

paras.html: Independence exists so that power is not concentrated in one branch. Divided power must be wielded by co-equal branches equally capable of independent action; without independence, one branch cannot check the arbitrary or self-interested assertions of another.
paras.text: Independence exists so that power is not concentrated in one branch. Divided power must be wielded by co-equal branches equally capable of independent action; without independence, one branch cannot check the arbitrary or self-interested assertions of another.

paras.html: For the Judiciary, independence means that individual judges freely resolve justiciable disputes, while the branch as a whole works free of restraint and influence from the other branches, save only those imposed by the Constitution itself.
paras.text: For the Judiciary, independence means that individual judges freely resolve justiciable disputes, while the branch as a whole works free of restraint and influence from the other branches, save only those imposed by the Constitution itself.

paras.html: Two concepts (citing Hood and Chan): decisional independence (a judge decides free from political or popular influence, based solely on the facts and the law) and institutional independence (the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive and Legislative; the collective independence of the Judiciary as a body).

paras.html: In re Macasaet (2008): individual judicial independence protects each judge's ability to decide with autonomy; institutional judicial independence protects judges as a class. A truly independent judiciary is possible only when both are preserved and public confidence in the Judiciary is maintained.

paras.html: Re: Fiscal autonomy
paras.text: Re: Fiscal autonomy

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy is "one of the most important aspects of judicial independence." Just as the Executive cannot physically stop a court from holding hearings and the Legislature cannot remove all jurisdiction from courts (U.S. v. Klein), courts may not be obstructed in their freedom to use or dispose of their funds for purposes germane to judicial functions.

Just as the Executive cannot physically stop a court from holding hearings and the Legislature cannot remove all jurisdiction from courts (U.S. v. Klein), courts may not be obstructed in their freedom to use or dispose of their funds for purposes germane to judicial functions.

paras.html: Although legislative control of the purse is generally unquestioned, any form of interference by the Legislative or the Executive on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy amounts to an improper check on a co-equal branch. To adjudicate, the Judiciary must be able to command adequate resources.
paras.text: Although legislative control of the purse is generally unquestioned, any form of interference by the Legislative or the Executive on the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy amounts to an improper check on a co-equal branch. To adjudicate, the Judiciary must be able to command adequate resources.

paras.html: Sec. 3, Art. VIII: the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy; its appropriations may not be reduced below the previous year's, and once approved shall be automatically and regularly released.
paras.text: Sec. 3, Art. VIII: the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy; its appropriations may not be reduced below the previous year's, and once approved shall be automatically and regularly released.

paras.html: Bengzon v. Drilon (1992): fiscal autonomy is a guarantee of "full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require"; it includes the power to levy, assess, and collect fees, fix compensation, and allocate and disburse funds. "Fiscal autonomy means freedom from outside control." If the SC says it needs 100 typewriters and DBM says only 10, autonomy becomes an "empty and illusory platitude."

paras.html: The Sandiganbayan has three months to decide: The 12-month period for "lower collegiate courts" in Sec. 15(1), Art. VIII refers to regular courts of lower collegiate level, which is only the CA. The SB, a special court with trial functions, must decide within three (3) months from submission under Sec. 6 of PD 1606 and its own rules, which do not distinguish between original and appellate cases. Motions for reconsideration or new trial and petitions for review must be resolved within 30 days.

paras.html: On July 29, 2000, the IBP Board of Governors, meeting in Los Baños, Laguna, adopted a Resolution on delays in the SB; on July 31, 2000, IBP National President Arthur D. Lim transmitted it to the SC.
paras.text: On July 29, 2000, the IBP Board of Governors, meeting in Los Baños, Laguna, adopted a Resolution on delays in the SB; on July 31, 2000, IBP National President Arthur D. Lim transmitted it to the SC.

paras.html: The Resolution invoked Sec. 16, Art. III (speedy disposition of cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative bodies) and Canon 12 of the CPR (lawyers' duty to assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice). It noted that the IBP had received numerous complaints from its members about serious delays in decisions and in the resolution of motions and incidents before the SB's divisions.
paras.text: The Resolution invoked Sec. 16, Art. III (speedy disposition of cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative bodies) and Canon 12 of the CPR (lawyers' duty to assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice). It noted that the IBP had received numerous complaints from its members about serious delays in decisions and in the resolution of motions and incidents before the SB's divisions.

paras.html: It also noted that SC Administrative Circular No. 10-94 requires RTCs, MeTCs, MTCs, and MCTCs to submit bi-annual docket reports and to post a monthly list of cases submitted for decision, but that the Circular had not been made applicable to the SB, which is also a trial court.
paras.text: It also noted that SC Administrative Circular No. 10-94 requires RTCs, MeTCs, MTCs, and MCTCs to submit bi-annual docket reports and to post a monthly list of cases submitted for decision, but that the Circular had not been made applicable to the SB, which is also a trial court.

paras.html: It recommended to the SC: (1) that AC 10-94 be made applicable to the SB as regards cases within its original jurisdiction; and (2) an inquiry into the causes of delay, with a view to measures that would avoid them.
paras.text: It recommended to the SC: (1) that AC 10-94 be made applicable to the SB as regards cases within its original jurisdiction; and (2) an inquiry into the causes of delay, with a view to measures that would avoid them.

paras.html: Re: The SB is a special court with trial functions
paras.text: Re: The SB is a special court with trial functions

paras.html: Under RA 8249, the SB is a special court of the same level as the CA, possessing all the inherent powers of a court of justice (Sec. 1), with functions of a trial court (Sec. 2: it holds sessions "for the trial and determination of cases"). It is not a regular court but a special one.

paras.html: "Special courts are judicial tribunals exercising limited jurisdiction over particular or specialized categories of actions": the CTA, the SB, and the Shari'a Courts.
paras.text: "Special courts are judicial tribunals exercising limited jurisdiction over particular or specialized categories of actions": the CTA, the SB, and the Shari'a Courts.

paras.html: Under Sec. 5(5), Art. VIII, rules of procedure of special courts remain effective unless disapproved by the SC.

paras.html: The SB was originally empowered to promulgate its own rules (Sec. 9, PD 1606). paras.html: (2) Effective December 1, 2001, to RELIEVE him of his powers, functions, and duties as Presiding Justice, and from presiding over trials as a justice and Chairman of the First Division, so that he may DEVOTE himself exclusively to DECISION WRITING until the backlog of cases assigned to him, and cases not assigned to any ponente (of which he shall be deemed the ponente), are finally decided. Chico-Nazario, as the most senior associate justice, shall take over the office of Presiding Justice until further orders.

paras.html: The SC supervises the IBP, including its elections: The IBP is "a sui generis public institution" (Tabuzo) whose officers perform public functions. "Implicit in the wording of Article VIII, Section 5 of the 1987 Constitution is the Supreme Court's power to supervise all the activities of the IBP, including the election of its officers." This power, though extensive, "should be exercised prudently."

"Implicit in the wording of Article VIII, Section 5 of the 1987 Constitution is the Supreme Court's power to supervise all the activities of the IBP, including the election of its officers." This power, though extensive, "should be exercised prudently."

paras.html: Sec. 14 of the Revised IBP By-Laws requires a link to an election: Sponsoring trips for IBP officers is not a prohibited election act where there is no concrete evidence that the giver intends to run and the electors (the House of Delegates) have not yet been elected. Hearsay, conjectures, and surmises cannot sustain a ruling.

paras.html: Excessive gifts to IBP officers are misconduct even if IBP officers are not public officers: IBP officers are not public officers under the anti-graft and gift laws (Tabuzo), but the Court may draw parallels from those laws for administrative liability. Support to the IBP must further its goals and directly benefit its members, and "should not solely be for the interest, use and enjoyment of its officers." Giving and accepting exorbitant gifts = Simple Misconduct under Canon II, Secs. 1 and 2, CPRA.

paras.html: Prohibits, whether by a candidate or any other member, directly or indirectly: (1) distributing campaign materials except within 7 days of election day; (2) campaigning while holding an elective, judicial, quasi-judicial, or prosecutory government post; (3) forming tickets or slates except within 7 days of election day; and (4) "[f]or the purpose of inducing or influencing a member to withhold his or her vote, or to vote for or against a candidate": paying dues or debts, giving food, drink, entertainment, transportation, or any article of value, or making a promise or causing an expenditure.

paras.text: Re: Canon II and misconduct

paras.html: Canon II: a lawyer shall "at all times, act with propriety and maintain the appearance of propriety in personal and professional dealings". Sec. 1 bars unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct; Sec. 2 requires dignified conduct and bars conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice law.

paras.html: Lawyers must uphold the Constitution and the laws and maintain high standards of morality, honesty, integrity, and fair dealing (Lim v. Bautista; A-1 Financial Services v. Valerio). It does not suffice that they are persons of integrity; they must also appear to be so (Re: Anonymous Complaint against Untian).

He never expressed intent to run, so what could he have campaigned for?

paras.html: Impeachment judgment is limited: A judgment in an impeachment case "shall not extend further than removal from office and disqualification to hold any office" (Sec. 3(7), Art. XI). Impeachment is purely political and is neither civil, criminal, nor administrative; "no legally actionable liability attaches" by a mere judgment of impeachment, so forfeiture of retirement benefits is not a consequence of removal by itself.
paras.text: Impeachment judgment is limited: A judgment in an impeachment case "shall not extend further than removal from office and disqualification to hold any office" (Sec. 3(7), Art. XI). Impeachment is purely political and is neither civil, criminal, nor administrative; "no legally actionable liability attaches" by a mere judgment of impeachment, so forfeiture of retirement benefits is not a consequence of removal by itself.

paras.html: Involuntary retirement: An impeached public officer whose civil, criminal, or administrative liability was not judicially established may be considered involuntarily retired from service, without forfeiture of retirement benefits. A later judgment of liability in a separate proceeding operates as a resolutory condition.
paras.text: Involuntary retirement: An impeached public officer whose civil, criminal, or administrative liability was not judicially established may be considered involuntarily retired from service, without forfeiture of retirement benefits. A later judgment of liability in a separate proceeding operates as a resolutory condition.

paras.html: Survivorship: Under Sec. 3, RA 9946, mere eligibility for optional retirement at the time of death, not actual retirement, suffices to grant survivorship benefits to the surviving legitimate spouse, absent the disqualifications in AC No. 81-2010.

paras.html: Renato Coronado Corona served 8 years as Associate Justice (appointed April 2002) and became the 23rd Chief Justice on May 12, 2010.

paras.html: Before the Court, he served in government as a working student in the 1960s (Office of the President, Office of Exec. Sec. Melchor, Dept. of Public Information, City of Makati); after private practice from 1975, he was Assistant Executive Secretary for Legal Affairs (1992), Deputy Executive Secretary and Chief Presidential Legal Counsel (1994–1998), Chief of Staff and Spokesperson of VP Arroyo (1998–2001), and Presidential Chief of Staff and Acting Executive Secretary (2001–2002).

paras.html: A year after his appointment as CJ, Articles of Impeachment were filed, and he was indicted by the HOR for betrayal of public trust, culpable violation of the Constitution, and graft and corruption [sic: the decision says "Section 2, Article VI"; fn. 3 quotes Sec. 2, Art. XI].
paras.text: A year after his appointment as CJ, Articles of Impeachment were filed, and he was indicted by the HOR for betrayal of public trust, culpable violation of the Constitution, and graft and corruption [sic: the decision says "Section 2, Article VI"; fn. 3 quotes Sec. 2, Art. XI].

paras.html: The HOR filed eight Articles, including partiality to the Arroyo administration (Art. I); failure to disclose his SALN under Sec. 17, Art. XI (Art. II); the status quo ante order in the Gutierrez impeachment (Art. IV); the TRO in favor of PGMA and her husband (Art. VII); and the failure to account for JDF and SAJ collections (Art. VIII).
paras.text: The HOR filed eight Articles, including partiality to the Arroyo administration (Art. I); failure to disclose his SALN under Sec. 17, Art. XI (Art. II); the status quo ante order in the Gutierrez impeachment (Art. IV); the TRO in favor of PGMA and her husband (Art. VII); and the failure to account for JDF and SAJ collections (Art. VIII).

paras.html: On May 29, 2012, the Senate, sitting as an Impeachment Court and having tried him on three Articles, found him guilty under Article II only by a vote of 20 Senators (at least 2/3), mainly for non-declaration of his SALN. The judgment, as quoted from Mrs. Corona's letter, imposed removal from office and disqualification to hold any office under Sec. 3(7), Art. XI.

paras.html: US origin: Impeachment was conceived as part of the US system of checks and balances, to discipline a President who abuses his responsibilities without creating a weapon to prevent him from carrying them out; the goal was to refine the separation of powers.

paras.html: Art. I, Sec. 3, Cl. 7, US Constitution: judgment "shall not extend further than to removal from Office, and disqualification", but the convicted party remains liable to indictment, trial, judgment, and punishment according to law.

paras.html: Fr. Bernas (quoting Justice Story): impeachment is "purely of a political nature", designed not to punish but to secure the state; it "touches neither his person nor his property, but simply divests him of his political capacity." Removal and disqualification are the only punishments; criminal and civil liability can follow, and prosecution after impeachment is not double jeopardy.

paras.html: No forum shopping / res judicata: Impeachment being sui generis, its culmination (dismissal or conviction) is not res judicata, because res judicata does not apply to purely political processes (Heirs of Sotto v. Palicte on the elements).

paras.html: No double jeopardy: A first jeopardy cannot attach on a judgment of impeachment, since impeachment is not criminal in nature (Cerezo v. People on the requisites).

paras.html: Quo warranto proceeds independently (Republic v. Sereno): impeachment is political (Congress is prosecutor, trier, and judge; vindicates breach of public trust; governed by the Constitution and congressional rules), while quo warranto is judicial (filed by the SG or a claimant; determines title or eligibility; governed by the Rules of Court; may impose additional penalties such as costs, Sec. 9, Rule 66).

paras.html: Conclusion: "A judgment of impeachment per se connotes mere removal from the post." Because the Constitution expressly limits it, its effects are confined within those limits; impeachment is separate, distinct, and independent from any other cause of action against the impeached officer, even one with a colorable connection to the impeachment grounds.

paras.html: Meaning of retirement: termination of one's career, usually by age, but also by serious physical impediments, personal choice, dissolution of the office, or the employer's prerogative; the term even covers judges who retire for permanent disability or who die in service (Re: Requests for Survivorship Pension Benefits).

paras.html: Voluntary vs. involuntary: voluntary = by one's own unilateral volition; involuntary = career terminated for reasons outside the worker's control. "Impeachment resulting in removal from holding office falls under the column on involuntary retirement."

paras.html: No deprivation without judicial determination: An impeachment respondent does not risk forfeiture of the constitutional rights to life, liberty, or property; a separate determination of liability by the courts is necessary. Without judicial conviction, the official is only removed, with the Senate having discretion to add perpetual disqualification.

paras.html: Gap in the law: No provision lays out the consequences of impeachment pending the resolution of other charges, and no law commands automatic cancellation of post-employment benefits of an impeached official. His death and the termination of the other cases compounded the issue; this is "fortified by the failure of the other forum to follow through".

paras.html: Equity: The fairer course is to consider him involuntarily retired rather than dismiss the claim outright without legal basis. "Equity is the material that fills in the open spaces in the silence, obscurity, or insufficiency of the law" (Reyes v. Lim); courts of law are courts of equity, and equity jurisdiction may be invoked despite applicable laws if their inflexibility would inflict injustice.

paras.html: Legislative exemptions from legal fees are invalid (rule-making): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress" (quoting the GSIS Resolution). The power to promulgate these rules is now the Court's exclusive domain, no longer shared with Congress, much less the Executive.
paras.text: Legislative exemptions from legal fees are invalid (rule-making): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress" (quoting the GSIS Resolution). The power to promulgate these rules is now the Court's exclusive domain, no longer shared with Congress, much less the Executive.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy: Legal fees under Rule 141 fund the JDF and the SAJF. Any congressional exemption from legal fees necessarily reduces these funds and is "constitutionally infirm," because it impairs the Court's fiscal autonomy (Sec. 3, Art. VIII) and erodes its independence → the exemption of cooperatives under RA 6938, as amended by RA 9520, no longer stands.

paras.html: Scope of "court and sheriff's fees": "All court fees" means the totality of legal fees under Rule 141 imposed as an incident of instituting an action. Even before the GSIS ruling, the exemption never covered the sheriff's actual travel expenses under Sec. 10, Rule 141.

paras.html: Citing Echegaray v. Secretary of Justice (1999): the 1987 Constitution molded an even stronger and more independent judiciary and took away the power of Congress to repeal, alter, or supplement rules concerning pleading, practice and procedure; the power to promulgate these rules is no longer shared by the Court with Congress, more so with the Executive.

paras.html: Doctrinal sentence (quoted from GSIS): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress."

paras.html: The separation of powers has erected an "impregnable wall" keeping the rule-making power within the sole province of the Court. The other branches trespass on this prerogative if they enact laws or issue orders that effectively repeal, alter, or modify the Court's procedural rules → a legislative grant of exemption from legal fees (there, Sec. 39 of RA 8291) necessarily fails.

paras.html: Legislative exemptions from legal fees are invalid (rule-making): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress" (quoting the GSIS Resolution). The power to promulgate these rules is now the Court's exclusive domain, no longer shared with Congress, much less the Executive.
paras.text: Legislative exemptions from legal fees are invalid (rule-making): "Since the payment of legal fees is a vital component of the rules promulgated by this Court concerning pleading, practice and procedure, it cannot be validly annulled, changed or modified by Congress" (quoting the GSIS Resolution). The power to promulgate these rules is now the Court's exclusive domain, no longer shared with Congress, much less the Executive.

paras.html: Fiscal autonomy: Legal fees under Rule 141 fund the JDF and the SAJF. Any congressional exemption from legal fees necessarily reduces these funds and is "constitutionally infirm," because it impairs the Court's fiscal autonomy (Sec. 3, Art. VIII) and erodes its independence → the exemption of cooperatives under RA 6938, as amended by RA 9520, no longer stands.

paras.text: Art. 61, par. (6), RA 9520 (Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008) provides:

paras.html: "(6) Cooperatives shall be exempt from the payment of all court and sheriff's fees payable to the Philippine Government for and in connection with all actions brought under this Code, or where such actions is brought by the Authority before the court, to enforce the payment of obligations contracted in favor of the cooperative."
paras.text: "(6) Cooperatives shall be exempt from the payment of all court and sheriff's fees payable to the Philippine Government for and in connection with all actions brought under this Code, or where such actions is brought by the Authority before the court, to enforce the payment of obligations contracted in favor of the cooperative."

paras.html: PHCCI claims this reiterates Sec. 62, par. 6, RA 6938 (Cooperative Code of the Philippines), which was the basis for the Court's own Resolution in A.M. No. 03-4-01-0 (15 July 2003) and OCA Circular No. 44-2007.

paras.html: The 2003 Resolution exempted cooperatives from court and sheriff's fees in actions under RA 6938, subject to guidelines: (a) the action is filed by the duly elected officers in the name of or on behalf of the cooperative; and (b) the action is filed under RA 6938 but limited only to enforcing the payment of obligations contracted in favor of the cooperative; otherwise, no exemption.

paras.html: Citing Echegaray v. Secretary of Justice (1999): the 1987 Constitution molded an even stronger and more independent judiciary and took away the power of Congress to repeal, alter, or supplement rules concerning pleading, practice and procedure; the power to promulgate these rules is no longer shared by the Court with Congress, more so with the Executive.

paras.html: The separation of powers has erected an "impregnable wall" keeping the rule-making power within the sole province of the Court. The other branches trespass on this prerogative if they enact laws or issue orders that effectively repeal, alter, or modify the Court's procedural rules → a legislative grant of exemption from legal fees (there, Sec. 39 of RA 8291) necessarily fails.

paras.html: SALN filing is not only a statutory requirement but a positive duty imposed by the Constitution [the duty is in Sec. 17, Art. XI; sic: fn. 80 cites "Article XII, Section 17" and fn. 81 "Article XII, Section 18"]. SALN laws were passed in aid of that duty.

paras.html: It shares the same category as the constitutional duty to owe allegiance to the State and the Constitution → offenses against SALN laws are violations of a duty owed to the State. "[T]he violation of SALN laws, by itself, defeats any claim of integrity", as it is "inherently immoral to violate the will of the legislature and to violate the Constitution."

Carpio found that after assuming office on August 16, 2010, she had to file a sworn SALN reckoned as of her first day within 30 days (by September 15, 2010).
