XI and, given her prior non-filing as a U.P. professor, a culpable violation of the Constitution committed while already an impeachable officer.

paras.html: Prima facie presumption of ill-gotten wealth (Sec. 2, RA 1379): It arises when (1) the respondent is a public officer, (2) who acquired a considerable amount of money or property during incumbency, (3) manifestly out of proportion to his salary and other lawful income. The State need only state the approximate amount acquired and the officer's known lawful income; the burden shifts to the respondent to show lawful acquisition by clear and convincing evidence. Respondents, not the Republic, must prove "other lawful income."

paras.html: Summary judgment: Denials for "lack of knowledge" of matters plainly and necessarily within the pleader's knowledge, and negative pregnants, are admissions that tender no genuine issue. Under Sec. 1, Rule 35, a claimant may move for summary judgment "at any stage of the litigation" after the answer is served; agreeing to go to trial is not a waiver.

paras.html: Admissions and estoppel: Admissions in a compromise agreement later declared void remain binding when the nullity has nothing to do with their truth. Laches and estoppel do not apply when the government sues as a sovereign.

paras.html: Dec. 17, 1991: the Republic, through the PCGG and represented by the OSG, filed a petition for forfeiture (Civil Case No. 0141) before the Sandiganbayan under RA 1379 in relation to EO Nos. 1, 2, 14, and 14-A, seeking to declare as ill-gotten wealth US$356 million (now over US$658 million with interest) held by five account groups of foreign foundations in Swiss banks: Azio-Verso-Vibur; Xandy-Wintrop: Charis-Scolari-Valamo-Spinus-Avertina; Trinidad-Rayby-Palmy; Rosalys-Aguamina; and Maler. It also sought forfeiture of US$25 million and US$5 million in treasury notes frozen at the Central Bank.

It also sought forfeiture of US$25 million and US$5 million in treasury notes frozen at the Central Bank.

paras.html: The petition detailed how FM and Imelda created the foundations through SKA/SBC lawyers and dummies, named themselves and their children as beneficiaries, used aliases "William Saunders" and "Jane Ryan" (and "John Lewis" for Maler), renamed and liquidated foundations, and transferred assets to successor foundations via Fides Trust. It also alleged the couple's only lawful income (salaries; ITRs showing a 1965 net worth of only ₱120,000 and suspicious "receivables" from FM's law practice).

paras.html: Imee and BBM: (A) the Republic was barred by estoppel by laches and had waived summary judgment by agreeing to trial; (B) RA 1379 is penal and must be strictly construed; the Republic failed to prove acquisition/ownership, the amount acquired during incumbency (Dec. 31, 1965–Feb. 25, 1986), and other lawful income (Sec. 3(c)–(e)), so the presumption never attached; (C) the Agreements are inadmissible under Sec. 27, Rule 130 (offer of compromise), and the "admissions" were taken out of context; (D) certiorari does not lie, as the SC is not a trier of facts.

paras.html: A judgment before trial but after both parties have pleaded, on affidavits, depositions, or admissions, where there is no genuine issue (Auman v. Estenzo; Sec. 1, Rule 35). A genuine issue calls for presentation of evidence, as distinguished from one that is "fictitious and contrived, set up in bad faith or patently lacking in substance." If affidavits, depositions, or admissions show the answer's issues are sham, trial is dispensed with.

paras.html: Denial for lack of knowledge is a recognized mode, but where an allegation directly charges a party with an act, a categorical denial is required (Morales v. CA). "[A] profession of ignorance about a fact which is patently and necessarily within the pleader's knowledge or means of knowing is as ineffective as no denial at all" (PBCom v. CA; J.P. Juan & Sons v. Lianga).

paras.html: Imelda and FM personally signed the foundation documents (Xandy, Trinidad, Rayby, Maler, "Jane Ryan" accounts), and she failed to deny their genuineness under oath (Sec. 8, Rule 8). Citing Sandiganbayan Justice Villaruz's dissent, the pattern of foundations, pseudonyms, dummies, beneficiary regulations, renamings, and liquidations shows FM and/or Imelda were the real owners. The ITRs and balance sheets were their own records, verifiable with the BIR. The children, as heirs and successors-in-interest, are bound by FM's acts.

paras.html: Negative pregnant: para. 22 of the Answer denied only that respondents "clandestinely stashed" the country's wealth, adding that the properties were lawfully acquired. This admits (1) that the Swiss deposits existed, and (2) that they totaled about US$356 million. "Where a fact is alleged with qualifying or modifying language and the words of the allegation as so qualified or modified are literally denied… the qualifying circumstances alone are denied while the fact itself is admitted." Paras. 47, 48, and 52-a (Rosalys-Aguamina; total of US$356 million) were not denied at all → deemed admitted (Sec. 11, Rule 8; Galofa v. Nee Bon Sing).

paras.html: Sec. 1, Rule 35 allows the claimant to move "at any time after the pleading in answer thereto has been served", with no fixed period. A question of first impression, so the Court looked to US law: like New York's Rule 113, our rules require issues to be joined first, after which the motion may be made "at any stage of the litigation" (Ecker v. Muzysh: allowed even after trial and submission).

paras.html: → The Republic, which moved after pre-trial and before presenting evidence, did not waive summary judgment by agreeing to trial. This reading serves the Rule's purpose of weeding out sham defenses and Sec. 6, Rule 1 (liberal construction). The Court also warned that, in cases with political undertones, parties delay in hopes that "a future administration sympathetic to them" may influence the outcome, which is "rank injustice."

paras.html: Laches = unreasonable, unexplained neglect to assert a right (Madeja v. Patcho). The Republic was never remiss: its first motion (1996) was denied because of the compromise, and it moved again after the Marcoses disowned the funds at pre-trial.

paras.html: Even assuming laches, "the doctrine of estoppel or laches does not apply when the government sues as a sovereign or asserts governmental rights" (Collado v. CA; fn. 73 also cites Sec. 15, Art. XI), and estoppel cannot validate an act contrary to law or public policy. Laches is principally a question of equity, and equity favors the Republic.

paras.html: Responding to the "penal statute / Sec. 3(c)–(e)" argument: it was not for the Republic to establish the Marcoses' other lawful income; respondents were in a better position to know and should have stated it in their answer. Allowing them to fault the Republic for missing SALs would reward their violation of the law.

paras.html: Quo warranto lies against an impeachable officer whose title is defective: Sec. 2, Art. XI ("may be removed") is permissive and does not make impeachment the exclusive mode of removal. Quo warranto tests title (eligibility at the time of appointment or election); impeachment tests fitness for acts in office. Per the Court's guidelines, an act or omission prior to or at the time of appointment that bears on qualifications may be raised in quo warranto; acts during incumbency by a validly appointed officer go to impeachment (if impeachable) or to disciplinary, administrative, or criminal action.

paras.html: SALN and integrity: Filing a SALN is a constitutional and statutory duty (Sec. 17, Art. XI; RA 6713; RA 3019). Its repeated non-filing, and non-submission to the JBC, negates "proven integrity" (Sec. 7(3), Art. VIII). This ineligibility is not cured by JBC nomination or presidential appointment; the appointee is a de facto officer removable by quo warranto.

Title to public office may be attacked only directly, by quo warranto (Nacionalista Party v. De Vera: prohibition cannot substitute).

paras.html: Text: "may" is permissive; an option to remove by impeachment admits of alternatives. Per Burke Shartel, expressio unius does not apply to one of several common-law remedies; the impeachment clause was made express to create a legislative check and to limit Congress, not to make it exclusive. The enumeration of impeachable offenses is not a complete statement of causes of removal. The Court rejected her reading that "may" refers only to lesser penalties, since Sec. 3(7) fixes removal and disqualification.

paras.html: Six reasons: (1) except for the President and VP under the PET Rules, impeachment is the only mode of removing impeachable officers (Sec. 2, Art. XI); (2) SALN submission to the JBC is not a constitutional qualification; (3) the one-year period lapsed a year after her 2012 appointment; (4) the JBC treated her submissions as substantial compliance, and any defect should have been assailed by certiorari before appointment; (5) non-filing under RA 6713 has its own procedure (Sec. 11), not quo warranto; (6) the OSG failed to prove non-filing, since the custodians' certifications lost value once other SALNs surfaced.

paras.html: Quo warranto lies against an impeachable officer whose title is defective: Sec. 2, Art. XI ("may be removed") is permissive and does not make impeachment the exclusive mode of removal. Quo warranto tests title (eligibility at the time of appointment or election); impeachment tests fitness for acts in office. Per the Court's guidelines, an act or omission prior to or at the time of appointment that bears on qualifications may be raised in quo warranto; acts during incumbency by a validly appointed officer go to impeachment (if impeachable) or to disciplinary, administrative, or criminal action.

paras.html: Prescription does not run against the State: The one-year period in Sec. 11, Rule 66 does not bar a quo warranto action brought by the Solicitor General for the State (nullum tempus occurrit regi), especially where the respondent concealed the defect.

paras.html: SALN and integrity: Filing a SALN is a constitutional and statutory duty (Sec. 17, Art. XI; RA 6713; RA 3019). Its repeated non-filing, and non-submission to the JBC, negates "proven integrity" (Sec. 7(3), Art. VIII). This ineligibility is not cured by JBC nomination or presidential appointment; the appointee is a de facto officer removable by quo warranto.

paras.html: Quo warranto is proper to question the validity of her appointment, unlike impeachment, which charges offenses committed in office. It is available even against impeachable officers (2010 PET Rules; Funa v. Villar; Nacionalista Party v. De Vera; Estrada v. Desierto; Lawyers League v. Aquino).

paras.html: "May be removed" in Sec. 2, Art. XI allows other modes (verba legis); her reading leads to absurdity. The Court has an Ethics Committee investigating its own Members (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC). Eligibility is a legal, not political, question.

paras.html: Impeachment (Greek eisangelia → British → US → 1935 Constitution; "betrayal of public trust" added in 1987) is political: the legislature vindicates breach of public trust by determining the officer's fitness to stay in office.

Title to public office may be attacked only directly, by quo warranto (Nacionalista Party v. De Vera: prohibition cannot substitute).

paras.html: Text: "may" is permissive; an option to remove by impeachment admits of alternatives. Per Burke Shartel, expressio unius does not apply to one of several common-law remedies; the impeachment clause was made express to create a legislative check and to limit Congress, not to make it exclusive. The enumeration of impeachable offenses is not a complete statement of causes of removal. The Court rejected her reading that "may" refers only to lesser penalties, since Sec. 3(7) fixes removal and disqualification.

parts.h: GUIDELINES FOR THE BENCH, THE BAR AND THE JBC (Part IV)

paras.html: Quo warranto to oust an ineligible official lies when the act or omission was committed prior to or at the time of appointment or election and relates to qualifications. Acts during incumbency by a validly appointed or elected official go to impeachment (if impeachable and an impeachable offense) or to disciplinary, administrative, or criminal action.

paras.html: Six reasons: (1) except for the President and VP under the PET Rules, impeachment is the only mode of removing impeachable officers (Sec. 2, Art. paras.html: The pardoning power cannot be limited by legislative action: The only instances in which the President may not extend pardon are (1) impeachment cases, (2) cases without a final conviction, and (3) violations of election laws, rules, and regulations without the COMELEC's favorable recommendation (Sec. 19, Art. VII; Sec. 5, Art. IX-C). "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

VII; Sec. 5, Art. IX-C). "Subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action."

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 of the RPC are harmonized, not applied rigidly: They only impart that the pardon of the principal penalty does not carry the remission of the accessory penalties unless the President expressly includes them. A pardon stating that the grantee "is hereby restored to his civil and political rights" substantially complies with the requirement of express restoration, because the right to seek public elective office is a political right.

paras.html: A whereas clause cannot make a pardon conditional: A preamble is not part of the operative language; absent a condition stated in the pardon itself, a "whereas" recital does not limit its scope or make its effectivity contingent.

paras.html: On September 12, 2007, the Sandiganbayan convicted former President Joseph Ejercito Estrada of plunder (Crim. Case No. 26558; RA 7080, as amended by RA 7659). Finding no aggravating or mitigating circumstance, it imposed the lesser penalty under Art. 63 RPC: reclusion perpetua with the accessory penalties of civil interdiction during the period of sentence and perpetual absolute disqualification. It also declared forfeited the Erap Muslim Youth Foundation deposit, the Jose Velarde account (₱189,000,000.00), and the "Boracay Mansion." [sic: the first forfeited amount reads "Five Hundred Forty-Two Million Seven Hundred Ninety-One Thousand Pesos (P545,291,000.00)"; the publisher notes the discrepancy between words and figures.]

paras.text: On January 24, 2013 [Leonen's dissent gives January 14, 2013 as the filing date and January 24, 2013 as the date of Estrada's answer], Risos-Vidal filed a petition for disqualification with the COMELEC (SPA No. 13-211 (DC)). She argued that Estrada is disqualified because of his plunder conviction and his sentence of reclusion perpetua with perpetual absolute disqualification, relying on Sec. 40 of the LGC in relation to Sec. 12 of the OEC:

paras.html: Sec. 40, LGC. The following persons are disqualified from running for any elective local position: (a) Those sentenced by final judgment for an offense involving moral turpitude or for an offense punishable by one (1) year or more of imprisonment, within two (2) years after serving sentence; …
paras.text: Sec. 40, LGC. The following persons are disqualified from running for any elective local position: (a) Those sentenced by final judgment for an offense involving moral turpitude or for an offense punishable by one (1) year or more of imprisonment, within two (2) years after serving sentence; …

paras.html: Sec. 12, OEC. Any person who … has been sentenced by final judgment … for any offense for which he has been sentenced to a penalty of more than eighteen months or for a crime involving moral turpitude, shall be disqualified to be a candidate and to hold any public office, unless he has been given plenary pardon or granted amnesty.
paras.text: Sec. 12, OEC. Any person who … has been sentenced by final judgment … for any offense for which he has been sentenced to a penalty of more than eighteen months or for a crime involving moral turpitude, shall be disqualified to be a candidate and to hold any public office, unless he has been given plenary pardon or granted amnesty.

paras.html: On April 1, 2013, the COMELEC Second Division dismissed the petition "for utter lack of merit." Having taken judicial cognizance of the consolidated 2010 resolution in SPA Nos. 09-028 and 09-104 and the En Banc resolution affirming it, it would "not belabor the controversy further"; Risos-Vidal failed to present cogent proof to reverse its standing pronouncement that the pardon restored Estrada's right to seek public office, and it would "no longer engage in disquisitions of a settled matter."

paras.html: On April 30, 2013, Risos-Vidal filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64, in relation to Rule 65, to annul the two COMELEC Resolutions for grave abuse of discretion. She raised five issues: the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion (I) in holding that the pardon was not conditional; (II) in not finding Estrada disqualified under Sec. 40 LGC for plunder, a crime involving moral turpitude; (III) in dismissing her petition because it involved the same issues resolved in the 2010 Pormento and Mary Lou Estrada cases; (IV) in not ruling that the pardon neither restored his right of suffrage nor remitted his perpetual absolute disqualification; and (V) in not disqualifying him motu proprio.

paras.html: The pardon was conditional. Estrada's express acceptance shows its conditional nature, and the condition is the third whereas clause (his public commitment to no longer seek elective office). That commitment impelled PGMA to grant the pardon; by filing COCs for President and for Mayor, he breached it, so "he ought to be recommitted to prison to serve the unexpired portion of his sentence" and is disqualified.

paras.html: Fundamental basis: Sec. 40 LGC in relation to Sec. 12 OEC. Plunder is punishable by imprisonment of one year or more and involves moral turpitude. The OEC exception does not apply because the pardon was merely conditional, not "plenary."

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 RPC are mandatory. A general restoration of "civil and political rights" does not restore the right to hold public office or the right of suffrage, nor remit civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification, unless the specific rights are categorically mentioned. They shun a general or implied restoration.
paras.text: Arts. 36 and 41 RPC are mandatory. A general restoration of "civil and political rights" does not restore the right to hold public office or the right of suffrage, nor remit civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification, unless the specific rights are categorically mentioned. They shun a general or implied restoration.

paras.html: Monsanto v. Factoran, Jr. Citing the concurring opinions of JJ. Padilla and Feliciano, restoration of the right to hold public office "cannot be left to inference, no matter how intensely arguable, but must be stated in express, explicit, positive and specific language." Express restoration is further demanded by the third whereas clause.

paras.html: Sec. 19, Art. VII lets the President grant reprieves, commutations, and pardons, and remit fines and forfeitures, "after conviction by final judgment," "except in cases of impeachment, or as otherwise provided in this Constitution." Sec. 5, Art. IX-C bars pardon for violations of election laws "without the favorable recommendation of the Commission."

paras.html: → The only instances in which the President may not pardon are: (1) impeachment cases; (2) cases that have not yet resulted in a final conviction; and (3) election-law violations without the COMELEC's favorable recommendation. "Therefore, it can be argued that any act of Congress by way of statute cannot operate to delimit the pardoning power of the President."

paras.html: Cristobal v. Labrador and Pelobello v. Palatino (1935 Constitution, similar phrasing): "subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution, the pardoning power cannot be restricted or controlled by legislative action." Reiterated in Monsanto v. Factoran, Jr. under the present Constitution: "a pardon, being a presidential prerogative, should not be circumscribed by legislative action."

This shows adherence to the "doctrine of non-diminution or non-impairment" of the pardoning power by acts of Congress.

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 "cannot, in any way, serve to abridge or diminish the exclusive power and prerogative of the President to pardon." A rigid and inflexible reading is unwarranted, "especially so if it will defeat or unduly restrict the power of the President to grant executive clemency."

paras.html: The codal provisions must be construed to harmonize the power of Congress to define crimes and prescribe penalties with the President's power to grant clemency. "All that the said provisions impart is that the pardon of the principal penalty does not carry with it the remission of the accessory penalties unless the President expressly includes said accessory penalties in the pardon." They still recognize the President's choice to pardon the principal penalty alone or both; they "only clarify the effect of the pardon."

paras.html: Applied (even under Arts. 36 and 41): The pardon's first sentence covers the principal penalty of reclusion perpetua (relieving imprisonment); the second sentence, "He is hereby restored to his civil and political rights," expressly remitted the accessory penalties. "Hence, even if we apply Articles 36 and 41 … it is indubitable from the text of the pardon that the accessory penalties of civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification were expressly remitted."

paras.html: A preamble "is not an essential part of an act"; it merely explains the reasons for it (People v. Balasa), and whereas clauses are not part of the operative language (Llamado v. CA). The clause "is not an integral part of the decree of the pardon" and does not by itself make the pardon conditional, make its effectivity contingent on the commitment, or limit its scope.

If PGMA intended a condition, "the former ought to have explicitly stated the same in the text of the pardon itself."

paras.html: Leonen: Arts. 36 and 41 are only "requirements of convention or form," a "procedural prescription" on how the President exercises the power; they do not reduce its coverage, so the President must state the restoration expressly.

paras.html: Ponencia: [sic: the ponencia here lapses into the first person, "With due respect, I disagree."] It rejects "the overbroad statement that Congress may dictate as to how the President may exercise his/her power of executive clemency." The form or manner by which a branch exercises its constitutional powers cannot be interfered with unless the Constitution so provides; this is the essence of separation of powers (BOCEA v. Teves), especially where non-compliance with a form imposed by one branch would diminish an exclusive prerogative of another. → Arts. 36 and 41 must be construed to give full effect to the clemency.

paras.html: "Absolute pardon" as officially defined: The Board of Pardons and Parole rules define an absolute pardon as one that "restores to the individual his civil and political rights"; the pardon used the BPP's wording, so PGMA clearly intended it to be absolute.

paras.html: Political rights include suffrage and the right to hold office (Simon v. CHR; ICCPR; RA 9225). Leonen's reading is "a very literal reading of 80-year old provisions"; the RPC predates the 1987 Constitution. Harmonized, the RPC form requirement is satisfied by restoring "political rights"; "full" is surplusage.

paras.html: II. Civil and political rights restored. The pardon substantially complied with Arts. 36 and 41. Monsanto favors Estrada: the absolute pardon there removed the disqualification, and the strict view of JJ. Padilla and Feliciano was not adopted by the majority, so it is obiter. He does not subscribe to Estrada's theory that Arts. 36 and 41 abridge the pardoning power. The omission of "full" may have been inadvertence; PGMA could have stated clear exceptions.

paras.html: Timeliness: The petition was a petition for disqualification under Sec. 40 LGC and Sec. 12 OEC, not a Sec. 78 petition (Fermin v. COMELEC); it was filed after the last day for COCs and before proclamation, within Rule 25, Sec. 3 of COMELEC Res. No. 9523.

VII) and the nuisance-candidate ground, not on Sec. 40 LGC; the subject matter differed (presidency v. mayoralty); the COMELEC's pardon statements were obiter; and Pormento ended in mootness, so there was no final judgment on the merits.

paras.html: Nature of pardon: "Forgiveness but not forgetfulness." Monsanto repudiated Garland, Cristobal, and Pelobello; pardon is a private, though official, act that does not erase the moral stain.

paras.html: Arts. 36 and 41 do not abridge the pardoning power: They do not reduce its coverage (Llamas v. Orbos); they are "requirements of convention or form" asking the President to state the intent "clearly, directly, firmly, precisely, and unmistakably." Public office is a public trust, while pardon is a private act; the phrase "as otherwise provided in this Constitution" requires reading Sec. 19 with the public-trust injunction.

paras.html: Clarifying Monsanto: Its "inclusion" statement was made in a comparative survey, relied on a U.S. case, and did not account for Arts. 36 and 41; it is superseded by People v. Casido and People v. Patriarca (citing Barrioquinto v. Fernandez) and Romeo Jalosjos v. COMELEC (2013).

paras.html: No express restoration or remission: The pardon is silent on suffrage, office, and perpetual absolute disqualification. Estrada relies on inference ("deemed subsumed," "substantial compliance"), which is exactly what "express" excludes. "Civil and political rights" is a collectivity or "basket" (ICCPR; Vasak; Simon v. CHR), while Arts. 36 and 41 single out suffrage and office. PGMA departed from the standard "full civil and political rights" formula and was silent; together these mean the rights were not restored. Estrada's other civil and political rights were restored.

paras.html: Preambular clauses: Even if ambiguous, the whereas clauses resolve it against Estrada (People v. Purisima). The third clause is "an indispensable qualifier": the pardon was premised on his promise not to seek office, consistent with the gravity of plunder (Estrada v. Sandiganbayan: malum in se).

paras.html: Nature of the writs: The writ of amparo is an extraordinary and independent remedy that provides rapid judicial relief; it is a summary proceeding that requires only substantial evidence. It does not determine criminal, civil, or administrative liability; it determines responsibility, or at least accountability, for the enforced disappearance or extrajudicial killing so the Court can craft the proper remedies. The writ of habeas data likewise protects the right to informational privacy without any finding of culpability.
paras.text: Nature of the writs: The writ of amparo is an extraordinary and independent remedy that provides rapid judicial relief; it is a summary proceeding that requires only substantial evidence. It does not determine criminal, civil, or administrative liability; it determines responsibility, or at least accountability, for the enforced disappearance or extrajudicial killing so the Court can craft the proper remedies. The writ of habeas data likewise protects the right to informational privacy without any finding of culpability.

paras.html: Command responsibility in amparo: The doctrine may be applied in amparo proceedings, but only to determine responsibility and accountability (who is accountable for, and has the duty to address, the disappearance), not to fix criminal liability or as a prelude to administrative proceedings. The President, as Commander-in-Chief, may be held responsible or accountable if the elements are shown by substantial evidence.

paras.html: Presidential immunity: Immunity from suit is concurrent only with the President's tenure (incumbency), not the term. A non-sitting President cannot invoke it, even for acts during her tenure (Estrada v. Desierto), and so cannot shield herself from an amparo court's determination of responsibility or accountability.

paras.html: The abduction, detention, and torture (6–17 September 2009):
paras.text: The abduction, detention, and torture (6–17 September 2009):

paras.html: 6 Sept 2009, 5:00 p.m.: Rodriguez reached Brgy. Tapel, Cagayan, on a tricycle driven by Hermie Antonio Carlos when four men forcibly took him into a car. The men tied his hands, sat on his back, and punched him, forcing him to confess to being an NPA member. Around 2:00 a.m. the car entered a military camp with a "Bravo" banner, which he later learned belonged to the 17th Infantry Battalion, Philippine Army.
paras.text: 6 Sept 2009, 5:00 p.m.: Rodriguez reached Brgy. Tapel, Cagayan, on a tricycle driven by Hermie Antonio Carlos when four men forcibly took him into a car. The men tied his hands, sat on his back, and punched him, forcing him to confess to being an NPA member. Around 2:00 a.m. the car entered a military camp with a "Bravo" banner, which he later learned belonged to the 17th Infantry Battalion, Philippine Army.

paras.html: 7–8 Sept: He was blindfolded, interrogated, repeatedly hit on the head, threatened with death, tied to a papag, and driven around Bugey and Mission to point out his "contacts"; a soldier pointed a gun at his head and threatened him and his family.
paras.text: 7–8 Sept: He was blindfolded, interrogated, repeatedly hit on the head, threatened with death, tied to a papag, and driven around Bugey and Mission to point out his "contacts"; a soldier pointed a gun at his head and threatened him and his family.

paras.html: 9–11 Sept: Soldiers made him their guide to an NPA camp in Birao. "Harry," a supposed NPA surrenderer, called him an NPA member. He noticed a soldier with the name tag "Matutina," whom other soldiers addressed as "sir." The soldiers threatened him and one "Elvis" with death; they spent three nights in the mountains.

paras.html: 12–13 Sept: Back in camp he was punched and kicked again, forced to sign documents declaring that he had surrendered and had become a military asset in May (he signed with a different signature to show coercion), and forced to sign a paper the soldiers wrote. He was beaten and electrocuted for about an hour.

paras.html: 15–16 Sept: He was taken on a military operation, where he saw Matutina again. He was then brought to the Enrile Medical Center, where Dr. Juliet Ramil found four hematomas; he lied that he had slipped because a soldier was watching. Soldiers photographed him eating with officers and pointing at a map, and made him sign a paper stating that he was a surrenderee who was never beaten, warning him not to talk to the media.

paras.html: Amparo: an extraordinary and independent remedy that provides rapid judicial relief; a summary proceeding requiring only substantial evidence. It is not an action to determine criminal guilt (proof beyond reasonable doubt), liability for damages (preponderance), or administrative responsibility requiring full and exhaustive proceedings (Secretary of National Defense v. Manalo).
paras.text: Amparo: an extraordinary and independent remedy that provides rapid judicial relief; a summary proceeding requiring only substantial evidence. It is not an action to determine criminal guilt (proof beyond reasonable doubt), liability for damages (preponderance), or administrative responsibility requiring full and exhaustive proceedings (Secretary of National Defense v. Manalo).

paras.html: It is preventive (breaks the expectation of impunity) and curative (facilitates subsequent punishment by leading to investigation and action).
paras.text: It is preventive (breaks the expectation of impunity) and curative (facilitates subsequent punishment by leading to investigation and action).

paras.html: Habeas data: a judicial remedy to protect a person's right to control information about oneself, especially information collected through unlawful means for unlawful ends (Roxas v. Arroyo). It is an independent and summary remedy protecting the right to privacy, especially informational privacy; no finding of culpability. If proven by substantial evidence, the Court may (a) grant access to the database or information, (b) enjoin the act complained of, or (c) order deletion, destruction, or rectification of erroneous data (Sec. 16, Rule on Habeas Data).

Carpio-Morales's Separate Opinion in Rubrico (quoted by the ponencia as "worth noting"): amparo's non-determination of liability should not abate the doctrine; Manalo and Tagitis do not preclude it (Tagitis held PNP/CIDG accountable through their incumbent Chiefs); RA 9851 treats superior responsibility only as a ground for criminal responsibility because of its purpose, not to rule out other applications; insulating high-ranking officers from amparo reliefs is dangerous.

paras.html: Boac v. Cadapan (penned by J. Carpio-Morales), which reiterated that opinion: Rubrico denies command responsibility to determine criminal liability, but recognizes a "preliminary yet limited application"; it "may be loosely applied in amparo cases in order to identify those accountable individuals that have the power to effectively implement whatever processes an amparo court would issue," pinpointing the superiors in the best position to protect the aggrieved party. Such identification may be a preliminary determination of criminal liability, still subject to investigation by the proper agency.

paras.html: Sec. 1: an official may be liable for neglect of duty if he knows a crime will be, is being, or has been committed by subordinates or others in his area of responsibility and takes no preventive or corrective action.

Responsibility covers participation by action or omission; accountability attaches to those with knowledge who bear the burden of disclosure, or who failed to discharge the burden of extraordinary diligence in the investigation.

paras.html: Secretary of National Defense v. Manalo: the right to security of person is a guarantee of protection of one's rights by the government, built into Art. III, Secs. 1 and 2, and a corollary of the State policy that it "guarantees full respect for human rights" (Art. II, Sec. 11). Protection includes conducting effective investigations, organizing the government apparatus to protect victims, and bringing offenders to justice.

paras.html: No statutory exemption from legislative inquiry: Sec. 4(b) of E.O. No. 1 ("No member or staff of the Commission shall be required to testify or produce evidence in any judicial, legislative or administrative proceeding concerning matters within its official cognizance") is directly repugnant to Art. VI, Sec. 21 and is declared REPEALED by the 1987 Constitution (Art. XVIII, Sec. 3). "A mere provision of law cannot pose a limitation to the broad power of Congress, in the absence of any constitutional basis."
paras.text: No statutory exemption from legislative inquiry: Sec. 4(b) of E.O. No. 1 ("No member or staff of the Commission shall be required to testify or produce evidence in any judicial, legislative or administrative proceeding concerning matters within its official cognizance") is directly repugnant to Art. VI, Sec. 21 and is declared REPEALED by the 1987 Constitution (Art. XVIII, Sec. 3). "A mere provision of law cannot pose a limitation to the broad power of Congress, in the absence of any constitutional basis."

paras.html: Scope of the power: the power of inquiry is co-extensive with the power to legislate, is "broad enough to cover officials of the executive branch" (Senate v. Ermita), and extends "to government agencies created by Congress and officers whose positions are within the power of Congress to regulate or even abolish." Sec. 4(b) also violates public accountability (Art. XI, Sec. 1), full public disclosure (Art. II, Sec. 28), and the right to information (Art. III, Sec. 7).

paras.html: Committees' contempt power; witnesses' rights: Sec. 21 is a direct conferral of the power of inquiry on the committees, carrying all powers necessary for its effective discharge, including contempt. Witnesses' rights must be respected, but there is no reasonable expectation of privacy over acts as officers of corporations in which the government has an interest, and the right against self-incrimination may be invoked only when the incriminating question is asked.

paras.html: Feb. 20, 2006: Sen. Miriam Defensor Santiago introduced SR No. 455, directing an inquiry in aid of legislation into the anomalous losses of POTC, PHILCOMSAT, and Philcomsat Holdings Corporation (PHC) due to alleged improprieties of their boards. Its whereas clauses cited: PHC's representation and entertainment expense rising to ₱4.3 million in the last quarter of 2005 (from ₱106,000 the previous year); over ₱73 million advanced in 18 months to a wholly owned subsidiary, Telecommunications Center, Inc. (TCI), without accountability reports; a reported ₱265 million release and a ₱125 million loan to a relative of an executive committee member (with an estimated ₱11.25 million interest income loss in 2004); and the need to protect the government's equity in these corporations.

paras.text: Re: Nature and breadth of the power of inquiry

paras.html: Origins: recognized in McGrain v. Daugherty and cited in Arnault v. Nazareno; American courts treated it as inherent in the power to legislate (Briggs v. MacKellar: "The right to pass laws, necessarily implies the right to obtain information upon any matter which may become the subject of a law").

MacKellar: "The right to pass laws, necessarily implies the right to obtain information upon any matter which may become the subject of a law").

paras.html: Arnault (citing McGrain): the power of inquiry, with process to enforce it, is "an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function"; a legislature cannot legislate wisely without information it often lacks.

paras.html: Executive agreements may implement existing treaties: the President may choose an executive agreement for matters involving foreign military forces provided it is not the principal agreement that first allows their entry, stays within the parameters of the law or treaty it implements (no new or expanded obligations), and is consistent with the Constitution and laws. Executive agreements must be traceable to express or implied authorization and are inferior to treaties and statutes. EDCA validly implements the VFA and MDT.

paras.html: 1947 Military Bases Agreement (MBA); 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) (concurred in by both Senates: mutual development of capacities to resist armed attack, and mutual defense); 1953 Military Assistance Agreement. The MBA expired in 1991 after the Senate rejected a new treaty. The 1987 Constitution added Art. XVIII, Sec. 25: after 1991, foreign military bases, troops, or facilities "shall not be allowed in the Philippines except under a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate" (and, if Congress requires, ratified in a referendum, and recognized as a treaty by the other State). The Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) was concurred in by the Senate and upheld in Bayan v. Zamora (2000); Lim v. Executive Secretary upheld the Balikatan Terms of Reference; Nicolas v. Romulo struck down the Romulo-Kenney Agreement as contrary to the VFA.

paras.html: After about two years and eight rounds of negotiations, the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) was signed on April 28, 2014 by the Defense Secretary and the US Ambassador; President Aquino ratified it on June 6, 2014. In June 2014, the DFA and US Embassy exchanged notes confirming completion of all internal requirements for entry into force. EDCA was not transmitted to the Senate, the Executive believing it unnecessary.

The Philippines retains ownership of Agreed Locations and permanent structures, has access, and keeps primary responsibility for security; prepositioned materiel excludes nuclear weapons; obligations are subject to available appropriated funds (Art. X(1)).

paras.html: Actual case – YES: against the OSG's claim that no Senator was deprived, the Senate itself took a contrary position in SR 105, and the Senators' abstention from suit is not decisive. The DFA's confirmation that "all internal requirements ... have already been complied with" was the last act before entry into force (Art. XII(1)) → ripe.

paras.html: Standing – NONE of the petitioners: as citizens, they asserted no specific public right; as taxpayers, there is no appropriation or disbursement (Art. X(1): obligations subject to appropriated funds); as legislators, the party-list Representatives lack standing because concurrence is the Senate's institutional prerogative, not the whole Legislature's (Pimentel v. Executive Secretary). The Senate as a body would have standing but did not file a pleading.

paras.html: Transcendental importance – YES: the Court weighed (1) the character of funds or assets, (2) a clear case of disregard of a constitutional prohibition, and (3) the lack of a party with a more direct interest. The issue is "rooted in the Constitution itself": Sec. 25 imposes a much stricter mechanism, and the DFA has confirmed completion → "this case is a proper subject for judicial review."

paras.html: Sec. 25 is unambiguous: all agreements concerning foreign military bases, troops, or facilities after 1991 must go to the Senate; the Executive has no choice of form. SR 105 cites Art. paras.html: Re: The President's constitutional role
paras.text: Re: The President's constitutional role

paras.html: The President's oath and Art. VII, Sec. 17 impose the duty to faithfully execute the laws, which is self-executory and includes ensuring compliance with treaties and executive agreements; it is followed by the commander-in-chief powers, and the duty to defend the country is unceasing. In foreign affairs, the President is "the sole organ of the nation in its external relations" (Curtiss-Wright; Bayan; Pimentel) and is accorded "a wider degree of discretion" (Puno's dissent in Lantion; Vinuya v. Romulo) → apart from express or implied limits, "the manner of execution by the President must be given utmost deference." Answering J. Brion, this does not let the President bypass Senate concurrence.

paras.html: Verba legis: "shall not be allowed" is a negative injunction; "allow" means to permit or consent to presence, and "in" denotes place. → "the constitutional restriction refers solely to the initial entry of the foreign military bases, troops, or facilities. Once entry is authorized, the subsequent acts are thereafter subject only to the limitations provided by the rest of the Constitution and Philippine law." The VFA already allowed entry of US troops (Lim). Verba legis applies even to provisions with a specific historical context (answering J. Brion).

VII, Sec. 21 do not include executive agreements. Executive agreements are concluded (1) to adjust the details of a treaty, (2) pursuant to legislative authority, or (3) under the President's independent powers.

paras.html: Two domestic distinctions: (1) executive agreements "must remain traceable to an express or implied authorization" and "cannot create new international obligations" beyond the law they implement; (2) treaties are superior: on par with statutes (later prevails), while executive agreements inconsistent with a law or treaty are ineffective. Both are subject to the Constitution. Constitutional limits include nuclear-free policy, tariffs, tax exemptions, foreign loans, and Sec. 25.

paras.html: The President's choice: "No court can tell the President to desist from choosing an executive agreement over a treaty ... unless the case falls squarely within" Sec. 25 [cited as "Article VIII, Section 25"]. Per EO 459, Sec. 9, the DFA determines whether an agreement is an executive agreement or a treaty. The Court's task is to check consistency with applicable limitations. Precedents of executive agreements adjusting details of military treaties: the Balikatan Terms of Reference (Lim) and the Romulo-Kenney Agreement (Nicolas, struck for inconsistency with the VFA).

paras.html: Re: The guidelines
paras.text: Re: The guidelines

paras.html: (1) An agreement allowing foreign military bases, troops, or facilities must be a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate. (2) Otherwise, the President may choose the form, provided the agreement is not the principal agreement that first allows their entry or presence. (3) The executive agreement must not go beyond the parameters, limitations, and standards of the law or treaty it implements, nor unduly expand its obligations. (4) It must be consistent with the Constitution and existing laws and treaties. Having chosen an executive agreement, respondents bear the burden of proving EDCA merely implements existing laws and treaties.

paras.html: Petitioners "cherry-picked" badges of exclusivity: the "return" of Agreed Locations is within activities authorized by the joint Mutual Defense Board and Security Engagement Board; "unimpeded access" is an adjunct to US ownership of its own prepositioned materiel, cleared by those joint mechanisms. The Court listed ten differences from the 1947 MBA (e.g., under the MBA the US had jurisdiction over bases and authority to control movement; under EDCA the Philippines has access to the entire area, US access is temporary, and the US cannot expropriate land) → "EDCA is a far cry from a basing agreement." EDCA is essentially a contract of use and access; ownership may coexist with transfer of some rights of control.

paras.html: Three standards from the ConCom: (i) independence from foreign control: "operational control" means command over personnel (as in Philippine law), not control over the Agreed Locations; US control over construction is limited and not unconstitutional. (ii) Philippine sovereignty and applicable law: the Philippines retains ownership and access, and primary responsibility for security; Philippine law applies and Philippine forces act as peace officers. (iii) national security and territorial integrity: fear of attack is "not in the realm of law, but of politics and policy"; the UN Charter (Arts. 2(4), 51) and international humanitarian law (distinction) do not make Agreed Locations lawful targets merely by US presence. Sec. 25's "bases, troops, or facilities" are three independent restrictions (Bayan v. Zamora).

paras.html: VFA scope: the VFA governs presence for "visits, joint exercises and other activities" (Sec. Siazon, Senate report); "activities" was left undefined (Lim); the DFA primer cited by petitioners is inaccessible and not binding; the Court alone interprets the VFA with finality.

paras.html: MBA comparison: an exchange of notes is not an amendatory treaty but a formal communication on routine agreements; it cannot amend treaty obligations (so the MBA's jurisdiction provisions stood, with only a contractual waiver). The differences make EDCA "a very different instrument" from the MBA. Petitioners' factual claims on US practices go to the wisdom, not legality, of EDCA; their remedy lies with the political branches.

paras.html: 1947 Military Bases Agreement (MBA); 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) (concurred in by both Senates: mutual development of capacities to resist armed attack, and mutual defense); 1953 Military Assistance Agreement. The MBA expired in 1991 after the Senate rejected a new treaty. The 1987 Constitution added Art. XVIII, Sec. 25: after 1991, foreign military bases, troops, or facilities "shall not be allowed in the Philippines except under a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate" (and, if Congress requires, ratified in a referendum, and recognized as a treaty by the other State). The Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) was concurred in by the Senate and upheld in Bayan v. Zamora (2000); Lim v. Executive Secretary upheld the Balikatan Terms of Reference; Nicolas v. Romulo struck down the Romulo-Kenney Agreement as contrary to the VFA.

paras.html: Re: The President's constitutional role
paras.text: Re: The President's constitutional role

paras.html: The President's oath and Art. VII, Sec. 17 impose the duty to faithfully execute the laws, which is self-executory and includes ensuring compliance with treaties and executive agreements; it is followed by the commander-in-chief powers, and the duty to defend the country is unceasing. In foreign affairs, the President is "the sole organ of the nation in its external relations" (Curtiss-Wright; Bayan; Pimentel) and is accorded "a wider degree of discretion" (Puno's dissent in Lantion; Vinuya v. Romulo) → apart from express or implied limits, "the manner of execution by the President must be given utmost deference." Answering J. Brion, this does not let the President bypass Senate concurrence.

paras.html: Verba legis: "shall not be allowed" is a negative injunction; "allow" means to permit or consent to presence, and "in" denotes place. → "the constitutional restriction refers solely to the initial entry of the foreign military bases, troops, or facilities. Once entry is authorized, the subsequent acts are thereafter subject only to the limitations provided by the rest of the Constitution and Philippine law." The VFA already allowed entry of US troops (Lim). Verba legis applies even to provisions with a specific historical context (answering J. Brion).

VIII, Sec. 5(2)(a) subjects them to judicial review. Romulo: the subjects are "not cast in stone."

paras.html: ConCom: after Fr. Bernas read Eastern Sea Trading, Comm. Aquino withdrew her proposal to expressly except executive agreements; Bernas confirmed that "international agreements" in Art. VII, Sec. 21 do not include executive agreements. Executive agreements are concluded (1) to adjust the details of a treaty, (2) pursuant to legislative authority, or (3) under the President's independent powers.

paras.html: Two domestic distinctions: (1) executive agreements "must remain traceable to an express or implied authorization" and "cannot create new international obligations" beyond the law they implement; (2) treaties are superior: on par with statutes (later prevails), while executive agreements inconsistent with a law or treaty are ineffective. Both are subject to the Constitution. Constitutional limits include nuclear-free policy, tariffs, tax exemptions, foreign loans, and Sec. 25.

paras.html: The President's choice: "No court can tell the President to desist from choosing an executive agreement over a treaty ... unless the case falls squarely within" Sec. 25 [cited as "Article VIII, Section 25"]. Per EO 459, Sec. 9, the DFA determines whether an agreement is an executive agreement or a treaty. The Court's task is to check consistency with applicable limitations. Precedents of executive agreements adjusting details of military treaties: the Balikatan Terms of Reference (Lim) and the Romulo-Kenney Agreement (Nicolas, struck for inconsistency with the VFA).

paras.html: Re: The guidelines
paras.text: Re: The guidelines

paras.html: (1) An agreement allowing foreign military bases, troops, or facilities must be a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate. (2) Otherwise, the President may choose the form, provided the agreement is not the principal agreement that first allows their entry or presence. (3) The executive agreement must not go beyond the parameters, limitations, and standards of the law or treaty it implements, nor unduly expand its obligations. (4) It must be consistent with the Constitution and existing laws and treaties. Having chosen an executive agreement, respondents bear the burden of proving EDCA merely implements existing laws and treaties.

paras.html: Petitioners "cherry-picked" badges of exclusivity: the "return" of Agreed Locations is within activities authorized by the joint Mutual Defense Board and Security Engagement Board; "unimpeded access" is an adjunct to US ownership of its own prepositioned materiel, cleared by those joint mechanisms. The Court listed ten differences from the 1947 MBA (e.g., under the MBA the US had jurisdiction over bases and authority to control movement; under EDCA the Philippines has access to the entire area, US access is temporary, and the US cannot expropriate land) → "EDCA is a far cry from a basing agreement." EDCA is essentially a contract of use and access; ownership may coexist with transfer of some rights of control.

paras.html: Three standards from the ConCom: (i) independence from foreign control: "operational control" means command over personnel (as in Philippine law), not control over the Agreed Locations; US control over construction is limited and not unconstitutional. (ii) Philippine sovereignty and applicable law: the Philippines retains ownership and access, and primary responsibility for security; Philippine law applies and Philippine forces act as peace officers. (iii) national security and territorial integrity: fear of attack is "not in the realm of law, but of politics and policy"; the UN Charter (Arts. 2(4), 51) and international humanitarian law (distinction) do not make Agreed Locations lawful targets merely by US presence. Sec. 25's "bases, troops, or facilities" are three independent restrictions (Bayan v. Zamora).

paras.html: EDCA substantially modifies or amends the VFA: (1) rotational stationing in locations with permanent facilities and prepositioned materiel; (2) prepositioning of warships, aircraft, vehicles, ammunition; (3) use of Philippine territory to launch operations within or beyond it; (4) new concepts (agreed locations, contractors, prepositioning, operational control); (5) effects on statutes (court jurisdiction, local autonomy, taxation). An executive agreement cannot amend a treaty. SR 105 shows the Senate did not intend the VFA to cover these. "History will now record that in 2016, it is this Supreme Court that said yes to the EDCA."

paras.html: Per Bayan v. Zamora, Sec. 25 covers bases, troops, or facilities, each standing alone. The VFA contemplates only visiting troops; EDCA is a general framework for US access to Agreed Locations, practically allowing bases or facilities → a new treaty requiring Senate concurrence (consistent with SR 105). EDCA gives the AFP unfettered discretion, without standards, on the size, location, and number of Agreed Locations. "There is no 'reasonable and legitimate' ground to violate the Constitution."

paras.html: MBA comparison: an exchange of notes is not an amendatory treaty but a formal communication on routine agreements; it cannot amend treaty obligations (so the MBA's jurisdiction provisions stood, with only a contractual waiver). The differences make EDCA "a very different instrument" from the MBA. Petitioners' factual claims on US practices go to the wisdom, not legality, of EDCA; their remedy lies with the political branches.

paras.html: EDCA substantially modifies defense policy, not mere detail adjustments (Eastern Sea Trading). Even if Agreed Locations are not permanent bases (given EDCA's ten-year term), they and their activities match the US Defense Department's definition of "facilities" (where forces live, train, operate, with prepositioned materiel), which alone triggers Sec. 25 (Bayan v. Zamora). The MDT covers resisting external attack and the VFA only joint training; EDCA legitimizes the functional equivalent of bases. Grave abuse was committed. Votes to GRANT the MR.

paras.html: A declaration of a state of rebellion is valid but legally superfluous: The President's authority to declare a state of rebellion "springs in the main from her powers as chief executive and, at the same time, draws strength from her Commander-in-Chief powers" (with statutory basis in Sec. 4, Ch. 2, Bk. III, Administrative Code of 1987). But in calling out the armed forces, the declaration is "an utter superfluity": it only gives notice that a rebellion exists, is "devoid of any legal significance," and cannot diminish constitutional rights or by itself justify warrantless arrests.

III, Administrative Code of 1987). But in calling out the armed forces, the declaration is "an utter superfluity": it only gives notice that a rebellion exists, is "devoid of any legal significance," and cannot diminish constitutional rights or by itself justify warrantless arrests.

paras.html: Calling-out power needs no declaration: Sec. 18, Art. VII grants graduated powers. Actual invasion or rebellion and public safety are required only for suspending the privilege of the writ and declaring martial law; the calling-out power requires only that it "becomes necessary."

paras.html: Moot but capable of repetition yet evading review; legislators' standing: A moot case may still be decided if it is "capable of repetition yet evading review." Members of Congress have standing when an executive act impairs Congress's powers; organizations, taxpayers and citizens must show direct injury (taxpayers: illegal disbursement of public funds).

paras.html: In the wee hours of July 27, 2003, some three hundred junior officers and enlisted men of the AFP, armed with high-powered ammunitions and explosives, stormed the Oakwood Premiere apartments in Makati City. [The Ynares-Santiago and Sandoval-Gutierrez dissents put the number at 323 and identify them as the "Magdalo Group."]
paras.text: In the wee hours of July 27, 2003, some three hundred junior officers and enlisted men of the AFP, armed with high-powered ammunitions and explosives, stormed the Oakwood Premiere apartments in Makati City. [The Ynares-Santiago and Sandoval-Gutierrez dissents put the number at 323 and identify them as the "Magdalo Group."]

paras.html: Bewailing corruption in the AFP, the soldiers demanded, among others, the resignation of the President, the Secretary of National Defense, and the Chief of the PNP.

paras.html: Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4:
paras.text: Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4:

paras.html: Later that day, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (PGMA) issued Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4, both declaring "a state of rebellion" and calling out the AFP (and the PNP) to suppress the rebellion. [Per the dissents, Proc. 427 was issued at about 1:00 p.m.]
paras.text: Later that day, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo (PGMA) issued Proclamation No. 427 and General Order No. 4, both declaring "a state of rebellion" and calling out the AFP (and the PNP) to suppress the rebellion. [Per the dissents, Proc. 427 was issued at about 1:00 p.m.]

paras.html: Proc. 427 recited that certain AFP elements had seized a building in Makati, planted bombs, publicly withdrawn support from the Government, and taken arms against it, acts which "constitute the crime of rebellion punishable under Article 134 of the Revised Penal Code"; it invoked Sec. 18, Art. VII and stated:

VII and stated:

paras.html: "NOW, THEREFORE, I, GLORIA MACAPAGAL-ARROYO, by virtue of the powers vested in me by law, hereby confirm the existence of an actual and on-going rebellion, compelling me to declare a state of rebellion."
paras.text: "NOW, THEREFORE, I, GLORIA MACAPAGAL-ARROYO, by virtue of the powers vested in me by law, hereby confirm the existence of an actual and on-going rebellion, compelling me to declare a state of rebellion."

paras.html: GO 4 directed the AFP Chief and PNP Chief to "immediately carry out the necessary and appropriate actions and measures to suppress and quell the rebellion with due regard to constitutional rights."

paras.html: By the evening of July 27, 2003, after hours-long negotiations, the soldiers agreed to return to barracks, ending the occupation.

paras.html: PGMA did not immediately lift the declaration. She did so only on August 1, 2003, through Proclamation No. 435, declaring that the AFP and PNP had "effectively suppressed and quelled the rebellion" and that "the state of rebellion has ceased to exist."

paras.html: Andrew Jackson: defeated South Carolina's nullification of the Tariff Acts of 1828 and 1832; in his Dec. 10, 1832 Proclamation he warned that "disunion by armed force is treason."

paras.html: Abraham Lincoln: joined the CinC and executive-power clauses into "the war power"; called for 75,000 troops, suspended the writ, issued the Emancipation Proclamation. In the Prize Cases (1863), the U.S. Supreme Court, 5–4, upheld his blockade without prior congressional declaration of war.

paras.html: Justice Irene Cortes (The Philippine Presidency): the Philippine President has residual power even greater than the U.S. President's, because of the "unitary and highly centralized" government (no counterpart of reserved state powers); the grant of executive power is plenary (citing Ocampo v. paras.html: "[I]n calling out the armed forces, a declaration of a state of rebellion is an utter superfluity" (see J. Kapunan's dissent in Lacson v. Perez). At most, it only gives notice to the nation that such a state exists and that the armed forces may be called to prevent or suppress it.

paras.html: It may "wreak emotional effects" on perceived enemies of the State or the nation, but the Court probes only its legal consequences: "such a declaration is devoid of any legal significance. For all legal intents, the declaration is deemed not written."

paras.html: TLDR: Votes to declare Proc. No. 427 and GO No. 4 NULL and VOID for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack of jurisdiction, together with all orders and actions based on them, especially after the Oakwood incident ended on the evening of July 27, 2003 (e.g., warrantless arrests).

paras.html: If the requisites for a warrantless arrest must still be present anyway, the declaration is a superfluity. She "shudder[s]" at a blanket affirmation of the President's power to issue declarations that may be untrue or may stay in effect after the rebellion has ended.

paras.html: Facts she adds (citing the Feliciano Fact-Finding Commission Report): Proc. 427 was issued at 1:00 p.m. while 323 soldiers occupied Oakwood; searches ran from July 27 to Aug. 1 and found staging points in Cavite, Makati and Mandaluyong; Ramon Cardenas (Asst. Exec. Sec. of the previous administration) was arrested, presented to the media in handcuffs, brought to DOJ inquest on July 28, and charged with rebellion (later allowed bail); on July 31, a DOJ spokesperson said the "indefinite" state of rebellion made warrantless arrests valid; police released "evidence" linking opposition figures (Sen. Honasan; Sen. Loi Ejercito and Mayor JV Ejercito).

paras.html: Factual basis ignored: The majority discussed only the abstract nature of the powers, without considering whether there was a factual basis for the declaration and when it ended → it returns to, if not expands, Garcia-Padilla v. Enrile, which overturned Lansang v. Garcia (judicial inquiry into factual bases). The 1987 Constitution's grave-abuse clause (Sec. 1, Art. VIII) was meant precisely to check executive abuse.

paras.html: Rebellion and coup d'etat ended with the surrender: Under Arts. 134 and 134-A, RPC, rebellion is committed only by rising publicly and taking up arms, and coup d'etat only by a swift attack; once these cease, the crime is no longer being committed. The "continuing crime" doctrine (Lansang; Umil v. Ramos) should apply only to subversive armed organizations such as the NPA.

paras.html: I. Facts she adds: The "Magdalo Group" (323 soldiers) aired grievances on graft in the military, sale of arms to "enemies" of the State, the Davao bombings allegedly ordered by ISAFP Chief Gen. Victor Corpus, increased U.S. military assistance, and "micromanagement" by SND Reyes. PGMA set a 5:00 p.m. deadline at 9:00 a.m., issued Proc. 427 and GO 4 at 1:00 p.m., extended the deadline to 7:00 p.m.; the soldiers left at 11:00 p.m. On July 28, the NBI searched Ramon Cardenas's house, and he was charged with rebellion; Mandaluyong police searched Laarni Enriquez's townhouses (alleged staging areas). After the lifting: an Aug. 4 coup d'etat complaint against Sen. Honasan and about 1,000 "John and Jane Does," and an Aug. 8 recommendation to prosecute Enriquez and Romy Escalona for rebellion.

paras.html: II–III. No constitutional power to declare a state of rebellion: Nowhere does the Constitution grant it. Under Sec. 18, the President may only (1) call out the armed forces, (2) suspend the writ, or (3) declare martial law. If the purpose was merely to call out, she could simply have ordered the AFP.

paras.html: The "unorthodox measure" is unbounded and leaves the people ignorant of their rights. The safeguards for the writ and martial law (public safety; 60 days; 48-hour report; revocation by Congress; SC review of factual basis within 30 days) are absent from a "state of rebellion" → "How can excess of power be curtailed at its inception?"

Maceda and hunted Honasan, Lacson and others, none of whom was caught in the act or arrested on personal knowledge → "In effect, she placed the Philippines under martial law without a declaration to that effect"; violates Sec. 2, Art. III and is unjustified even under Sec. 5, Rule 113.

paras.html: Congress's concurrent power: Emergency powers should be exercised jointly with Congress (Sec. 18 report and revocation; Sec. 23, Art. VI). By declaring a state of rebellion, PGMA disregarded that concurrent power; "the accumulation of both the executive and legislative powers in the same hands constitutes the very definition of tyranny."

paras.html: IV. U.S. cases do not support the majority: Every proposal to confer uncontrollable power on the U.S. President has been rejected. In re Debs was eroded by Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (Steel Seizure Case), quoting Justice Jackson's concurrence [the opinion says "Mr. Justice Andrew Jackson" (sic: Robert H. Jackson)] on "loose and irresponsible use of adjectives" like "inherent" powers; and by United States v. U.S. District Court (rejecting inherent power for warrantless domestic surveillance). The Prize Cases concern foreign affairs, where executive power predominates; in domestic affairs, the executive role is ancillary to Congress.

paras.html: Four groups of presidential appointees (Sec. 16, Art. VII): (1) heads of executive departments, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain, and other officers whose appointments are vested in the President in the Constitution; (2) all other officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for by law; (3) those whom the President may be authorized by law to appoint; and (4) officers lower in rank whose appointments Congress may by law vest in the President alone. Only the first group requires the consent (confirmation) of the Commission on Appointments.

paras.html: In the 1935 Constitution, "in the President alone" made sense as an exception to the general rule of CA confirmation. In 1987, confirmation is the exception, and the second sentence already vests the appointment of officers authorized by law in the President without confirmation → "alone" is redundant, a literal import from 1935, and cannot prevail over the clear intent of the framers.

paras.html: Inquiry vs. question hour: Secs. 21 and 22, Art. VI are complementary but distinct powers. Appearance of department heads in the question hour (Sec. 22, oversight) is discretionary; appearance in inquiries in aid of legislation (Sec. 21) is mandatory. "When Congress exercises its power of inquiry, the only way for department heads to exempt themselves therefrom is by a valid claim of privilege." Only the President and members of the Supreme Court are exempt from the power of inquiry.
paras.text: Inquiry vs. question hour: Secs. 21 and 22, Art. VI are complementary but distinct powers. Appearance of department heads in the question hour (Sec. 22, oversight) is discretionary; appearance in inquiries in aid of legislation (Sec. 21) is mandatory. "When Congress exercises its power of inquiry, the only way for department heads to exempt themselves therefrom is by a valid claim of privilege." Only the President and members of the Supreme Court are exempt from the power of inquiry.

paras.html: Executive privilege: it is recognized only for certain types of information of a sensitive character, not for categories of persons; "the presumption inclines heavily against executive secrecy and in favor of disclosure." A claim "must ... be clearly asserted", with precise and certain reasons, and may be invoked only by the President (or the Executive Secretary "By order of the President"). An implied claim, as authorized by Secs. 2(b) and 3 of EO 464, is invalid per se.

paras.html: Right to information and publication: an issuance that unduly limits disclosures in generally public legislative inquiries "necessarily deprives the people of information", and because EO 464 affects that right, it had to be published before implementation (Tañada).

paras.html: Sept. 28, 2005: President Arroyo issued EO 464, "Ensuring Observance of the Principle of Separation of Powers, Adherence to the Rule on Executive Privilege and Respect for the Rights of Public Officials Appearing in Legislative Inquiries in Aid of Legislation," effective immediately (Sec. 6). Its key provisions:
paras.text: Sept. 28, 2005: President Arroyo issued EO 464, "Ensuring Observance of the Principle of Separation of Powers, Adherence to the Rule on Executive Privilege and Respect for the Rights of Public Officials Appearing in Legislative Inquiries in Aid of Legislation," effective immediately (Sec. 6). Its key provisions:

paras.html: Sec. 1: in accordance with Art. VI, Sec. 22, all heads of departments "shall secure the consent of the President prior to appearing before either House of Congress"; when security or public interest requires and the President so states in writing, the appearance is in executive session.

VI, Sec. 22, all heads of departments "shall secure the consent of the President prior to appearing before either House of Congress"; when security or public interest requires and the President so states in writing, the appearance is in executive session.

paras.html: Sec. 2(a): executive privilege covers "all confidential or classified information between the President and the public officers covered," including presidential conversations and correspondence; military, diplomatic, and national security matters; information before the conclusion of treaties and executive agreements; closed-door Cabinet discussions; and matters affecting national security and public order.

paras.html: Sec. 2(b): "who are covered": senior officials of executive departments, AFP generals and flag officers, PNP officers of chief superintendent rank or higher, and senior national security officials, each "in the judgment of" the department head, AFP Chief of Staff, PNP Chief, or National Security Adviser, plus others the President may determine.

paras.html: Parliamentary origins: the 1973 question hour (Art. VIII, Sec. 12(1)) made ministers' appearance mandatory, suited to a parliamentary system. The 1987 framers made it discretionary to conform to separation of powers. But this makes Congress's right to executive information under Sec. 21 "more imperative" (Schwartz).

paras.html: → Sec. 21 elicits information for legislation; Sec. 22 obtains information for oversight. When Congress merely seeks to know how laws are implemented, its right is less imperative than the President's, so it may only request appearance. When the inquiry is in aid of legislation, appearance is mandatory (Arnault). Oversight may be facilitated by compulsory process "only to the extent that it is performed in pursuit of legislation."

paras.html: Exemptions: department heads are exempt only by a valid claim of privilege, not by being department heads. Only the President is exempt (reachable only through impeachment; long-standing custom), and members of the Supreme Court (separation of powers, fiscal autonomy, judicial independence), as Senate counsel Sen. Joker Arroyo admitted.

paras.html: Holding: because Sec. 1 refers specifically to Sec. 22 and not to inquiries in aid of legislation, it is construed as limited to the question hour (construe issuances to render them constitutional) → valid on its face. It cannot be applied to inquiries in aid of legislation; Congress need not respect a department head's refusal to appear "unless a valid claim of privilege is subsequently made, either by the President herself or by the Executive Secretary."

paras.html: Coverage: Sec. 3 requires prior consent from all officials in Sec. 2(b): senior department officials, AFP and PNP officers, and national security officials whom designated heads judge to be "covered by the executive privilege," plus others the President determines (read by ejusdem generis as also based on privilege).

paras.html: Misuse of doctrine: Sec. 2(b) "virtually states that executive privilege actually covers persons"; privilege is invoked for categories of information, not categories of persons. Read with Sec. 2(a), "covered" means the official possesses information the head of office judges privileged.

Read with Sec. 2(a), "covered" means the official possesses information the head of office judges privileged.

paras.html: Implied claim of privilege: the consent requirement bars appearance unless the President lifts it. So an official's invocation of EO 464 is "an implied claim" that the information is withheld on the basis of executive privilege, by the President's authority. Ermita's Sept. 28 letter illustrates this: it neither invoked privilege nor gave grounds, but its unstated premises amount to a determination that the information is privileged.

paras.html: Privilege may be validly claimed even against Congress (Chavez v. PEA: presidential conversations and Cabinet discussions "cannot be pried open by a co-equal branch"), so Sec. 3 is not invalid merely for sanctioning claims of privilege. But claims are assessed case by case.

paras.html: Invalid per se: the implied claim "is not accompanied by any specific allegation of the basis thereof"; Congress is left to speculate which ground in Sec. 2(a) applies. "Congress has the right to know why the executive considers the requested information privileged." A message that does not look like a claim of privilege is "more pernicious," leaving Congress "doubly blind."

"Congress has the right to know why the executive considers the requested information privileged." A message that does not look like a claim of privilege is "more pernicious," leaving Congress "doubly blind."

paras.html: A claim "must ... be clearly asserted." U.S. v. Reynolds: "There must be a formal claim of privilege, lodged by the head of the department which has control over the matter, after actual personal consideration by that officer." Without a specific basis, no one can tell whether it falls within a traditional privilege or should be respected in context (as in Almonte and Senate Select Committee v. Nixon). Also A.O. Smith v. FTC, U.S. v. Article of Drug, Mobil Oil v. DOE ("precise and certain" reasons), and Black v. Sheraton ("An improperly asserted claim of privilege is no claim of privilege"). Respect for a co-equal branch demands that grounds be stated (McPhaul v. U.S.).

paras.html: Degree of particularity: Congress must not require reasons so specific as to compel disclosure of what the privilege protects. Analogy to self-incrimination (Hoffman v. U.S.): it need only be evident that a responsive answer "might be dangerous because injurious disclosure could result."

paras.html: → The claim under Sec. 3 in relation to Sec. 2(b) is invalid per se: "It is not asserted. It is merely implied." It merely invokes EO 464 plus the absence of consent, "woefully insufficient", and severely frustrates the power of inquiry.

paras.html: Unlawful delegation (petitioners' second ground): Secs. 2(b) and 3 presume a head of office's determination bears the President's authority, so the President authorizes claims "by mere silence." Given its "highly exceptional nature," the power to invoke the privilege is limited to the President, who may authorize the Executive Secretary to invoke it on her behalf, stating it is "By order of the President" (meaning he personally consulted her). She may not authorize subordinates, much less by silence → Sec. 3, with Sec. 2(b), is "further invalid on this score."

paras.html: Procedure going forward: an official summoned on a matter he thinks may be privileged must be given reasonable time to inform the President or Executive Secretary. If neither invokes the privilege after that time, Congress is no longer bound to respect his non-appearance and may use legal means to compel it.

paras.html: The Memorandum as a jurisdictional challenge: the President, asserting that an inquiry is not in aid of legislation and belongs to another body, may object to it (Senate v. Ermita). "The forum to address such jurisdictional claim is the Senate and its committees themselves": under Sec. 3 of the Senate Rules of Procedure Governing Inquiries, a jurisdictional challenge "must first be resolved by the Committee before proceeding with the inquiry."

paras.html: Congress passed unprecedented appropriations for the pandemic. The DOH alone received ₱77 billion, of which ₱37 billion was for personal protective equipment (PPE).

paras.html: The COA's 2020 Annual Audit Report noted a deficiency of ₱67,323,186,570.57 in funds for the COVID-19 response, prompting a Senate Blue Ribbon Committee investigation of the DOH's budget utilization.

paras.html: Senate resolutions: SR 858 (Zubiri: vaccine procurement by LGUs and the private sector); SR 859 (De Lima: COA findings on DOH unspent funds, misstatements, irregularities, and deficiencies, "identifying and holding accountable those responsible"); SR 880 (Hontiveros: PhilHealth payment claims with private hospitals).
paras.text: Senate resolutions: SR 858 (Zubiri: vaccine procurement by LGUs and the private sector); SR 859 (De Lima: COA findings on DOH unspent funds, misstatements, irregularities, and deficiencies, "identifying and holding accountable those responsible"); SR 880 (Hontiveros: PhilHealth payment claims with private hospitals).

paras.html: The Blue Ribbon Committee said its inquiry covered: (1) the DOH's underutilization of its 2020 budget; (2) vaccine procurement by LGUs and the private sector; (3) DOH unspent funds and COA findings; and (4) PhilHealth payment claims. Questions included whether key purchases underwent public bidding, how appropriations for health workers were spent, how expensive the PPE purchases were, whether officials did due diligence on suppliers, and why contracts went to foreign rather than Filipino suppliers.

paras.html: After several hearings, President Duterte complained of the alleged "browbeating" of Executive officials appearing as resource persons.
