paras.html: Oct. 4, 2021: through Executive Secretary Medialdea ("By order of the President"), he issued a Memorandum stating that: the hearings had gone on for nearly two months; Executive participation was "greatly affecting its ability to fulfill its core mandates," most of all the protection of the people's right to health [the ponencia's second excerpt of the same passage reads "the violation of our people's right to health"]; and the hearings were "conducted not in aid of legislation, but to identify persons to hold accountable for alleged irregularities already punishable under existing laws," so the Committee "stepped into the mandates of other branches" and "deprived itself of the only basis to compel attendance."

paras.html: (1) No actual case: the hearings were really an exercise of the oversight function (Sec. 22, Art. VI), aimed at identifying persons accountable for anomalies in PPE, face mask, and face shield procurement and whether health-worker benefit laws were executed. Jurisdiction belongs to the Joint Congressional Oversight Committee under the Bayanihan Acts, which as special laws supersede the Senate Rules. Under Sec. 22, attendance cannot be compelled without the President's consent. The Senate suffers no direct injury since it lacked jurisdiction.

paras.text: Re: Requisites of certiorari

paras.html: Certiorari (Rule 65, Sec. 1) requires: (1) a tribunal, board, or officer exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions; (2) action without or in excess of jurisdiction or with grave abuse of discretion; and (3) no appeal or other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy. The Court "focus[ed] on the third requisite": where such a remedy exists but is peremptorily omitted, a Rule 65 petition will not prosper.

paras.html: Re: The power of inquiry and its scope
paras.text: Re: The power of inquiry and its scope

paras.html: The power is inherent in the power to legislate (Senate v. Ermita) and broad, since a legislature cannot legislate wisely without information (Neri). Senate Rules, Sec. 1: inquiries may refer to the implementation or re-examination of any law or appropriation, proposed or future legislation, or matters vested in Congress or the Senate. They need not result in legislation (Romero II v. Estrada), but must be "material or necessary to the exercise of a power vested in it by the Constitution" (Bengzon).

paras.html: May the President object? Yes, per Senate v. Ermita: the inquiry "might not properly be in aid of legislation," abuses are "remediable before the courts, upon the proper suit filed by the persons affected, even if they belong to the executive branch," and in exceptional cases of "a clear pattern of abuse," executive attempts to forestall them may be judicially sanctioned.

paras.html: But the forum is the Senate: "Notably, the forum to address such jurisdictional claim is the Senate and its committees themselves," in respect of its own Rules. Sec. 3, Senate Rules of Procedure Governing Inquiries: "If the jurisdiction of the Committee is challenged on any ground, the said issue must first be resolved by the Committee before proceeding with the inquiry." If the Committee, by a majority vote of its members present, there being a quorum, finds the inquiry pertinent to legislation or other constitutional matters, it overrules the objection and proceeds; only one challenge on the same ground is allowed; and pending criminal or administrative actions do not stop an inquiry.

paras.html: How the Senate could have overruled it: under the 2020 Rules of the Senate, the Blue Ribbon Committee has 17 regular members plus 3 ex officio members; a quorum is one-third of regular members (Sec. 4), so 6 members, and a majority of those present, 4 votes, overrules a challenge. Filing the petition directly would have overruled the challenge "only if the Petition was filed by at least six members." Here, only Sen. Gordon among the regular members joined; while four Committee members filed, there is no certainty there was a quorum when they decided to file.

paras.html: The power of inquiry is implied (Arnault) and became express in Art. VIII, Sec. 12(2) of the 1973 Constitution, retained in Sec. 21. Its limits exist to prevent past abuses such as intimidating witnesses and grandstanding. Under the 2010 Senate Rules of Procedure Governing Inquiries (Sec. 1), the definition is broad: so long as the inquiry relates to a matter vested in Congress, it is in aid of legislation.

Its limits exist to prevent past abuses such as intimidating witnesses and grandstanding. Under the 2010 Senate Rules of Procedure Governing Inquiries (Sec. 1), the definition is broad: so long as the inquiry relates to a matter vested in Congress, it is in aid of legislation.

paras.html: The four subjects of the hearings "are obviously related to the implementation of laws," namely RA 11469 and RA 11494. Since these laws delegated emergency powers (legislative in nature), the Senate has "even greater reason" to investigate their exercise, especially given the COA report on misuse of public funds, of which Congress is guardian. The Joint Oversight Committee does not have exclusive jurisdiction; nothing in the Bayanihan Acts says so, and statutes cannot supersede constitutional powers.

paras.html: No valid claim of executive privilege: the Memorandum makes no express claim on state secrets, informers, or internal deliberations; the President merely decided for himself that the hearings were not in aid of legislation. Without an express claim, the Court must "presume that the action of the legislative body was with a legitimate object."

paras.html: Ermita controls: there, the officials' absence under EO 464 made the case ripe even without an actual withholding of consent; here the Memorandum directly prohibited attendance, a stronger case. Gudani v. Senga: when the President withholds consent, Congress's remedy is to go to court, which may command the President to compel attendance.

paras.html: The President's public statements: the petition cited his Sept. 30, 2021 address (challenging the Senate to use its contempt power, threatening to arrest the Senate Sergeant-at-Arms, instructing the PNP and AFP to disobey arrest orders) and Oct. 6, 2021 remarks ("Baka 'yang inyong 'in aid' maging first aid 'yan") → no doubt the President would not allow attendance; the action was "complete and ripe."

paras.html: Sec. 3 does not apply: the nature of an action is determined by the petition's allegations (Padlan v. Dinglasan). The Executive never lodged a jurisdictional challenge with the Senate; the Memorandum was addressed to Executive officials, not the Senate or the Committee. Requiring the Senate to rule first would be "a trivial and vain exercise"; the Senate questions the constitutionality of a co-equal branch's act, which only the Court can decide. Dismissal "effectively cloak[s] the President's actions with some semblance of legitimacy."

paras.html: Presidential immunity is personal to the President and may be waived: The privilege of immunity from suit "pertains to the President by virtue of the office and may be invoked only by the holder of the office; not by any other person in the President's behalf." An accused in a criminal case where the President is the complainant cannot raise it as a defense. Nothing in our laws prevents the President from waiving the privilege; the choice to exercise or waive it is solely the President's prerogative.

An accused in a criminal case where the President is the complainant cannot raise it as a defense. Nothing in our laws prevents the President from waiving the privilege; the choice to exercise or waive it is solely the President's prerogative.

paras.html: Personal determination of probable cause (Sec. 2, Art. III): The Constitution requires the judge to personally satisfy himself of the existence of probable cause, not to personally examine the complainant and the witnesses. He may (1) personally evaluate the fiscal's report and supporting documents and issue the warrant on that basis; or (2) if he finds no probable cause on that basis, disregard the report and require supporting affidavits of witnesses.

paras.html: COA may create special audit teams: The Constitution gives COA the exclusive authority to define the scope of its audit and examination and to establish the techniques and methods therefor (Sec. 2(2), Art. IX-D). Pursuant to it, COA Memo No. 2002-053 (drawing force from COA Res. No. 2002-005) lets the General Counsel deputize a special audit team. A party's complaint should refer to the conduct of the audit, not to the validity of the auditing body, and must be raised through COA's own procedure.
paras.text: COA may create special audit teams: The Constitution gives COA the exclusive authority to define the scope of its audit and examination and to establish the techniques and methods therefor (Sec. 2(2), Art. IX-D). Pursuant to it, COA Memo No. 2002-053 (drawing force from COA Res. No. 2002-005) lets the General Counsel deputize a special audit team. A party's complaint should refer to the conduct of the audit, not to the validity of the auditing body, and must be raised through COA's own procedure.

paras.html: Exhaustion before COA: COA provides an appeal ladder (Auditor → Director → Commission Proper; Sec. 48, PD 1445). Resort to Rule 65 is premature unless an exception applies, and the party invoking the exception bears the burden of proving it. Courts must exercise caution when intervening in disputes involving the independent constitutional commissions.

Courts must exercise caution when intervening in disputes involving the independent constitutional commissions.

paras.html: Prohibition and injunction: Prohibition lies only against judicial, quasi-judicial, or ministerial functions; issuing an order constituting an audit team is none of these. A writ of preliminary injunction requires a clear legal right; a threatened, not-yet-issued notice of disallowance shows no urgency.

paras.html: COA created the Special Audit Team (SAT) under Legal and Adjudication Office (LAO) Order No. 2004-093 (dated 30 September 2004), issued by COA Assistant Commissioner and General Counsel Raquel R. Ramirez-Habitan, "[p]ursuant to COA Memorandum No. 2002-053 dated August 26, 2002."
paras.text: COA created the Special Audit Team (SAT) under Legal and Adjudication Office (LAO) Order No. 2004-093 (dated 30 September 2004), issued by COA Assistant Commissioner and General Counsel Raquel R. Ramirez-Habitan, "[p]ursuant to COA Memorandum No. 2002-053 dated August 26, 2002."

paras.html: The SAT was to conduct a special audit of selected GSIS transactions for 2000 to 2004, "with particular attention on the creation of subsidiaries such as GSIS Properties, Inc., missing paintings, cash advances and allowances/benefits of the Officers and Members of the Board of Trustees," within 10 working days, and report within 5 days after completion to the Director, LAO – Office of Legal Affairs.

paras.html: A rule of thumb for every Rule 65 petition is the unavailability of an appeal or any "plain, speedy, and adequate remedy" (Rule 65, Secs. 1–3). Certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus are extraordinary remedies that historically require extraordinary facts (citing J. Johnson's separate opinion in Garcia v. Sweeney, and Ongsitco v. CA) to correct errors of jurisdiction.

paras.text: GSIS's claimed exceptions are all baseless:

paras.html: First, a threat to issue a notice of disallowance is speculative absent actual proof; even if real, it falls under no exception because the COA rules (Rule V, Sec. 1) provide an adequate remedy to dispute a notice of disallowance.

paras.html: Second, COA's inaction on GSIS's petition/request is explainable by the CA's TRO and writ of preliminary injunction; the cited two-month delay is not so unreasonable as to require trampling procedural rules. [The COA petition/request was filed on 15 April 2005 and the CA petition on 18 July 2005.]

paras.html: Fourth, partiality and bias are questions of fact already before COA. A question of law arises when the doubt is as to what the law is on a certain state of facts, not as to the truth of alleged facts (Vigilar v. Aquino; DBP v. Go; Mendoza v. People; Cabaron v. People). Questions of fact generally cannot be decided in a Rule 65 prohibition petition (Padua v. Ranada), which applies to jurisdictional flaws (lack, excess, or grave abuse of discretion).

paras.html: Exhaustion rationale (Ongsuco v. Malones): if resort within the administrative machinery can still be made, it must be exhausted first; "[t]he premature invocation of the intervention of the court is fatal to one's cause of action." It entails lesser expenses, speedier disposition, and comity and convenience, giving the agency every opportunity to correct its error.

paras.html: Re: constitutional commissions. The 1987 Constitution created the constitutional commissions as independent bodies with specific roles requiring expertise (Art. IX). COA's role: "the power, authority, and duty to examine, audit, and settle all accounts" of the Government, including GOCCs with original charters (Sec. 2(1)) [the decision cites "Art. IX, Sec. 2(1)"; the provision is in Art. IX-D]. COA is empowered to define the scope of its audit and examination and to promulgate auditing rules (NIA v. Enciso).

paras.html: This falls short: a preliminary injunction is proper only when the plaintiff appears clearly entitled to the relief and has substantial interest in the right (Power Sites and Signs v. United Neon); there must be "a right to be protected and that the acts against which the writ is to be directed are violative of the said right" (NPC v. Vera). "[W]hile the existence of the right need not be conclusively established, it must be clear."
paras.text: This falls short: a preliminary injunction is proper only when the plaintiff appears clearly entitled to the relief and has substantial interest in the right (Power Sites and Signs v. United Neon); there must be "a right to be protected and that the acts against which the writ is to be directed are violative of the said right" (NPC v. Vera). "[W]hile the existence of the right need not be conclusively established, it must be clear."

paras.html: Lacking a clear legal right (Fua v. COA; Rosario v. CA), the remedy should not have issued, all the more because the factual support had not been established. Courts cannot reverse the burden of proof, for that "would assume the proposition which the petitioner is inceptively duty bound to prove" (GSIS v. Florendo). This is not a mere technicality: every case requires a cause of action (Republic v. De los Angeles).

paras.html: COA has the power, authority, and duty to examine, audit, and settle all government accounts (Sec. 2(1), Art. IX-D). (Sec. 2(2), Art. IX-D).

paras.html: COMELEC's residual power over plebiscite dates: As the body mandated to "enforce and administer all laws and regulations relative to the conduct of an election, plebiscite, initiative, referendum, and recall" (Art. IX-C, Sec. 2(1)), COMELEC has the authority to modify or alter the dates of a plebiscite, even beyond the period the law prescribes (Cagas v. COMELEC). It "cannot be paralyzed by the literal interpretations of a guiding law," and the Court will not strike down its actions unless there is a clear showing of grave abuse of discretion.

paras.html: Cagas v. COMELEC: the law creating Davao Occidental required a plebiscite within 60 days of effectivity, but COMELEC suspended all plebiscites to prepare for the May 2013 elections and reset it for Oct. 28, 2013. The Court upheld this: COMELEC has "all the necessary and incidental powers" to hold free, orderly, honest elections; OEC Secs. 5–6 let it postpone or reset elections; and "The COMELEC thus has residual power to conduct a plebiscite even beyond the deadline prescribed by law."

COMELEC: the law creating Davao Occidental required a plebiscite within 60 days of effectivity, but COMELEC suspended all plebiscites to prepare for the May 2013 elections and reset it for Oct. 28, 2013. The Court upheld this: COMELEC has "all the necessary and incidental powers" to hold free, orderly, honest elections; OEC Secs. 5–6 let it postpone or reset elections; and "The COMELEC thus has residual power to conduct a plebiscite even beyond the deadline prescribed by law."

paras.html: Thus, COMELEC has the authority to modify or alter the dates of the plebiscite. It "cannot be paralyzed by the literal interpretations of a guiding law" (Pangandaman v. COMELEC). Prioritizing strict compliance with the period over a safe, honest, and successful plebiscite would defeat the purpose of holding one.

paras.html: Specificity. Allegations of fraud, violence, or intimidation must be supported by conclusive or convincing evidence; bare allegations without detail on how the fraud was committed are not enough (Marcos, Jr. v. Robredo: the power to annul an election is exercised with the greatest care, and the specificity requirement deters fishing expeditions).

paras.html: Limits on the CSC's rule-making power: The CSC's rule-making power is subsumed under its designation as the "central personnel agency" (Sec. 3, Art. IX-B). As a constitutional grant, it is an aspect of its independence and cannot be withdrawn by Congress. But it "is still limited to the implementation and interpretation of the laws it is tasked to enforce." Its rules "must not override, but must be in harmony with, the law it seeks to apply and implement."
paras.text: Limits on the CSC's rule-making power: The CSC's rule-making power is subsumed under its designation as the "central personnel agency" (Sec. 3, Art. IX-B). As a constitutional grant, it is an aspect of its independence and cannot be withdrawn by Congress. But it "is still limited to the implementation and interpretation of the laws it is tasked to enforce." Its rules "must not override, but must be in harmony with, the law it seeks to apply and implement."

paras.html: Congress may legislate exemptions: The CSC's constitutional authority over the civil service does not divest the Legislature of the power to enact laws providing exemptions to civil service rules. A GOCC with an original charter stays within the civil service (Sec. 2(1), Art. IX-B), so the CSC still enforces position classification there, but "under the terms that [the GOCC] has itself established."

paras.html: "Endeavor to conform as closely as possible": This language allows deviation from RA 6758; it requires an effort to follow RA 6758's principles and modes, not full, exact, and strict compliance with the entire law.

paras.html: TIDCORP is a GOCC created under PD 1080. It functions as the government's export credit agency.
paras.text: TIDCORP is a GOCC created under PD 1080. It functions as the government's export credit agency.

paras.html: Its charter was amended by RA 8494. Section 7 provides:
paras.text: Its charter was amended by RA 8494. Section 7 provides:

paras.html: "The Board of Directors shall provide for an organizational structure and staffing pattern for officers and employees of the [TIDCORP] and upon recommendation of its President, appoint and fix their remuneration, emoluments and fringe benefits: Provided, That the Board shall have exclusive and final authority to appoint, promote, transfer, assign and re-assign personnel of the TIDCORP, any provision of existing law to the contrary notwithstanding.
paras.text: "The Board of Directors shall provide for an organizational structure and staffing pattern for officers and employees of the [TIDCORP] and upon recommendation of its President, appoint and fix their remuneration, emoluments and fringe benefits: Provided, That the Board shall have exclusive and final authority to appoint, promote, transfer, assign and re-assign personnel of the TIDCORP, any provision of existing law to the contrary notwithstanding.

paras.html: All positions in TIDCORP shall be governed by a compensation and position classification system and qualification standards approved by TIDCORP's Board of Directors based on a comprehensive job analysis and audit of actual duties and responsibilities. … TIDCORP shall be exempt from existing laws, rules and regulations on compensation, position classification and qualification standards. It shall, however, endeavor to make the system to conform as closely as possible to the principles and modes provided in Republic Act No. 6758."

paras.html: The 1987 Constitution created the CSC as the central personnel agency of the government, mandated to establish a career service and promote morale, efficiency, integrity, responsiveness, progressiveness, and courtesy in the civil service (Sec. 3, Art. IX-B). It is a constitutionally created administrative agency with executive, quasi-judicial, and quasi-legislative (rule-making) powers.

paras.html: The CSC's rule-making power as a constitutional grant is an aspect of its independence as a constitutional commission. It places the grant outside the reach of Congress, which cannot withdraw the power at any time.

paras.html: Administrative rules are entitled to great respect, but their conclusive effect is not absolute: they may be issued only to carry the law into effect; they cannot extend the law nor amend a legislative enactment; and in a conflict between the basic law and an implementing rule, the law prevails (Land Bank v. CA, citing Peralta v. CSC, Toledo v. CSC, and Shell v. Central Bank).

paras.html: Dual endorsement: Rep. de Lima endorsed the second complaint and then the third, calling it an "improved version" and saying "walang prohibition for any endorser to endorse more than once." Either the second was sufficient (so no need to improve it) or it was not (so the first endorsement lacked care) → the good-faith premise is undermined. A "not prohibited" stance is "textual minimalism."

paras.html: Borrowing the civil pleading rule (A.M. No. 19-10-20-SC; Montemayor v. Raborar; Palm Avenue Holdings; Zuñiga-Santos), ultimate facts are the constitutive facts: "who, what, when, where, how, by what act, by what authority, in what amount, through what document, against what duty, and with what personal participation." They differ from evidentiary facts, conclusions of law, and generalized accusations.

Raborar; Palm Avenue Holdings; Zuñiga-Santos), ultimate facts are the constitutive facts: "who, what, when, where, how, by what act, by what authority, in what amount, through what document, against what duty, and with what personal participation." They differ from evidentiary facts, conclusions of law, and generalized accusations.

paras.html: Impeachment is personal, not institutional; office-level irregularities or subordinates' acts cannot be imputed by command responsibility. Hearsay, media reports, and unauthenticated files are "leads for investigation," not ultimate facts. "A constitutionally sufficient impeachment complaint must be a complaint, not a prospectus for investigation." Ultimate facts also serve fair notice (due process).

paras.html: At threshold the Committee performs a legal gatekeeping function, not advocacy. Members who endorsed or advanced the complaints are "institutionally aligned with the survival of the charges"; one cannot be prosecutor and judge at once (Cojuangco v. PCGG in text; the footnote cites People v. Cojuangco, G.R. No. 160864). Due process requires both actual impartiality and its appearance; their failure to inhibit aggravated the arbitrariness. [The petition does not name the members.]

paras.html: A. Immediate relief: (1) TRO restraining the respondents from any act implementing or continuing proceedings on the third and fourth complaints, including (a) treating them as sufficient; (b) hearings, meetings, or votes; (c) any subpoena or compulsory process; (d) compelled witnesses or documents (SALNs, tax and corporate records, audit materials, archived proceedings); (e) any committee report or resolution; (f) any Articles of Impeachment based on them; (g) any act that would render the petition moot. (2) After hearing, a WPI.

paras.html: B. Final relief: (3) DECLARE GAD in sustaining the complaints under a relaxed, selective standard; (4) DECLARE the complaints infirm and dismissible at threshold; (5) DECLARE that participation of aligned members tainted the proceedings; (6) DECLARE the Mar. 25, 2026 compulsory-process acts void for overbreadth and lack of nexus; (7) ANNUL and SET ASIDE the findings, the hearing proper, the ground rules, and the subpoenas; (8) issue a Writ of Prohibition permanently restraining further proceedings on the complaints. Other just and equitable relief.

paras.html: Petitioners' core theory (not a ruling): The Committee on Justice's threshold review (sufficiency in form, Rule III, Sec. 4; substance, Sec. 5; grounds, Sec. 7) is a mandatory constitutional gatekeeping function. III, Sec. 1) → grave abuse of discretion.

paras.html: Dual endorsement: Rep. de Lima endorsed the second complaint and then the third, calling it an "improved version" and saying "walang prohibition for any endorser to endorse more than once." A "not prohibited" stance is "textual minimalism."

paras.html: Re: The ultimate-facts standard

paras.html: Borrowing the civil pleading rule (A.M. No. 19-10-20-SC; Montemayor v. Raborar; Palm Avenue Holdings; Zuñiga-Santos), ultimate facts are the constitutive facts: "who, what, when, where, how, by what act, by what authority, in what amount, through what document, against what duty, and with what personal participation." They differ from evidentiary facts, conclusions of law, and generalized accusations.

Raborar; Palm Avenue Holdings; Zuñiga-Santos), ultimate facts are the constitutive facts: "who, what, when, where, how, by what act, by what authority, in what amount, through what document, against what duty, and with what personal participation." They differ from evidentiary facts, conclusions of law, and generalized accusations.

paras.html: Impeachment is personal, not institutional; office-level irregularities or subordinates' acts cannot be imputed by command responsibility. Hearsay, media reports, and unauthenticated files are "leads for investigation," not ultimate facts. "A constitutionally sufficient impeachment complaint must be a complaint, not a prospectus for investigation." Ultimate facts also serve fair notice (due process).

paras.html: Breach of a conditional pardon may be determined by the President alone: Where the President opts to proceed under Sec. 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code, "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court", before the convict may be recommitted for violating his conditional pardon.
paras.text: Breach of a conditional pardon may be determined by the President alone: Where the President opts to proceed under Sec. 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code, "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court", before the convict may be recommitted for violating his conditional pardon.

paras.html: Two options, and the choice is the President's: The Executive may proceed either under Sec. 64(i), RAC (administrative recommitment to serve the remitted portion of the original sentence) or under Art. 159, RPC (prosecution for violation of a conditional pardon). The choice is an exercise of executive prerogative and is not subject to judicial scrutiny. But a final conviction is still required before the penalty for the new crime, or the Art. 159 penalty, can be imposed.
paras.text: Two options, and the choice is the President's: The Executive may proceed either under Sec. 64(i), RAC (administrative recommitment to serve the remitted portion of the original sentence) or under Art. 159, RPC (prosecution for violation of a conditional pardon). The choice is an exercise of executive prerogative and is not subject to judicial scrutiny. But a final conviction is still required before the penalty for the new crime, or the Art. 159 penalty, can be imposed.

paras.html: Due process is not always judicial: Because due process is not "semper et ubique" judicial process, and the convict already received judicial due process when tried and convicted of the original offense, Sec. 64(i) is not afflicted with a constitutional vice.

paras.html: Re: The state of the case law (three propositions):
paras.text: Re: The state of the case law (three propositions):

paras.html: (1) The grant of pardon and the determination of the terms and conditions of a conditional pardon are purely executive acts not subject to judicial scrutiny.
paras.text: (1) The grant of pardon and the determination of the terms and conditions of a conditional pardon are purely executive acts not subject to judicial scrutiny.

paras.html: (2) The determination of a breach of a condition, and its proper consequences, may be either (a) a purely executive act under Sec. 64(i), RAC, not subject to judicial scrutiny; or (b) a judicial act, i.e., trial for and conviction of violation of a conditional pardon under Art. 159, RPC. Where the President opts for Sec. 64(i), "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court". [sic: the decision says the convict may be "recommended" for the violation; context indicates "recommitted."]
paras.text: (2) The determination of a breach of a condition, and its proper consequences, may be either (a) a purely executive act under Sec. 64(i), RAC, not subject to judicial scrutiny; or (b) a judicial act, i.e., trial for and conviction of violation of a conditional pardon under Art. 159, RPC. Where the President opts for Sec. 64(i), "no judicial pronouncement of guilt of a subsequent crime is necessary, much less conviction therefor by final judgment of a court". [sic: the decision says the convict may be "recommended" for the violation; context indicates "recommitted."]

paras.html: (3) Because due process is not "semper et ubique" judicial process, and the convict was already accorded judicial due process for the original offense, Sec. 64(i) is not afflicted with a constitutional vice.

paras.html: This is not the prosecution of the parolee for a subsequent offense in the regular course of the criminal law. It is only the ascertainment of whether the convict breached his undertaking that he would "not again violate any of the penal laws of the Philippines," for purposes of reimposing the remitted portion of his original sentence.

paras.html: In proceeding against a conditionally pardoned convict who allegedly breached the conditions, the Executive Department has two options: (i) Sec. 64(i), RAC; or (ii) Art. 159, RPC, which imposes prision correccional, minimum period, on a convict who, "having been granted conditional pardon by the Chief Executive, shall violate any of the conditions of such pardon."

paras.html: Sales, quoting Fuller v. State of Alabama (45 LRA 502): the statute "supervenes to avoid the necessity for any action by the courts." paras.html: Revocation of amnesty requires congressional concurrence: Art. VII, Sec. 19 is silent on revocation, but “the revocation of a grant of amnesty must be with the concurrence of the Legislature”; allowing the President to revoke alone “renders futile the participation of the Legislature in its grant.” [This is stated in the body; the fallo only declares Proc. No. 572 void.]
paras.text: Revocation of amnesty requires congressional concurrence: Art. VII, Sec. 19 is silent on revocation, but “the revocation of a grant of amnesty must be with the concurrence of the Legislature”; allowing the President to revoke alone “renders futile the participation of the Legislature in its grant.” [This is stated in the body; the fallo only declares Proc. No. 572 void.]

paras.html: Amnesty may be revoked, but only within limits: Where a grant is subject to conditions that are not met, it may be revoked, but the revocation must comply with the Constitution and any procedure in the grant or its rules. The President's power of control cannot be used to revoke a DND amnesty decision that has become final and immutable.
paras.text: Amnesty may be revoked, but only within limits: Where a grant is subject to conditions that are not met, it may be revoked, but the revocation must comply with the Constitution and any procedure in the grant or its rules. The President's power of control cannot be used to revoke a DND amnesty decision that has become final and immutable.

paras.html: Effect of amnesty on a later prosecution: Where the accused moves to dismiss on the ground of amnesty, double jeopardy applies, even though the dismissal was on his motion. An executive issuance that strips a person of an amnesty violates the ex post facto clause even if it is not a penal law.

paras.html: Admission of guilt: It suffices that the applicant admits (a) committing the acts covered by the amnesty and (b) that these acts are criminal; an admission of the specific crime charged is not required.

paras.html: Trillanes is a former active member of the AFP (Philippine Navy) with the rank of Lieutenant Senior Grade.

paras.html: July 27, 2003: Trillanes led the Magdalo Group of armed soldiers in taking over the Oakwood Premier Apartments in Makati (the Oakwood Mutiny). He and others were charged with coup d'etat (Art. 134-A, RPC) before Branch 148, RTC Makati (Crim. Case No. 03-2784) (the “Coup d'etat Case”).

paras.html: While the case was pending, Trillanes won a Senate seat in the 2007 elections.

paras.html: November 29, 2007: During a hearing in Branch 148, Trillanes and the Magdalo Group walked out of the court and took over the Manila Peninsula Hotel, calling for the ouster of PGMA (the Manila Peninsula Incident). They refused to receive a warrant of arrest for direct contempt, so the police broke into the hotel to arrest them. Trillanes was charged with rebellion before Branch 150, RTC Makati (Crim. Case No. 07-3126) (the “Rebellion Case”).

paras.text: Proclamation No. 75 and its implementation:

paras.html: November 24, 2010: President Aquino issued Proclamation No. 75, granting amnesty to active and former AFP and PNP personnel and their supporters for crimes connected with the Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off, and the Manila Peninsula Incident. Sec. 1 provides:
paras.text: November 24, 2010: President Aquino issued Proclamation No. 75, granting amnesty to active and former AFP and PNP personnel and their supporters for crimes connected with the Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off, and the Manila Peninsula Incident. Sec. 1 provides:

paras.html: SECTION 1. Grant of Amnesty. — Amnesty is hereby granted to all active and former personnel of the AFP and PNP as well as their supporters who have or may have committed crimes punishable under the Revised Penal Code, the Articles of War or other laws in connection with, in relation or incident to the July 27, 2003 Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off and the November 29, 2007 Manila Peninsula Incident who shall apply therefor; Provided that amnesty shall not cover rape, acts of torture, crimes against chastity and other crimes committed for personal ends.
paras.text: SECTION 1. Grant of Amnesty. — Amnesty is hereby granted to all active and former personnel of the AFP and PNP as well as their supporters who have or may have committed crimes punishable under the Revised Penal Code, the Articles of War or other laws in connection with, in relation or incident to the July 27, 2003 Oakwood Mutiny, the February 2006 Marines Stand-Off and the November 29, 2007 Manila Peninsula Incident who shall apply therefor; Provided that amnesty shall not cover rape, acts of torture, crimes against chastity and other crimes committed for personal ends.

paras.html: Sec. 2: applications are filed with the DND ad hoc committee within 90 days from publication; the committee receives and processes applications (and oppositions) and determines entitlement; the DND's final decision is appealable to the Office of the President by any party, but is immediately executory even if appealed.

paras.html: G.R. No. 256078 (Rebellion Case): Branch 150 held only a summary hearing on affidavits and documents. In its Order of November 25, 2018 [the CA's fallo refers to the “Orders of 25 September and 18 December 2018”], it held that Proc. No. 572 did not violate Trillanes' rights, credited the Andrade Certification, found that he filed no application, declared its 2011 Dismissal Order void ab initio (so it never became final), and granted the warrant and HDO (bail at ₱200,000). MR denied (December 18, 2018). Trillanes filed an R65 petition with the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 159811); its TRO was denied. On March 1, 2021, the CA granted the petition: Proc. No. 572 is valid, but a void order must be attacked through an independent action or collaterally, not by a mere motion in the same case, and the denial of an evidentiary hearing violated due process. The Orders were set aside. The People filed an R45 petition with the SC (March 24, 2021).

paras.html: Nature: amnesty is the “general pardon to rebels for their treason and other high political offenses” (Villa v. It has historically been granted to groups who committed crimes with political color.

paras.html: Effects: amnesty “looks backward and abolishes and puts into oblivion the offense itself”; the grantee stands as though he committed no offense; it has the force of law → farther-reaching than the general pardoning power.

paras.html: Questionable process: the government looked specifically for Trillanes' form seven years later without any apparent reasonable ground, and the President issued Proc. No. 572 without notice or hearing. No rule expressly requires notice and hearing before revocation, but notice and hearing are the essence of administrative due process. Given (a) seven years since the grant, (b) full enforcement and long-dismissed cases, (c) a factual ground he could have explained, and (d) revocation far beyond the period for reversing the DND, fair play required notice and an opportunity to be heard.

paras.html: Congress gets only one JBC seat: Sec. 8(1), Art. VIII gives Congress "a representative" in the JBC. Following Chavez v. JBC as stare decisis, any member of Congress, whether from the Senate or the House, is constitutionally empowered to represent the entire Congress. The six-month rotation adopted by both Houses is in line with that mandate and does not deprive Congress of full participation. To add a member or increase Congress' representation, "the remedy is not judicial but constitutional amendment."

paras.html: (I) certiorari is proper to correct the JBC's denial of his votes because Chavez is defective/flawed; (II) mandamus is proper to compel the JBC to count his votes because the JBC's reconstitution is defective and unconstitutional; (III) the rotation is impracticable, absurd and unconstitutional and creates an institutional imbalance between the two chambers; (IV) the Constitution requires participation and voting by representatives of both the Senate and the House (bicameralism was decided belatedly and must be deemed incorporated; there was a technical omission the Court should rectify; full representation requires both chambers; both chambers' presence upholds co-equal representation of the three branches).

paras.html: Locus standi is a personal and substantial interest such that the party has sustained or will sustain direct injury from the challenged act (Imbong v. Ochoa). The party must show (1) actual or threatened injury, (2) fairly traceable to the challenged action, (3) likely to be redressed by the remedy sought (Lozano v. Nograles).

paras.html: Citizens, taxpayers and legislators have been given standing when specific requirements are met. Per Francisco v. HR: a legislator may sue "to question the validity of any official action which he claims infringes his prerogatives as a legislator"; a member of the House has standing "to maintain inviolate the prerogatives, powers and privileges vested by the Constitution in his office."

Enriquez: although the petition of 16 Senators was not authorized by the Senate, and two other petitions had no enabling resolution, the Court held that a member of the Senate or House has standing to question a presidential veto or a condition on an appropriation item: "To the extent the powers of Congress are impaired, so is the power of each member thereof." An act injuring Congress causes a derivative but substantial injury that any member may question. (It contrasted Gonzales v. Macaraig, where the Senate itself sued under Senate Res. No. 381.)

paras.html: The constitutional intent is proper community and branch representation and removing partisan politics; the focus is proper representation, not numerical limits. A deadlock is no problem since JBC voting is not by "yes" or "no."

paras.html: Bicameralism: Art. VI, Sec. 1 vests legislative power in a Senate and a House. They differ in election (national vs. district/party-list), term (6 vs. 3 years), officers, rules, journals, records, discipline, even addresses. There is no presiding officer or journal of "Congress"; no Senator can carry House instructions and vice versa → no member can represent Congress as a whole. Only Art. VII, Sec. 18 requires joint voting.

paras.html: Appointment is a process: all four elements must concur for a valid (complete and effective) appointment: (1) authority to appoint and evidence of its exercise; (2) transmittal of the appointment paper and evidence of the transmittal; (3) a vacant position at the time of appointment; and (4) receipt of the appointment paper and acceptance by an appointee who has all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications. This applies "regardless of when the appointment is made, whether outside, just before, or during the appointment ban"; there is no valid appointment if the process lacks even one step.
paras.text: Appointment is a process: all four elements must concur for a valid (complete and effective) appointment: (1) authority to appoint and evidence of its exercise; (2) transmittal of the appointment paper and evidence of the transmittal; (3) a vacant position at the time of appointment; and (4) receipt of the appointment paper and acceptance by an appointee who has all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications. This applies "regardless of when the appointment is made, whether outside, just before, or during the appointment ban"; there is no valid appointment if the process lacks even one step.

paras.html: Ban on midnight appointments: subject only to the exception for temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies will prejudice public service or endanger public safety, appointments within the period (two months before the presidential elections up to the end of the term) are automatically prohibited, regardless of the appointee's qualifications or even of the President's motives. An appointment accepted (oath or assumption) during the ban is a midnight appointment and is void; EO 2 is valid.

An appointment accepted (oath or assumption) during the ban is a midnight appointment and is void; EO 2 is valid.

paras.html: Transmittal through the MRO: release of the appointment paper through the Malacañang Records Office is an unequivocal act signifying the President's intent to issue it. The President or Executive Secretary may still hand the paper directly to the appointee, but the appointee then bears the burden of proving it was given to him.

paras.html: MRO evidence: MRO Director IV Marianito Dimaandal testified that appointment papers (with stamp mark, barcode, and hologram, plus a transmittal letter) are normally forwarded by the Office of the Executive Secretary (OES) to the MRO and released the same day with a delivery receipt; that the MRO is the Palace's "gatekeeper" and cannot certify a paper that never passed through it; that a faxed copy is at best an "advanced copy"; that there was a steep rise in appointments in March 2010; that only 133 of the 800+ March appointments were released through the MRO; and that blank receipt dates on OES-released papers were "highly irregular." Division Chief Ellenita Gatbunton testified that the papers of Garafil, Tamondong, Rosquita, and Villanueva were not released through the MRO but merely turned over to it later, already stamped "released" by the OES.

paras.html: Based on prevailing jurisprudence, an appointment takes several steps: the President's signing of the appointment paper to a vacant office, its official transmittal (preferably through the MRO), its receipt by the appointee, and the appointee's acceptance, evidenced by an oath or assumption of office. This applies to every valid appointment, including one made under the Sec. 15 exception.

paras.html: Re: Origin and purpose of Sec. 15, Art. VII (Aytona)
paras.text: Re: Origin and purpose of Sec. 15, Art. VII (Aytona)

paras.html: Aytona v. Castillo (1962) is the basis of Sec. 15 and defined "midnight or last minute" appointments. On 29 December 1961, his last day in office, President Garcia submitted 350 appointments, including Aytona's as Central Bank Governor. President Macapagal, who assumed office on 30 December, issued AO No. 2 on 31 December recalling all appointments made after 13 December 1961, and appointed Castillo. The Court dismissed Aytona's quo warranto and declined to disregard AO No. 2.

On 29 December 1961, his last day in office, President Garcia submitted 350 appointments, including Aytona's as Central Bank Governor. The Court dismissed Aytona's quo warranto and declined to disregard AO No. 2.

paras.html: Aytona reasoned that 350 appointments in one night could be regarded as an abuse of presidential prerogatives, a partisan effort that deprived the new administration of the chance to make its own appointments; that the appointees' equitable rights were doubtful given the "rush conditional appointments, hurried maneuvers"; and that they cooperated, wittingly or unwittingly, with the "stratagem to beat the deadline."

paras.html: Response – glaring absurdities: if acceptance is excluded, (1) in case of non-acceptance, the position is considered occupied and nobody else may be appointed; (2) an incumbent appointed to another office is automatically deemed to have resigned his first office upon transmittal, even if he refuses; and (3) a President unhappy with an incumbent can remove him without cause or due process by appointing him elsewhere. → chaos in public service.

paras.html: Re: The four elements of a valid appointment
paras.text: Re: The four elements of a valid appointment

paras.html: The following must always concur: (1) authority to appoint and evidence of its exercise; (2) transmittal of the appointment paper and evidence of the transmittal; (3) a vacant position at the time of appointment; and (4) receipt of the appointment paper and acceptance by an appointee who possesses all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications. They operate as a single process; there is no valid appointment if the process lacks even one step, and no need to distinguish effective from ineffective appointments.

They operate as a single process; there is no valid appointment if the process lacks even one step, and no need to distinguish effective from ineffective appointments.

paras.html: Lacson v. Romero (1949): Lacson, provincial fiscal of Negros Oriental, was nominated and confirmed as fiscal of Tarlac but never accepted; Romero was appointed to Negros Oriental in his place. Held: Lacson remained fiscal of Negros Oriental; there was no vacancy, so Romero's appointment was invalid. Nomination and confirmation are a mere offer; the last step, acceptance, rests solely with the appointee ("there is no power in this country which can compel a man to accept an office," citing Borromeo v. Mariano).

paras.html: Rejects Garafil's argument. To "preserve and defend [the] Constitution [and] execute its laws," the Executive must interpret; this is recognized in the Administrative Code (executive orders implement constitutional or statutory powers). The power is broadest within the President's own sphere and narrows where other branches are involved; it is always subject to judicial review, and the Court's rulings bind the other branches. Sec. 15 had not been previously interpreted by the Court.

paras.html: By fixing a period, Sec. 15 removed the need to inquire into undue haste, partisanship, or bad faith; appointments outside the period are presumed regular. Thus the CA erred in saying "not all midnight appointments are invalid" and in relying on Sales v. Carreon and Nazareno v. City of Dumaguete, which involved outgoing local chief executives and CSC rules. No referral to the OP was needed: an appointment within the period is void, and no evaluation by the President can validate it.

The broad sense fits cases where the first two stages are unquestioned (e.g., Javier v. Reyes).

paras.html: Issuance (not mere signing) is the last act showing the President's choice. Until acceptance, the President retains control and may recall the appointment, so non-acceptance does not make the post "occupied" or hold the President hostage. Acceptance is still indispensable to assumption, so no incumbent is automatically resigned or removed. The ponencia's view would reduce the President and OES to a "virtual housekeeper" monitoring acceptances.

paras.html: Amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime: "when an accused maintains that he has not committed a crime, he cannot have any use for amnesty." It is "rank inconsistency" to seek forgiveness for an act one claims not to have committed. The contrary rule in Barrioquinto, De Los Santos, and Viray (admission not a condition precedent) has been superseded and deemed overruled by People v. Llanita and People v. Guillermo.
paras.text: Amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime: "when an accused maintains that he has not committed a crime, he cannot have any use for amnesty." It is "rank inconsistency" to seek forgiveness for an act one claims not to have committed. paras.html: Confession and avoidance: the invocation of amnesty admits the allegations but disclaims liability on account of intervening facts; where the proclamation imposes conditions, it is incumbent upon the accused to prove the existence of such conditions.

paras.html: In the CFI of Quezon, petitioners Gaudencio Vera, Restituto Figueras, Lorenzo Ambas, Justo Florido, Paulino Bayran, and 92 others as John Does were charged with the complex crime of kidnapping with murder of Amadeo Lozañes, alias Azarcon. [The decision's opening paragraph does not name Jayme Garcia, a petitioner in the caption; the Commission's order spells his name "Jaime Garcia."]
paras.text: In the CFI of Quezon, petitioners Gaudencio Vera, Restituto Figueras, Lorenzo Ambas, Justo Florido, Paulino Bayran, and 92 others as John Does were charged with the complex crime of kidnapping with murder of Amadeo Lozañes, alias Azarcon. [The decision's opening paragraph does not name Jayme Garcia, a petitioner in the caption; the Commission's order spells his name "Jaime Garcia."]

paras.html: Lozañes was a lieutenant of the Hunters ROTC Guerrilla, then engaged in the resistance movement. He was kidnapped, tortured, and later killed on February 13 and 14, 1945. [The decision spells his name both "Lozanes" and "Lozañes."]

paras.html: Upon petitioners' motion invoking the benefits of the Amnesty Proclamation of the President, series of 1946 (Proclamation No. 8, September 7, 1946), the case was referred to the Eighth Guerrilla Amnesty Commission, which actually tried it.

paras.html: During the hearing, none of the petitioners admitted committing the crime. Gaudencio Vera, the only defendant who took the witness stand, categorically denied the killing.

paras.html: Commission decision (January 12, 1956): it held that it could not take cognizance of the case, because the benefits of the Amnesty Proclamation could be invoked only by defendants who, admitting the commission of the crime, plead that it was in pursuance of the resistance movement and perpetrated against persons who aided the enemy during the Japanese occupation. It ordered the case remanded to the court of origin for trial.

It ordered the case remanded to the court of origin for trial.

paras.text: Order denying MR (January 11, 1957): the Commission made these findings:

paras.html: The motive for the kidnapping and killing was the keen rivalry between Vera's Guerrilla Party and the Hunters ROTC Guerrilla. General Vera had driven the Hunters away from Pitogo in December 1944, and after the killing, Mayor Ramon Isaac of Unisan was in turn kidnapped by the Hunters.
paras.text: The motive for the kidnapping and killing was the keen rivalry between Vera's Guerrilla Party and the Hunters ROTC Guerrilla. General Vera had driven the Hunters away from Pitogo in December 1944, and after the killing, Mayor Ramon Isaac of Unisan was in turn kidnapped by the Hunters.

paras.html: Leopoldo Miciano, secretary of Col. de Luna of Vera's Guerrilla Party, testified that General Vera told him he suspected Mayor Isaac was kidnapped in reprisal because he (Vera) had ordered the liquidation of Lt. Lozañes ("dinispatcha").
paras.text: Leopoldo Miciano, secretary of Col. de Luna of Vera's Guerrilla Party, testified that General Vera told him he suspected Mayor Isaac was kidnapped in reprisal because he (Vera) had ordered the liquidation of Lt. Lozañes ("dinispatcha").

paras.html: Since Lozañes was then a lieutenant of a guerrilla group in the resistance movement, the killing could not be said to further the resistance; rather, it would tend to weaken the resistance movement against the Japanese.
paras.text: Since Lozañes was then a lieutenant of a guerrilla group in the resistance movement, the killing could not be said to further the resistance; rather, it would tend to weaken the resistance movement against the Japanese.

paras.html: Nothing in the record showed that Jaime Garcia had any participation in the crime, nor that he admitted or disclaimed any role; hence there was no room either for his conviction or for applying the amnesty proclamation.
paras.text: Nothing in the record showed that Jaime Garcia had any participation in the crime, nor that he admitted or disclaimed any role; hence there was no room either for his conviction or for applying the amnesty proclamation.

paras.html: Petitioners appealed to the CA. On July 27, 1959, the CA certified the appeal to the SC because of the legal issue involved: W/N persons invoking amnesty should first admit having committed the crime. On August 13, 1959, the SC docketed it as G.R. No. L-15803.

paras.html: On petitioners' motion, the SC returned the record to the CA because of factual issues: petitioners claimed that Lozañes's death did not spring from personal motive or guerrilla rivalry, but from his having sided in the enemy's war efforts, as a member of the Japanese-sponsored Philippine Constabulary and as one of those who arrested and massacred innocent civilians and guerrillas in Catanauan, Quezon.

paras.html: Petitioners argued in their MR that they had impliedly admitted their participation in the killing. The CA held that "mere implied admission is not sufficient", because DOJ Administrative Order No. 144 (October 11, 1950), amending AO No. 179 (November 17, 1949), directs that, for offenses under the RPC (other than crimes against chastity) committed between December 8, 1941 and the liberation of the province or city, "in order that the Amnesty Commission may take cognizance of the case, the accused or respondent must allege or claim verbally or in writing that he committed the acts charged against him in furtherance of the resistance movement or against persons who aided in the war efforts of the enemy," for amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime.
paras.text: Petitioners argued in their MR that they had impliedly admitted their participation in the killing. The CA held that "mere implied admission is not sufficient", because DOJ Administrative Order No. 144 (October 11, 1950), amending AO No. 179 (November 17, 1949), directs that, for offenses under the RPC (other than crimes against chastity) committed between December 8, 1941 and the liberation of the province or city, "in order that the Amnesty Commission may take cognizance of the case, the accused or respondent must allege or claim verbally or in writing that he committed the acts charged against him in furtherance of the resistance movement or against persons who aided in the war efforts of the enemy," for amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime.

paras.html: Since petitioners made no such claim and instead verbally denied the charge, their case should be tried by the ordinary courts.
paras.text: Since petitioners made no such claim and instead verbally denied the charge, their case should be tried by the ordinary courts.

paras.html: The CA declined to rule on the factual issue (whether Lozañes aided the enemy): any ruling would be "premature and prejudicial, but also useless" because the case came from a body with no jurisdiction; jurisdiction may be raised at any stage.

paras.html: Amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime: "when an accused maintains that he has not committed a crime, he cannot have any use for amnesty." It is "rank inconsistency" to seek forgiveness for an act one claims not to have committed. The contrary rule in Barrioquinto, De Los Santos, and Viray (admission not a condition precedent) has been superseded and deemed overruled by People v. Llanita and People v. Guillermo.

paras.html: The motive for the kidnapping and killing was the keen rivalry between Vera's Guerrilla Party and the Hunters ROTC Guerrilla. General Vera had driven the Hunters away from Pitogo in December 1944, and after the killing, Mayor Ramon Isaac of Unisan was in turn kidnapped by the Hunters.

paras.html: Leopoldo Miciano, secretary of Col. de Luna of Vera's Guerrilla Party, testified that General Vera told him he suspected Mayor Isaac was kidnapped in reprisal because he (Vera) had ordered the liquidation of Lt. Lozañes ("dinispatcha").

paras.html: Petitioners argued in their MR that they had impliedly admitted their participation in the killing. The CA held that "mere implied admission is not sufficient", because DOJ Administrative Order No. 144 (October 11, 1950), amending AO No. 179 (November 17, 1949), directs that, for offenses under the RPC (other than crimes against chastity) committed between December 8, 1941 and the liberation of the province or city, "in order that the Amnesty Commission may take cognizance of the case, the accused or respondent must allege or claim verbally or in writing that he committed the acts charged against him in furtherance of the resistance movement or against persons who aided in the war efforts of the enemy," for amnesty presupposes the commission of a crime.

paras.html: JBC may set its own criteria: The JBC has the authority to set standards/criteria in choosing nominees for every judicial vacancy, "subject only to the minimum qualifications required by the Constitution and law for every position"; it has "sufficient but not unbridled license to act." The five-year requirement is necessary and incidental to its constitutional function.
paras.text: JBC may set its own criteria: The JBC has the authority to set standards/criteria in choosing nominees for every judicial vacancy, "subject only to the minimum qualifications required by the Constitution and law for every position"; it has "sufficient but not unbridled license to act." The five-year requirement is necessary and incidental to its constitutional function.

paras.html: Equal protection: The classification between first-level judges with at least five years of service and those with less satisfies the rational basis test; it is reasonable and intended to gauge "proven competence" (Art. VIII, Sec. 7(3)). Five years is not the only factor in selection.
paras.text: Equal protection: The classification between first-level judges with at least five years of service and those with less satisfies the rational basis test; it is reasonable and intended to gauge "proven competence" (Art. VIII, Sec. 7(3)). Five years is not the only factor in selection.

paras.html: Publication: The policy need not be filed with the ONAR (the Administrative Code's publication rules exclude the Judiciary), but it should have been published because it is a qualification standard affecting applicants, not an internal rule. The non-publication did not prejudice the petitioner, who has no legal right to be included in the list.

paras.html: WARM filed a Petition for Review on Certiorari (Rule 45), assigning six errors: (1) the CA failed to apply environmental-law principles; the Precautionary Principle requires respondents to prove compliance and the absence of harm; (2) the CA failed to recognize respondents' violations of PD 1151, PD 856, the Water Code, RA 9275, and the Continuing Mandamus, and their operation without an ECC; (3) the CA ignored the environmental damage from dumping raw sewage in heavy rain, despite its own Decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 112023 and a Philippine Medical Association certification, and ruled without a hearing; (4) failure to properly operate a sewerage system is itself a violation remediable by the writ; (5) failure to comply with the Continuing Mandamus is itself a violation remediable by the writ, and, now that the case is before the SC, jurisdiction cannot be denied; (6) the CA failed to find the extreme urgency that justifies a TEPO, as the dangers of wading in sewage-contaminated floodwater may be taken by judicial notice.

paras.html: Sec. 1, Rule 7, Part III, RPEC: the writ is available to a natural or juridical person, entity authorized by law, people's organization, NGO, or public interest group accredited or registered with a government agency, on behalf of persons whose constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology is violated or threatened by an unlawful act or omission, involving damage of such magnitude as to prejudice the life, health, or property of inhabitants in two or more cities or provinces.

paras.html: It is a special civil action and an extraordinary remedy, available against an unlawful act or omission of a public official or employee, or a private individual or entity (LNL Archipelago Minerals v. Agham Party List, citing Paje v. Casiño).

paras.html: Elements: (1) an actual or threatened violation of the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology; (2) the violation arises from an unlawful act or omission of a public official or employee, or private individual or entity; and (3) it involves or will lead to environmental damage of such magnitude as to prejudice the life, health, or property of inhabitants in two or more cities or provinces.

paras.html: Abogado v. DENR: the writ is a highly prerogative writ that issues only on a showing of actual or imminent threat and such inaction by the relevant administrative bodies as will make an environmental catastrophe inevitable. It is not an excuse to invoke judicial remedies when administrative forums remain. It is not an all-embracing remedy to be wielded like a political tool; parties must exhaust the political and administrative arena, and legal action may be entertained only when a concrete cause of action arises from facts provable by substantial evidence.

It is not an all-embracing remedy to be wielded like a political tool; parties must exhaust the political and administrative arena, and legal action may be entertained only when a concrete cause of action arises from facts provable by substantial evidence.

paras.html: Braga v. Abaya: the Court denied a writ of continuing mandamus and/or kalikasan against the PPP concession of the Davao Sasa Wharf for prematurity and lack of merit. The petition cited general studies on port impacts but failed to identify threats from the project itself (the port had operated since 1900; the project was a modernization) → allegations were "hazy and speculative." The Court lacks the technical competence to assess the project, which is lodged in the DENR acting through the EMB in the EIA process; the bidding process itself cannot cause environmental damage.

paras.html: No actual impairment of the right to travel: Proclamation No. 475 does not impair the right to travel "in its essential sense"; its bearing on travel is "merely corollary" to the closure, a necessary incident of rehabilitation, and only temporary. Since it does not restrict travel, it does not substantially alter the relationship between the State and the people; it is not a law, and the President did not usurp legislative power.

paras.html: Police power: Even if it were otherwise, the closure is a valid police power measure: a lawful subject (environment, health, and general welfare) and lawful means (reasonably necessary and not unduly oppressive). Absent a clear showing of grave abuse, unreasonableness, arbitrariness, or oppressiveness, the Court will not disturb the executive determination.

paras.html: April 26, 2018: President Duterte issued Proclamation No. 475, "Declaring a State of Calamity in the Barangays of Balabag, Manoc-Manoc and Yapak (Island of Boracay) in the Municipality of Malay, Aklan, and Temporary Closure of the Island as a Tourist Destination." The closure took effect the same day.

The closure took effect the same day.

paras.html: Its Whereas clauses cite the State's duties on health, ecology, and marine wealth (Secs. 15 and 16, Art. II; Sec. 2, Art. XII) and the findings of an Inter-Agency Task Force (DENR, DILG, DOT): fecal coliform averaging 18,000 MPN/100ml against a 400 standard at Bolabog; most establishments and residences not connected to sewerage; only 14 of 51 shoreline establishments compliant with RA 9275; coral cover down ~70.5% (1988–2011); solid waste of 90–115 tons/day against a hauling capacity of 30 (~85 tons left daily); damaged habitats; only 4 of 9 wetlands left, with 937 illegal structures on forestlands and wetlands and 102 on easements; DOST findings of beach erosion; 18,082 tourists a day, up over 160% from 2012 to 2017; and the NDRRMC's recommendation under RA 10121 for a state of calamity and temporary closure.

paras.html: Dispositive provisions: a state of calamity in the three barangays; "temporary closure of the Island as a tourist destination for six (6) months starting 26 April 2018, or until 25 October 2018" subject to applicable laws; remedial measures under RA 10121; departments to augment LGU services; the state of calamity to remain until lifted by the President, notwithstanding the lapse of six months; all departments, GOCCs, and affected LGUs directed to implement the closure and rehabilitation per the Boracay Action Plan; law enforcement to act with restraint; and the Municipality of Malay to ensure that no tourist is allowed entry until the President lifts the closure.

paras.html: Due process: property rights include the right to work and earn a living; by banning tourists and non-residents, the proclamation deprived petitioners and everyone working in the island of their livelihood. Environmental laws have specific penalties for violators; making the innocent suffer violates due process.

paras.html: The right to travel properly concerns regulations that directly restrain a person's freedom of movement (curfews in SPARK, hold-departure of accused, deployment bans, quarantines) — a "ball and chain" on persons. Proclamation 475 is a "place-based" regulation, akin to "cordoning-off" calamity areas; affected persons remain free to move elsewhere → no need for a Sec. 6 statute.

paras.html: But the President is not thereby automatically authorized. Proclamation 475 is not a law but an executive issuance with statutory imprimatur: the Administrative Code and RA 10121 authorize the declaration of a state of calamity upon NDRRMC recommendation and proposals to restore normalcy; closure is a necessary implication of executing those laws (ex necessitate legis). With RA 9275 (DENR emergency clean-up) and the Code (DENR, DILG powers), the Executive had sufficient authority; the President, through control, can integrate those functions. No need to rely on residual powers.

paras.html: Legislative power (decided): the President validly issued Proclamation 475 as subordinate legislation under RA 10121: the law defines disaster risk reduction broadly (prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response) and allows restrictions on movement (e.g., evacuation, no-settlement zones); it delegates rule-making to the NDRRMC; the proclamation is germane and meets sufficient standards (public safety, health, disaster mitigation); agencies' contemporaneous construction (PHIVOLCS alert levels, PAGASA signals, Marikina's alarm levels) treats evacuation as including restriction of entry; Congress's oversight committee has not corrected it.

paras.html: Rights issues (declined): the rights to travel and due process are not absolute; the real question is reasonableness, which requires evidence (e.g., whether a shorter or barangay-by-barangay closure would suffice). Cases petitioners cite (White Light, Lucena Grand Central, MMDA v. Viron) were first tried in the RTC. The proclamation enjoys a presumption of validity, which requires evidence to rebut (Ermita-Malate, citing O'Gorman). Local autonomy likewise turns on facts.

paras.html: Sec. 6, Art. III is clear: travel may be impaired only for national security, public safety, or public health, "as may be provided by law" — an explicit statute (Genuino v. De Lima). The provision does not distinguish direct from incidental restrictions (ubi lex non distinguit; Shapiro v. Thompson, Soto-Lopez, State v. Burnett, SPARK). Not a "cordoning-off" case, since LGUs are already authorized by law to close roads (Sec. 21, LGC).

paras.html: No law grants the President power to close an island: RA 10121 only lets the NDRRMC recommend a state of calamity; it allows only limited remedial measures (price ceilings, fund reprogramming, no-interest loans) and favors local actors. Police power rests primarily with the legislature and needs valid delegation (Review Center Ass'n v. Ermita). Calamity powers (calling out, emergency powers, takeover, supervision of LGUs) do not include it. RA 9275 gives the DENR water-treatment measures, while LGUs handle contingency plans.

paras.html: Source and scope of the disciplinary power: The SC's authority to discipline lawyers stems from its constitutional mandate to regulate admission to the practice of law, "which includes as well authority to regulate the practice itself of law" (Art. 8, Sec. 5(5)); it is also an inherent power incidental to the administration of justice. It is broader than the contempt power: it may be exercised whether or not the misconduct also constitutes contempt.

It is broader than the contempt power: it may be exercised whether or not the misconduct also constitutes contempt.

paras.html: Free speech and criticism of courts: Freedom of speech "is not absolute" and "needs on occasion to be adjusted to and accommodated with" the public interest in the integrity and orderly functioning of the administration of justice. A lawyer may criticize the Court, but the criticism must be bona fide and "shall not spill over the walls of decency and propriety" (*In re Almacen*). A lawyer's free expression may be more limited than a layman's, and a Special Prosecutor's duty of respect is heavier than a private practitioner's.

paras.html: Nature of the proceeding: Disciplinary proceedings are sui generis: an investigation by the Court into the conduct of its officers, with no plaintiff or prosecutor; the Court is not "complainant, prosecutor and judge." Referral to the IBP or the SolGen under Rule 139-B is not mandatory, "especially where the charge consists of acts done before the Supreme Court."

paras.html: The SC, as regulator and guardian of the legal profession, has plenary disciplinary authority over attorneys, stemming from its constitutional mandate to regulate admission to the practice of law, "which includes as well authority to regulate the practice itself of law" (Art. 8, Sec. 5(5); Rule 138, Secs. 27–29). Apart from this, it is an inherent power incidental to the proper administration of justice.
paras.text: The SC, as regulator and guardian of the legal profession, has plenary disciplinary authority over attorneys, stemming from its constitutional mandate to regulate admission to the practice of law, "which includes as well authority to regulate the practice itself of law" (Art. 8, Sec. 5(5); Rule 138, Secs. 27–29). Apart from this, it is an inherent power incidental to the proper administration of justice.

paras.html: The SC also has the inherent power to punish for contempt, "necessary for its own protection against an improper interference with the due administration of justice"; it "is not dependent upon the complaint of any of the parties litigant."
paras.text: The SC also has the inherent power to punish for contempt, "necessary for its own protection against an improper interference with the due administration of justice"; it "is not dependent upon the complaint of any of the parties litigant."

paras.html: The disciplinary authority is broader than the contempt power. Contempt may be committed by lawyers and non-lawyers, in and out of court. Where the respondent is a lawyer, the disciplinary authority may come into play whether or not the misconduct is also contempt. → A lawyer, as an officer of the court, who "visibly tends to obstruct, pervert, or impede and degrade the administration of justice" commits both professional misconduct and contumacious conduct.

paras.html: Acts of a de facto officer are valid: A de facto officer is "one who is in possession of an office and who openly exercises its functions under color of an appointment or election, even though such appointment or election may be irregular." His acts "are as valid for all purposes as those of a de jure officer, in so far as the public or third persons who are interested therein are concerned." Even without the ruling settling his citizenship, Justice Ong was a de facto officer during his Sandiganbayan incumbency, so a decision he signed is valid.

paras.html: What Kilosbayan held: Kilosbayan Foundation v. Ermita did NOT rule that Justice Ong was not natural-born. It only held that he could not accept or assume the post of Associate Justice of the Supreme Court "until he shall have successfully completed all the necessary steps, through the appropriate adversarial proceedings in court" to show that he is natural-born.

paras.html: An anonymous complaint was filed before the Office of the Ombudsman-Mindanao against petitioner Zoleta, Mary Ann Gadian, and Sheryll Desiree Tangan for participating in a scheme of questionable grants and donations to fictitious entities using provincial funds.

paras.html: The COA conducted a special audit of Sarangani Province. Among the irregularities found was a ₱20,000 financial assistance to Women in Progress (WIP), a cooperative whose members were mostly government personnel or relatives of provincial officials.

paras.html: On the COA Special Audit Team's report, the Ombudsman conducted a preliminary investigation and, through the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP), charged petitioner, Vice-Governor Felipe Constantino, Violeta Bahilidad, Maria Camanay, and Teodorico Diaz before the Sandiganbayan (SB) with malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents under Art. 217 in relation to Art. 171(2) and Art. 48 of the RPC.
paras.text: On the COA Special Audit Team's report, the Ombudsman conducted a preliminary investigation and, through the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP), charged petitioner, Vice-Governor Felipe Constantino, Violeta Bahilidad, Maria Camanay, and Teodorico Diaz before the Sandiganbayan (SB) with malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents under Art. 217 in relation to Art. 171(2) and Art. 48 of the RPC.

paras.html: The Information alleged that on January 24, 2002, Constantino (Vice-Governor), Camanay (Provincial Accountant), Diaz (Provincial Board Member), and Zoleta (Executive Assistant III), conspiring with Bahilidad (a private individual), took and misappropriated ₱20,000 by falsifying Disbursement Voucher (DV) No. 101-2002-01-822 and its supporting documents, making it appear that WIP, "represented by its President, Amelia Carmela C. Zoleta," had sought financial assistance when no such request was made and no amount was received. The funds were released through encashment of LBP Check No. 36481 dated January 24, 2002, issued in Bahilidad's name.

paras.html: First: all accused except Bahilidad are public officers under the RPC definition (Constantino, Vice-Governor; petitioner, Executive Assistant; Camanay, Provincial Accountant; Diaz, Provincial Board Member).
paras.text: First: all accused except Bahilidad are public officers under the RPC definition (Constantino, Vice-Governor; petitioner, Executive Assistant; Camanay, Provincial Accountant; Diaz, Provincial Board Member).

paras.html: Second: the funds belonged to the Province of Sarangani and are public in character.
paras.text: Second: the funds belonged to the Province of Sarangani and are public in character.

paras.html: Third: Constantino and Camanay were accountable public officers. The Government Auditing Code defines an accountable officer as one who, by reason of office, is accountable for public funds; Sec. 340, LGC expands this to other local officials who become accountable through their participation in the use or application of funds. Local officials are accountable (1) by the nature of their functions or (2) by participation in the use of funds (Frias v. People). Their signatures are required for any disbursement; no check can be prepared without them → control and responsibility over the funds.

The Government Auditing Code defines an accountable officer as one who, by reason of office, is accountable for public funds; Sec. 340, LGC expands this to other local officials who become accountable through their participation in the use or application of funds. paras.html: Fourth: they took or permitted the taking of the funds when they signed the DV. Approving a DV certifies that the expenses were necessary and lawful, the supporting documents complete, and cash available (Atienza v. Villarosa). Camanay also signed the ALOBS and Constantino signed LBP Check No. 0000036481, enabling Bahilidad to encash ₱20,000. The request was purportedly from WIP, yet the check was payable to a private person, Bahilidad; per COA team leader Helen Cailing, no document proved she was WIP's treasurer.
